The rest of the go, he just sighed and accepted that our tomatoes were never going to be safe from the wildlife.      Nothing escapes them, really. It’s like the countryside is planning to outnumber us humans and run the show next!

Rather skip the new DVD and go through the request cards first.      Ah, like... What's a card?      I can take it or we can take a peek.      Look I know what you're saying. But it was my card and all the holidays, I don't think they want to know if it's not all roses.      I think they do. Why'd you not send your mother a picture last week?      She's got her own cards. But, but the new DVDs came out... like three months after I left.      What's that?      My turkey, my turkey bird!      Ten more, ten more! You're on, pick one I'll get the little pigs.      Oh! Wait breakfast, no breakfast then?      The morning goes on, you ever looked at that, you'd think it's the weekend.      Water and weather, you get it, I listen to the radio in short bursts.      It's not like today is a launch date or anything.      That's relative.      I'm not pushing, but the other day, I had a new set of tests and they said something about bone.      That's not good. Our parents all said cancer was a lifestyle.      That's oddly sour.      I didn't mean to sound sour, I just meant... I don't know how else to say about bone.      Bone! She said bone! Both our thighbone and your thighbone that supports you!      Maybe I should have just stayed in for the day.      Mm hmm. I remember when your dad used to give you vitamins and he used to call it his special little ones.      Yeah that's right. And every once in a while, I think maybe that's the same path I should've been on.      I think it's more go out and get your own if you don't mind walking.      It's not like we were boxers or something. But your legs... you know how bent it made me to bend and pick up after them.      It's a family farm we've got there over the centuries. Cows, chickens, that kind of thing.      My doctor suggested I go for a walk, but it's cold out and I haven't seen the doctor yet.      Shouldn't we be writing something off then? Like, you're on the right path still, you're not a hundred percent on the line yet.      Mm, and her father.

Rather lovely walk today, isn't it? I needed this. A bit of fresh air and no students asking when the next essay is due.      I know what you mean. It's a bit of a change from the lectures and the coffee fumes at the campus. And it’s nice not having to talk about Newton-Raphson methods for once.      Agreed. I saw that hot air balloon this morning before we left. Do you remember the time we watched one go up just outside Norwich? It was just coming into town when the wind picked up suddenly.      Oh, I nearly lost my hat—literally! And we were out in the fields with the dog. Remember Mylo? He was going absolutely bonkers chasing bursts of wind and pretending they were rabbits.      Poor little thing—now he’s all calm in the cottage, snoozing on the sofa no doubt. I swear he’s still a bit in awe of his own reflection ever since we walked past that duck pond near the farm.      He did try to fight his own shadow for five minutes. Honestly, I don’t know what got into him. Did you tell the story at the book club on Tuesday?      Oh yes, got a good laugh out of it. Although, I think some of them thought I was making it up. You know how they are—nothing like a bit of British countryside absurdity.      There’s also this funny thing with the birds here. I swear the jackdaws just follow us around when we’re out. Probably think we’re a source of snacks.      Maybe they’re waiting for you to drop your sandwich again. That bird does have a memory! Anyway, speaking of snacks—have you thought about this weekend? The camping trip you mentioned?      Definitely. I’ve just been waiting for the weather forecast to look steady. I don’t fancy sodden tents and soggy biscuits again. But I think it might hold.      I hope so. I’ve got that new sleeping bag of mine ready—warm as toast. Of course, it was probably the same price as our last holiday in Cornwall, mind you.      Oh come on, it was an investment in comfort. And seriously, at that camping store? I don’t think I’ll be buying a new tent anytime soon. They must be making a killing.      Oh, I checked out the warranty after I bought it—two years to be exact.

Rather annoying isn’t it, this weather? One minute it’s sunny and warm, the next it’s like someone’s turned on the hose. You’d think April would be more predictable by now.      Yeah, can’t complain about the lack of rain though—my patch of grass in the back’s finally green again. Still, today was a good session out on the court—kept me on my toes. A lot of the younger lot in this clinic, funny enough, but they’ve not got a clue about technique.      Funny you say that, I was reading a book on coaching methods the other day. It’s made me rethink a lot of the ways I teach my Spanish classes. The idea of mirroring, for example—where the teacher’s body language and energy directly reflect the learner’s, helps build confidence and trust. Makes me wonder whether your job is a bit like teaching too.      I suppose in some ways it is—building rapport with people, setting goals, pushing without burning them out. Although the analogy stops once I stop grading essays and start grading personal best jumps. Still, I listen more now than I used to. When I first started, I thought it was all about correcting form. These days, I find out where they want to go and help them get there.      That actually sounds really smart. I’ve had a few students in the past who just needed their method tweaked rather than completely overhauled. For example, one of them had been in an exam environment for over a decade, and it just wasn’t working for her—job-based learning is what did the trick. She’s now running a social enterprise in Barcelona.      Nice! I hear a lot of stories from the gym too—people doing part-time stuff on the side, or starting their own small businesses. Doesn’t always work, mind you—had one fella last year who left construction to start up his own childcare venture. Bit of a gamble, but his wife was giving him the third degree, so he did it. Took off, actually.      That’s brilliant! He probably learned a lot faster once he had to do it for real. That's how I teach—set real-life contexts. For example, if I’m teaching vocabulary for travel, we don’t just sit at a table reading off a textbook.

Right, thanks for coming in today. You're all very welcome. I know it's a bit of a trek from Hull to Malton, but I’m so glad we can finally get together after all this time. I've got tea made and some scones—your favourite, Martha.      Bless you, Eleanor. You always think of us. Still baking like royalty in your sitting room? I swear that plate rack by the door still holds every single spoon in the house since 1980.      And I still trip over the same rug, don't I? You'd think after three decades of visiting, I’d’ve memorised where the furniture is, but no. Tripped over that My Fair Lady rug again last week. Fun Tuesday.      [laughs] You're both so silly. I think the world should just float you in for visitors instead of you coming here. Or hoverboards. I've been wanting to get one in my room. I showed the teachers in school, and they said it's not a valid form of transport for walking exams.      [chuckles] Well, I don’t think your exams as it is will be the real challenge with that one. But please—have a seat. I’ve set the table by the window so the light’s good for the scones, and the cats have been herded off the settee.      You’ve done well, Eleanor. Still ruling the roost, then? Who’s in charge of the bulbs in the garden this year? That’s been a familial point of contention for years.      Oh, you know Margot’s had a hand in it, but I did most of the actual planting. I’m afraid she still insists crocuses should be watered twice a day. They don’t like dramatics, Bert. They’re not in a West End show.      [mimicking Margot] “But Eleanor, they’re brown at the tips!” Do I have to spell it out for her that crocuses come out of the ground and that sometimes being  outside  is their job?      [giggling] Yeah, like you once told her that sunflowers like the sun. No one go there with the pond life, though. If I remember right, she once tried to give pond snails a midnight snack of cereal.      Snails. It was a big night for conservation, if not for digestion. [chuckles] Anyway, Eleanor, we’ve come for more than snacks and stories. We’ve got a bit of a plan—Margot’s been eyeing up her cottage.

Rather skip the new satnav eh?      Aye, it's pointing me up a dead-end again. Never mind them local knowledge road signs. I'd take a blind date over that thing any day.      Look, just keep going straight at the roundabout, past that old red phone box, and then the first turning on your left after the church.      Aye Aye, captain! Got that! I swear, navigation these days is like reading poetry – you gotta interpret it.      Funny you mention poetry, I read that lovely one you wrote about the fells. Mary at the gig last night said it gave her shivers.      My turkey dinner must have done something to me then. It tried to lift itself off the plate and walk!      Aye? That’s an odd one. Mine just gave up and fell on its face. I said to Brian, “Well, if it can’t be roasted, then we fritter it.”      That’s your lot—always one for a bit of drama in the kitchen. Remember I told you, your mother-in-law still sends me Wolfram patterns for my bookcase. I tried knitting one once. It turned out like a suicide note from a recluse.      Ha, that’s the spirit! You’ve got her hands in every stitch now. Anyway, about the gig—did we sort the mics? There’s no way someone at the back is gonna hear me trying to explain a ceilidh.      We’d better have a sound check. I’ve got Paul DJ’ing again, and last time he thought a didgeridoo was a type of brie.      Oh for goodness’ sake—he fails at both technology and culture! I swear it, if we run out of folk music, we’re cutting to treacle siphoning.      Aye, the crowd’d love it. At least it’d be a novelty. Speaking of crowds, did I tell you about that time I crashed the village feast and got mistaken for the Town Crier?      Was it the year you walked in with a chicken under your arm?      That one! The vicar nearly had a stroke. But I told him it was part of the performance. “Avian storytelling,” I said.      Well, I’ll be thanking you if you keep that chicken at home today. I’m not keen to explain farm animals in the sound booth.      Fair enough. But if I go down in history for integrating rural livestock into avant-garde poetry, so be it.

So did you talk to Lucy last night?      No, she hasn’t been replying to anything. I’m starting to get worried. She said she had a meeting with Redrow about that housing project… but honestly, I don’t think things are going well.      Yeah, she mentioned something about the client making ridiculous changes and the site manager not actually… well, managing. I feel for her. I know that kind of stress.      It’s tough working under a brief that’s moving the goalposts every week. Did your uni project go any better?      Not really. Our group is still arguing about whether the building should be modular or traditional. One person thinks it needs to be fully sustainable with no compromise, another says the cost would be astronomical. We haven’t even started the schematics.      Cats and dogs, breakfast, and laptops then?      Exactly! Speaking of, you ever had a Full English with the works?      Only once, and I overheard the waiter say it used to belong to the guy who owns the land next to the site. I think he owns everything.      Doesn’t everyone in West London from the 80s? Mate of a mate of a guy who owns it, boom, you’ve got a building permit.      You know what I’m thinking though? Maybe we should just form a co-living project.      Now? After just one conversation about Lucy?      No, I mean seriously. The client is asking for  rooms in a building  not people about people. We’re not designing boxes—we’re designing spaces where people live, laugh, maybe date, and maybe cook your eggs for you.      Maybe I’ll start with designing  that  room. Ensuite. Bigger than hers.      Oh you’re on. Do it.      You know I did? Last Saturday. I had this cute girl from a different project trying to draw the same idea. She thought the same thing—communal kitchens where you meet people. Said it was like the Netflix version of gothic architecture meets co-vaxing.      Co-vax? Is that like… group showering? So did you lot see the pair of heels I bought last week? I know it's mad ‘cos like... we’re not exactly going out in them unless we find a fancy dress-up event      A fancy dress-up event? That’s like what you call a gig in a night club in eeny weeny heels yeah? Or are they like proper heels?      No I mean yeah heels are fine if you know how to walk in them. Oh but are they stilettos or clomps or sommat?      Nae, clomps... like three inches max. I mean I can still run to the bus stop in em if needed. But like, My nan still asks if I’m going to a wedding every time I put em on.      Eww, nah she should just take a back seat cos we’re gigin it. Or is that just me?      Oh don’t I know it. I once told my gran I was going out in the clomps and she said “well do tell the lads I say hello from up here”      Hahahahaa, that is classic though. My gran says the same. She says, “If you’re out clubbin Matey, don’t let the boys think it’s serious”      It’s not like we all have boyfriends or anything, we’re literally just out for a daft night.      Yeah. I just like the way they look. I buy them and then wear flip flops in the end.      I do exactly the same. I nearly did a backflip walkin in them buggers the other night. It was a whole mission walkin outta cabby Andy’s!      Maybe we’re all just rebeling agin the whole “expected” high heels thing. Demo that we can wear em if we want but not have to wear em cos it’s way too restricting.      Yeah, and shopping for shoes is a right faff with 'em too. They’re either too tight, too wide, or you try a pair on with socks and think they’re brilliant, go out with no socks and you suffocate      I once bought a pair that had like a plastic box thing inside the sole. Must’ve been size 8 or sommat and they hurt like hell      I think I’m over heels to be honest. I’ve moved over to boots. Practical and them big ankle bits help. I can even sit cross legged without falling over      Boots?

So do you ever imagine going back to a different time in history and living it out for yourself?      Honestly? Yeah, I do more than I'd probably admit.      Oh? When would you go?      Hmm. Maybe the 1960s? I like the idea of all that change, the space race, the music, the rebellion. A lot of it would’ve been exhausting, but it felt like a turning point.      You’d be the kind of rebel who starts a revolution or the one who just grumbles about the lack of baked beans on the shelves?      [Laughs] Probably the second one. I like my revolutions served with a solid breakfast.      Fair enough. I suppose I’d want to go back to ancient Egypt—build pyramids, wear flowy linen, get called “Great Soul” by people who still think the sun is a disk on chariot wheels.      You’d have the personality for it too. Always trying to explain things, whether people want it or not.      Hey, I credit early education for everything. Have you ever thought about watching how the pyramids were built from the best seat in the tent?      No, I imagine they had a huge “You Can’t Have Entry Without Ten Bottles of Silphium” rule. You ever heard of the pharaoh’s coffee barista?      That’s unfortunately a myth, dear. [Sips coffee] Though, speaking of spiritual journeys, have you ever thought about whether we all had a soul mate out there?      I think about it from time to time. I mean, I like what you said once—you know that line you used in the argument about soulmates?      Which one?      “Maybe it’s not one person who’s your soul mate, but all the people you grow from.” I liked that because I don’t think you necessarily grow  toward  one person—you grow by the people you keep and the ones you leave behind.      That’s beautiful. I like that you remembered that even after I ranted for three-and-a-half minutes about monogamy and metaphysics in the bath last week.      You were in the bath  with  me, I might’ve been the one ranting against the soap.      Okay, fair point. But still—what if we had to go to an imaginary party? Like, all the dead people and fictional ones?      Oh yeah, I did a version of that. I hosted one in my head when I was stuck on a train in London.

So did you manage to sort out that knitting pattern, Claire? I remember you said it was a bit fiddly with the cables.      Oh I did, thanks! I found a video on YouTube that walks you through each step, and it made such a difference. Honestly, I don’t know how I got by without it before. I’m just on the last few rows now. What about you, Fiona? Still knitting those baby blankets?      Oh yes, bless me, I’ve started a new one. My daughter’s due later this year, right? So I’ve got to get another three ready by then! It’s so much easier with the right needles, though. You know, like that set you lent me with the ergonomic handles—it made such a difference on my hands.      I know exactly what you mean. I tried to take up knitting about a year ago after seeing all the TikTok videos, but I gave up after two rows. My hands just didn’t want to cooperate, ha! Still, I can do the basics now, and that helps me feel like I’m not being left out of all the sweater culture.      Honestly, I think knitting is like everything else—there’s a generation gap. We younger ones rely too much on videos and tutorials, but it’s got to be better than none, right?      Definitely. It’s not just about the skill anymore. It’s about the connection with your family, the sense of making something with your own hands. And with everything moving so fast these days, it gives a bit of calm.      You know, being an admin head, I’m surrounded by computers all day. I do miss the old craft skills sometimes. My mam used to knit every pair of socks for my dad, and even now her grave is marked with a tiny sock planted beside the headstone to remember her.      That’s such a lovely idea. I’ve been thinking about tombstones a lot lately. My gran passed last year, and we’re just waiting on getting her memorial stone done. I had to have a say in the wording, and honestly, I think it was one of the hardest decisions I’ve made in ages.      I can imagine. When I did my dad’s, I wanted to keep it real. You know, not all of that fancy poetic stuff. Just a bloke who loved trains and steak-and-kidney puff.

So did you lot hear about what’s going down at the student union next week?      What, another quiz night? Or is it more of that fancy dress nonsense like last time with the “80s comeback” and Liam in a dodgy leg warmer set-up?      Haha, yeah Liam still sends me the photo where he looked like he stepped out of a Graham Norton show reject reel.      No, no, it’s a   free pizza session  . For everyone. They’re trying to get more people in, but honestly, I don’t get the appeal of free food these days when we’re all broke.      Bro, if you’re broke, you haven’t met enough overdrafts yet. Ten o'clock on a Wednesday and I’m already past my limit.      I was about to say something about money when you said that. I just happened to get a student tax rep email today, you ever get one of those, Hayley?      Yeah, that’s the one with the robotic woman reading out your name like she’s in a sci-fi film.  “Due to the current economic pressures, we’ve ensured… ”      “ …relevant national funding – allocated… ” I’ve got like, half the email saved as a ringtone. “Philip, funding has been allocated.”      It’s not funny, though. Our房租 here is full price. No student discounts. I just paid mine and thought I’d definitely die before paying another one this year.      I feel like all I do is spend money on rent and about five square meals. My motivation to study drops dramatically the closer it is to midday and the hungrier I get.      Yeah, uni student transformation: step one, go in for lectures with treble clef enthusiasm. Step two, faint halfway through econ because your blood sugar levels have dropped lower than the FTSE 100.      Ugh, I just remembered we’re also meant to be revising for the big English paper next month. We going over that set text,  Jane Eyre ? Anyone care to explain gothic elements on a life-affirming level again?      I’m still figuring out why the boxset binges count as ‘research’ but the lecturers seem to be okay with it.      I think I’m half-way to a degree in binge-watching over this one. Celine, remember that guy from the Wednesday lecture who tried to pronounce “ Bildungsroman ” as “bildingsomethingroman”?      How could I not? It sounded like he’d just discovered the dictionary and was speaking directly to it.

Rather skip the starter and just go for the whole grilled octopus. I’m starved, honestly.      Maybe go for the soup, love a bit of something warm first. Beans and tomato is always reliable.      Can I just get the spaghetti with tomato sauce again? That’s what I had last time.      Sure thing, Harry. Though I reckon you’re ready for something a bit more adventurous now, son. You're not five anymore, are you?      I like what I like. It tastes the same every time.      Honestly Dad, give him a break. What’s the point in coming to a nice restaurant if you're gonna be forced to try new stuff all the time?      Oliver, maybe pick something a bit lighter. Lamb? Or the fish, if you’re not too far into your studies again. I know you’ve been busy with tutors.      I'm not  obsessed , Mum. I just want to finish on a good grade and do well, is all. I’ve got an interview for a teaching placement next week.      That’s brilliant news, love. You’ll do great. Have you put your tattoo on your CV – the one of the wolves?      No! I covered it up with a black jacket. You can’t exactly go into education looking like you’re about to join a biker gang.      Fair point. Though a bit of edge never did anyone any harm. Just don’t let them get you into a rigid system. Education is all about flexibility in my opinion.      What’s the interview like, Ol?      Loads of questions about pedagogy and how you’d deal with a disruptive class. Maybe I’ll have to say ‘firm but fair’ or something. All the others did.      I remember your time at Priory Primary, Oliver. You used to run off with your stick while you were waiting for the bus.      Ol wasn't the one with the stick, he just carried it. That was me. Then I got told I couldn’t take it in the classroom on day one.      You made my life a misery for a week. I had to sit by the window while your teacher talked you into deleting your Facebook photos of me with ketchup packets on my face.      Fair play to me for doing that. You looked mad.      Now now, enough of the nostalgia. Speaking of, Clarice, how's the hospital been treating you?

Rather skipper, you've got to see these pictures. I've printed them out—the lighthouse in St Ives, the kids at the YHA, the Cornish sea air, blimey, it was something else. Not quite as scruffy as we usually get in Norfolk!      Hasn’t that been the place for holidays for decades? I remember taking the bus all the way with a gang of children from my flat one summer. Of course, it was easier when they were all in nappies. We didn’t do much cycling then!      Oh, but you did get the chance to walk around, didn’t you, Bob? I read up a bit about the lighthouse they had—Fistral Head, I think it was. It’s supposed to be one of the finest in the country, and I hear the views? Truly something you don’t forget.      Aye, it’s proper grand. They told me in the YHA’s little handbook it was built back in the 19th century. One of those real old guard ones with the kerosene lamps, I reckon. Got one of the keepers’ daughters to show me around. Kind soul, still remembers her dad pointing out the crabs trotting about in the rocks.      Crabs, eh? I still remember that time I tried to catch one and got pinched clean enough to draw blood! You know what kids are like—never seem to learn from the old-timers who have already made the blunder. You’d have had half the YHA kids running out with buckets, wouldn’t you, Bob?      Aye, and I spoke to a few of them. Some young ones doing the "Yorkshire in a Day" sort of vibes—modern-day madabouts! Going by that cycle race route they had up near the headland. I doff my cap to 'em. Me, I’d have been about halfway up and already dossing it down a telephone box with a bacon sandwich.      You’re not wrong. As good as it sounds, being 70 and trying to do Yorkshire in a day? I’ve got enough trouble with Manchester to Cambridge on a train these days!      Anyway, Bob, I think it was wonderful of you to go and help out at the YHA. I imagine they could do with all the help they can get these days. So many young people in and out of there—just like I used to with the children I looked after.

So do you lot ever actually go out for meals or is it always just takeaways or ready meals? Cos I got to say, I love a dining out more than I used to, probably due to my job and doing a lot of events with spread stuff and buffet things.      Nah, it’s all takeaways, honestly. I got one meal handed over to me today on a building site next to a ladder. That’s if I’m lucky.      Oh, bless. I know someone once who had their wine and cheese delivered to them in a scaffolding tunnel.      That’s decent, even if it’s tragic.      Yeah, I do get that. But Myra, you work in events—you must have experienced some fancy dinners by now.      Definitely, and I’ll be the first to say most of it’s a bit of a farce, but I love the stories. One event last week in Brighton—candlelit tables, waiters, you name it—it was so poshy, I felt like I was in one of those Merchant Ivory films, and I was the one holding two different flutes of sparkling wine and forgetting the brand names.      Sounds like fun. But I’m out of my depth in that world—never had a table cloth on my dinner, let alone a waiter who’s into my sommelier trivia.      Oh, it’s not that bad. And let’s be fair, someone at every one of those events is trying to spot a romantic partner. I met a guy with a ridiculous name at a conference in Manchester—Tobias. Can you imagine?      Tobias? I like that. Or I prefer "Adam the labourer," which is what most of my romantic stories sound like.      I mean, it does sound like something out of a pub quiz. “Name the construction guest.” Answer: Adam.      Ha, it is a nickname I live with. But I dunno, I haven’t been out much. Feels like every time I try to get a date, it’s either a complete disaster or I’ve got to schedule it in like you schedule delivering a container.      Yeah, go for it on your own if you don’t mind walking two miles in heels just to go out for a pint. But, bloke, if you can get a woman to put up with you, lucky you.      And if you don’t like heels, just say so.

Rather skip the new barista café near the marina, do you?      Oh, I don’t know—new place, new music, new blend of something or other. Beans imported “directly from the moon,” they claim.       Deer in headlights eeny-meeny-miny-moey moment.  I reckon this is about as authentic as a Turkish Delight coffee latte.      Fair enough. Though personally, I quite like moon beans. Especially when grinding through the nightmares of running a start-up, or as I call it, a frozen financial Russian roulette.      Ah yes, I’ve only ever had to run against time and turkey sandwiches. You know, school budget left’s week? Tenpence to the psychiatrist and the rest to the milkman. A world of its own.      Now, breakfast, now—milkman happened. I once tried to barter GCSE grades for milk in a shopping mall in Tunbridge Wells. Real highlight of my twenties. The man nearly fainted when I told him I’d rather have an A in geography than a pint.       Stubborn, cheeky… reminiscent of the parents we dealt with when we told them that national curriculum – no, not with the moon, with the swans—wasn’t the cheapest option around .      You know what I miss? When education meant learning, and the coffee was just a full English. Strictly no moon stuff.      Funny thing—job histories are like coffee stains. You start with being ‘prioritised,’ but over time, you’re just a flammable misfit searching for motivation and a latte that’s not fizzy.      Tell me about it. I once accidentally opened a shop near a sewage plant. My idea of business development was hiding the GeoTrac under a chaise lounge and pretending I was a minimal planner.      I tried being a personal organiser once. Ended up lost in Lagos and discovered a passion for Websites陉.      So what’s the plan? Coffee, no coffee—what’s the source?      Coffee go bad? I think life improvements do. If I go wrong, I simply line my suitcase with curriculum vitae and return the boxset of "Doctor Who."      I might seriously quote that when writing a tribute to my start-up exit.      Just don’t say ‘cyber crime’ or ‘moon beans.’ I’m not entirely sure what that means, and I’ve been in the education sector for over two decades.      Oh, alright, then—how about this—"The moon-employees dismantled their empire, one delusion at a time, on their quest for tea, truth, and a functioning payroll system."      Would highly recommend that to any A-Level English student looking to stretch a paragraph.

So did you talk to him about the music last night? Like, I know it's not  that  loud, but I was trying to study and I couldn’t even hear myself think.      Yeah, I did. I said I know he’s just having fun and all, but it’s kind of messing with the others too. Not just you.      Yeah, I mean I don’t want to seem like one of those housemates who are always on each other’s backs or anything. But you’d be surprised how annoying it is when your brain’s trying to focus on essay hell and someone’s playing One Direction at 9 p.m.      Fair enough. I said it’s cool if he wants to play it during the week, just maybe keep the volume down after seven on school nights and I think he got that. Or at least he nodded a lot and said something about, um… “not being a total housemate monster.”      Oh great, he’s given himself a nickname now? “The Housemate Monster”?      You know what I mean—trying to make it seem like a joke to avoid the grief. Typical. Honestly, we’ve got a brilliant setup here, don’t we? Five people, no parents, just trying to figure out how to not be on each other’s nerves.      Mate, if you say one more thing about “figuring out,” I swear I’ll start throwing things.      Just trying to keep a sense of perspective. I mean, what’s the alternative? We moan and then split up and live under a bridge with a posse of raccoons about our standards of quiet time.      Oh, very funny. I’ve already had to remind Sarah that she shouldn’t be laying around the kitchen in her bathrobe at 11 a.m. like she owns the place. And by the way, I told  you  before she was doing that.      I did not expect your brain to run such a tight ship. Let’s be real, you were asleep on a couch in your pyjamas last week.      That’s different. I was watching a film go out of my mind. I wasn’t  being  anyone else.      You're always being someone else—valedictorian, queen of the biology tutorials, fluency award winner in German roles. We know you're just hiding under that disguise of casual chaos.      Oh, I’m chaotic? Because I’m the one who remembered to buy cleaning supplies last week?

Rather do this than go in the cold again, eh? I swear the shops out there would put paid to a man's health, let alone his legs.      I know! It’s a miracle we made it back with all those bags and that rain! You wouldn’t think it was November when it’s pouring like this, would you?      Aye, and them cabs out there! A penny for your thoughts and they want a quid. Still, we’ve done it, ain’t we? All the milk, the veg, the lot.      You did fetch the heavy ones, George! Not that I don’t appreciate it, mind, only I do feel like I’ve done a shift at the factory again. Fun though. It’s been a while since I had to argue with a deli man in a queue.      Ha! That one with the breakfast roll—“We don’t do half rolls here.” I said, “Well, neither do we have any, then, have we?” That got a few chuckles, I think.      You always say just the right thing! Sometimes I think you’ve still got it when it comes to dealing with cheeky young folks. I reckon you should be out there running a market stall or a newsagent again, just to keep you on your toes.      Would you? All that standing and the phone calls? No, no, no! This is me prime activity now—chatting in an armchair with me wife after a day out fetching tins and veg. Some folks paint, some folks play skittles. Me lot? Margarine labels and tinned peaches.      Well, I’ll be honest, it was nice to get out. I missed doing things for someone else other than me. I mean, it is a bit strange now that the last child I minded is grown and married!      Aye, I remember when you would come back from a day at the creche tired as you were waiting on tables. We used to kid you were the busiest person in Norfolk—“Where do you go?” and “You been doin’ the rounds again, then?”      Truth! I had my own go-to bin on Number One if I needed a sneaky one! You always said it was “me green bench,” didn’t you?      Reckon I said it was me special conservation centre for grown-ups, didn’t I? Never had the heart to tell you it was just the loo.      Well, I’m not one to miss a chance at a good laugh.

Nan, can I ask you a question?      Course, love, what is it?      You’ve got more questions than a maths exam, lad.      Not like that, Grandad. I was just wondering—what would you do if I left the house  this  messy every day?       [chuckles from kitchen]  I don’t know if I’d have a heart attack, but I’d probably go pick up a duster.      Oh, you’d not want to start with a duster, like. You’d want a  plank . That’s the only thing that’d calm you down!      You’ve met his room, haven’t you? Probably need a bulldozer, Viv!      Oh, don’t exaggerate, Grandad. It’s not  that  bad. I mean, I did put the washing in the basket today.      Aha! That was the Good One, wasn’t it? I told your gran—personally, I think the washing basket should legislate a curfew. It don’t live on the floor, no. It lives  in  the wardrobes.      Mate, you got a sneaker in the soup pan  last  Tuesday. That wasn’t in the basket, was it now?      That was an  accident , Grandad. Spontaneous arrangement.       [walks into the room with a mug of tea]  So, Connor, you being ‘spontaneous’ with your ballet slippers in the fridge about five days ago—was that spontaneous too?      Okay… fair. Maybe I should start tidyin’ up when I’m not tired.      That’s the ticket.      And when you  are  tired, the bin is your best mate. I once dropped a stone in it. You’d think it’d crack, but it just… lived.      So, Nan and Grandad—was it always like this in  your  house?      Oh love, go on then. We didn’t have  choice  but to be tidy! Your grandad here, he once tried to box a badger when it wandered into the shed. It won. The badger won, mind you. We never saw him after that.      That was a ‘temporary holiday’! I was just giving the badger some time to think over things.       [now seated]  And let me guess, Viv, you made the sandwiches?      Ah, you got it in one! Ham, of course—no ifs or buts. The badger had beliefs. It didn’t like the rocket. That was a tough one.      Wait, the badger turned down the rocket?      Wasn’t rocket, don’t be silly. Coriander. Women these days—want rocket? That’s no lunch! That’s a  delinquent  sandwich!

So did you lot see the latest health supplement post on TikTok? I swear it's just a glorified protein shake and some fancy sea moss.      Honestly, I think they just dress it up with fancy ingredients to make you feel like you're doing something unique. Sea moss was in my nana’s bath when I was a kid. Smelled like the seaside.      Ha! A lot of those trends are just repackaged old stuff with a new Instagram filter. But you gotta admit, some of the tech they show off is actually useful, like the portable vegan blenders or the smart mirrors that scan your face and tell you what skincare you need.      Yeah, My uncle still uses a landline. Doesn’t get on the internet much, but if I text him a photo of my mates in our uni hoodies he forwards it to about 20 cousins. Copy and paste old man vibes.      My nan’s the same. She texts me, “Look at this photo of me and your dad, we were so young!” Then she asks me to explain what a “TikTok” is.      It’s wild how fast things change. I remember not having a mobile until I was like 14. My brother had one of those old Siemens phones with the swivel antenna. Bet you’ve never seen one of those.      No, I didn’t even get a pay-as-you-go until uni. Spent my gap year playing PlayStation with my mates and just using the family computer.      So, what’s the plan once we finish uni? I’m thinking of doing a masters in about five years, but I need to travel the world first. Have you considered going back home or staying in the city?      I’m still deciding between London and Bristol. My flatshare here is killing me, rent’s passed 900 quid. But the culture here is something else. I love how it’s way calmer than London, but still buzzing with good pubs and art.      London’s not all bad though—you can do anything if you’ve got the money and a serious level of hustle. I’ve met so many go-getters on the train from Swindon.      I’ve got a cousin who just started box fitting in South London. She says it’s the only way to get fit if you live in a flat and don’t want to step into a gym.

Right, I’m just going to write up a shopping list for tomorrow. Who needs what?      I’ll need some mugs—ours are all chipped by now after all this years of tea drinking. Not to mention those dicky George things!      Yeah, and I need more pasta. We’ve got one sad noodle left.      I want crisps. Salt and vinegar, no questions.      Right, crisps, pasta, and mugs. What else? Oh! Do we need painkillers? I got a bee sting on the leg last week and I still feel it sometimes.      You had that one? I thought it was a jellyfish left over from Pompey!      It  was  a bit unusual. I tried to take it off with a credit card first, like you do for jellyfish. Should’ve stuck to kitchen remedies like vinegar.      You can’t do that. You have to use Sting Spray or nothing helps. I saw it on a video.      Bah, your YouTube videos don’t know grief when they see it. I’ve dealt with far worse bites than a little wasp from the garden. Though I swear that one looked like it was from a sci-fi movie.      [Speaking with a slight London accent] You know what it probably was—an Asian tiger mosquito, they’re spreading this far north now.      Oh aye, and I’ll thank you not to make it sound like a Marvel villain. It’s bad enough dealing with the  real  monsters in my line of work.      Like the ones who leave their kids in pushchairs on the Tube!      So, back to the shopping list. Painkillers, anti-itch cream, and maybe some calamine?      Sounds like it’ll do. Oh, and Terry brought home another spider today. You know the one who kills everything in the house. He’s doing a real good job with that.      I took the kettle over there and  boiled  it. That’s the proper way to go. Unless it’s a man-spider or something      Oh, no, it's just a box spider—harmless really, but you don’t have to tell it to Terry.      So, anyone got anything else? Oh right, we need chips for the weekend. They promised to do a fish supper. You know Terry—he’s got that football theme going.      And let’s not forget the Arsenal lager. Got to keep the spirit alive during the game, right?      Aye, we’re not in the Premier League for tea and biscuits!

I haven’t had that phone since like 2015.       laughs  Same with mine! I tried to explain that I’ve "updated my information slightly" but it just delete me and says too many attempts.      Honestly, like, do they not understand the word "cancel" or are they just evil?      It's like they want to make us throw our phones out the window, only to log back in like minutes later. Just, I don't know, like why is this so hard?      But anyway, I think our P.E. teacher is actually, like, onto something. Wait, you heard about that new system they’re using for PE in Year 10, right?      Yeah, so? They made us do fitness tests like Water-Polo, Climbing, and then some weird yoga one that I don’t think I’ve done since I was ten and fell off a mat in ballet class.      Right? So she's using some app where you scan your face, and then it gives you a fitness score. I didn't want to laugh out loud when Silas was scanned. The app read '0.8 kg' for his bicep strength. Honestly.      Oh my god, I  should  have taken a video. Or at least whispered it through my hand so no one heard me.      Yeah, but hey, you can just blame the machine, right? Not like a teacher can say anything if it's data-based.      Maybe. Although, I found out that the app gives different results depending on how much sleep you had the night before. Science class is going to be so  useful  next year.      Not to mention, like, our entire lives are just being recorded with weird machine data and videos of us trying to do yoga. My sister just walked in the room with a snack and started watching the video go viral of my failed downward dog.      You’re lucky it’s not science class. I tried to do that volcano experiment at home and it  exploded  in my brother's face.      Wait, really?! You didn’t use baking powder and vinegar or something overkill?      I used the one my mum gave me for a project, the instant kind. All you do is add water and light it.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You think they'd do something about this cold in time for when they start planning the conference, but no luck. I’ve been sniffing and sniffling for a week now.      That is a bummer. You can't be much use writing up all that conference content with a runner nose and brain fog. Did you at least get the vaccination? I remember that was a requirement this year, wasn’t it?      Yeah, I got that done. Two weeks ago was the last one. Didn’t even get a sniff then. Honestly thought I was sorted. But then I bloody made the mistake of eating at the Indian place near campus. Never again.      Oh no! The chilli chicken one? I think I had food poisoning after the last time I was there. Fair enough, I can see how that would’ve dropped your guard. I still can’t figure out whether they were using a dodgy rep or what, but ever since then I’ve stuck to the pizza place down the street.      Water under the bridge, maybe. But I’m not up for much short of a hot bath and Netflix. I only started watching that series with Lloyd Grossman—what was it? The one about the AI and body language recognition for security cameras?      Yeah,  MindFrame ? That one is actually quite thought-provoking. Silly as it looks, the concept of using AI to spot fake emotions feels all too near. I remember reading a paper a few years ago that tested AI against a bunch of students acting out fear and surprise in the lab. The tech got better every time.      Exactly! I mean, imagine what a setup like that could do in a hospital waiting area. If a machine can tell if you're nervous before you even open your mouth, does that change how we treat anxiety, or does it just create new ones? All that data about your emotions floating around without your say-so?      There’s a question. I suppose when you’re doing a PhD you start looking at things like this academically, trying to find nuanced angles and ethical models to hold it all together. But when you’re a normal person with a cold and the TV on, it's just weird stuff that you can't unsee.      Completely. It’s like they’ve taken something very human and made it algorithmic.

Right, I just played "artisan" on a double word score. That had to be worth  something.       Maybe you're finally using your transcription skills! Erm, I just put down “claret,” but honestly, I have no idea what that word even means in context.      Claret is a type of red wine. I think.      Oh aye, I used to have claret every Sunday after tea, unless we had sherry. But that was years ago in my school days, when I used to run the staff mess.      Right, claret it is. I’ve no idea what it means, but if Nell says it’s a real word, I’m going with it. Speaking of school days, did I tell you I still use my schoolmaster planner today? It’s bursting at the seams with doctor’s appointments and forgetful grandchildren breakfasts.      Seriously, Dad? The same planner that’s got five different inks on it and looks like a timeline of the Wars of the Roses?      Haha, fair enough. Though I might take notes from your planner as well. I’ve got ten emails waiting today, plus this transcript I have to finish by tomorrow. It’s got “coordination” and “best-practice” in there like, 37 times. I swear, no one says those words out loud anymore.      You young folk talk about "work-life balance"—in my day it was either work or a jam jar of plum chutney left on the stove hotter than the summer sun.      Still, Margot, I do like the way you talk about balance. I try to take the dog round the block for a walk every afternoon. It’s like my own kind of “wellness.”      You mean when you’re not browsing for vinyl on the music magazine stand at the supermarket.      A man can dream. Those records are bloody pricey though. At my age, I can’t afford a tour of the 70s. Though I did nearly buy Led Zeppelin recently—only to find out it was fake, of course.      Right, but back to the game. I go next. I think I’m going to go for “queued” next, just in reference to that brutal hour we spent waiting at the butcher’s the other day. It felt like the queue was going to circle the entire town centre.      Tell me about it. I had forgotten how bad gridlock is at the shopping centre on a Saturday. There’s more cars than I’ve seen since the time the ring road collapsed in 2008.

Rather a lot of people here today, isn't it? I do love these working parties, even when they're a tad on the quiet side.      Oh, you're right about that. I was at an exhibition in Germany the other week—some 300 or so people came through, and now  this  is a breeze! But I reckon it depends on where you come from. You’ve been all over with your artwork and antiques, haven’t you?      Oh, wasn’t nothing fancy like the exhibitions you’ve run in, but I did a few small art fairs near Exeter and Bristol—those were nice, short and sweet, no crowds to speak of like that one you had in Berlin!      Ah, well, the crowds were partly because we had this whole new printing system showcased there. It was one of my proudest projects back when I was still working. Spent years developing a system that combined offset and digital, and it took off like wildfire in the industry.      That sounds like something I could tell you a thing or two about—offset I mean! Back in the day, I had a little print shop in Taunton. Nothing on the scale of your invention, mind, but I had my own system of preparing prints for the antique frames and labels I sold.      Now there’s a craft! You always were a dab hand with the aesthetics of things. I remember you once told me you painted one of your catalogues by hand—something about it being oddly satisfying.      Oh aye, I thought it through very carefully—I wanted the patrons to feel they were buying a piece of history, not just a product. But talking of printing systems, what made you take on Germany for exhibitions?      Well, it wasn’t so much that I wanted to ‘take on’ anything, it was more about the opportunities. The German print industry was booming then, and if you wanted to show something new, Germany was where you did it. We had to pitch, then negotiate, then ship out everything. Sometimes with very little notice.      Blimey, you must have had a few interesting adventures! I recall you once goin’ on about a time you had a broken wheel on your camping van just outside of Nuremberg.      [chuckles] Aye, that was a classic! Wheel came off one night, and those locals, bless ‘em, stopped to help me and ended up fixing it with tools we had to them!

So do you know how long we're gonna be on the road today?      We should be there by tonight if we don't stop more than we have to, probably after dark, depending on traffic. But don't worry—I timed it so we can stop at a service station for lunch again and maybe even a cream tea if we find one with good scones.      That would be amazing, but can we have a detour to Bude? I read there's a farmer’s market and you said we could go foraging for wild mushrooms if we had time.      Only if you promise to not throw a tantrum the moment we don’t find truffles like in My Neighbor Totoro. I swear, last time we tried to find fungi, you were half-convinced the whole forest was cursed.      Well, you did nearly step on a pig while whispering to a dandelion like in a horror film, so no wonder I thought something spooky was going to happen.      It wasn’t a pig, it was a very sturdy manure pile I mistook for land. Anyway, let's get serious for a minute—did you pick a university course yet?      I’m thinking of doing English Language with Philosophy. I love grammar, but I also find ethics and the meaning of life quite interesting. It’s all very abstract, but I like that.      Sounds like someone who might one day write books that no one buys and then write bad reviews of those books themselves.      You think I’m not serious? I actually  want  to understand how words have changed over time. Like, why "through" is spelt like that but pronounced completely differently. It drives me nuts.      Spelling’s a bit of a mess, isn’t it? I still say “pronunciation” wrong, even after all these years.      Do  you  spell it correctly?      Not really. I just spell phonetically. It’s always been: P-R-O-N-O-N-I-A-T-I-O-N… and then I get lost around the N.      Mm, it’s P-R-O-N-U-N-C-I-A-T-I-O-N. But it's always the quiet letters that get people. Like “knight” or “psychology.”      I think those silent letters are just leftovers from old English. Just forgotten ghosts that sound overconfident when they speak.      You know I did that poster for class?

Rather skip the newfit meat eh?      Aye, it's all mad expensive. I got the lamb from down the road, proper farmer’s market, bit pricey, but smells wicked.      You do know the rest of us ain't got student loans to make up for, don’t you? I’ve been feeding the cat kibble and water for the last two days!      Oh, don’t be a drama queen, Tim. If you’d done what I said and brought a whole chicken, we could’ve at least had some leftover meat.      Chicken’s dry, Claire! Not everything can be a posh conference dinner, you know. I like my food to hit the spot, not sit there like a brick.      I reckon you're just too picky. If it walks like a piece of meat, you eat it.      He’s got a point. Honestly, I used to live on Tesco Value chicken when I was working full-time and studying—and I still survived. Barely.      Aye well, I’m not up for that sort of torture.      And what, pray tell, is on your brilliant lamb tonight, Jamie?      Garlic, rosemary, lemon—bits I grew in my mam’s garden before she kicked me out.      That sounds lovely! You know what I could kill for? A bit of those roast potatoes you make at your nan’s—proper crispy on the outside, soft in the middle.      Ah, now that, I can cook. Still got the recipe in my head from when I was a kid about five. My gran made the best bangers and mash too, but I haven’t had one in years.      I’d take it. I haven’t seen my nan in, like, six months. She still texts me recipes in all caps.  cook me a yorkshire pudding she said, as if it’s a crime .      We should make a night of it. Potatoes, lamb, Yorkshire pudding… we can call it “Jamie’s Grand Heritage Evening” or something.      Pfft! Jamie’s Heritage Evening go bad? I’ll see you lot trying not to fight over the last brussels sprout.      That might be the only sprout we’ll see. I asked if I could bring any, and Jamie looked at me like I’d asked him to bring a cactus on a picnic.      C’mon! It’s a sprout! Unless I got confused and brought courgettes instead.      No, don’t you dare! I haven’t had a proper oven-ready meal in weeks.

I can't believe the bar’s still shut for another week. Cheapest pint in town, and they’re piling in the deep clean or whatnot. It’s mad, innit? Yeah, it must be tough running a bar right now. Especially after the tax rises and everything. You must be missing the place, huh? Definitely. I’ve been popping in here just for a bit of coffee and a breather before heading back to the bar. Oh, and checking out the new baristas. Know what I mean? They’re all uni students or somethin’. You don’t get the same vibe as back in the day. That’s true. From what I remember, university bars were always chaotic. Fun in bursts, but most of the time you’d end up with a student and a broken taps. I did spend most of my time there during my first year. Not sure if it helped me learn German, though. I imagine it depends on what kind of German phrases you picked up. Maybe not ones you’d want to teach in class. I try to keep it as PG as possible when I’m at work. I’ve got a bunch of teenagers, and I’m sure they’d find it hilarious if I shouted “Herzlichen Glückwunsch” at someone’s birthday. Anyway, enough about me. How did you manage through uni if you're working part-time now? That must’ve been tough. It was a bit of a grind, yeah. Bartending at night, lectures during the day, and some study in the café. But you get used to it after a while. Guess it all depends on how much caffeine you can handle. Sounds like quite the schedule. I remember doing some shifts at the library to plug gaps in my income. Less glamorous, but it kept me going. And reading was kind of a bonus. Yeah, I could never do it without a salary sacrifice. Speaking of, I tried to apply for waiting at that new Italian place down the road. Drives me up the wall how they've got to keep the “hiring hold” thing going. Got any experience trying to get a job lately? Honestly, it’s wild. I had to start applying again for some part-time college work in the holidays, which was like explaining my academic background to a chatbot. It’s funny how much things have changed since I was your age.

Rather skip the queue and take a shortcut through the shops, do you?      Oh, I don’t fancy driving anywhere after this lot sorted out my oil leak, do you?      Not to worry, the coffee’s already on the table. We’ll make do with a bit of peace and quiet before the rush.      Rush? It’s half past ten in the morning, Phyllis!      If you refer to it as 'rush', then you might as well start ringing the bells for it, Jerry.      Not to worry, I won’t be driving anywhere near the roundabout today, not after last week's near-miss with a lorry that thought it was heading for the Gambia by mistake.      Ah, and I hear the traffic there’s even faster than it is round here!      I’ve been thinking about creating a donation box in my garden. You know, for people walking by, to give spare change to a worthy cause.      That’s very kind of you, Phyllis. I’m sure quite a few people would appreciate it. Just make sure someone remembers to collect it—it would be a shame if it was all taken by someone playing at being Baptiste Munchausen, and claiming it for a long-lost cousin.      Now, you mention donations, what about those banners you had made for the charity fair in June?      Yes, they were a bit of a struggle to get up—piece of string and a breeze, and I thought it was a wind tunnel!      You know, I considered binding them to a bell tower just to keep the wind at bay. Not much else you can do! Though it might attract the local bell ringers.      My, my! You lot certainly do get amongst things. I was just planting some new shrubs the other day. Proper bloody late for the season, but I suppose it's never too late if the bell doesn't mind.      Gardeners never do keep to the schedule! They're all about going with the flow and delivering something beautiful.      Yeah, go on then, Phyllis—why not make a proper donation box out of it? Stick a nice bench beside it, blooming plants, and your banners. It could be something the whole village talks about—better than my business making those plastic signs nobody even reads!      And if you overdo it, just be sure to hire someone to ring the bells all the way to the Channel, so people know it's happening!

Okay, thanks a lot for dinner, honestly. Your grannies cooking is just as good as real Polish pirogi and I mean she’s German now but still somehow I can tell by the smell where she's been doing it. Not quite traditional, but I mean—some people wouldn't say it was Polish at all, but she doesn't care. She says 'I make what I like.'      She probably just makes it up as she goes! I mean, I've had this stew before, and she once added tarragon to it. Tarragon? That’s French.      Yeah, but it worked! It made it taste a bit more like the countryside, you know? Or like that one movie where the German farmer makes his own food and no one questions it, because it's their home cooking and that's just what it is.      Honestly, I would have been too brave to even try that. Like, "why tarragon in a stew, nonna?" But, you didn’t have the guts to ask why, did you?      Not a chance. I mean, if I ask questions, she leaves. And once she leaves the kitchen, everything turns to mush. I’ve seen it.      Tell us what we can’t?      No comment. Anyways, back to why we're all here. We did say we'd have a movie night. And we’ve already picked the horror one. Our group chat said Spooky Tales 21: The Hairdresser of West London.      That is a terrifying title if I've ever heard one. A hairdresser in London doing something spooky in about five square feet of a bathroom?      Oh come on, they showed what the budget was. This wasn’t like some big Hollywood series. This was probably shot entirely on an iPhone in someone's spare bedroom.      So it's just bad, but the kind of bad where you all comment on how intense it is, but you're convinced your friend is really into it.      Exactly. It’s that kind of horror where you hear the “screaming in the sewer” and you’re like, “I swear that was my go-to room on Number 11 bus.”      I just started smiling when that green screen waterfall randomly flipped upside-down.      Look, I’m not here for special effects, though. I'm here for jump scares and clichés. True to horror genre: the dolls turn over, the lights flicker, someone yells.

Rather annoying this, having to get stuck in a car for an hour and a half just to come up and see you lot. Never used to be this bad when I were younger.      Aye, I remember when you could drive from Costessey to Norwich in under half an hour and not see a single car. Now it’s like bloody Times Square out there.      You should have taken the bus! Got one every hour, it stops just outside the village shop, easy as that.      Oh no, don’t get me started on buses. Mine broke down three times last week! Sitting there on the side of the road, wind blowing in through the window like a pinched face. Driver had to get out and fumble around with a spanner like he was Oliver Hardy trying to fix a leaky tap.      Aye, better than breakfast, no doubt. I had a driver once told me in his sleep he’d be five minutes! That was an hour ago.      You’d have to be mad to leave the house without a car these days. I mean, don’t get me wrong, I like the bus, but only because there’s nowhere to park here. Had to park half a mile away last Sunday and –  ha!  – I was almost flattened by a cyclist zigzagging across the road like he was racing to the next postcode!      You heard that bloke shouting at the cabbie in the village last week? All he was doing was turning left, and the guy with the red bus nearly ran into his windscreen and still got out and started slagging him off as if it were a personal slight!      Aye, well, I blame the young ones. No clue how to drive. I see these kids trying to park a £30k estate car, like it’s the first time they’ve held a steering wheel. Banging it into a lamppost and not giving a hoot. I tried to stop them waiting on me once and the bloke tutted at me as if I were the one with the problem!      Some people, no respect for anyone, least of all older drivers! I had a woman go flying past my pond-side about a week ago, so fast I thought she was in a race, and she had the box of the car full of bloody takeaway boxes! Could have been planning to fill up the koi pond after work!

Rather annoying this new traffic light system, isn't it? I swear they've added three more since we first set off from Manchester.      It’s a bit of a slog, but at least we’re not dealing with the weather they have in the north today. Imagine trying to drive through that lot on the motorway.      Yeah, I reckon it’s not as bad as it could’ve been. I still can’t get over this though—how much easier it used to be back in the eighties! You’d just hit the M6 and chase the sun or the sunset. No hold-ups like this.      Aye, and no Facebook spammers either. You know, like that Myra chap. I swear he sends me five ads a day about replacing radiators now I’m moving house, even though I bought a whole house inspector to check everything for me!      I feel for you. I mean, house moving is such a chore. I remember the time I moved, and the lorry got stuck in the village for three hours. I was over it by the end of the day. Honestly, I don’t know how anyone does it without losing their mind.      It’s not for the faint-hearted, that’s for sure. I helped out my sister once when she moved, and I ended up with tennis elbow from carrying the kitchen drawers. It took me weeks to recover.      You don’t say? I’ve never managed anything that dramatic, but my back certainly wouldn’t survive another one. Besides, I had a chest infection last week—just a mild one, but the doctor told me to take it easy for a bit.      Oh no! That does sound awful. You still coughing?      Not much now, thank heavens. Still, I’m taking it easy, mostly because I have to, not that I’m complaining. I didn’t work for twelve years, and now I suffer the consequences!      Fair point, but at least you’ve got us here to crack you up as you recuperate. Although I’m not sure the lunches we keep bringing are helping—my chocolate cake the other night? Still trying to get around that!      Honestly, that cake was a life-and-death risk. But you two have made my kitchen my new second home. Honestly, I’ve never had so many people coming through my front door at once since I bought this place.

Mummy, did you actually get my bike back?!      Yes, love! We got it back a couple of days ago. It was down at the warehouse by the docks where they found this whole group of stolen bikes and stuff. Your name was on the frame, so it was lucky they checked!      No way! Are you serious?! But how did it not get sold or something?      Honestly, I’m not sure. The police think some guy was trying to sell bikes off in the car boot on the weekend when he got caught with a whole load of dodgy ones. One of the other sellers saw a bike that looked just like yours and reported it. So that’s how it all came back!      Omg, that is the best news. But why was I not told straight away? I was worried for ages!      Well, love, I didn’t want to get your hopes up in case it turned out not to be you. But when they confirmed it was definitely yours, I thought I’d give you a big surprise!      I’m so happy! I’ve still got grief from that, like, someone just rode off with it during lunch. I thought it was gone for good.      I know, and I know you were trying to be the mature one saying don’t worry, but I could see you were upset. You don’t talk about it much, but I know it matters.      Thank you for not giving up, mummy. I had all this weird DMs and fake profiles being like “I saw your bike” or “I might know who did it”... most of it was just trolls trying to wind people up. Honestly, it made things worse!      I know it does. Social Media can be so tricky, can’t it? Sometimes the less you say about it, the better. Just stick to the facts if you have to write anything.      Yeah, I did stick to my story as much as I could. Even mentioned it in one of my college essays by the way. Not in the creative writing part—just a personal statement. I was like, “This is goin’ on my life…”      Well, I’m sure the colleges will understand. And the good thing is, your bike’s all back and in one piece. The chain was a bit bent, but I’m going to get that fixed for you this weekend.

Right, I just drew a card. "From Bristol to Coventry." That's a hop. But first... who's hungry? I could do with some more tea. This game gives me the munchies!      I'll have some tea as well. Just don't let it get cold on you like last time, Mairin. You   did   leave it on the windowsill with a fan blowing on it by mistake.      Excuse you,  you  are the one who moved the fan in the first place! Didn’t even ask me.      Right, I’ve just united  Swansea  with  Exeter . That’s a bold one. But what’s for lunch? I’m starving!      I made a chicken salad, assuming someone might want something not too heavy for playing board games in the cottage. But judging by Gareth breakfast, no doubt someone has second thoughts.      Excuse you, Elaine! That muesli puffin is a national treasure. I would expect nothing less from Welsh breakfast standards, and I loved it.      Right, as if you’re choosing food over trains. Tell me there was something on the plate, Elaine.      There was – but it looked like a puffin and I had to confirm whether it was the real thing or not.      If I’d seen that, I might’ve carried it out in a torchlight procession and played a bagpipe. Puffins and pipes – that’s a theme for you. Also, I think the tea’s burning here!      Look, let’s make a rule about tea from now on: it must be stirred   and   tapped on the side of the mug three times. Ceremonial stuff.      No, we’re not starting a  tea ritual  like the ones Dad does at 5am on the weekend with a teaspoon and his newspaper. That’s  too  intense.      Honestly, Gareth, if you had that much energy in your day job, the lunches would be on time and we wouldn’t be eating lukewarm sardine sandwiches around this table.      Let's refocus! This game is about  strategic placement , not my breakfast choices. Dylan, you're currently in control of the main line. Pass it over!      No, no way, Elaine. I’m holding the line until I get a coherent explanation of why you changed from Geography to Education. C’mon! It's a  close  family game, so no hiding behind the board.      Okay, firstly, Geography is a lovely subject, and secondly, I thought I was going to be in a career long enough to actually enjoy travel, not teach about it to people still too young to get a train pass on their own!

Rather skip the starter and just go for the main, don't you?      Oh, come on, it's not every day I get to play board games on a rainy Sunday afternoon with my wife in my in-laws' conservatory.      Fair point. Got a glass of red? I’ll pour one for us both.      You know I always do. What game are we playing this time? Risk, Catan or are you going to dump something complicated on me again?      Oh no, don't worry. I thought we'd try out a brand new one— Azul . It's a tile-based game. Quiet and a bit more strategic than Catan, I think.      I’m intrigued. You know I’m more of a "place the little pigs" man, but by all means, if it doesn’t involve murder then I’m in.      You say that, but back in London when we hosted the Christmas dinner and that man from the third-floor flat—personally, violently—attacked the tapas spread with a fork and a grief of ten, remember?      How could I forget? He was like “I’m lactose intolerant!” while he stabbed the cheftini with a smile.      All that aside, this whole drinking culture is bizarre, isn’t it? In London, the supermarkets just chuck out full bottles of wine every evening. You’d walk by and there they are, waiting— just waiting —to be trampled and forgotten.      Yeah, it’s absurd. I mean, I know marketing does that to the wine, but it’s still depressing. At home, we make sure we finish the bottle or we give it to the next-door neighbour to do something less wasteful.      True. Back here in Norfolk, it’s a totally different pace. People don’t drink as much during the week, unlike London, where you could live off pubs and Aldi’s 99p Indian meals.      That’s the difference between the cities and the country—drinking in London is fast, loud and go-to-war on your own if you don’t get a table in time. Here it’s all about the weekend sips, blokes on the patio with straws and smoothies.      Although, I’d miss those nights, don’t get me wrong. Do you ever feel that post-lecture, when we head to that little bar off the Holloway Road and just talk about anything—neuro-linguistics, the 80s, or whether the flat white has enough caffeine to keep you awake until 2am?

So do you not like meatballs?      I love them. I just think there was... like, a thousand of them.      Well, I've been cooking for a week, hun. Not sure I'll have time to cook again for a week after moving.      Moving? I thought the place was all handed over to you already.      It is, but we still have to unpack this stuff, and then we're due at a friend’s place to do a photoshoot next weekend. You're coming, aren't you?      If you're bringing baked Alaska shots, I probably will.      That was a  disaster . I still can’t believe you made it to the end of that night, Emma.      I was sad in slow motion for a month afterward.      Yeah, breakfast, baked Alaska, and brussels sprouts... I don’t know what’s more Welsh than that combo.      Well, it’s  Welsh brussels sprouts , love, not just any old sprouts. I put in a dram of whisky to the sauce and everything.      Real craftsmanship there, Nana. Absolutely top-tier culinary humblebragging.      I’m not proud, I just  know  what the lads in my poker club would like for their tea if they weren’t too busy counting their losses, huh?      That’s right. And speaking of... are the bins outside sorted yet?      Sorted? Love, I  lost  the black bin lid again! Looked like it ran off with about half the milk bottles.      Maybe it had a midlife crisis.      Oh that was you! I was up at the shop for my usual bunch of fags and thought someone left the bin lid out like it was giving me a sign. Took me ten minutes just to figure out it was mine.      I think your bin lid’s got a bit of a personality now.      Speaking of personality... what are the plans with the white goods? Still trying to get the fridge and freezer delivered the same day?      If I could just  convince  the lad at the warehouse, yeah. He thinks we can box four fridges and a freezer into a Vauxhall Corsa. I’ve been writing emails, mind you. Properly formal ones with all the boxes ticked and the dotted lines.      Or just call the guy and go,  “look, we need those things in two days or the fridge’s owner is going to be me, and I make spicy potato dishes, not oven-ready meals” .      She means chilli-infused, right?

Rather annoying this traffic, isn't it?      It's always mad through Finsbury Park on a Thursday afternoon. You’d think more people could work from home.      Yeah, but honestly, I don’t know what people were thinking building all these one-way systems. It’s like a maze.      Maze, yes. You'd think with a bit of A.I. they could route this lot better. Still, easier said than done.      You saying the TLS got another print issue out last week?      Yes, I did. Honestly, I can't fathom why the print department still exists. It's like printing the turkey on Christmas Day. There's just not the appetite for it anymore, unless you count the Downton Abbey set who think it's somehow posher.      Yeah, I see what you mean. I mean, I read some in uni and everything, but ever since I started writing, it’s always been digital submissions.      Eventually, it’ll all get phased out. But until the last subscribers drop, they’ve got to keep printing it. For now, I’m just thankful they don’t print it any heavier than they already do.      Speaking of which, you still writing that Belgium book?      It’s moving, slowly. I've been drafting some of the chapters at the weekend, and I might take someone with me when I go back to France to do a bit of archival work. Would you want to come with? I know you like to tag along.      Yeah, that would be cool. I've always been interested in how stories from the past get told in the present. I might even help out with research. Not that I’d get it published beside yours, but still.      That’d be lovely. A proper mini-road-trip. We'll go to Paris for the afternoon, take the train, meet some people, and I’ll get a crack at the archives. Perfect.      Do you plan on bringing anything from here with you?      I might bring this vintage typewriter I got from Dad. It’s one of his old ones. He used it at the Express when he started out. I think it'll go with the vibe.      Cool. If it’s too much of a hassle, we could just pick it up from you when we go to France.      That’s not a bad idea. I’m always leaving my keys and one of my mismatched gloves in the car.

Right, so I am telling you, the whole holiday in Spain was a bit of a write-off. We’d got to the airport at six in the morning, ready to go, then someone left their passport in the bin at home. We had to go back, collect it, get back in time for check-in and then we were  not  allowed on the plane.      Wait, why? Did they lose your stuff?      No, easier than that. We were pulling suitcases onto the conveyor belt and me being the “expert” in airport security said, “No meat products, but I guess baked beans are fine.” Big error, cos the beans had pork in them. They made us re-pack, we missed our flight. Fun.      And you still moaned about it the whole way there?      What was I supposed to do, breakfast on the plane then? I mean, realistically...      Honestly, I remember that flight, didn’t we have to do the whole plane full of blokes in one row, because of the inappropriate costumes?      Right! Because Steve and Adam tried to be “disguised” in bow ties and socks with sandals and flip-flops. “It’s European chic,” they said. The guy in front actually asked if they were escaping a zombie film.      And then we all had to sit in the hot room for two hours before they sorted someone out to rebook us.      That’s when we started the bucket challenge in the departure lounge. Or at least  pretended  to. I had to get away with it most of the time. Steve finally pulled the plug when the security guard gave him “the look.”      Oh that was brilliant! I mean it was a  hot  departure lounge and we had to put wet socks on our hands after. Steve did it twice and then told us the security guy told him he was banned.      You mad bints. I’m just glad we got on the next flight and got there with lunches to keep us going. I’ve still got the chip in my bag from that sandwich I had onboard.      Look on the bright side, we had a few extra days in the country and we got to see the Spanish countryside in a taxi that looked like it had seen better days. It had a seatbelt on the driver’s side only and a sheep in the back.      Oh yeah, and the guy asked why we were surprised.

So I heard you've been out wild winter camping, Alistair? That sounds like it takes some guts! What's the appeal?      Aye, it's wild, no mistake! But it's probably the most alive I've ever felt—especially in the cold. There’s something about being out in the open, miles from nowhere, with just a bivvy and your mates. The silence you hear at night when the wind dies down... it's like nothing else exists. It's just you and the elements.      That doesn't sound very comforting to me. I mean, I like to have a warm bed and a safe house, thank you very much! But I do get the draw of the wild, I suppose. I used to hike with a group back in Edinburgh, but I never went into it this far.      It's not for everyone, Mhairi. I still have moments where I think,  “What am I doing in a blizzard five miles from the nearest road?”  But the benefits? They’re real. You learn so much about yourself—like your resilience, your ability to cope, your limits. It strips everything back to the essentials. Food, heat, shelter, survival… it’s basic, but it’s deeply grounding.      I can see how that would be therapeutic, in a way. It’s the opposite of the fast pace and noise of the city. For someone who splits their time between labs and literature, the idea of someone sitting in one place and meditating on the stars? It just sounds oddly appealing. Though I’m not sure I have your cold-weather tolerance.       laughs  Oh, trust me, I didn’t always have it either! I started in the summer, then gradually moved into autumn. Now I take it easy—I choose sites with a bit of protection, bring decent gear, and never go alone. Safety’s the biggest rule. Though I once did venture into the Cairngorms alone after a storm cleared, and it was intense. The way the snow shimmered under moonlight… it was beautiful. Though I’ll never forget how frigid that bivvy got by morning.      You’re lucky you came back with stories and not frostbite! Honestly, it’s wild that people are still trying new things like this at their age. I’ve got a group of people in my therapy sessions who are always chasing some form of self-discovery, but seriously, why not just take up painting or something less dangerous?

So did you watch The Last of Us on HBO yet? I’ve been trying to get you into it like ages.      Yeah, I did actually. I binged the first season last week. I wasn’t sure what to expect, but it’s cracking good.      Oh I'm glad! I’ve been rating it to the moon. It’s basically like all them post-apocalyptic films but with real heart. Not like that  World War Z  blether, you know?      Definitely. The writing’s so tight. The way they explored the relationship between Joel and Ellie felt so real—it even made  me  emotional, and I’m not one to blub at blockbusters.      Oh you big softy. It’s just like, the real horror isn’t even the Cordyceps or the fungus nonsense— it’s the loss and the choice of letting go . Bucks the trend of most films, which is just running and guns, you know?      True. And the performances. Pedro Pascal is immense, like always. But tell me—personally, are you Team Ellie or Team Joel?      Honestly? I’m Team Ellie. She’s got so much grit, and it’s such a coming-of-age thing too. Mate, I’ve been devouring fantasy novels because of this show. I’ve gone back to read  Station Eleven  and  The Stand —and oh, I even started  The Passage  again.      No way! I read  The Passage  ages ago. Some good stuff, but it’s a bit over the top with the microbes and all that future stuff. Still, it made about five films, didn’t it?      Oh I know. It’s like the holy grail of that genre. I mean, it’s a classic for sure, but I found  The Last of Us  less “over the top” and more just bleak, man. I’d say it was all  very  relatable, you know? Like, could see us there, as people. Even being in a car like this with someone, stuck on the English roads with no signal and a flat battery—it’s a bit of a taster.      Mm, don’t I know it.
