Any road, have you read anything else? I’m between choosing  The Quiet Before  and  The Road . Thought you might have an opinion.      Yeah, I think  The Road  is like, the bleakest of the bleak, but very moving. Only read it at night, though. You’ll go all melancholy for a week.

Right, who’s ready for a story tonight? I’ve got a few new ones in my ‘read-aloud’ folder on the laptop. Or would you like to make one up this time?      Let’s make one up, like we usually do.      Yeah, Mummy! Can I start it with ‘Once there was a robot that wanted to be a wizard’?      That sounds brilliant, bud. Go on then.      Once there was a robot that wanted to be a wizard. But the problem was he didn’t have any magic. He even tried to wave his arms like a wizard and shouted, “Fizz-wizzle pop!” But it just came out “bleep bleep bleep”.      That’s silly. He should’ve said “zoom zoom zoom”!      No! Wait! He met a typewriter that happened to be a bit grumpy and said, “You can never be a wizard, robot. You have wires, not wands.”      Oh no! That’s cruel. What happened next?      Did the robot cry?      No, the robot got really cross then. He said, “I – am – not – a – typewriter.” And he turned on the typewriter and hit the space bar so much it typed “DISSSMISSSSS”!      Oh someone’s full of imagination tonight.      Can we have a bit of Excel in the story?       laughs  Okay – where do we start? Maybe the typewriter had formulas in its keyboard?      And robot wizard had a spreadsheet of spells.      Yeah! He had a column for ‘Hair-Pulling Jinx’ and ‘Nose-Itching Charm’ and he did VLOOKUPs for extra effectiveness.      Genius. I am writing this down when I get older. This is good stuff.      Then the typewriter finally said, “You are the wizard of the 21st century, robot!” Because it was too slow to keep up.      And the robot said – “I made you do it, typewriter!”      You two are your mother’s children. Alright, what happens next?      The robot made a potion in Excel, called it “FizzPopWizzle potion 3.0” and cleaned up the typewriter’s keyboard so all the keys danced and sparkled.      And then they built a tower out of Lego and called it the Control-tower of Magic Logic, and now they run a wizard school in… in…      The cloud!      The – cloud!      Wow, that’s pretty advanced for a bedtime story. That feels like it came out of my own Psychology degree! If you didn’t mention the Lego tower, I’d say it was a case study.      Is that what you study in your work, Mummy?

Rather than chuck a wobbly, I just chuck my scruffy clothes on. Don’t even know if I got the right socks on some days, do I?      I saw you this morning, Sue. Not only do you have the wrong socks on — one is green, one’s navy — but you were  reading the paper with one boot on and one on the floor.  It’s a wonder you’ve taught a postgraduate class before.      Oh, don’t start, John. This place is my sanctuary. Scruffy and warm. Right when I get the fire going and the kettle’s on, it’s like  this is where I’m supposed to be.  That’s why I won’t sell the house, by the way — not to the students, not to the council, not to the foreigners with their silly architectural ideas.      It is a bit of a place. Your breakfast, though — if I may say — has a certain rugged charm. Toast, black coffee, and that marmalade you bring back from the fruit farm every summer?      Aye, that’s Rhian up near Harrogate — runs a farm with her brother and dad. They’ve still got the old-country ways. Doesn’t bother with fertiliser from the big supermarkets. Grows all organic: plums, figs, blackcurrants — and she gets a proper crush out of that marmalade. If I could, I’d bring back the whole bloody lorry just for the jam.      You’d have to clear out the junk mail first — you know, the lot that says you’ve won a free trip to Mauritius  for winning a Prime Minister most likely to make me want to die.  I binned ten of them this morning.      Oh! You know that lot comes in because I have the unwise habit of signing up for websites like  Update Your Address for a Free Historic Map of a Deserted Medieval Village!  And the next thing you know, my doorstep looks like it was hit by a printer explosion.      Those  Update Your Address  Websites are always trying to catch you off guard. At least the village map sounds interesting. You like that kind of thing.      Oh, go on then — tell me about your morning. Any roadworks causing you to rethink your entire philosophy on life?      You know what your problem is, Sue? You take  such  delight in the roadworks. As long as I’m delayed for half an hour more on the M1, you’re in the middle of my car like  John, I’ve been watching that collision from my window — did you see the articulated lorry?

Right, I just wanted to go through the medication again before we get the rest of the food sorted. We don’t want another cold brew mishap this week, do we?      Haha, I don’t think we do. That coffee fiasco at the dinner table on Christmas night was not one for the holidays, I’ll say that.      Okay okay, but come on—it was genius. You tried to make cold brew from a recipe on Facebook and it looked like motor oil. Honestly, it was gold.      Didn’t even look like it was safe to drink, like, was it even mostly  water ?      I still can't get the taste out of my tongue. I’ve been gargling with peppermint mouthwash ever since.      But hey, I think it turned out alright. It added character to the evening at least. I still haven’t recovered from the time you tried to drive in Ashford and got lost five times in one shopping centre.      That was  one  time—okay, fine, maybe a couple of times. But I got there in the end.      And then you tried to hide the fact that you didn't know how to give directions from the kitchen to the living room?      That was  not  my best day. Let’s just move on.      Anyway, what about the Christmas presents? Did we manage to wrap them all? I found one for Mum in the back of the wardrobe behind old tax papers.      Yes, I think so. I helped with most of them—I even wrapped your grandmother’s knitting set in gold about an hour ago. Just don’t tell the cat, she had a field day with a roll of tape earlier.      I’m still not sure sending the knitting set was the best idea for her. She always guestimates the tension.      Well, the scarf you sent was ‘chunky’ in the loosest sense of the word, Dad.      I’ll have you know that it’s  modish . Chunky is in now.      Still, I think she liked it. She sent a photo back of her walking the pond with it on.      You’re just saying that because that was your scarf.      Anyway, all jokes aside—I ordered the new flu jab online via the NHS site after I saw those ads on Facebook. You should check it out, it’s much easier than waiting in the GP queue.      I did mine last month.

So did I! The episode last night was mental — that twist at the end was so out of nowhere. I texted my sister mid-show, like, “Is  this  what happens next?!”      I know, right?! I think I gasped so loud that my flatmate een came out to check I hadn’t choked on my tea. Honestly, I’m all for good drama, but that was a bit much.      No, but I’m not mad about it. It just made me  more  invested. Didn’t it get your head spinning trying to work out who did it?      Honestly, I’m still trying to piece it together. I had one theory, then the next episode completely shot it down. But hey, I live for the rollercoaster, I guess.      It is brilliant storytelling, even if it makes you tear your hair out. I mean, has anyone taken in how slowly the investigation is going in real life? They didn’t even say when they’ll solve the case properly. I was glued to the news this morning, hoping they’d cracked something.      Same. I even started reading old articles online just in case there was a clue we missed in the show. You ever do that? Mate of mine at uni said, “You know you’re hooked when you’re googling real-life crime,” and he was  not  wrong.      God, yes. I just watched a four-year-old documentary on a case that wasn’t even mentioned in the show. I’m getting obsessed.      Anyhow, enough about that — how’s work going? I heard about the new project you mentioned the other week.      Honestly? It’s chaos. My manager is doing this “no emails only meetings” thing, so I’ve had 17 catch-ups just to discuss one request. I swear, if I get another Teams invite at 8 a.m., I’m going to scream.      Sounds like the same nonsense as when I did that admin job before uni. Do lunches cost a mortgage there now? My boss took an hour over pizza just to decide where to put the printer!      That bad? Okay, maybe I’m exaggerating. But I’m just not in the mood to be micro-managed while I’m trying to write some dodgy copy at 10 p.m. and dreaming of my bed.      It’s a rough time for everyone, isn’t it? Work-life balance has flown out the window.

Rather skip the gym today, eh?      Aye, just haven’t got the energy yet. I’ve been up since the crack o’ dawn doing some desk work for the new manuscript I’m attempting.      That’s the one you were telling me about, was it set during the war or something more contemporary?      Both, actually. It’s fiction, but with a lot of real-life research in it—do you remember that house we used to visit in Ilford? Well, I'm basing the setting on that. Apparently, the owners had a secret room under the floorboards during the war. I’ve been digging through archives to make sure I get the details right.      You’ve always been the detail-oriented one. Unlike me, I stick to what I can remember from history class in school!      Well, that’s part of why I still enjoy it. It keeps me sharp, which I suppose is a bit of exercise for the brain, even if the body’s lazy.      I’d like to get into writing, maybe start a blog or something. I’ve never really tried it as a proper thing, only for university essays. But there’s something appealing about it.      You should. Start small—maybe food writing, since you’re always rattling on about recipes. I imagine that would do quite well.      Oh, I could! I cook more often now that the kids are older. Spent last week making a Sunday joint—slow-roasted lamb with rosemary and carrots. Just the way our mum used to do. But you know, I’ve had to get a bit creative with the salt and fat content these days.      Ha, I had that for lunch on Sunday and thought you were wasting your efforts! I mean it was bloody brilliant, but I do wish you’d stop cutting the fat off my potatoes!      Aye, leave the man his indulgences. Speaking of, I hear house prices in your area are going wild. How are you managing that?      It’s tight, I won’t lie. My partner took an early redundancy, so we’ve had to be careful. We’ve been looking at go-only properties on the edge of town. If we can afford it, I’d love to do some renovations. Maybe even a big kitchen extension.      You could have me in for free help—my job’s all paperwork anyway, I never even leave the office!

I can't believe the new Budget was announced last week and no one’s talked to me about it since. Honestly, no one I’m at work with talks about it either. It’s a bit frustrating because I don’t see how the government expects things to improve if they’re just cutting budgets again and again. It’s ridiculous really. My friend at the university works in housing and said that grants have been reduced by over ten per cent. They’re struggling to keep staff as it is. Yeah, I mean, I run a small civil engineering firm now – not huge, but I’ve got two people working under me and it’s tough out there. The government needs to stop biting the hand that feeds them, you know? I hear you – I’m in admin, so I’ve not got the same pressure as you, but still, funding is definitely tighter. I’ve been working more hours just to keep the same level of service. That’s the thing, everyone is feeling it. And I don’t see any sign of it stopping, which is why I’ve been thinking about expanding the business into property as well. Civil and structural assessments, that kind of thing. It’s stable, it’s needed, and it gives more flexibility. That could be a good way to diversify, especially if the construction boom doesn’t pick up again like it did a few years ago. Have you heard anything about the railway projects in this area? Just a bit – a new line’s been proposed through Cambridge, but it’d be a few years before anything really comes through. If I’m honest, I’m not holding my breath about massive investment unless there’s a real push from the government. Honestly, you could write a play about the current Budget. It’s got drama, disappointment, and the smell of scandal for the ending. I know – maybe I should open a theatre. Or a musical at least. I bet you’d do well with a West End-style review of the entire 2024 financial situation. I’d definitely buy a ticket. Still, I’m more likely to be booking the cast somewhere away from the buzz of capital cuts if you know what I mean. Oh yeah, I’m serious about doing a weekend trip soon. Maybe to Brighton?

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You think they'd do something about the gutters by now. We had proper rain and it just poured through the hole like it hadn’t even been fixed      Aye, proper nightmare. Look I got a bloke at the garage who knows a good eeny weeny firm, if you want I can get 'em out tomorrow      Aye, that’d be brilliant Cheers mate. I got to be honest, I’m not quite pulling my weight with this whole painting and gardening business      Nah, it's not too bad. You seem right sorted, honestly. I mean, you’re the one who still turns up with brushes like you’re painting a proper gallery piece      I suppose I was brought up like that, my mum was always into art. Knew a few proper artists in Germany, even did a bit of stage design for plays and stuff      Oh aye, you ever fancied getting on stage yourself?      I fancied it once, when I was younger—personally I think I'd have been luvverly as Romeo      Luvverly? You watching that BBC Romeo and Juliet on then?      Mate it's got Joseph Fiennes and I take the blame if I was into that sort of thing      Aye, well no worries you're more the lecturer type then, eh?      Fair point. Though truth is, teaching is alright. You get paid to watch people pretend they care about Shakespeare and be surprised when they don't      Sounds a about like me doing the same with tourists trying to get the exact change for the ferry from Toxteth Pier      Aye, it is a kind of strange kind of life, isn't it?      I know. The other day me mate said I should just give up the cab and get myself a flat in some little town, tour groups about to places like Chesterfield or Stockport or something      That sounds better than the Alternative Society Line, no doubt      Course. I told 'im no go, I need the life, you know      I do. I think that's what we were talking about earlier on when I said about goals in life.      Oh aye, I'm all about the simple things like new tyres to go on the road or fixing over this bloody gutter      That’s it mate. I think that's exactly it.      And always remember to borrow me telly remotes for when you fancy a film

Rather skip the new bar in Tarnów, shall we? I've had just about enough of stringy mince and dubious €5 shot offers for one trip. I prefer a good textbook and a proper café where I can finally alphabetise my teaching resources and not spill anything on them.      Right, yeah, I don’t mind one bit. I reckon it’s about time we sorted out a bit of our stuff too. I’ve got this box back here that’s basically a graveyard of old phone chargers and one pair of socks I lost and gave up chase for, but still left in the van... like it might walk back in.      Oh, I’d help but I have this habit of throwing useful things away first. The last time I tried this back home, I chucked out what turned out to be the only functioning kettle in the flat.      Yeah, I see that—maybe I'll just reorganise for now. Walk through, touch the object, say, “Keep, toss, keep, toss,” like it’s some kind of van therapy session. You know, I’ve had hitchhikers in this van before. One guy drove me absolutely mad, kept flicking the odd-country-loo switch for ten minutes in a row just to see what would happen.      Oh, that’s par for the course. I’ve had quite the journeys as well—on a slower note, one guy once stayed with me for two days in Kremsmünster. He ended up proposing to me in the van. I had a €7 flan waiting to be eaten in the sink and here he is with a ring!      No flan was harmed in the making of that romantic proposal, then?      No—he had to know that was off-limits. But it does kind of show that the most mundane things can turn into treasured memories. Though I don’t think that €7 flan will ever leave a dent on my pottery shelves. I tried to make my own once, but it crackled and died like a sprite being stepped on by a hobbit.      Okay, but the pottery class thing sounds like a learning experience. This van journey, though—it's kind of a smorgasbord of social experiences so far, innit? Between language students, hitchhikers, box contents that could be solved one day with a good PSU, and Tarnów on the horizon, it’s starting to feel like a choose-your-own-adventure book made real.      Exactly.

So do we go via the motorway or down the old road through the villages again? I think mummy got lost last time.      Oh don’t worry, I've got GPS this time. I downloaded the exact route and everything, so we shouldn’t be lost. But it might be good if you remind me if I seem to be driving the wrong way, okay?      Yeah, but only if I don’t get side tracked staring at funny cows or something. There was this time someone saw a unicorn at the side of the road when we came through, but I think it was just a frozen cow or something.      That’s the problem with GPS, you think you’re following it but you still need to pay attention. Fun fact—when I was a lad, I used to drive a route between Manchester and Preston every week for work. It used to take me forever to get it right, no laptops then, just a paper map.      I remember the Queen coming to visit our town once for a charity event. My mum would never let me miss it, even if I had homework. She says it impacts development if you miss a royal event once in a while.      Real important watching the Queen, yeah. Well, I got more homework than that – I had three exams last week, and none of them were on the British monarchy.      Aye, I remember doing exams. Mine were in the old Bolton library—this big dusty place with shelves knocking. Strict as anything. You had a time limit for each room. Now they’ve got all this technology and still can’t get it right.      Yeah, there was a train strike last week that messed up the entire schedule. I had to take the bus to work and ended up arriving three hours late. Not ideal when you’re trying to impress new clients.      That must’ve been worse than missing my Geography test. I ended up getting told off for it, but it was all because the school’s computer system crashed right when I was doing the exam—      Let me guess—logged you out?      How do you do that every time? Yeah, exactly.      I had a similar go at my old job—keyboard got swallowed by a cat one day.      Lucky it was just the keyboard, not the laptop. I once had a system at work that crashed during a call

Rather skip the newfit lot eh?      Aye, it's mad they think piling bits on a mobile app is the same as tidyin’. Not everyone wants their life in a categorised scroll!      That's the truth! I wouldn't know where to start wi een beginning if I tried. I’m still twitchy about touchin’ that thing – last time I tried cleanin’ up my inbox I ended up deletin’ me holiday pictures from 2008!      Nan, you can always just chase the cloud or something. You know, fetch the pixels back like magic!      Oh, don’t mock me lad. It’s a strange world you’ve all got us left in. But I’m here to help, mind, if it's mental sorts of issues you're talkin’ about now.      I appreciate it, Winnie. It’s not just tidying up at the moment, it’s been rough, you know? With the class pressures and everything. Sometimes I just feel like I’m juggling a hundred things and everything keeps dropping!      Aye, and grief of that, love. You’ve got a roof, you've got rhythm in your day, you’re okay. My Mate Laura used to say, “if you’re slap pariah, you’re not sommat of a disaster.”      She said that? That's classic. I miss her. She always used to tell me the funniest stories when I was down—about her uncle who wore a red trilby and claimed he was a goblin hunter in the hills of Kendal about forty winters ago.      Oh, she had a mind for tall tales. But they weren’t wasted words, you see. She used to say, “laughter’s the bin for the overfilled cup.” Got it out ofinnie tragedy, really.      Oh aye, she was a grand lass. Strong stuff for when the winds howl. As for you, Dottie, if it’s always too heavy, why not take it one day at a time?      I try, Winnie. I just get so caught up in everything I'm supposed to do or be.      Then go out and kick a football about with blokes on the park. Or forget you exist for an hour. Play a stupid game on the PS5 where you wrestle monkeys in belly of a flamingo farm—like that one!      Aye, that sounds the cure! The great big world's got room for all kindsa silliness, love.      It’s not used to hearing that from you before, Martin, but I’ll take it.

Right, lads, take a look at this beauty. I’ve been saving up for ages for this—finally got the new laptop with all the jazz.      Nice one, Anon. You done well with the specs. Look at that hinge! You wouldn’t know it was a real laptop, feels like a space helmet.      Yeah, it’s like they made a fan just to cool your brain while you’re using it.           Oh, sod off. You’re just jealous cause you're still running Windows 7 on a meat grinder from 2009.      What can I say? My job doesn’t pay for me to keep up with tech. I got students who could fix my laptop in their sleep. D’you know one of them kids turned my USB port upside down for about 20 minutes before I told him to stop? He thought he was doing some kind of “reboot spell.”      You paid him to shout at your hardware, didn’t you? I do that, get told I’m banned from the garden centre’s computers.           Tell me about it… I reckon the IT guy there thought I was some kind of tech cult leader trying to summon Windows back from the dead.      Let’s test it out—YouTube, mortal kombat, a load of stuff. See how it runs.      Oh, I’ll show you a real man's stress test—load up a retro game hotter than the summer sun. Or better still…      come on, let’s have about five browser tabs open, all of them the BBC, all watching different rugby matches. Let’s see if it becomes sentient.           Nah, I just want it for editing stuff. Got a gig coming up—podcast, audio editing, that sort of thing. Proper bloody stressful when the computer freezes halfway through you saying  "this chair is so comfortable..."  and then goes off to dreamland.      That’s the bane of all artworkers, isn’t it? You’re halfway through a sentence, and the laptop go  "I need to see if your audio clip is real first, thank you."       You’re blokes alright, what your lives are like. I just take care of plants. No dramas, no glitches— unless  I water them with my phone still on it. Then they overgrow and turn into green aliens.      Oh I like that— green aliens , nice one. You ever think about getting into YouTube, Louis? Just make a channel called  Plant Whisperer  or something.

Rather skip the new bar across the road. That’s where they get the people in, don’t they.      Yeah, I’m more of a bistro person anyway. It’s a little more... cosy.      Mm, well, the place was doing good on opening day. I mean, the owner was actually   seated   at the counter, not behind a table. A real touch.      They gave me a free latte, which is something. Usually you have to hit the third visit for that in Poland.      Right, but it’s mostly  promising . I mean, the décor, the chairs, even the playlist feels more...   me   than the standard Polish bistro vibe.      You're into the atmosphere and the   story  , aren't you? I was thinking the waitstaff looked like breakfast-shift students from the local university.      Well, I expect the service will improve, you know, once they get a rhythm. It’s still early days. I do like the way the owner speaks, though — I mean, with quite a bit of accent, but   clearly  , as if he was taught to speak English for work.      Maybe he’s from Bucharest or Sofia.      Could be. Though his hands move quite a lot when he gets excited. I think it’s Italian, at the end of the day. They all talk with their hands. But maybe not.      I do wonder what made them decide to open   here   in Tarnow. Not like it’s a tourist hotspot or anything.      I think they’re from   Lviv  , originally. There’s a whole new restaurant chain idea going that way. I mean, it’s a classic case of dreaming. My sister had that. She left construction and wanted to open a bakery. A dream? Yes. Realistic? Not any bloody bit.      I understand. I did a while back too, actually. Though I kept it short-term. I mean, I wasn't chasing anything serious like owning a restaurant. Just   existing   after a while became a dream itself.      But life doesn’t let you drift for long, does it? Eventually, you’re either pushing forward or lying in bed at 7 a.m. counting the ceiling tiles.      Yeah, I think those of us who had addiction, or just heavy stuff in life, learn over time to avoid the silence. You   need   the noise of something to hold on to.      That's one way of putting it. Another way is that you've learned to want meaning in the small things.

So did you get the tickets for the Dorset Steam Fair yet, Gran? I saw it’s on next weekend, and I thought we could all go together.      Oh, I’ve been meaning to sort that out! I rang the box office yesterday, but they were a bit booked up on the main days, but I did manage to get us on the Sunday. They said it’s a bit less busy then, so that’s probably best for your nan, isn’t it, Jean?      Yes, dear, the crowds on the Saturday would be too much for me. I saw on the website that they’ve improved the facilities for wheelchairs and people with mobility issues. There’s now a viewing platform by the main engine display.      That’s brilliant news, Nan. I didn’t know they’d made changes like that. It must make it a lot easier to enjoy. I was actually thinking earlier this week about how inaccessible some of these events are, especially for disabled people or the elderly. It’s a shame it took so long for places to catch up with the rest of society.      I agree with you, love. When I was young, places like that were just for the able-bodied—and it used to be a real struggle if you had kids who weren’t mobile, or if you had old parents. Things are definitely improving, though. Now don’t go making me feel old, Jean!      Oh, don’t you worry. I think it’s also nicer to not have to fight the crowds. I can admire the engines without getting jostled. So, have you still got that cat, Gran? The one that used to knock over your walking stick?      Oh, that old rogue—yes, he’s still around! Hasn’t knocked over anything in a while, thank goodness. I’ve bought him a ‘cat TV’ like yours, Julie. He watches birds on a screen now.      Oh my goodness, you haven’t! I’ve got one too, but the cat just ignores it. He’s more interested in the spiders in the corner of the room.      That sounds like my Jack. He’s a bit of a scatterbrain, poor thing. I think he was hit by a car once. But he’s a good mouser, so we put up with him knocking stuff over.      Well, I suppose all of this sounds quite domestic against the background of the steam fair—but it’s true that we talk about the ‘bigger picture’ far too much these days.

Rather do I go up in the living room to get me a cup of tea.      What dear I’ll get it for you.      No I’ll get it. I don’t wanna be stuck here the whole time being stared at.      Hasn’t been that long has it?      Since what?      A lot when you're ten and this is your grandma’s house.      Oh. Well you might not like the company when you're considerably older but.      Right, I think it's just because I like me tea when the fire’s on, warm house and like that.      The weather left’s a bit of a mess to be honest. Drove up this morning I think it turned round at least three times before breaking the M6.      I've been wanting to move for a while now. This house is getting a bit, you know, cramped. Especially with the publishing gigs I’ve had taking off over the last few years.      I never thought I’d hear the day you’d say moving sounds like a good idea. You used to love it here.      I still do but it's got a bit, I dunno, parochial. I’m trying to make connections with other writers and publishers who aren’t all from Kendal!      You could at least bring us with you! That way I wouldn’t have to go to the village with you each week to have a word with the vicar!      Can we watch something? Not school about movies or anything. Just like whatever’s on the telly.      There was a drama on last night that I meant to tell you about, dear. The one with the farmers and the big flood.      Aye, I remember that. Thought it was passable, though the actor who played the vicar was mad.      Vicars are always mad, nan.      They better be. Not many people would want to be stuck delivering sermons with tuppence for their troubles.      Right, you two stop it or I’ll turn the television off. It’s not polite to talk about clergy like that when the one from here’s in the next village.      I’d say those jokes are fair considering the amount of gossip I’ve heard about him from over half the congregation.      You know my philosophy on that. Always listen, but never believe it.      Right, right. Just make sure when we’re planning the moving, you remember there are people in this house who’ve lived here their entire lives.

Right, so today is rather exciting, isn't it? Both of you have birthdays today, even though they're technically a day apart—Easter is messing with the calendar! How do you feel about that?      Aw, I like sharing a birthday with my brother. We can get extra cake and all the Easter chocolate!      Yeah! Plus, I got to have Monet’s dad bring me some radishes from the garden this morning. They’re weird but cool. He said they’re good for your teeth.      Didn’t your dentist say the other week you need to floss more, Aaron?      Ugh, I know, I know. But they said My hearing is fine, at least. I got checked last week during the school health day. You get your ears pressed and you hear beeps and stuff. It was weird but not too bad.      I need to go for a hearing test too! My teacher’s been saying I don’t listen, even though I  do !      Oh, I know she says that, Erin, but maybe you are tired in the morning.      It’s not fair. I’ve got a friend named Anon. She says when her friend Ashaad was at the dentist they showed him a movie, and he got to eat a huge lollipop.      Ugh, that’s better than radishes.      There’s also this school trip in May to a castle near Cambridge. I heard it counts for history and geography. Some students had to do some maths to work out the distance and cost per person. Maybe your teachers are trying to make us do something fun without us even realising it.      I’m really bad at maths. I need you to explain it again, Mr. Grant does  not  make it easy.      I get confused between percentages and fractions. They just all blur into the same blurry mess.      I’ll write you a little note with some examples. Maybe we can go over it again after we’ve finished tidying the kitchen. It’s your day—you don’t have to clean, but you  have  to help.      Ugh, fine. But if you promise not to make me listen to another dentists’ story, I’ll be the best big brother in the world.      I can help too! I might even eat some of the radishes, maybe?      Is that a hidden ‘ask’ for more chocolate?      Nope! Radishes for me, and cake for everyone else.

So did I! The turkey was decent, I suppose, but everything else was just lukewarm. Honestly, I don’t know what’s wrong with that oven. I’ve asked for someone to look at it three times now.      Yeah, it's been like that since I moved in. My friend Natalie, the one who used to rent the flat before me, had all sorts of issues too—microwave wouldn’t work properly, the taps all squeaked. Oh, and she had some sort of rodent problem at one point.      Ugh, I remember her telling me about that. She even left a note on the door once—well, I only found out about it after she’d gone. It said something like, “If I find one more squirrel, I swear I’m moving out and setting fire to every single patch of grass within a ten-mile radius.”      That sounds like Natalie. She’s got a bit of a dramatic streak, you know. Anyway, I’m ordering a new stove tomorrow. This one is clearly on its last legs.      I hope it doesn’t take two weeks like the last time. Did you know the kitchen felt like it had its own ecosystem for the first two days it was being fixed? The guy left a power drill in the sink, and I found it three days later covered in mold.      Honestly, I considered putting up a ‘fix it or flog it’ sign in the hallway at one point. But I don’t know—something about just leaving it alone and pretending it’s charming has kept me here. I mean, it’s not bad otherwise.      Not bad about the house or your sense of humor? Because talking about mice and mold is most definitely a charming trait.      Okay, fair. But listen, while we’re on the subject of things falling apart—your guest bedroom light needs rewiring. The bulb flickered so hard the other night, I thought it was reacting to someone being too loud in the room.      Oh yeah, I nearly mentioned it. Do you think I can get one of the same? I almost bought a replacement once, but I had no idea what the number was or go back to get it unless I wanted to look like a confused shop assistant.      Honestly, go with a smart bulb. You can just say, “Alexa, I am 30% more in control of my home environment than I was yesterday.”

Rather skip the new bar in town, isn't it? I think they've just changed it into some kind of art café.      Yes, I heard it's attached to one of those cycle shops now. Not quite sure what the plans are—some fancy exhibition space in a barn. Got eeny weeny grant from the town council for 'rebranding'.      Aye, I read about it in the local paper. Old barn converted, you know. It's interesting 'cause it wasn't nothing to begin with and now it's a proper cultural hub. Tore me heart out to see it changed, mind—those old stone walls were the real thing. Still, I suppose it beats what it was before—a derelict car garage.      I know what you mean, Frank. I remember when the town centre was alive with proper shops, and now it's all second-hand and gone up in rents. They tried to 'revive' it, but it's like reviving a ghost—it's still got holes in the walls and nothing holding it up.      Oh, but I think there's quite a plan to bring back the old facade on High Street. One of the shops had a proper Victorian rhythm in it.      Mate, I often say I'd still take that slap-up cycle ride I had when I was a kid to wander them lanes at will. No traffic, just you and your bike, and the old man chuckling in the back seat.      That's oddly romantic. You ever think about doing that now with a quad-bike and hillside cafe stops?      Not nearly about to climb them hills again.      Oh, but let’s not be too gloomy. The last planning meeting I noticed was about solar panels up on the school. Passed, I think. Maybe it’ll put us in the future after all.      It's something, yes.      Speaking of passing things, I just read about a clever way to get into a theatre when it's 'sold out'. They told me someone asked if the play was any good and, after a nice tiff with the box office woman, was given a spare ticket from the stage door.      That’s cheek, I like it. That bloke could’ve been your patient, George. I remember you used to sail on conference trips, after all.      Oh aye, we did. Know where I once had a lecture at sea?

So do you think an online version of our case study resource would have the legs to stand on?      I think it could, especially with the schools and universities looking for more accessible teaching tools these days. But how would we differentiate it from the standard LMS stuff they’re already using?      Good point. We need to make it interactive—maybe include role-play scenarios? You know, like real-life examples students can navigate as if they’re part of a communication breakdown in a school or something. We can use the moving image case studies you've been working on.      Yes, that could make it more engaging. I've got the video content on resolution of conflict in classrooms that Myra shared from Manchester Uni—a few solid case studies on specific strategies teachers used to rebuild relationships after a major issue occurred. I think it could be adapted.      Exactly. And if we can tie it into social skills development for education professionals—like emotional intelligence, cultural competence, and communication, we might hit a niche area that the bigger ones aren't covering.      That sounds like a good idea. I could also tag a few teacher friends and ask if they’d contribute as co-case analysts or peer reviewers. You know, give it a bit more credibility.      I’m down with that. And while we’re building the platform, maybe we include a social aspect—like a forum where teachers can share their own experiences. It’s all about community.      And not everyone has a big professional network like we do. Some teachers are very isolated—especially in rural areas.      Absolutely. So, how would we structure the membership model? Subscription-based? Or offer the basics for free and upsell premium case studies or analysis tools?      I’m leaning toward a tiered system—free with limited access for basic content, and paid for full access and exclusive case-study groups. Maybe a student version too?      That way you can build a strong user base while still making a profit. And as we get more content, the network effect starts to happen—you know, more users, more contributions, more credibility, more users.      Exactly. And we need to figure out our branding angle. Maybe something like "EduShift" or "MindShiftED" to suggest transformation in education.      “MindShiftED” sounds good—smart, modern, and hints at personal and intellectual development. But we need a solid elevator pitch for this thing.

Rather skip the queue and just go through the side doors, do you?      We’d be taking the mickey out of ourselves, more than I think.      It is a bit funny, isn’t it? We’ve both picked our own careers, and we’re now lecturers at different uni’s.      True. Almost as if we were a bit ambitious, but not entirely serious about it.      I watched a clip of someone trying to do the wine sommelier version of the sea when we were kids. You know the one, where they walk around with their arms out like a seagull?      Oh yes, you mean seas captain Marco?      Yes! I think I still have the photo, he was quite the character.      You’ve got to admit, when you’re a kid and you’re playing with a sea in your back garden, you think it's quite something, don’t you?      I still like to go for walks by the sea, though. There's something about the smell, the way the wind flicks the leaves, it just puts everything in perspective.      Be careful what you say. You might find yourself talking to the sea, and then it really  does  feel like a sommelier.      If the sea could talk, I’d ask it what its opinion was on wine. That’d be quite something.      I can definitely picture it opening a crate of Chablis and commanding the bottle to be poured like a glass of sea water.      I think I might have mentioned the sea the other day in my lecture. To be fair, not about wine, but more about the environment and how unspoilt bits still do exist, like that little cove by that lighthouse.      The one where it used to surf on wooden decks and there were no regulations about restricting your performance based on tides or suchlike.      Except we were always told not to go near the lighthouse path because of the rocks.      But we did it anyway, didn’t we? Always chasing after something or other.      I suppose it’s part of being young, isn’t it? You think all of the sea is yours to explore and to bend to your will.      And then as adults, we find we can only get over half of the rocks and struggle to carry both a homemade cup of tea and a sense of adventure at the same time.      I did try to teach a class on adventure and the sea last week, but I think half of them fell asleep by the time I got to the part about the lighthouse.

So do you lot reckon it's still in to wear wide-legged trousers or have we officially flipped back to skinny? Like, I saw this look in York last week and I was like, sure, but then I saw it in Leeds and thought, “Blimey, that's a lot of denim.”      Honestly, I think it depends on the   fabric  . Like, if it's a tailored wide leg, it still works—classy and comfortable. But if you're rocking flowy, dump-truck legs and you're not doing the "fashion chase," it can look a bit… makeshift.      I mean, I wear wide legs at the school supply store, but when I’m dressing up, I definitely go back to skinnies. It’s just more practical to move between classrooms, don’t you think?      Haha, fair enough. But you’re not breakfast, brunch, then late-night gym class like I am in Donny. I need moves, not hides.      Also, the way you style it matters—voluminous tops, cropped jackets, or a good crop sweater can make or break a wide-leg look. I think the  vibe  is in, not just the cut. Like, when it gives “millennial Pinterest – but with a budget.”      Okay, but what are the shoes doing? It’s not just what you wear, it’s how you wear it! I swear, those chunky white boots with full-on dressy dresses are blowing my head off. Like, is it a Mary Jane? Is it a sneaker? What  is it ?      That’s the new norm, I reckon. Mid-street, mid-pretty. People want to look put-together without being fussy. Like, that new trend where you layer a   latex skirt   over leggings. My sister tried that and I was like, “Is that comfort or confidence?”      Oh, I saw that too! Was it confusing or just misunderstood?      I think it's  intentionally  chaotic. Like Gen Z fashion—“I don't care if it clashes, it makes  me  happy.” I had a kid in the class the other day wearing a Harvard jacket over a football top and denim shorts. I was like, “Alright mate, individuality with a capital  I .”      So are we planning to go to that vintage shop in London next week? I need to grab a couple of pieces to channel the  wide-leg meets streetwear  aesthetic.      S’all go if I can get a day off. My boss is a nightmare, but I’ll figure it out.

Mummy, I've got this photography project at college now. We have to take photos of real life—like, everyday stuff, not just landscapes or anything.      Oh, that's lovely, hun. What kind of stuff have you been taking photos of?      I did this one of the ice cream van outside the park where we used to go as kids. The man behind the wheel had these muddy wellies and this big, funny squint. I thought it would be like something out of a book.      Oh, I remember that van. It used to play this jangly tune—what was it, “A-Tisket, A-Tasket”? My gran still hums it sometimes.      Probably, yeah. I showed the photo to Dad and he said it looked like a scene from one of his uni lectures—something about "ordinary details in everyday life."      Oh, he’s using his postgraduate knowledge on you now, is he?      It’s not bad, really, but I don’t think he takes photos of people with wellies as much as he used to.      Probably not. I remember photographing you when you got your first bike—he wouldn’t let me take a photo with you on it for  months  because he said you looked like you were going to fall over.      I might have, huh.      But you didn’t. You just kept smiling like you were doing a pose for a magazine!      Hey, I was  eight . I had ballet and drama and all kinds of posing down.      Oh, you had it all sorted. I used to say you were going to grow up and be the next big photographer or a Hollywood star. My sister still thinks you look like someone from her telly.      Probably a Strictly contestant. I think I look a bit like that dancer from when I was little who did the Argentine tango.      Yes, that’s right. She had those long legs and the dramatic eyelashes.      Anyway, the point is, I’m really enjoying this photography thing. It makes me feel like I’m capturing something real, you know?      Oh, I can see that. You’ve always been observant. You remember when you were six and you made that whole scrapbook of things from the farm—like the cow over the gate, the tractor with the missing window? You called it  "The Quiet Life of Animals."       Yeah, I did! Missus Sandwell in the shop still keeps a copy.

Rather annoying this, putting in an application form for what, do we need one for the bloody cockerel?      Yes, poor thing got loose last week, chased half the village! You need a licence now to keep livestock, even a chicken!      A cockerel is a  rooster , not a bloody   livestock  ! Proper government waste, I reckon. A lot of money would be better spent on social care than registering a bird.      Well, to be fair, if he’s outside when he shouldn’t be, you’re technically breaching noise bylaws! Not to mention the kids who live next door, still wet behind the ears like that—      The kids left their windows open last night, the wind came in, smashed the pipe and I had a flooded bathroom! Blimey, I’ve never known!      Was this while you were sleeping?      No, I didn’t sleep at all. Sorted the water, sorted the mess, and by the time it was done—my back gone out again! I can barely get out of a chair without popping a pain tablet.      Sounds like you've got quite a task on your hands. How’s the 3D printer coming along, by the way?      Doesn’t work! Had to be sent back for a third time already! When I get the hang of it, I wanted to print one of those little robotic birds to keep an eye on the nest by the patio—      Oh, I saw it through the window the other day, those little birds in the Apple tree. One of them fell out, such a thing, we had to put it back in.      Not you! I didn’t want a  nesting project  on my hands! Just needed something quiet that didn’t make too much mess.      You could always take the whole lot down and pop it in a little box or something? Not sure how you’d feel about being the caretaker of baby birds, though.      I’ve got no problem looking after a couple of cockerels and the odd baby bird go so far as to raise a generation of  kids  at the same time!      That’s a fair point—and I’ve had some of them myself at the childminder days. Oh gosh, some of those parents, never had a clue. I’ve had kids coming in with overcooked emotions, food allergies, and half the time the problem wasn’t the child at all.

Rather than going up there and trailing through the cold and grumbling about the mountains, it would be so much better if she came here with us. Brighton has more than enough going on, and we’d have a proper flat with sun and proper washing-up facilities and not those tiny little apartments like the one I stayed in during the war holidays, where we had one tap and   no heating!        I agree. A lot. I just worry that this is a bit much for her, what with all the upheaval. She’s been in Switzerland for twelve years now, teaching, settling in… You don’t want her to feel like she’s  being dragged back.       That’s where you’re wrong, Myra. She wrote me last week and said she’s  worn out.  She says she misses her brother, and I think—well, I know you feel it too—that she’s better off here, near her family.      I suppose she’s not the only one getting worn out, is she? I mean, I know why you suggested it, after Mum went into the care home and we both agreed—what I mean is, well, as much as she loved the idea, it still took a toll on her. Doesn’t have to be that way again.      No, no. I wouldn’t dream of subjecting her to something like that. We don’t have to go through the  whole  family trauma routine. We could make it happen gently. A trial visit, maybe for a month. That way she can see how it is here, meet some friends, get used to the idea of starting again.      I like that. A trial visit. I mean, I know she’s used to the English weather, but Switzerland—well, it’s different. The pace is slower, you barely need to walk anywhere. Brighton’s got that electric buzz, even for someone who left when they were young.      Precisely. I remember when she was little—oh, I tried to take her to the pier when she was seven and she  ran off  to a hot dog stall with a ten-pound note and tried to haggle the man over condiments. Came back with this enormous dog and the sun burning away goopy sweat on her neck, and absolutely  beaming.       That’s true. She always had a spark—unlike the rest of us, who were content to sit and read on the beach.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh?      Which part? The referendum, or the fact that we still好像 don’t have a clue what to do about it?      Both probably. Though I think we’ll survive the chaos. By the way, did you hear I’ve got a job interview at the uni in Stirling next week?      Oh yes! That’s fantastic. A lecturer post? That must have felt like a relief after your last few applications.      Well, nothing was coming quickly and I was starting to get worried. But then came the offer. It’s a short contract, only a term, but at least it’s something worthwhile. It’s about doing what you love, isn’t it?      Ten out of ten sentiment for you, mate. Always thought you’d be the type for teaching at uni level. My old colleague from back when I was at Brighton Grammar said they’d still be offering tutors if they saw the quality of your last paper.      Yeah? That’s actually what I was thinking of sharing with you, maybe tonight?      I’m listening.      I’ve started something with my daughter—she’s watching a bit of documentary stuff on YouTube. About Scottish history. Pretty basic stuff, but she’s devouring it, and I thought, why not help her out a little? So I started talking about the Empire and the Union and everything in between. It’s kind of like someone said, "Here’s the system: read it, react to it, and preferably understand what you react to."      Sounds like you’re bringing up a  very  well-read child. I about blocked the internet after she asked what “industrial relations” meant on an old document.      Oh that was you! I remember it. You said it was like the 17th century version of arguing about office politics.      Classic me. You know, I was thinking the other day, I wonder if you’ll be passing on your passion for history into her.      I hope so. She’s a little bit of a question bomb, but she’s got a good head on her.      Yeah, go her. I remember your partner telling me once about how she comes out with line after line of that “everything’s unfair” bloke on her YouTube list.      Yeah, she’s been obsessed with one video of John Stuart Mill arguing about freedom of speech. She’s trying to say that “the government should let everyone be them” like that.

Right, I just unearthed the Mousetrap board game from the back of the bookcase. The box is all dusty and it looks like it hasn’t been opened since the 1970s!      Haha, I bet there’s a dead mouse in it by now. Has anyone ever won this thing properly?      Honestly, I’ve only ever known a few people to actually play this properly. Most of the time, it ends with someone falling over, pulling someone else over and then blaming the board.      I remember bringing this over to my cousin’s house in America once. They were stunned. All the rules, all the characters. It was like a Mycroft Holmes fan club in that room!      I didn’t know you'd worked in the US, Nick. Did you?      Mm, back when I was younger. I was posted in Washington DC for a couple of years, thanks to the civil service being, well, civil. Kept the papers over, built a couple of relationships and came back a wiser man. Though the American way of life did make one thing abundantly clear.      What’s that, sir?      You really don’t want your kids growing up thinking pizza is a way of life. I mean, the portions were enormous.      You know what struck me about American kids? When we went out for food someone always asked for a fizzy drink. And not a 'fizzy drink'—it was always specifically Coca-Cola. It was like some strange loyalty oath.      Oh, come on, I mean I’m British and I still prefer Coke over Fanta or whatever. There’s a reason it’s the drink of champions.      You sound like my cousin. My god, that lot took it very seriously.      I have to say, it was a bit alien to me. At home, we just drank tea or lemonade. Not fizzy stuff. I remember being sent out for dinner by the lunches of a couple of English friends in Texas, and their children were sipping Diet Pepsi around the dinner table!      That sounds horrifyingly American.      You’re just in denial because that’s what you were doing when you were 14 and pretending you were at a grown-up dinner to impress someone.      I don’t like fizzy stuff much. I like chips and stuff, but when I was at catering college I once made mac ‘n’ cheese for a theme night. My teacher said I should put ketchup in it because ‘that’s how the Americans do it’.

Right, I’m just in the living room sorting through post. Have you had a good day?      Exhausting. I was at the school doing an interview for the new faculty representative position. I’ve just come from a departmental meeting that was  literally  about folder colour-coding. I think it’s a coping mechanism to avoid the real issues.      Sounds familiar. I had to remind one of the interviewees that this is a post to engage with staff welfare—not rearrange the water cooler.      Exactly. I’m not sure if I’m annoyed I missed the job, or just sad that the world is this absurd most of the time.      Maybe both. I just happened to volunteer a bit in advance and the Head of Department looked grateful that someone didn’t ask for a laptop budget.      Ah, classic subtle sexism—personally I think they’d have given it to a man as long as he didn’t mention  emotional  stuff in the interview.      You got that from the one who said they’d “revisit curriculum alignment”? Please,  revisit  is a new word for “don’t touch it at all.”      God, I just wanted to ask someone at the meeting, “Are you trying to solve a problem, or just fill a room with fluff?”      Hey, look at it this way—now you can fully commit to being about folder colour-coding. You could be the Renaissance woman of green folders.      That’s it—I’m starting a union for it. Green Folders United. We’ll go international.      I will attend your first rally with pride. Just don’t let them assume you’re bringing the tea again.      My one reward from such absurdity. You can call me Monica Wooden Tea Tray.      Perfection. We’ll go down in history together—albeit in very poorly coded departments.      If I survive this academic hellscape, I might just name my memoir after that green folder committee meeting.       In Defence of Indexing .      That’s it. I can die happy now.      Then I’ll be your junior co-author:  Academic Life—Objectively Absurd .      Signed and podcast-ready, darling. Let’s get our CVs out. We could be the next big thing.      As long as I can cite your folder colour-assessment on the back cover.

So did you go through all the boxes last night?      Yeah, most of them... got to the shower gel and mugs before I collapsed on the bed. My brother’s gotta be kidding me with all that stuff. If you can teach me how to do the language thing that you do with the boxset bloopers, your foreign phrase folder—I could have died laughing at “Min kaffe, ta!”      You’re welcome to it. Right, lads, I’ve been doin’ a bit of research on accents today, ‘cos I had this bloke from Scotland in the studio today, and I swear he said “mooth” instead of “mouth” and I couldn’t figure out why—thought he’d had a stroke for a sec!      Haha, that’s   loch   for you—rolling “l”s and soft “th”s. Some of their vowel sounds are so different. It was the same when I taught in Manchester. Leeds lads and Londoners called the same fruit ten different names.      Honestly, I grew up in Cyprus for a few years, and when I came back and tried to speak English again, I had   zero   clue how to sound like a normal Londoner for weeks. It was like I lost the language for a bit—my accent was halfway between Middlesbrough breakfast and a Greek taverna!      Bro, that sounds mental. I mean, we’re all from Bedfordshire and Luton, so we all sound like Waterstones rejects, if I’m honest. But I’ve always wondered if we all said “guitar” like the real purists do. Try saying “  gw  uitar” without it coming out like “goo-jar.”      I can say it properly if I’m buying gear online and trying to impress someone with my tech-savvy. But in real life, I say “guitar” like I just got full in my boots. “I got me a new   gwy-tar  —look at the pickups!” It's like I'm being paid in premium.      Haha, I did an article about accent variation in verbal feedback from English learners. Turns out, most students pick up sarcasm fails if their teachers are too RP or too Scouse. No one can trust the tone.      Speaking of accents, passed my mate yesterday at the cycle path by the Asda. He was all “I’ve been training for MMA, waiting to fight a   mole  ,” and I’m like, “Dude, it’s not a mole it’s a   Muay Thai   class, you prat!”      Man, I tried Muay Thai once on a dare from my cousin. First round I got countered into a headlock and nearly had my arm torn from its socket—and I thought your accent was dodgy at the time!      Yeah, I think those kinds of environments are where regional differences get more… explosive. I mean, I’ve been working at the language school since lockup, so I hear everything from “ I was in the   outhouse   last night ” to “ I saw a   chappy   at the chippy last week .”

So do you ever think about getting a car? Your commute is like forty-five minutes each way.      I know, it’s brutal. But I can’t see the point in spending a fortune on a car when the train only costs ten quid a day.      I mean if you  shared  the cost with someone who lives further out, it could actually save you a bit. A lot of people do that in this area.      Maybe, but you’d have to find someone you trust. You don’t wanna rely on someone who forgets you on a Tuesday.      Haha, fair point. I had a friend who left in the middle of a journey because she forgot her metrocard left at home. Ten minutes down the road I had to turn around and pick her up.      That’s a nightmare. I guess when I was younger, I hated driving. My dad tried to teach me and I failed five times!      Oh my god, why?      Nerves, mostly. I’d freeze at the roundabouts and struggle with the gears. I didn’t even know what colour the traffic light was pointing to.      That’s funny. I remember my first lesson: I mistook the handbrake for the accelerator. The instructor looked like she was about to cry.      Oh man, at least you didn’t cause an accident.      Just a stressed instructor and a lot of muttered words. Anyway—what about the environmental cost of cars? I feel bad driving even when I need to.      I get that. I hear all these stories from work about office colleagues who drive and just  complain  the whole time about traffic. I’d rather handle the train any day.      True. Plus, parking in cities is such a hassle. I had this one job where you’d have to walk twenty minutes to find a spot. Not worth it.      Yeah. Though being able to listen to a podcast on the way and not having to do anything? Bliss.      Then again, if you owned a car, you could do the same thing from your own house to work. Still, I think it’s all about what you’re used to.      Exactly. So are you planning to save up for a nicer one after next year?      Maybe. I want to see if I can upgrade from the dreadful green hatchback I’m currently driving. It’s like a collision waiting to happen.

Right Aaron, the bins need goin’ out tomorrow, do you thinks you can get ‘em done first thing? I’ve got a train to catch at eight and I don’t want the council givin’ me a right bollocking again. Blue’s for glass and tins, green’s for recykle, red’s for the rest. You remember that one, love?      That’s the same as thirty years ago, Alice. Aye, and I’ll have you know, I once turned up with a Christmas pudding and that went in the recycle bin, didn’t it? Took me hours to find it again.      And then you tried to hide it in the back of the larder and then blamed the cat.      Well, it was  hiding  from us somethin’, that’s for sure!      You should’ve been a magician, Wilf.      And you a card sharp, Darcy.      So, Alice, have you worked out that tea towel situation yet? I saw those red ones you brought home about five years ago. Still not used.      Ron put them out yesterday. Said they were ‘a bit worn out’ but I reckon that’s just a ‘cos they look like he did in his Geography A-level. Not many people can work out how many faggots you need to feed the dinner lady in govt exams.      I think that’s history, not food math.      Pass me a faggot then, I’ll show you how it’s done.      You don’t need to feed the dinner lady, Darcy, we’ve moved on!      Speaking of food, Nana, do you still keep the jar of jam under the sink that no one uses?      That’s my special jar. ‘Reserve Stock’ we call it. Only comes out for emergencies or when Alice renders tea out.      And don’t you start, Darcy. The emergency jar’s stayed put this month.

Rather skip to the part when they actually shackled him in that Arabian port.      Oh yes, and rather well she shot the boat!      Erm, where are we?      Yes, the boat...      Erm, in '81 I went out to Jeddah to teach at a big British school.      A British school in Jeddah?      No, but they were terribly British there, it was a private school anyway, full of expats.      Were you living with the other British teachers?      No, we had separate houses, but we were in like a compound.      So it was quite a fortified place?      D'you know, I think it turned out to be an excellent preparation for the Catskills.      The Catskills?      Oh, no, sorry, not the Catskills, the...      The Arabian Nights?      Yeah, maybe.      I mean if you were teaching in Saudi Arabia, weren't you on non-met?      Yes.      So no beer at the bar?      No, because they don't really sell alcohol there unless you've got a very strong foreigner’s license.      Erm, and did you?      Well, I had my own.      Oh.      I had a secret gin and it poured forth at regular intervals.      Not in public obviously.      No, it wasn't, but mind you they didn't exactly prohibit anything.      I mean it is a Muslim country but to some extent, they realized they needed to liberalize.      A bit.      And was that all during the very intense Islamic revolution stuff or was it sort of after the 70s?      No, the '70s were over by the time I got there in '81, after the oil boom.      So that really meant that life was more or less.      Yeah, the oil boom had genuinely.      Changed what your actual social world could be like.      Yeah, we had amazing hours off, never had to worry about work.      Sounds very idyllic, until the boat incident. What happened there exactly?      Well, I had a friend, an Australian who was trying to sail from Cyprus to Jeddah, and I got involved in some sort of.      Sailing...      Boat trip...      We ended up in the middle of the Red Sea, our boat had malfunctioned, and somehow, the authorities in Saudi Arabia caught hold of us.      They arrested you for taking the boat without a permit or something?      Something like that. Erm, and the most bizarre part was, the other one was particularly terrified of me.      Of you?      Because I had a dental magazine in my...      A dental magazine?      From the States, about some orthodontist who showed people the different ways of using caps and things.

Right, thanks a million for helping us out with the grills. I know it's such a busy time with the weekend and everything, but it really saved us. I can't thank you enough.      Not a problem at all, love—grills are like the biggest night in-house, aside from holidays, I reckon. It was my pleasure.      Yeah, I mean obviously Aiden wasn’t keen on doing too much, to be fair. I remember when I was his age, work experience felt like a rite of passage.      I’d be lying if I said I wasn’t a bit surprised when he told about his new boyfriend. Just the other week, talking to my cousin Jane, and she said what with this generation, it’s easier to get a girl pregnant than unplug a plug socket. My, they move fast.      I know. But once I met the lad, I think it was probably the right path. He’s far more grounded than Aiden. Plus, he’s into sport— go figures he gets that life from somewhere.      I just started refereeing, by the way— box team in the high school. It’s actually really nice. I get mats to jump and tackle roles in, and hours of pretending I’m not as clumsy as I look.

So do you ever find it funny how people request things in such strange ways? Like today, someone came up to me and said, “Erm, do you by any chance take an interest in language?” I was like, “Well, I’m the one collecting data on it, so yeah, I do!”      I don’t think they actually realized who they were talking to! Though honestly, I’ve been in meetings too where people test the water like that to avoid being confrontational. It’s interesting, actually. We use so many polite buffers and qualifiers just to ask simple things.      Yeah, I guess it does depend on the context. Like at the press, people tend to get straight to the point, but around here, especially in the academic or creative departments, there’s a lot more subtlety and politeness.      Exactly! I was at a café this morning and a guy asked me if I mind him asking for a recommendation in a tone that was almost apologetic. I mean, it’s a recommendation, not a secret bomb location! Sometimes I feel like people feel guilty for existing in other people’s space.      It is what it is. But let me tell you, when I’m at work and I’m managing digital campaigns, no one wants to hear about your day. I ask people, “Can I confirm the schedule is still tight?” It’s not “Do you have a second to talk about the schedule?” It’s just… concise.      But also, maybe people read too much into it. I had a client email me recently saying, “I hope you don’t mind me replying so quickly but your colleague’s feedback is most welcome and I shall take it under advisement.” I had to read it three times to understand it was thanks and not criticism.      That’s classic formal English for “Thanks, I’ll read that and do something with it.” Though I suppose it depends on the relationship too. You can be a lot more direct with people you know well, but in professional settings, people stick to scripts.      Also, regional differences probably play a role. I’ve noticed people in the North tend to be far more direct, where around here it’s a bit more diplomatic. I remember being on a call with partners from Manchester, and one of them just said, “Y’know what? That idea blokes on.”
