I suppose. I still go out of my way to avoid getting their food, though. Genuinely off-putting that it's always in your face during games now. Pass the remote—let me have a look at the highlights and see if they’ve dyed their hair McDonald’s yellow as well.

You’d think the government would’ve worked out by now that people like me exist. Someone who’s unemployed and never got the hang of work. You’d think they’d make it a bit simpler to claim benefits, but no—every £2 I spend on the George Foreman is tracked like I’m gonna buy a yachting holidays out of it.      Yeah, it all feels completely nonsensical. A lot of people would love that kind of social security. You’d think they’d be pulling you to do something with it, like take a course or chase a job or something. But not you... like, I’ve even seen people doing dead-end jobs with no future, and still, people on JSA get the lectures like we’re living high on the hog’s back.      You're telling me. Last week, I turned up at the jobcentre for my claim and this twerp behind the desk practically sneered at me. "You haven’t updated your CV, have you?" he says, like ordering puffin eggs from a supermarket. I said, “Yeah, I do, you know, every day. My CV impacts me shortlisted land a job to update it again.” Hilarious.      I tried to get a little laugh out of it, too – but it's exhausting. I mean, I know you don’t like to talk about it, but have you considered taking something online? If nothing else, just to make your CV look better? Like, someone at the jobcentre might take you a bit more seriously if you’ve done a course on email writing or something?      I did once—something called  “Digital Workforce Skills for Beginners” . I lasted two weeks before I bailed. Learning to take “cringe document format” into “gradually less cringe document format” didn’t sound worth £10 to do. But they said I needed to show “engagement,” so I signed up. Then I bailed.      Fair enough. I mean, I understand. I could see the appeal of that kind of course being academically-traumatic. But, I mean, what are the options? Since you’re stuck in Kent, you’re not exactly surrounded by the metaverse gig economy. Unless you want to be a tour guide for Kent ramblers or something?      I tried doing eBay last week, what can I say. I ordered something from China and it looked like a Greek tragedy had taken place in the delivery box.

Rather skip the new drive-through café near the station, have you noticed the queue for it yet?      Never mind queueing, I’d rather wait! I saw someone nearly hit a lamppost trying to reverse out of there the other day—  Lorry   in a carpark is one thing, but  not  a lorry!   Vauxhall Astra   nearly finished it.      Ay, that’s just plain daft. If I was going to drive like that, I’d give it up before I hit the motorway, don’t you think? I saw the crash near Peterborough last week—plane crash, they said it was, only it turned out to be a MyBallonInMyFaceTV kite! Ten minutes I had watching the fire engines turn up, and I’m thinking the poor man had an almighty shock.      Well, if I ever see a kite flying into a chimney at my age, I’ll call the felling-in-the-bath alarm!      My Bob—my late husband—he used to have that sort of luck. Left to go to the shops for something simple as bread and milk and come back with a trotter in a Tupperware. Not much for organisation, but at least he brought something home!      Ah, trotters are nice when done right! You know what I blame for everything? That warts and all business. someone said to me last week, “You know, a lot of people get rid of them with lasers now,” and I thought,   Me? Lasering my warts? No, I’ve got enough problems in about five square inches of skin as it is!        I had one removed last month. The nurse was like, “This is it!” and I thought to myself, “You’re cutting the whole of my hand out here!”      You both know my sister had a spinal operation and came out waiting for a spoon? Not to feed her, but to stir her tea! Of course, she wasn't allowed to do anything with it!      That’s a nice idea. I told my doctor I go out walking on the lake if it's not raining or snowing—still got my specs on, mind. He said, “You should be proud your legs still work!” I said, “Well, doctor, if one of them goes down, I’ll just push myself along with the other one like a shopping trolley!”      You lot should be at the Channel Five quizzes, you’re both brilliant at it.

Okay, I just wanted to say, our English teacher is going mental today. Did she ask  everyone  to read out our essays? Like, is she trying to make us all die or something?      Haha, yeah, I know. I was half-asleep when it was my turn and I read my  entire  essay on 'The Great Gatsby' in like… two minutes. I probably sound like a robot or a raccoon.      You sound like a raccoon? Please. You sound like you’re reciting the alphabet when your dog just knocked your maths homework into the toilet.      Haha, okay, but honestly, I can't stand that new trainee teacher, Ms. Price. She just left after one lesson and said, "Oh, you're all so creative and I think I'll just go spend an hour in the staff room drawing faces on breakfast cereal boxes."      Ugh, no! That was  Ms. Price ? I didn’t even see her go! I thought she just sat in the corner and whispered poetry into a bookshelf or something. She looked like she was about to faint from the weight of the spelling test.      I reckon she tried to take a shortcut from the staff room to the classroom but got lost in the art corridor and ended up in the gym instead. You know what the gym looks like? Just a whole bunch of tape on the wall and a mexican standoff with the PE teacher.      Let me not even talk about the gym. I had a lesson with Mr. Hardy this week and he couldn’t even be bothered to set up the dumbbells. He just said, "Here, try lifting a chair!" I mean, come  on . It was like a mission impossible workout.      At least you have PE. I had double science. My group  still  can’t agree on what generates electricity. One person said squirrels, another said it was a magical toaster, and the last one tried to argue it was mad scientists in a fridge.      That’s nothing! Our art teacher recently told a new student that "impressionism is when you drop paint on a canvas and then pretend like you meant it." Then go and give it an A if you like wavy lines.      Oh no, I need to go to secondary school forever if the art teacher is going to be that cool. I’ve been obsessed with drawing on my iPad for weeks, though.

Right, so the question is—what do you think about nuns?      Like... real nuns, or from  The Matrix ? I mean, I've seen nuns in movies, but I don't really know what they do outside of that.      Well, real nuns—they used to be very strict. I remember when I was your age, going into a convent with my Sunday school class and being told off for coughing in a chapel. It was very intense.      That sounds like the nuns from  Sister Act .      Mama!  Sister Act  is when the nun sings hippo?      No, sweetie, it's not a hippo. It’s "Open Your Heart," and it's very sad. A nun singing about loving an angel, not a hippo!      I've never met a real nun in real life. I know some of my friends talked about their grandmothers being in the church choir, or that kind of thing, but not full-on nuns. Do they still exist?      Oh yes, they do. Some people go on retreats or spend time in religious orders, but they’re not as common as they used to be. I think a lot of people don’t really see the point of it in the modern world.      Well, what about religion in general? I mean, someone at school said their aunt joined something called Scientology. Is that like a cult or a proper religion?      I think the word ‘cult’ is a bit rude, but there’s definitely a line between religions and groups that use manipulation or charge a lot of money. Scientology is… a complicated one. It started as part of science fiction, and it evolved into something else.      So it’s kind of fake?      Not fake, necessarily. It just isn’t widely accepted. People believe what they want to believe. Some religions stick to ancient texts, and others create their own systems. What matters is what gives a person peace of mind.      Do nuns believe in Santa Claus like we do?      Santa Claus is more of a… festive tradition, love. Nuns, like most Christians, believe in God, Jesus, and what your teacher talked about in RE class—like the 10 Commandments and all that.      True, but isn’t religion kind of overrated? Like, if aliens landed and destroyed everything, I wonder what religions they’d have. Probably not about nuns and Christmas trees.      Maybe they’d have religions about technology or flying saucers, you never know.

So did you watch The History of England on iPlayer yet? I’m trying to get into that show. It’s got a bit of Old English in it, and I find it funny how they overemphasise it in some bits.      Yeah, I did! It was alright. I think the presenter liked pretending to be a medieval professor. But he did actually know what he was talking about. I found the part about how the old English measurement system confused everyone absolutely hilarious. Imagine trying to build a road with just inches and leagues!      Honestly, the worst bit was when they tried to explain it with modern-day equivalents and still got it wrong. I mean, how do you convertitunes [corrects] tons to metric without a calculator? I’m not sure I want to live in their Domesday Book anymore.      It is a mess, and you’re not wrong. Maybe that’s why I switched to watching a doc on aging and ageism last night. There was this part where they interviewed a doctor who worked in a hospital and said that patients over 65 get sent home quicker than they really should. It puts your head in a twist, y’know?      That does sound awful. I remember when my nan needed help, and the doctors were just like, “She’s old, just give her painkillers and send her home.” It’s like they don’t even consider the best treatment anymore—they just treat the age.      Exactly. And it’s not just the NHS, it’s everywhere. My friend works in the corporate world and says if you hit 40, you’re basically over the hill in their eyes. I mean, I’m not even there yet, and the thought of being treated like a relic is already scaring me.      Don’t listen to them. You’re just a ‘young’ bloke from Harpenden passed off as a late bloomer.      Oh, I’m very disappointed in your enthusiasm for my looks, honestly. But to be fair, I do feel like I’m always trying to catch up with the latest trends—like this virtual reality stuff. Have you seen those headset ads? They say it's the future of go-karting.      No, I thought the future of go-karting was just go-karts that go faster. But if virtual reality makes people rich enough to afford to build karts, then I’m down with it.

Right, so we've got about two hours to kill before we get to Poreč, so does anyone fancy stopping and grabbing some lunch? There was that market down the road a few miles back where we saw stalls with fresh olives and cheese. That place had some of the best tasting oil I’ve had in a while.      I was just thinking the same thing. I’ve been trying most of the places we’ve driven through and the food from those local stalls is outstanding. The woman there, Ante or Ana—Antonia was her name—she insisted we try her olive oil with some local meat. Super rich without being heavy, honestly made me feel like a local for a moment.      But what’s the point if we’re going to have another meal later? I’m not hungry right now, can we pick up snacks instead? I’m up for some of that Croatian biscuit stuff if it doesn’t kill me before I hit bed. Mum said I could stay at the hotel for five minutes and I’ve already stared at Netflix for two hours. I’m determined to surf the Waterboy.      Who’s this Waterbody? You don’t need determination to binge-watch a show for two days. You’ve got a three-year-old mindset. Still, yeah, let’s grab something at the market. Bring in the snacks, and maybe pick up a bottle of something local. I’m quite taken with the place so far. If I weren’t back in London by Monday, I might even consider someone buying me an apartment here. Just not a caravan, those places look oddly depressing at night with all the lanterns going.      Don’t knock the caravan thing too fast, Dad. Not everyone about to fall off the social ladder can afford the Renaissance Palace of Rovinj. I’ve seen your holiday photos. Caravan with barely a chair and a car boot turned into a fridge. That’s not 'romantic’ that’s ‘low maintenance’.   Speaker_2 :   Bless him, he had a bit of a shock when he first saw your brother’s trailer park experience. But honestly, Istria is so beautiful with or without a hotel. The vineyards, the olive groves—it’s like a living painting.      Yeah, go on then, make it about your antiques again. But personally, I just want to see that art festival we were talking about earlier.

So do you lot remember when we were all sat in that flat in Cambridge and Ash played us that song like... off the top of his head after we dared him?      Oh my gosh, is that what happened to that video? I mean, you were all like "Deer in the Headlights" or whatever and we were just filming and   recording his panic face  ? That’s a classic.      Yeah! And I swear to God, he didn’t   expect   someone to be taping him. I think for like the whole first minute of the song he looks like he’s about to wet his pants. And then he just gets into the vibe, you know? It goes from "what the hell did I get myself into?" to "I’m just gonna go for it."      We should make a playlist of all the chaotic stuff we’ve recorded. Like the Domino breakfast, the Bucksy anal therapy session, and... I don’t know, the time Mega challenged us to eat floor to ceiling pizza and he got food poisoning?      Oh yeah, the pizza one is gold. Mega takes three falafel wraps and one slice and then falls asleep for twelve hours. We were in   Doncaster   that day, remember? We got him pizza from that takeaway Mate’s been going to since uni and, boom, chaos.      And don’t even get me started on the Bucksy thing. I don’t even know what she said in that video but when we played it back to her she just sat there like "WHY do you all think this is funny???" and we were all being like "no, no, your   facial expressions  , we were just transcribing conversation."      She said something like “the thimble is your failsafe""... I still don’t know what that means but it's in the bin, so for posterity it lives forever.      Honestly, I think we should just make a YouTube channel called  Four Girls, No Filter . Imagine when our nan finds out. She’d tut and then watch every video out of pure spite.      Nan would do it justice, let’s be real. But serious now—who are we gonna ask to upload it for us? I don’t know how to clip or edit.      Oh no, I don’t want to know how to do it either. Can you just sum it all up for me? Like "Add video → press upload → ???

Right, I swear the sandwich shop near campus is charging more than they did last year. What’s up with that?      Oh, I completely agree. I had a chicken and bacon roll for £8 the other day. I thought, is that what a sandwich costs now? It was smaller than a fiver!      Yeah, I nearly dropped my coffee when I saw the prices. I’ve taken to bringing my lunch in every day just to save money. Honestly, it’s easier and cheaper to do a whole week’s prep on a Sunday.      That’s not a bad idea, Gemma. I tried that once, but forget about the turkey, I grabbed the left-overs and Myra still managed to eat half of it before I even got back to work.      Roast leftovers are the best anyway. But if you’re making your own lunch, what do you all usually have?      I’m in a kind of lunch rotation. Usually, it’s either pasta bake or a stir-fry. I divide it into five portions and stick it in the fridge. Keeps it from getting boring.      I still live on salad sometimes, can’t be bothered to cook anything. Doesn’t work if you want to stay warm in Salford this time of year. I nearly froze on the way to campus today.      Haha, you and me both. I’m wearing three jumpers and I’m still cold. I just don’t get how some people don’t even wear a coat here. Must be a Manchester thing.      Or just Russian and being used to winter. Look at some of the people who come in about five minutes before classes start — they just sprint in the frost like it’s nothing.      Going back to the food thing, I was thinking about sending a complaint to the uni about the overpriced sandwiches. They’re supposed to help students cut costs, not contribute to the student debt.      Be careful though, you might get a response like, “We’re a learning institution, not a cafeteria.” Then you’ll be back where you started with digestive problems and high prices.      You’re not wrong. Last time the facilities got goaded too much, they stopped giving away free tea and coffee in the staff room. Imagine that, I was sipping from a cold mug for weeks.      That’s harsh! I’ve had enough of it, I’m off to find someone from the university to complain to properly.

So do you lot ever actually use social networking to promote library services or is it just us in Salford doing all the shouting?      Haha, we use it, but mostly we use it to complain about how we wish we had better Wi-Fi at our branch. Or to post pictures of accidentally sticky chairs after a long weekend. It’s like   50%   of all our content is a PSA that coffee should never be allowed in the library.      Oh,   New Zealand   libraries do a lot more with social media than I expected. We do virtual book clubs on Facebook, Instagram story quizzes, even TikTok challenges—like "What book is this? Guess before we do!" It’s mostly kids, but it’s fun! The eccentricities of a librarian’s life, right?      I’d say   TikTok   is an excellent idea, but I’m not sure if it would work if your community manager’s name is   Gloria   and she’s not 15, doesn’t have a laptop, and once excluded Holocaust memes from the database because "they weren’t pleasant" — and I mean I don’t disagree, but as a Librarian,   facts   are still facts.      You know what’s funny? We tried running a   Twitter   account a while back, and it died because the only tweet we ever posted was “It’s Wednesday,” just like   47 times  . Then we deactivated it and made a meme out of it. Now people still ask if it's back. That's the Internet for you.      Ah, I   love   that. In   NZ  , we once had a colleague, let’s call her about   30 years old  , who thought the   library’s Facebook page had been hacked   because someone changed the profile picture to a   horse in a suit  . She spent two hours trying to get rid of it and crying gently about her ability to multi-task. The rest of us were just laughing because she was being nice and trying to preserve the library’s dignity when it was just one of my kid’s   jokes   from a different account.      That poor woman must have thought the world had exploded. I remember the time we tried to do Facebook Live of a go-kart on the lake because we thought “interactive outreach” meant "no line of sight." It was a   disaster  —9 minutes in due to technical difficulty. It just kept repeating, “  Loading... Library live stream starting soon!  ”

Rather than going the entire way along through the whole consultation, do we need to just do it through the first couple of sections and then put them temporarily on hold so we could get a few specific heads of steam going first?      No, I think we need to take things through the full process. The consultation is there for a reason—we’re building trust   and   getting the best feedback. You don’t want to be accused of starting something off in a silo, especially with a project of this scale.      Fair point. I suppose when you're considering the rationale for the location, you can’t just go with habit or convenience—especially when dealing with health services. Tunbridge Wells has some real strengths in the local care ecosystem, but I’m wondering whether it’s the most strategic footprint for the new hospice.      That’s why we’re commissioning the Business Case and working with consultants. We need to look at population demographics, existing provision for end-of-life care, proximity to existing hospices, and even the transport links so people aren’t excluded from access. I’ve been in discussions with a couple of hospices—there are definitely synergies out there as well as gaps we need to plug.      That would also help with relationships and continuity of care. I’m thinking about how we can ensure the nursing care and patient health support are integrated from the start—not bolted on after funding has been secured.      Exactly. We’ve been advised to form an advisory group with people from hospices, local GPs, and even patient advocacy groups. It’ll give us something of a built-in coalition and improve the   rationale   for where we allocate resources, especially when it comes to   health budgets  .      And what about the use of an estate agent for this kind of property? Do you think we should handle it in-house, or bring someone in?      Definitely bring in an estate agent, but one with experience in healthcare or third-sector buildings. We need to look at not only cost, but long-term usability. We’re not just looking for somewhere to put a building—this has to be a space that reflects the patient journey from admission through to bereavement support.      Agreed. I can go ahead and map out what a new building might look like. I’d love to suggest separate wings for individual therapy rooms, a communal area for families, and some quiet zones.

Rather skip the newfit incense. You know what, let’s go with her former job.      Her former job.      Erm, she’d been a temp for a while before she started at the GP surgery as a CCA. But it was in that eeny weeny chemist’s shop on the high street where we used to get all our Nurofen from. A lot of people would walk in from the social clubs. Oh, and she was quite strict with the kids wanting to buy gummy sweets and stuff.      Were you one of the kids?      No, no, the real supply and demand was on the gummy My turkey still walks around with melamine though. I’m not sure why, to be honest. Darcy, pick one: black or white?      Black.      Black then. Now, are you alright for eggs or shall I cook you some bacon again?      Eggs are fine. I don’t want to overstuff the tummy before we start taking photos.      What did you say your grief support meeting was called today?      Green trotting gallop.      Mate, I don’t know, I think it was something to do with the Royal Ascot.      You know what it is, don’t be dumb, she said it was someone who found an old racehorse they’d read about in the dictionary.      Oh, is it a documentary or real life?      Real horse, real lady. I about blocked her horse after she mentioned turd manure again.      Ron, that’s part of the charm. That’s the bit where she uses the fertilised manure, not the actual Pooh stuff.      Yeah, but I still don’t want a horse turd in my garden.      I don’t know, hearing her talk about rural life gave me a bit of the lunches. I miss the English countryside.      Do you ever think about trying it out yourself?      I think life would suffocate me eventually. I think I’d just spend the day trying to teach the sheep how to baa properly.      Fat chance. You’d probably spend all day in the kitchen pretending to make pies and ignoring the horses outside like a complete uncaring oaf.      It would be the only way I could beat the temperatures they were having in Spain. They were suffering, weren’t they?      They were, yeah. It was like, you know, it was a few degrees off being like the coldest in the whole of Europe.      Cheeky birds. But I mean, our weather’s not helping much—endless rain and that typical grey sky.

Rather skip horror films tbh. I do not like 'em. I had a nightmare for a week once after watching  The Conjuring .      Ohhh, c’mon Liv! You’re 23, not 13. You gotta watch them now and then. They’re eenjoyable!  Hereditary  is brilliant, really atmospheric if you like that sort of thing.      I don’t  like  things where someone suddenly jumps out and blocks the light and someone screams. That’s just not me. Give me a chase through the woods with a big knife any day.       Friday the 13th ? Yeah, that’s classic! But that one turkey, Jason, is more scary to me cos he looks like he’s had a bad day in a mullet and a hockey mask. You know he’s coming for you, and he ain’t breakfast, he’s brunch and a punnet of rage.      And the silence! That’s what gets me. Like when the characters stop moving, and you know something is about to happen—person is holding a knife up, you can hear your own heart beating and you’re like,  please, someone go in another room.       Oh, yes—I love that bit. Mate, I got a real one in my house the other day. I was watching  The Babadook  and the phone rings. I panic, press pause, and answer it and it's just someone selling solar panels. Honestly, I screamed my head off. Rattled the cat out the room like it'd seen a skunk.      Awe! Look, it’s not all bad, innit. There are the funny ones, right?  Scary Movie  and stuff like that. Satirical is the way to go. Give me Steve-o as Chupacabra with a ‘ My Poop’  shirt any day.      Oh man, I forgot how funny that one was. Steve-o tried way too hard to be scary. We crack up every time he goes after the Chupacabra. And that one bit where he whines about being rejected by his parents—it just  kill  me.      Yeah, go for the fake stuff. I rated  The Belko Experiment —even though it’s not funny, it’s just mad blokes getting random what your death is and you have to do it.      That one is nuts! I think someone got set on fire by a guy in a ‘Best Girlfriend’ T-shirt and he was like  trying , I swear he wanted to die or get famous. Either way.

Rather skip the newfit one eh?      Aye, it's always that same ponce with the white coat and the Italian dining table music. I prefer a bit of real noise with a little hum in the background.      Fair enough. I'll just order from the old eeny-meeny-miny-moe one with the garlic and pepperoni combo they do. It’s a classic, right? Like Dad's old cider and pie place, but with more cheese.      Aye, and I'll have what you're having, but with pineapple. You don’t like that sort of thing, do you? Still, it's the only way to have it, in my opinion.      Ha! You and your pineapple. Ten more years and you’ll be asking for rocket and balsamic drizzle on it. But sure, no problem. Got the Domino's app open ready to go.      The app? When’s the last time you used a phone to do something that didn’t involve a scroll, a double-tap, or a face-time call?      I’m with you on that. But credit where it’s due, the app’s got a brilliant loyalty scheme. For every pizza, you get points. Ten points – another pizza. True story.      You mean like one of them newfangled payment systems? You swipe, tap, and then ‘Balances updated via instant pay’ – all this faff when in my day we paid in coins or a five-pound note.      Yeah, but it’s easier and faster. Anyways, while I’m ordering your pineapple, how’s your Apple tablet doing?      That thing! She’s had it for years. I’ve tried and tried to get that ‘Screen Time’ thing to kick in, so I don’t fall asleep watching that series about the war. But no luck.      Ah, the modern version of the ‘get me the remote’ call. I miss waiting ten minutes for a crackly tune as it warms up. Websites load in two clicks now, and the whole whack of the news is there in under a minute.      Speaking of which, Dad go out today on that Airbnb place you've been using for his birdwatching trips in Cornwall?      That bloke? Aye, went out on the 11th. He sent me a heart-felt email hours after he left. Wrote about the contrast of the hills and ‘the poorer furniture’s charm’. Imagine! It astonishes me how they all chase about for a place that doesn't have soft carpet or remotely romantic.

Rather skip ahead a bit, eh, Brucefield Farm is such a great spot for reading, especially when it’s got the big fire going. Been reading that Dava Sobel book again, the one about longitude and maritime navigation. Not quite beach reading, but it brings back some vivid memories of our trip to St Kilda.      Aye, that one’s a good read—very well written. I’ve been revisiting  Poor Things  too, the one by Alasdair Gray. It’s like it was written with Edinburgh in mind. You get the whole city feeling through the story. You remember that little shop near Grassmarket where we tracked down a second-hand copy the last time we were in town?      Och, you’re not serious. That bookshop by the castle was the one with the spiral-bound maps of every single world capital? Man, I’d forgotten the name of it. I still have that copy at home—battered cover and everything. Says a lot about the city when you can follow the history of a place through the stories people write.      Aye, reading is like a form of travel in itself, even if you’ve read the same book ten times. Like we’ve read  The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle  a few too many times. Though I remember that one bookshop near Montrose had such an array of Tolkien copies. One time, I picked up a copy of  The Silmarillion  and the guy at the counter, dressed in old tweeds and full beard, just smiled and said, “Ah, welcome back, friend.” Turns out he had the same edition from his childhood.      Awe, that’s a good story. I love how places like that stick with you. I had the craziest experience in a bookshop in Lisbon. Going for that Pedro Lains biography and it turns out the owner was originally from Perth, had moved out for the quiet waters. He passed me a glass of port and told me the whole story of how he ran away to sea and ended up opening a little Artesanal bookstore. Feels like books can root people in a place, or take 'em elsewhere.      That’s the magic of it, innit? You travel via imagination, and then end up wanting to map your own stories somewhere. I think next time we go on a trip, we should pair it with a themed book—like reading Kipling before India or W.G. Sebald before Germany.

Mum, thanks again for taking the time to look at my application. I know it's not exactly your field... but I thought you might have a fresh perspective as someone who's had to apply for jobs before.      Of course, love. Anytime! I wouldn't dream of missing the chance to read what my daughter has written. It's like watching a history book unfold in your lap.      Fair enough! Honestly, I’m feeling a bit daunted by it all. This place is so different from the kind of smaller firms I’ve worked at.      Why’s that, then?      Well, the studio’s based in Canary Wharf now and the application process is pretty formal — interviews, portfolios, all this stuff I’m not used to.      I think it’s brilliant. You should feel proud about applying for something better. I still remember when you were just mastering CAD for a local housing rep at sixteen, and now look at you, thinking about working for a global firm!      I mean, it is exciting—personally and professionally. But I also worry that I might not stand out. I only started designing residential as my specialism… plus, I’m up against masters from all over.      Well, love, you’re still way ahead of most if you’ve already got experience. It’s not just what you have on the page, it’s what you say in the interview. People want someone who knows what they’re talking about and can explain why they designed something the way they did.      That's the bit I’m least confident about. I’m used to working in teams and being about the process... but an interview is such a high-pressure situation to present your ideas.      You know what I think? Confidence isn’t always about knowing everything. It’s just about  owning  the things you do know. And besides, if they ask you something you can’t answer? Just be honest. People respect that more than pretense.      You’re not wrong. I’ve seen colleagues fluff their way through a question and ruin their chances.      Precisely. So have you thought about the questions they might go for? I remember your old teacher always said, “If you expect the question, you can study the answer.”      A bit — but it’s still all so new. Maybe I could practice with someone?      I’ll ask your old workmates on the forum if they fancy doing a mock interview.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You used to be able to get a house in this area when we were young and now it's all bally nonsense with prices. I mean, my son nearly had a fit trying to buy a flat in Norwich the other week—  £300,000  ! Madness!      Aye, if it wasn’t all concrete and glass I’d probably be tempted to move back in one of those newer places. But no, I’d rather rot in Costessey with nothing to do than live somewhere that smells of builders' tea and underfloor heating.       laughs  You two are both the same, still moaning about the cost of living like it's the war all over again. I remember when I was a childminder and I could afford a whole week in Bognor Regis with cash in hand. Now you have to get a loan even to go to the seaside!      It’s the government! That’s what it is. All the time, they bleed us dry and then act surprised when people are struggling. I’d say voting would make a difference, but it’s all the same grief. One lot takes over, does the same as the last, and then blame the people who voted for them.      I know, I know, but imagine what it must be like for the young these days. My Silas was lucky—I got him a flat while the prices were still in this world—but now he’s looking at mortgage rates like they’re a punishment from God. I tell him, “Just get a van, live in the back, and hitch across the country like in the good old days”!      A van, eh? Ha! You’re trying to make me envy him! I sold my Citroën two years ago. It was a good car, mind, but for the price you’d pay for an MOT these days, I just handed it to the scrapmen. Walks all day, does I. Strong legs from waiting on stationmasters all those years! She said the Aussies were open but also… very particular about proper workwear in certain industries.      Mate, I got a few funny looks for speaking with a broad Brummie-Yorkshire accent! Back in Sheffield, I used to say “I’m bin at the shops” and the Australians just couldn’t get their heads around it. All my students thought it was hilarious.      They’d laugh at me too, but for being an old sod trying to speak like one o’ them young buggers from Sydney. I tried to adopt the accent for a while but gave up. I’ve got this Norf-East burr that won’t shift!      I grew up in Gloucestershire, so no one’s quite passed me about my accent. But I used to work in a school in London, and there I learned something about Southerners versus Northerners from the kids.      Ah, yeah? What’s the difference besides the accent?      The Northerners I worked with were more likely to speak their minds. The Southerners tended to be more... subtle. Not that one is better than the other, mind. But it did affect the teaching style. Though all of that pales in comparison to teaching Aussies, eh?      Oh, we had one student who kept trying to say “Brisbane” when we were in Queensland.

Rather skip the new series of Doctor Who do you think. I've got one episode left and they've already gone off and changed the Doctor again. I’m more than a bit tired of it all, to be honest.      No, I kind of like the new one. He’s got that eeny kind of passive-aggressive vibe, you know? But he’s still not as… well, I suppose that word is too strong— less cartoonish  than Jodie. I watched a couple of episodes on my train commute to Leeds. They do keep the chase scenes, don’t they? You know, like, every five minutes there’s a new alien threatening to destroy the world, only to fail spectacularly.      Oh, you watched it on the train? Ten thousand years to the rescue and then back again, and I’m sitting here with a piece of vegan kale pizza the size of a car tire, no doubt dripping with dairy-free cheese. Haha—excuse me, you ever looked at that stuff, Bridget? It tastes like the inside of a bicycle inner tube.      Oh, I’ve had the occasional falafel patty as a substitute. Honestly, I’ve seen more appealing wallpaper. Still—it’s fun, right? I mean, the way it all works—saving the planet with a sonic screwdriver, barely getting any sleep, brushing the dirt off of his coat and calling it a day. If I could live like that, I’d live like that. Less marking essays, more saving the universe.      That’s oddly sour coming from someone who’s got herself a job in the real world being an actual English teacher.  You  are out there saving people’s grades, I hear.      Only when they finally finish writing their essays on time and not at 4 a.m. the night it’s due. Maybe I’ll do a podcast about that. Maybe call it “Full Marks at 4:00:01 a.m.” Catchy title, don’t you think?      I could see the trailer now— “Where dreams of a perfect grade are traded for the soul-deadening crunch of instant ramen, and the road to salvation is a red pen.”  I could be in it. I have 47 years of social media woes and existential dread ready to be mined for content.      Well, if you can get a vegan smoothie to rise to the occasion of kinaesthetic metaphor, you can write the whole bloody thing.

So did I, but it was weird.      What was?      You know, when we were lying there after and I said something, or didn’t say much, and he… well, he just… sort of faded off. Didn’t even get to the  pretending to snore to avoid awkward questions  bit?      No, no, nuffin like that. Just like, boom, he was out. I thought maybe I hadn’t made him feel good enough or summat and I started gettin’ all anxious an’ was about to try giggin’ breakfast on to cheer him up, an’ he just rolls in his sleep and’s like,  “Sleepy, didn’t have a good night” .      Poor thing. Might’ve had PD or summat. I mean, don’t make him feel like it’s serious or nothin’ but there’s… there are problems, you know.      Yeah – but it’s new. Honestly, some of them aren’t even on the same page unless it’s to draft a five-year plan for their savings or lectures about the best way to hang a shirt.

Okay, I just took the roast out. That smells mad.      Yeah, like... proper weekend roast vibes. You're doing that cauliflower cheese properly, aren’t you? But I wanted to make it a bit healthy extra friendly by using some of that zero-cal syrup to drizzle over the veggies.      You mean the one that tastes like artificial nectar, but the packet says “natural zero-calorie monk fruit goodness”?  laughs  I tried it once and I swear Siri asked me if I wanted to try turkey katsu next. And we can cancel the rest of our week with one meal? Yes! That way we’ll have to work harder to burn them off and still sabotage ourselves with a calorie-free gin and tonic later.      Oh, we most certainly will. I’m already warming the bottle of the clear stuff. We can pretend it’s a healthy herbal infusion.      I’m up for that.
