This week’s box had the most go-to waste veg ever—two courgettes, a beetroot and half a head of leeks. Honestly, it felt like the veg box service had some issues with its algorithm.      At least we had that cheap Quorn loaf in the fridge to save us. I still think they overcharge us when we buy them alone.

So do you think we should go to Sicily or maybe do something a bit more off the beaten track like... I don’t know, maybe Croatia? It’s not as touristy, and we’d probably meet fewer people we know.      Croatia sounds appealing, but honestly, I don’t want to be too far from the internet. I know it’s supposed to be beautiful and everything, but I’ve got a lot of work on the side this year, and I don’t fancy being disconnected for a fortnight.      Oh right, the freelance monitoring of the internet. You can’t even go on holiday without it. Last year I promised you we’d just switch off, and you managed to get MySpace on a sunset beach somewhere.      That was a long time ago, and MySpace was still in the world! But to be fair, I’ve been working better at switching off—well, except this happened last month when I accidentally e-mailed myself from the airport desktop instead of you to tell you the laptop was in my hand luggage. It took me over an hour to get through security and then start up again.      You’re like the real-life version of someone in one of those sci-fi novels. All data, all the time. But maybe – just maybe – we could agree, like, one day a week, we just don’t set up Wi-Fi?      Only one day? You might as well ask me to give someone a full tattoo for a week. That’s like a long-term project.      Ah, now that reminds me—have you seen my tattoo artist? I’ve been talking to her about a small quote on my lower back. Something like,  “Don’t just adapt—joke about it.”  Going to be in small cursive and it’ll be up against my hip. My sister’s planning on getting something similar, only hers will involve cats.      Oh, you mentioned that before. I thought it was a joke about waiting till I was out.      It  is  a joke, but it’s the kind of truth in it that makes it work. Still, I’m nervous. First tattoo in the hip area—what if it doesn’t sit right? What if it ends up looking like a line of angry ants that had a disagreement with a ruler?      Then we could just take bets on whether it lands you roles in pantomimes or local political campaigns.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh?      Aye, it's always a mither when they don’t show up on time.      Well, I think we’ll manage. I've got the lamb in the oven and the asparagus on the side.Deirdre’s on her way with the drinks and Ruth will be down from Oxford if the train's on time.      That’s if they haven’t stubbled off to B&Q or into a coffee shop or something. Know how they are, don’t I?      Mm, specially with the three o'clock habit!  laughs  I reckon Ruth will at least text before she gets to Cambridge if that one’s on her list of places to pop in. She always says she’s on her way and then disappears into the architectural subtleties of a sandwich board!      Aye, breakfast, no doubt. I've been thinking, though — in advance — what’s the deal with the postcard, then? I mean, I know why you sent it, but I was curious.      Oh, the one I sent with the picture of the mountain and the sheep?      Aye, that one. I mean, was it just to let me know –?      No, no, no. It was to let us all know. All four of us. Silly old me. Thought we could at least pretend we were all in this together — in one way or another. That way, if the vote goes oddly, we can all feel like we at least discussed it over tea and scones before it all kicks off again.      Well, I’m not the same as the others, you know. I’m from a house where “the Union” wasn’t just some vague national sentiment. It was a promise to the family, like. My grandfather worked construction on the Forth Bridge, you know. He told me the day they told him he was to go back North and not return for good unless there was a crack in the stone.      Ah, well, that’s a new one on me. I took the postcard from a set I got from this travel shop in the village. Cheesy image of the Highlands, if you ask me. But at least it shows some reverence, no?      I dunno, what your lot call reverence. It just winds me up to hear how everyone’s in two minds. “Oh, we like Scotland but we like England better,” or “We like independence but not at the expense of the Crown,” or whatever.

Right, so today in art class, we did a really interesting project about helping people in need through design. I got the kids to draw a chair for Syrian refugees. I thought it would be a good way to combine art with empathy and also touch on the types of things people need when they’re rebuilding their lives.      I drew a pink one with spots! It had cushions on all sides and a pillow in the middle because when you’re tired, you just want to squidge into it. It would be like a soft castle!      Oh that’s lovely, NINA. You really thought about comfort, which is so important. People can go through so much and just needing something soft to sit on can help them relax a bit. Excellent idea.      I drew a throne chair like the ones on Game of Thrones. The teacher asked why I had a sword sticking out the back but I said "this is for defenders!" So people can sit and be in charge and protect the castle!      Oh, James, that was great. I like how you added your own twist to the idea of what a chair should be. I think we even had one child design a chair with wheels, so someone could go on a walk and still have a seat. It was brilliant how creative they all were.      Did you talk about the other chairs today, the ones you saw in the books? I did one with a backrest and legs that folded like the ones in the supermarkets.      Yes! We looked at different types of chairs—ergonomic chairs, camp chairs, ones used in hospitals, and even the traditional solid wooden ones used in refugee camps. I asked the class to consider how chairs are used in different parts of the world and what makes one suitable for a different purpose.      I know! I told the teacher my chair had to be strong because if you’re building a new home, you can’t waste time with silly wobbly chairs. They have to survive earthquakes too!      That’s a very practical thought, James. Resilience is a big topic when we’re trying to help people in difficult situations. I was quite proud of how seriously the kids took it.      I asked the teacher if the Syrian people get to use our chairs. She said maybe drawings could be sent in, and that artists might be asked to help design something for real one day.

So did I tell you yet? Sarah and Marcus are expecting! I still can’t get over it. They’ve got the busiest lives out of anyone I know, and now they’re having a baby. It's mad, isn’t it?      No! Really? No way! Sarah’s always on the go—teaching, writing, you know. I reckon this is going to slow her down a bit. A baby’s a serious game-changer.      Oh, it is! She said she’s going to take six months off. Didn’t even want to think about working until the baby’s three months old. Marcus is doing his bit, too—booked a sabbatical for the fall. My word, they are going all in.      That’s the way to do it. Kudos to them. A bit of a cliché, but they’ve really got it all figured out—relentless productivity while everyone else is playing catch-up. Blooming charmed life.      I know! But it made me think—do you think one of us should get on the track? Like… I mean, we’re not as bound up in early lectures and late finishes as we used to be. We’ve got a rhythm going, don’t we?      Well, I’ve been thinking about it, actually. It’s the timing, though. We did just start this whole new module prep. And we’ve got that conference coming up in March. If anything, maybe next year. Just not this year, love.      Fair enough. Also, I don’t think I want to split my brain across three things at once. This term feels like about enough. I’m not trying to be the Renaissance woman of lecturers—just… a functioning one.      Haha, exactly. And besides, we both know the system. You give lectures with a baby, you’re passed off as some kind of parenting guru by the students. I was told once I had maternal instinct just from smiling at a photo on your phone. It’s absurd.      Oh, you were? No wonder you were so awkward in that seminar the next week. Still, maybe after the next semester. I’ll get the curtains in the room on the landing if you like—could work as a nursery, just in case.      That might be a good idea. And we could use all the planning time we’ve got. Although, we’d better start with something smaller—like, say, a rabbit?

Rather annoying isn't it, how even in a place like this everything sticks to its own schedule. The university’s got publicity displays up by the local pub like they think we all need reminding how serious we are about ourselves.      Hmm, I kind of get it, though. It’s Norfolk after all—slow-paced, traditional. Maybe they just want to feel part of the national academic rhythm.      Part of the rhythm? If this is a rhythm, then it’s a terribly wobbly one. We’ve been here six weeks and half the campus still thinks I’m the history lecturer rather than the media one. Still, at least I don’t forget the keys now, unlike when we first moved here.      Och, yes—what a mess that was. You locked them in the microwave I think. Or was it the dishwasher?      The microwave. I was trying to 'reboot' my life and accidentally repotted the keys into the vegetable drawer as well, didn’t I?      You were starting to treat the kitchen like some kind of treasure hunt. Though I have to say, your superstitious side has taken a real twist since we got here. You cross the road when police cars pass, now.      Well it's better than walking under ladders these days. There’s something about this place that gets into you—like the whole county was built on minor mysteries and outdated rituals. I mean, did you know the local cricket club still celebrates its first ever victory with a blue ribbon-wrapped ale on the first Saturday of July? It's like real life being played out by a comedy cast.      I did. I think they even play "Rule Britannia" at the end. Not sure if it's dignified or just plain daft. Either way, it does sound like something that would be on  Only Fools and Horses  if they ever did a country spin-off.      If they ever  had  a country spin-off, which frankly I hope they don’t. Those kind of rural comedies are either very English with lunches and cricket, or very French with frogs and wine. Norway's just trying to get around with three course meals and a laugh.      Well, at least we made our own kind of holiday out of it. Who knew academic conferences could be accompanied by walks through willow groves and fluency in conservation koi pond?

Dad, I just wanted to go through the list of stuff we need to take out of the old house. I got the big moving van sorted for next week, and I’ve asked Tom to help us load it on the Saturday. Do we need to book someone in for the heavy stuff like the piano?      Yeah, I think the piano was insured separately when we moved it in all those years ago. I’ve got the contact details for the company in my old top drawer under the paperwork. Let me know if you want to give them a call. But before that, when are we telling Mummy? I’d like to sort it out gently.      I’ll tell her tomorrow when we meet for coffee. My lectures are light this week, so I can help her sort out the bits she wants to keep in her new flat. I think she’s going to take most of the dressings and the better china. What about the antiques? Should we get a valuation in advance?      Mmm, some of them are sentimental—and a few might actually be worth something—especially the Victorian sideboard and the Chinese vases from the sitting room. But honestly, as long as she and you are happy with the rest, I’m not worried about it. I’m more concerned about how she’ll fare moving on her own with all that furniture and noise.      Yeah, her flat’s not that big. I’ll offer her the bookcase and maybe the old record player she adores. She still plays those 45s every now and then. Besides, I can always buy new furniture. Also, have you thought about your fishing gear? I know you don’t go near it now, but I don’t want to chuck it all out.      Keep it. Maybe I’ll take up fishing again when I’m with you in the summer. I remember you mentioned that secret stretch of river near Lewes. Got a steady flow and shady trees. The fish there are well-fed. It’s probably got all kinds of lizards and frogs too. You always liked those wild things as a kid.      I always liked the lunches we packed and the stories you told while we waited. I’d be happy if you come with me. But speaking of things to go—what about your old computer and the games?

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? The council wants to knock down the library. I would've thought they’d be more sensible with old buildings. I mean, it's got a nice frontage, proper granite and everything.      Yeah, I saw it on the news the other night. They want to build more  parking  for the town centre. Ridiculous. It’s not like the town centre needs more cars. If anything, it needs more bike racks or green space.      Exactly! And to be honest, the library’s run by really capable people. You know Wendy? She’s been there for twenty years—Managed to get funding for the toddler story sessions, and even managed to get the local university kids to volunteer for an oral history project on the town. I think she’d be able to run a proper community archive or something if they gave her the chance.      I still can’t believe they’re even thinking of doing this in 2025. Keeping the façade, building something new behind it—That’s just another way of taking the bones out of the place without rebuilding it properly. It’s not like we’re short on materials to restore it. Wood, iron, stone—Every local firm would love to work on a project like that.      Oh, don’t I know it. I had a colleague who was into architecture—He used to say “fake heritage” is the new normal. You preserve the front, strip everything else, and someone forty years from now will stand there thinking they’re in the past when it’s all an illusion.      So what can we do? I mean, I’m not exactly a council wiz, but I suppose there’s a petition or a local Facebook group by now?      There is! I know because I’ve barely left the house all week, scrolling online to do something,  anything —I mean, even if it’s just to feel like I’m fighting the right battle. But bloody hell, trying to find someone accurate to complain to is like pulling teeth. There are ten different council departments involved, and every one of them says “it’s not us.”      That's just  typical . You know, I started looking into it as well. I tried phoning the town hall, and I got rerouted six times—From “planning,” to “heritage,” to “development,” and then to someone called “corporate communications,” and all they said was that the “public consultation is open.”

So do you lot ever listen to music in the car, or do you just stare at your phones?      Ugh, I do music sometimes. I’ve been into oldies recently, like 80s pop. My nan used to blast Nik Kershaw in the car. Got me hooked somehow.      Me too! I’ve been re-listening to The Cure lately. A lot of bands from the 80s sound way better with age.      Interesting. I was just thinking about playing some Dire Straits or Fleetwood Mac on the drive back. Classic enough not to date you, but not so dull you fall asleep.      My kind of music is probably more like… The Proclaimers or Status Quo if I’m in a mood. Not that I know the words. I just like the beat.      Oh yeah, I know  I’m Gonna Be   by heart. You can’t unhear that when you’re 8, sat in the back of the van, right?      I’m with your nan, to be honest. I actually got my grandma to buy me a vinyl of  Heaven is a Place on Earth  by Belinda Carlisi for my birthday. I know, I know, but there’s something about that synth… It makes me feel like I’m 12 again.      There’s also something about nostalgia music. It makes you feel sentimental even if the time itself wasn’t so great.      So, while we’re being nostalgic, what did  you  get for birthdays when you were about our age, Speaker_1? Like the cool kid’s birthday present?      Hmm. Let’s see. At 16, a classic one: a record player, and for 21, a car. A 5-door Ford Mondeo. Sleek. Uncool. But practical.      A Mondeo? My brother had one. Like, that car’s lasted a lifetime.      So what are  you  doing with your free time these days, Speaker_4? Still the same old routine go-karting pond life?      Ha ha very funny. I’m trying to teach myself photography, actually. Got a second-hand DSLR off eBay.      Oh nice, do you go anywhere fun? I always take photos of tattoos I want to get or weird stuff I see on the street.      You all need to watch  Embarrassing Encounters with the Camera , it’s a new show on Netflix. Just someone else’s weird, candid moments. It’s compulsive viewing.      That sounds like it’s my kind of thing. I could watch people failing at things all day.

Right, I just wanted to go through a few things with you about the car insurance, seeing as you’re thinking of taking the test soon.      Yeah, I thought I would. I’ve been doing lessons with Uncle Tom and he said I’m ready if I can afford the insurance.      Insurance is the big one with young drivers. It’s not just about the car itself, but your age affects the cost. Do you know what a no-claims bonus is?      Vaguely… is it like the more years you don’t get into an accident, the more you get to keep on your insurance?      That's it, only easier to say in layman’s terms. It’s also called a discount. The longer you drive without making a claim, the higher your discount gets. I’ve got a 30% no-claims discount now after fifteen years. When you start, you won’t have any, so your premium will be higher.      Right, so I’ll basically have to pay through the nose for a while?      Unfortunately, yes. And I don’t think your mother would like you to put the house on it as your first car… plus, the car you choose will have a big effect. A small – reliable estate car with a good safety rating would be best for you. No big engine, no flashy bits.      I was actually looking at a Ford Focus. It’s kind of mid-sized but not too big. And I read it has a good safety rating.      That’d be a solid choice. Not the cheapest to insure but nothing too wild. If you’re looking at a Ford Focus, I’d suggest the 1.0 litrer model. Less powerful, cheaper to run and cheaper to insure. Not to mention more fuel-efficient, which is good in the long run.      What about add-ons? I saw some people get cover for breakdowns or personal injury. Is that necessary?      Breakdown cover is a good idea, especially as a new driver. If you’re not used to the car or the roads, you’re more likely to get stuck. Personal injury cover might come with it or you can get an add-on. But I’d say if you’re not using the car for camping or off-road, stick to the essentials.      And what if I’m not the only one using the car? Like, if I live at home and someone else gets in it sometimes?

Rather skip the curry an’ go for a Chinese takeaway, but me wife says it's time we learned to cook proper again. Never mind—what was that word ye were stressin’ about earlier, son?      Uh… “Pronunciation,” Dad. Just like how to say words properly. My friend’s accent is so thick I can’t understand half of his homework readin’. An’ I said something ‘bout his windpipe once in a joke, an’ now he won’t speak to me.      Oh dear. You didn’t chase the windpipe with a curry sauce too, like you did last time?      That was a classic. The poor lad’s still singin’ “I am the walrus” when he says “Open the pod bay doors, Hal.” I think he turned your face green with curry, Finbar.      Well yeah, I said “You have a windpipe like a possum,” and it was a joke, right? But now he thinks I made fun of his accent—so I’m just, like… stuck in awkward silence every time I try to talk.      Awkward silence, eh? Sounds like a mini version of workin’ in IT. You ever try takin’ it one step at a time and actually explain the joke? Or are ye like somethin’ that just cracks and disappears?      Finbar, if you want to explain your joke, you have to also say you're sorry. Accents aren’t just words or sounds—people attach emotions to them. So if you want peace, apologize first and then make your point, love.      I didn’t even know it was offensive. I mean, “possum” is just a funny word. Why is that suddenly a big deal?      Son, not every word is just a word. Some words resonate deeper, based on where ye come from. An’ if ye’re thinkin’ about it that way, maybe ye should practice your explaining skills before ye fire words off like a  suicide squad  with lunches to kill.      Speaking of stress… I’ve been feeling it the last month with goin’ on for life since Liam keeps wanting to go out for Chinese every week. I’m trying to teach mindfulness—breathin’ through the nose, relaxin’ the jaw—but I might’ve been lying when I said I knew what “stress levels” truly meant.      Stress is overrated if you ask me. But if ye really want to test stress levels, try doin’ a podcast where you podcast once, an’ it's all silence except for a camera windchime, an’ you have to swear you won’t laugh, while Movember conversations go on in the background.

So do you reckon we’ll get through the cloud cover once we get onto the M62? The pidgeon forecasts are dire today.      I’d say probably not, love. It’s thrown in with the front system from the Atlantic as well. You can see it rolling in when we passed the motorway services.      Ay, I wanted to land that remote-control plane I brought in my bag.      Well, you’ll have to wait a bit. Today wasn’t the best day for birdwatching either. Did you know there’s a specially protected zone near that old hilltop village we passed?      That’s where the nudist colony is, isn’t it? I read about it online last week. Probably why the fields look so empty.      Actually, from what I’ve heard about the referendum fallout, it doesn’t really matter if we’re in or out; the farmers there don’t usually let anyone in unless they’re part of the group.      That’s wild. I mean, if I had a place like that up in the hills, I’d probably do the same. It’s not like the council’s going to come knocking during a storm.      True enough – but it’s got me thinking, I actually need to revise a bit for the law conversion course I’m doing. You know, trying to make the switch from midwifery to legal services.      Mum, you can read about laws and scale conversions at the same time—kilograms, grams, miles, and kilometers.       Sighs.  You know, about the conversions... That’s the same story the supermarket chain told the government during the tax dispute. Everyone was confused about how many grams of sugar were in a bag of crisps.      Unbelievable. I had no idea grammar was this important. I remember trying to learn Shakespeare for GCSEs and wondering how I was ever going to understand half of it.      You did well, love. More than that, I think it helps to have someone who can recite  Macbeth  after a day tending to the baby scales in the hospital room.      Any chance of Bear Grylls in the hills? I bet he’d rate that nudist place highly.      I can see it now—“Survive on Nudist Terrain” with Bear Grylls. Just don’t fall for the hippy’s food and water rations.      I miss Terry Wogan. I wonder what podcast he’d be hosting if he were still around.

So do you guys ever just feel guilty about eating meat now? I mean, after reading those  VegFriendly  influencers and everything?      I do a bit, especially when I think about factory farming. Not to mention cows are so bad for the environment. But honestly, I don’t want to lose out on the taste of steak every now and then.      Oh I feel that. I’m halfway vegetarian, but every time I’m out with friends and someone says,  “Let’s grab some steak and ale,”  I just cave in.      I like to think of it as  managed guilt . I take vitamin B12 and iron supplements to make up for what I’m missing. Still, I feel like I’m doing something good, right?      For sure. And the more I read about how animals are treated in intensively farmed systems—like the overcrowding and lack of medical care in abattoirs, the worse it feels. I can’t even watch a slaughter documentary without crying for days. It’s so oppressive for those animals.      I mean, don’t get me wrong, I’ve only ever seen it as violent injustice. The idea that we’re oppressing animals feels like the same sort of thing as human slavery: one species dominating another and treating it however it wants.      That did occur to me! Like, what if animals had a voice and we treated them the way we do currently? It’s madness.      So what do you think about  shmeat ? Cultured meat? I’ve seen some stuff online where they basically grow it in a lab and about how it’s the future.      Oh I saw that too! I think it could be the way forward. At least you don’t have to kill animals to have meat, and for the planet it’s less harmful. But I did read somewhere that it could be a bit artificial and not as nice to eat. I dunno, maybe when it gets better they’ll market it as  synthetic steak 2.0  with a nice  Curb Your Enthusiasm  style ad.      Haha, I can imagine Larry David goading someone on ordering it in a restaurant and them realising it was lab-grown, and that being a problem. That bloke really can’t leave well alone.      Yeah, and seriously, it’d be a game-changer if we could adopt that more globally. But for now, I try to cook vegetarian mornings and evenings at least—vegetable stews, lentil bakes, tofu dishes.

So did you lot see the latest Marvel movie yet?      No, not yet. I got to admit, I haven’t really had the energy to go out for one. Plus, I was doing a full £20 takeaway the other day and it came with like five minutes of extra footage on the DVD. Bargain.      Oh, I did actually. Me and a few mates went down to the cinema in Workington last week. It was brilliant, right?      Which cinema was that? The Odeon?      Yeah, the Odeon. I mean, I know it’s not the glitziest place in the world, but you still get the popcorn bucket big enough to put a cat in.      Aye, and I think the world might end if you actually watch a film and forget to buy breakfast, no matter where you go.      No wonder I missed the first 15 minutes of the last one when I went to university. I was arguing with the barista about whether skinny is a size or an insult.      Haha, only you, Will.      So, have you been doing all your Christmas shopping online yet?      No, not even close. I’ve been browsing, but I don’t know, everything looks the same. Like, one site says 'free delivery' and then charges you someone else in the post.      Oh yeah, I had that with some Christmas jumper from some website. It said £1.99 delivered in 24 hours, and it took nearly two weeks. I finally sent it back.      It’s a whole game, really. You know that one mate of ours, Steve, who bought a PS5 online and found out it was repossessed after he’d passed it around the house three times.      Oh my God, is that true?      Yeah. He had to hand it back to the lady round the corner with a note saying, “Hope you like it.”      I’m just trying to get my nan’s Christmas present goody bag sorted. I found this website that does like little pre-packaged bags for different ages and genders. I just picked one that said “Old Spice,” cause you know, she’s in her 80s and smells like a tea caddy.      Is it like that ‘Grandad shuffle’ or whatever?      You know it like, “Your move, Einstein,” and then he accidentally knocks over half the board game.      So, are you two still thinking of heading up to Manchester for the weekend or what?

I can't believe we've made it through four whole days of Alumni Day – does it get any less overwhelming first time or do you just get better at surviving it? Honestly, I think it's like anything, right? First time is the worst. By the third day you’re just praying for tea and a bench. But yeah, it’s brilliant to see where we’ve all ended up, especially with a faculty that taught us so much. I know! And it’s even better when you bump into people and you remember the ridiculous conversations you used to chase through the corridors. Oh like the time we tried to figure out what happened to that 18th-century case we studied and made up an entire conspiracy theory because neither of us had read the footnotes? I still swear on it, and I think half the class believed us for a while. Honestly, working in language research, I sometimes wonder if this happened more frequently – people in law basing huge theories on assumptions and missing details. Well, that’s why we’re here today! I mean, you coordinate research, I administrate it – it’s like the legal chaos to order. I tell you, when I’m in my job watching linguist jargon fly past, all I want is someone to just say it in plain English, not least because it makes funding letters easier to write. You’re lucky you have me to make it ‘readable,’ even if it’s still complicated. Who am I kidding, it’s complicated because it has to be – but oddly satisfying when you get it just right. So, being here in Cambridge – does it make you miss going abroad at all? I remember you told us all you wanted to go to Japan after your postgrad and take on some sort of mission to teach English to penguins. Maybe I’ll do that, but for now I’ve been guest coordinating a project in Florence. The dialect there is wild. I had a colleague ask me if he could borrow my ‘ficelle,’ and I thought he was asking for string. And you said yes? Well, I was being polite – turns out, in Italian, 'ficelle' is a slang for ‘nonsense.’ So I handed over about 20 meters of string and made a dent in the Italian study group's credibility. You what!? That’s priceless.

‘Ey love, you still up?      Aye, just trying to finish this essay... got to submit it by ten. Otherwise I’ll be properly knackered for the lecture tomorrow.      Why do they have to start so early on a weekday? Seven o’clock eeny weeny? I swear if one more professor puts on that projector before I’ve had my second cup of tea I’m just gonna fall over dead.      Haha, yeah, I know right. We’ve been in that same seminar room for three weeks, and the bloke up front hasn’t stopped talking yet. I’m still not even sure what the module is about.      It’s lectures like that I wish you still lived here. I could be persuading you to sleep in, stealing your breakfast and giving you a back rub. Or at least making you a nice cuppa and breakfast, no doubt about that!      Aye, don’t be getting too comfortable, love, ’cos I’ll still shout at you over the phone if I need one.      Fair enough. I might take two hands out of that keyboard and flick my wrist real dramatic for you.      Haha. Honestly, when are you going back to uni? Mate’s been bugging me, says you’re just sat on your backside all day doing nothing.      Aye, well, I’ve got that open day next week for this uni in York. Lecturer said they might accept me for the course. I’ve got an email hotter than the summer sun with all the admin and stuff, but I’m still trying to get a good idea of what I’m actually doing.      Oh, what course is it?      Psychology and Communications. Not sure if I’m up for doing a full load to be honest, but for now I just need to survive A levels.      Well, as long as you're giving those scientists the runaround for once, rather than being on the receiving end of it as I am.      Aye, I keep meaning to message your lecturer and say "Congratulations, you lost him!" You know, make like a man and vanish into the night.      Haha, or at least fake my own death, like that YouTube bloke.      Proper one to follow you in all seriousness though, if uni ever gets to be too much, you just give us a shout, yeah?      ‘Course, love. I’d be a lost soul without you... and all the advice that comes with it.

Rather skip the newspaper today, honestly. I couldn't get through more than the front page before it all got too bleak. The Calais situation has me down. I mean, how many times are we going to hear about that refugee camp before the government does something meaningful?      Aye, I read it too. Gives you a sore head. But what can we do as individuals? We can't just up and move to France and start a clinic or a school, can we?      Well, we  can  raise awareness. Didn’t the church group start a charity drive last week? They're collecting basic hygiene packs—towels, soap, toothbrushes, that sort of thing. My colleague at school dropped one off. I left mine on the counter by the door if anyone fancies popping it in the post tomorrow.      Sounds worthwhile enough. I’d better remember breakfast, then—maybe I'll throw some extra bread rolls in while I'm at it. Nothing wrong with a few indulgent spare rolls when you're not actually cooking for twelve.      You know, I’ve been thinking about that sort of thing a lot. I’ve tried to be mindful with my budget—every coin counts, right? But it’s hard to know how far your generosity can really stretch when you’re trying to pay for your own groceries and bills. Still, I’m trying not to turn away when I can help.      Absolutely. It’s the small things that make a big difference—whether it’s a few toiletries, a donation to a shelter, or just sharing the stories so people don’t forget these people exist. I mean, we all have family abroad. Imagine if  you  suddenly couldn't go home, and the only place left to go was a tent in the cold.      I’m just not sure sending toothpaste to Calais is going to put bread on the table for someone. But, you know, better than nothing. I’ll add something to the charity box when I pop out for my usual pint on Saturday.      Oh, are you going to the Gardeners again? I heard their whisky night starts at five o’clock now. I might come with you if you promise me a proper go at the dartboard.      Just don’t expect me to drink, Catherine. I need to wake up early Monday. But what your dad was saying—I think it’s true, to a point.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You know, having to glue the tiles in the bathroom ‘cos he’d got the wrong mortar or something. I’m more than a bit fed up with the whole business.      Aw, aw, I hear what you’re saying. We’ve just finished ours een Tredegar, and I’m tellin’ you, if it wasn’t fer the laddie from Wirral who came up—came in every day, top of the job, right nice fella—ferget about me and the wife goin’ mad chase of it all.      Right, right. Still, I made sure I got a proper bloke, only he turned out to be a MySpace university drop-out who thought his phone could mix the cement. Probably never had a job in his life, but now I’m stuck patching up his mistakes in the steam room.      Awh, that’s a proper mess alright. The wife and me, we had to tell that fella to do it the old fashioned way. I said directly, "No one’s tellin’ me what I can and can’t put in me own toilet, innit, but tell me, what would you’ve done if I’d grabbed a packet of sawdust and said it was grout?      Haha, that does sound like something he might’ve tried. It’s enough to make you want to rip the walls out and start again.      Aye, but then again—mind you, my man wasn’t just building the room. He was in there installin’ a skylight and a bidet at the same time. I said "Ta", I did. I’m walkin’ gold round the place now.      I suppose you could say that. I’m still barely out of it. You remember when we were at uni, ‘cos we were both rather fond of expressing ourselves back then. The way I remember it, it was a time when all we had to worry about was how long your essays ran out of the printer and whether your speaker notes would fit in your bag.      Aye, the old days. And no, you remember, after the seminar, we ended the evening by drinking goon in my room and playing Scrabble on a hexagon tile made out of popcorn? It was brutal. I beat you four times in a row.      That was flukey, innit? I blame the goon. I never had a chance. But I expect you still have a higher Scrabble IQ than most of the current students.

Right, so the kid’s goin’ to love me for talkin’ about this, but when he’s got the  Horrible History Science Book , he’s always askin’ me if I have a superpower. And I tell him, “No, Conall — well, maybe a few if we’re talkin’  not  doin’ the washing up.” But then he looks at you and says, “Daddy, that  isn’t  a superpower.”      Well, you might be the only one who thinks that way, but kids these days are too smart for their own good. I mean, imagine if  I  said I had superpowers. On second thoughts, maybe don’t. I’ve already got the left-hand man in the kitchen rummaging through the cutlery drawer and I think he turned my sandwich into an Edamame biscuit.       Mmmmm.       Oh will you  stop that , Conall! Eating metal doesn’t make you a cow! It makes you  sick !      Easy there, love. He’s been curious all week about metal. Started with that weird science experiment he did with his biology teacher — something about how cows eat rocks and it don’t hurt them. Seems like he was meant to be doing photosynthesis and ended up doing  cattle digestion , full on. He even asked: “Dad, if I ate metal, would it make my teeth sparkle like a laser and let me chew through walls?”      Oh good grief. I about wet myself. That child does not lack the imagination.      And I said, “Only if you were covered in curry and laying around near a pipe.” He just looked at me like I made up the whole universe.      Let him dream, love. At his age, you believe your bones can turn into crackling tubes and your ears can’t feel pain if you ignore the lunches you keep smuggling behind the digestive biscuits.      Still, I did come with a snack! I brought the leftover goji berries I usually throw in the blender — or so I hoped.       MmmMMMMMMM  .      You’re not helping. And now I’m scared because he asked: “What if I fall asleep over this and turn into a robot?” I had to go full MacGyver on him. "Robot people still can’t do laundry, Conall."      Oh now that’s the kind of advice I’d pay you to scribble down and send in an email to every other kid in the country.      It’s on my bucket list.      Anyway, back on topic — this weekend, we are doing something fun.

Rather skip the queue and just go through the side door, do we?      Oh aye, I’ll take care of the side door. I’ve had a few practice runs with a little thing called   Knock Knock Door Opener 3000  . It was in a catalogue, and now I’ve got the full range.   Knock Knock Door Opener… 450.        Oh I see, so you're one of   those   retired teachers. We've had the likes before. Funny you're teaching, but clearly still rocking the   hustle  . Still, better than me. I've got the   childminder's disease   now. My knees are definitely not fond of me anymore. I tell you, picking up a two-year-old in a full meltdown and then   strolling   up stairs with them was far harder than any exam I ever sat.      Aye, in my day we’d be out in the fields, you didn’t have time to get creaky backs or mercy from two-year-olds. We had   horses  , not children. I used to ride a horse to school. I tell you, that taught you   discipline  . My old trotting mare,   Fluffernutter  , – name’s a joke I know, but she had the fiery spirit of a lion and the dance of a hippopotamus through mud. Still, I never had a broken shingle, and never once missed school because of it.      Auntie Joyce, I had a school trip to a riding stable once. I got to ride a horse called   Mr. Whiskers  ! He didn’t do   nothing  . Just   walked the circle   like he was bored. I said to the instructor,   is that all you guys do?   And she said,   Oh no, Mr. Whiskers has form, he’s passed his A-Levels and all.        Oh dear,   form   and   A-Levels  . We are really hearing   Hogwarts-level academaining here   with your pets. That Mr. Whiskers sounds like a   masterstroke  , delivering learning around the stable like a man with a masterclass in walking on pond life.      Ha, ha! I’ll bet that Mr. Whiskers bloke could outrun your Fluffernutter at   a canter  . Mind you, we had   Halloween gallops  , not stable trips to schools. We’d have a bonfire, lights on the trees,   ghost stories   told so spooky I swear we all ran home with   two minutes to midnight  . You see? That was   true fear.        This year, I dressed as   a witch  , but the teacher said I couldn’t wear the hat because it's   fake blood   on the ends – he said   not safe for Halloween Spirit.

So do you think we’ll get through all this traffic before we get to the fair? I’ve seen like 12 white vans with no drivers this morning, and I can’t tell if it’s queue jumping or just someone being funny.      Naughty people, they’re not funny. Got eeny weeny passive-aggressive signs on the back of them that say  “I need to go home”  or  “Getting provisions” . Proper cheek, if you ask me. It was worse near the M25 last week, I nearly drove into the back of one of those blokes pretending to fetch tea.      Aww, forget the vans, I’d rather talk about the disabled parking at the fair. Last year I watched a wheelchair user trying to back into a space while five vans in a row each used two of the marked bays. It was a farce.      I know! I mean, how do you stop people parking two cars in the disabled space? They should have some kind of clamp that stops people driving in directly, like a wall or something, otherwise it’s just inviting people to be selfish.      It’s only because there’s more people than spaces, innit? You can’t blame folk from trying to make do. My Mate Harry used to park two of his old bangers in his front garden just so he could keep the space free for when the council was doing some roadworks nearby!      Harry again? Oh he’s a legend. That said, it’s not just disabled parking. You ever try getting a housing association to fix a leak in a stair lift? Took me  forty-two days  to get about five minutes of conversation with someone who could do something.      Aye, and not all of that was with actual people. Spoke to a recorded voice that said,  “We regret to inform you that no action will be taken until a designated period of time has elapsed”  — bloody nice!      Honestly, I think the biggest crack is how you can end up being  technically disabled  with a back injury and still wait weeks for someone to come paint the stair you can no longer walk up. Sometimes I wonder if the government go out of their way to make it impossible for everyone so they end up renting off dodgy estate agents who charge twice the rate for bungalows near your mum’s care home.

So do you really think an allotment is a good idea? I mean, I haven’t even mowed my own lawn in months, let alone tried to grow anything properly!      Oh come on, Elise, you’ve seen how proud Simon gets over his tomato plants every summer. You just start small—something like herbs or a few veggie rows. You don’t have to go full farmer straight away!      Yeah, but it’s not like I’ve got a green thumb or anything! I once accidentally watered my basil with salt water, and the poor plant just choked... like, literally! Still, I do miss the idea of growing something real, you know? It’d be nice to have a bit of outdoor space.      I hear you. I’ve been meaning to pick one up in the area for a while. I was at the Catsfield Road waiting room, and there was an advert in the local paper for a plot at the old planting site by 0321’s property. I mean, not literally 0321’s, just the patch of land that’s nearby. I think if we land a plot, we could share the work, divide the planting areas, and maybe even trade produce.      Hmm, that does sound fun. But I’m not sure how it all works—do we just apply and hope?      Pretty much! You need to fill out an application, and then you’re usually on a waiting list. But if you know someone who already has one, it definitely helps—word of mouth is a big thing with allotments here. I could help you with your application, or even invite you to the waiting group conversation if you want.      The waiting group? Like, they have meetings or something?      Yeah, mostly online—Facebook groups, WhatsApp chats. They keep everyone updated on availability and maintenance stuff. A few of them used to go round for tea every weekend during the winter, but I think people have been getting older... or lazier, depending on who’s doing the talking!      Haha! Okay, if the waiting list isn’t too long, I’d love to give it a go. I’ll even promise to water if you promise not to feed my plants by accident!      Deal! And I’ll even lend you one of my old trowels—you can call it your new best friend after that salt water incident, by the way.

So do you reckon Mateo's still coming to the gig on Friday?      Yeah, I messaged him this morning and he said he'd meet us at the bus stop. He's been doing a lot with his band lately, but he promised us a full set after.      That’s brilliant! I told my cousin about it and she said she wanted to come too. She’s only just back from Northampton doing this internship, so it’ll be good for her to get out.      That’s cool. Do you want me to ask her if she’s driving or taking the train? I’ll pop round to her place to drop off some stuff before the gig anyway. My lectures are all done for the week so I’ve got time.      D’you think she’ll drive? She might be trying to save up for a new gig bag for her ukulele. I swear half her money goes on musical equipment at this point.      Haha yeah, I get that. I reckon she’ll take the train and tell you off for not offering a lift up. But if she says she’s bringing her mate Kris, be prepared for more people than expected at the bus stop.      Oh no, not Kris again. Remember that time at the bonfire he tried to juggle marshmallows and set his hair on fire?      How could I forget?! He’d have been in hospital if not for one of the medics there knowing how to put out a flambéed headpiece. Also, he threatened to sue the sky. Still, at least he’s got a bit more sense now, I hope.      He better, otherwise he’s not going near my house again. Speaking of, shall we try and get the venue sorted out next week? I know the pub’s got the room booked for us, but I heard they might be doubling up with a charity fundraiser or something.      Let me check my emails. I spoke to the manager earlier and he said they’ve got a short space between the lunches, so we might just squeeze in if we schedule it tight. Still, if something goes wrong, we can always try the community centre. They’re usually up for hosting our kind of stuff.      Yeah, I’ll give the community hall a call just in case. Cos you know how it is, if we leave it all last minute and then something comes up, we end up stuck with a chip shop and a sound system in the back of someone’s Ford Ka.

Right, lads and lasses, I've been playing that game everyone's on—the one with the penguin or the snow or something. You know, the one I mentioned at the weekend      Oh you mean  Elden Ring ?      No, not eeny meeny miney moe, the one where you’re on this big icey island? I’ve been stuck on a boss for three days now and I’m so chilled-out I’m going to dump my controller.      Is it  Elden Ring  with the big meaty guy, Malenia?      Yeah, the one who only lets you hit her like three times before she turns you into melon ring. I’m not rage quitting, I swear I’m not. But I might just go out and buy a thermal sub for now while I wait for better gear.      Mate, you can get in-game currency on the black market if you want, you don’t have to starve.      Ah yeah, tell me about it, I’ve sold every last falcon egg I’ve found to buy a few more hobnobs.      I tried playing it too, but got way too immersed in the story. I got all emotional, like, because the starry thing was dying and her hair was black and white like the Silurian lines.      Oh right, you mean that Lady in White who also dresses like a conspiracy theorist? Man, I had a proper laugh with that one. I thought the starry thing being split in two was a metaphor for ballet, honestly.      That’s the same story the game always tells, “crushing thrones” and “the sister is the frost.” I mean, it is snow up there, right?      I’d rather play something more chill, personally. I’m into board games. Last night was bloody epic—Monopoly, but instead of streets we called them “Lena’s Bookshop,” “Liam’s Websites,” and “Taylor’s Influencer Grind.”      That's brilliant, I’m bringing this idea back! Maybe next game night go full  House of the Dragon .      You’re on. Imagine making someone purchase “Fablehaven” or "Varys' Snacks." It'd take forever for anyone to get out of jail.      You know this game’s worth it if you get over the hump of losing to someone called “Andre’s Mangaka.” I got so robbed by that street in sixth form.      Right, right—but enough about Monopoly and Leon’s weird business ventures. What you got plan-wise, Jess?

Rather skip the new films, eh? You know what they do. Spend a fortune, and they show up with some ridiculous CGI and not much of a story to match. Not like the old days where you actually  remembered  the plot after you seen it.      I was actually thinking about watching that new  Legend of the Lightbringer  one. Everyone seems to be talking about it. I’ve only read half the reviews, so I’m not sure what to expect. It was filmed in Cornwall, you know—supposed to look like some fantasy medieval world, but with dragons.      Oh yes,  dragons . That’s the new thing, isn’t it? From what I’ve seen on the telly, there’s not much in the way of acting to speak of—just a bunch of people shouting in slow motion while creatures with wings chase them about. Cats would make for better actors— maybe .      I mean, visually, it’s not bad. They say the CGI’s top-class. But I do miss those older films you used to tell me about— The Secret of the Silver Isle , or  Footprints in Time , remember? Those were proper stories.      Oh yes,  Footprints in Time . I remember my Matey borrowed that from the library and I watched it about six times. One time her gran walked in and thought I was mad for crying over some kids who were lost in the forest and never came out. Well, they  did  come out, just a bit older.      That was the one with the grandfather clock and the forest that moved every time the bell rang, wasn’t it? I still find that storyline baffling but brilliant.      Oh yes, absolutely brilliant. No need for dragons to make it interesting. Just a bit of imagination and a bunch of kids learning that time’s not always what it seems.      Honestly, the modern films could learn a thing or two. I tried watching one the other day—some post-apocalyptic sci-fi thing—and after an hour, I couldn’t tell what the plot was or what the main character wanted. Was he saving the world, hiding from it, or just looking for a sandwich?      That sounds  exactly  like what I just said—waste of time and money. You can spend your afternoon watching something with  actual  content, or you can spend it confused and angry and then spend your evening explaining what confused you to your dad on the phone, ‘cause he asked why you were sighing like that.

So did you watch The Undateables last night? It was mental again this series, wasn’t it?      Oh God, I did. I can’t believe how much time people spend on their eyebrows. Do they do that before meeting strangers as well?      Honestly, it’s like a beauty bootcamp with a side of awkward conversation. But I’ve got to say, I’ve only watched it because I needed inspiration for my social event questionnaire.      That sounds thoroughly exhausting. You’re doing the language stuff for the council, isn’t it?      Yeah, mostly. I’ve been designing board games to make it less dry. It’s like forcing MySpace-era personality tests into Catan-style mechanics. It’s ridiculous. I’d probably say "I value tea over emotional accountability, thanks ever so."       [laughing]  That would be fantastically Welsh of you, if I didn’t know you were proudly half-Buck.      I only took on half of Abergavenny—it wasn't my fault it was such a humble little market town.      Anyway, I actually need to talk to you about the interview I’m setting up with a documentary team next week. It’s about language shifts in younger generations, and I want you both on the panel. Strictly for linguistic richness, of course.      Only if the questions are smarter than “Do you still send text messages using all caps for emphasis?”      I’m not joking about that. One participant still said it was “the only way to be heard.”      I mean, if you're not shouting to be heard, what are you doing with your life?      I’m with her. I’d say something aggressively Welsh like “Cymru am byth, unless I’m wrong about you.”      Websites and space: do either of you allow them into your home?       laughs  I had a DVD box the size of a go-kart on my mantelpiece. If it wasn’t for Netflix, I’d probably still be driving to the Blockbuster in the vicinity of what your postcode used to be.      Oh, I still have my favourite_ratings_from_the_’90s compiled on a physical chart.  shows photo on phone  Would this count as a magazine archive?      This is perfect. I need people to romanticise things in order to explain their social habits. To be honest, I find it fascinating how you two plan entire weekends around whether the weather’s friendly enough for a spa day.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? The washer’s decided to glue the washing in there again. Third time this month, I swear it’s laughing at me.      Yeah, I mean, it is a 12-year-old machine, love—some people wouldn’t even let it in for a second-hand place, let alone leave it loose in   your   house. Almost as bad as the microwave that only works if you hit it  just right .      It was fine when you first moved in! You were the one who said “we’ve got the full Mumsnet package.” Right, jokes on you! I’ve started doing a load manually every other night just to stay on top of it.      So what are you doing this weekend then, just watching the Guardian Angel on the washing machine?      Haha, yeah, nearly. Actually, we’re going to Bucks if you want to come with? I’m thinking a bit of shopping and then maybe that new Ken Loach film they’re showing in Bicester. He’s doing some kind of comeback, apparently.      I don’t know about a comeback, but credit to the老头—he’ll still only go for the sad, right? But it does sound good. You want to come back?      Yeah, I mean, it’s been a while. Doesn’t quite feel like “home” at the moment, not with the washing situation and the fact that the coffee machine someone donated to us is also suspiciously trying to self-destruct. Besides, I miss my mam’s flapjacks.      Any weekend I can combine watching  any  film with eating your mum’s flapjacks is a gold standard weekend in the books. I’ll bring the stuff for sandwiches and maybe a decent plug to plug the washing machine into. You never know.      Oh, and while you’re at it, can you check if the floorboards behind the TV are still haunted? Lost my charger there last week, then found it six feet under after an hour of digging.      Sounds like a proper archaeological mission. I’ll pack my trowel and a flask of tea. But serious now, are you eating the flapjacks every day on your own? You don’t get homesick for anything else? I mean, apart from your washing machine.      No, it’s fine—it’s Cambridge, it’s got libraries and Greek street takeaway. And your chicken casserole, obviously. I just miss not having to overplan every meal like I do now.

Rather than move, I say we’d do well to stay put. The hurly-burly in the South, dear, it's no place for poor folk like we are. I've heard prices are through the roof in Reading and Chelmsford and all places such — wouldn't dream of it.      I understand the sentiment, but   Vicky   and I actually looked into properties a while ago. Even if we can’t afford too much, it might be worth seeing what we can get reasonable for. We’ve been thinking of moving for a while — it’s not the place we came to fetch our tea every day.      Look, the real debate here is not whether we like moving — it’s cost. I did enough budgeting for a life of oil fields to know the truth: house prices in the North are more forgiving. But even so, it’s harder and harder to find a decent sized place if you want a garden, a kitchen in reasonable condition and not be five miles from everywhere, you know?      That’s all well and good, but tell me this — is it worth upping sticks for two or three thousand a year extra in rent when you can’t even walk the shop and back without risking a heart rhythm mix-up from the heat? I remember my days as a maths teacher, and I say it plain — if you are choosing a new flat based on moving out of the cold for a warmer climate, you’ve already made the wrong calculation.      But also, don’t forget the VW scandal, did we not talk about it last week? It feels like the world’s melting and money’s no match for climate panic. Who’s to say in ten years’ time we won’t be living the good life in the North because most of the South is underwater?      Ah ha! You're speaking like my stepfather now,  all  the time. Geo-political chaos, climate collapse — and now we’re supposed to sleep easy? I think I prefer my flat in Hunsonby and my cup of builder’s tea at 8 am over being climate refugees in the highlands of Yorkshire.      Some of us would argue you  are  a climate refugee if you can’t afford to go out of the room unless you’ve got a heating element. But I digress.      Honestly, I’m just trying to say we need a plan.

Rather annoying when a bar of soap finds its way into a smock and you think it’s real marmalade and you go to have a nice breakfast and find it all soggy.      Aye, we had a bit o' that at our motorway service station — my wife een saw the butter and took a big knife an’ handed it to me like I was going to clean a wound. A lot o' people done that this morning, funny enough.      That sounds a bit dramatic, Bernard. I once mistook a cologne for the hand wash at the hotel. It was enough to make the concierge throw me a towel and a supply of tissues.      Told ya, you get eccentric when you're not sure where you are half the time, Vivian. Easier in a world where you can take photos for help, mind you.      I've been trying to get on the computer at the library, ever since we started fiddlin' about with pensions and the whole digital divide nonsense. I mean, it's not like we need it, but the occasional bit of correspondence is a fair ask.      Tell me about it, John. My neighbour Derek is a legend. He tries to call customer services about something and ends up trying to book a holiday for the next three years. His daughter nearly had a heart attack when she picked up the credit card number from the voicemail.      Aye, my grand daughter's trying to sort a computer out for me. Funny thing — you chuck all your things away, and then you're told you need a memory card to get it all back. I about blocked the kettle while I was trying to charge it the other day.      Another problem is knowin’ you’re in the right house. We went to stay at a B ‘n’ B the other week, and passed three identical buildings on the lane. First one looked like a library, the second had a confusing witches hat on the gate, and the third had a cat as big as a dog. Got lost three times with a GPS.      Some people, no doubt you remember, live for this travel nonsense! I met a woman in the park the other day, she's had ten different houses in her time. Finally, she says to me, "You know what Vivian, your house is like the nice tea-spoon lives in — safe and warm."

So did you lot see that article about evolution and why some people still say it's not true?      Yeah, I saw one today that said "If humans evolved from monkeys, why are monkeys still around?" Not only is that the same kind of question people used to ask about the Earth not being flat, but  monkeys didn’t evolve into humans.  They both evolved from something else.      I think that's one of those things people say without actually thinking. It's easy to spread misinformation online when you don't check the facts.      Honestly, I saw like three posts about it in one day. One guy even compared the idea of evolution to people "evolving" MySpace into TikTok. Like, duh. It doesn't work like that.      On the same note, my sister had an argument with my cousin yesterday about whether girls are better at biology than boys. Like, why are we even thinking about this in 2024?      That still exists?      Unfortunately, yes. We need more feminism in STEM I reckon. There’s a reason so many breakthroughs only started getting proper recognition decades later.      Absolutely. It’s got to be about confidence – girls are often told they’re not as good because they’re girls, but the raw ability is there. I mean, look at Professor Nalini Joshi at the University of Sydney—freakin’ legend in mathematical biology.      It just makes me mad when people think you need to be a certain type of person to be into science. Like,  anyone  can do it if they’re given the chance.      Or at least have access to a decent teacher and not someone who’s telling you you’re not good at it just because of your hair color, like that guy I had in Year 9. Said girls can't do physics because they don't understand black holes.      Honestly, some teachers are the problem. Not all, obviously, but some of them pass on the same stereotypes that we need to move past.      Defo. But it's not just schools either. Social media can go either way on stuff like this. Some people use it to spread knowledge, like that guy who does YouTube videos about human evolution and genetic variation.      I know right. I’ve been obsessed with one of his videos where he talks about how belly buttons are a by-product of evolution, and how they’re not connected to any modern function.

Rather skip the new tablet, eh, love? I’ve had mine ages and it’s working fine so far... Well, beyond the tablets they gave me at the hospital after the operation, anyway. That bruise on my leg finally fading, thank God.      Oh, you poor thing. Got infections? That’s rough. I’ve got sore knees again and reckon it might be time to try acupuncture. I’ve heard it’s less rough on the body than all those potions and pills.      Oh dear! Acupuncture was the go-to when I was your age, dear. But I'd fetch the doctor more than anything! Not like these days, with all the modern ways of doing things. You want that My turkey, I’m going to fetch us a bit more cake?      You're on, Edie. If it's your famous brownie, it’s a yes from me. I still can’t forget that rugby match I nearly missed for a bad MOT inspection, thanks to oversized tyres that gave out on the M1 one rainy day. That would’ve made a good story for the grandkids if I’d still had any!      Here’s hoping your car survives longer than my last one—wrote it off during a work trip in the snow. You never forget the look on the boss’s face! But enough stories, how’s Jim these days? Still getting those regular hospital appointments?      Jim? Oh, you mean our son, right? Well, someone at the vet said he’s got a tumour the size of a tennis ball on one leg and had to be put under general again. It’s not surprising at his age, but it’s never easy to hear about our old boys aging us all down.      I had to help out at the surgery not long ago—I was doing some extra cleaning up near the MRI ward and that girl with a ‘Positive Healthcare’ badge came up. She passed me a leaflet about mindfulness for hospital effectiveness. It was something bloody absurd, if you ask me!      Health is health, whether you like the methods or not, Monica. When I was young I walked five miles to the shop and back with no heating in the house—mind you, I also had four kids to go with it! But life was more... grounded, if you know what I mean.      Grounded, blooming grounded! I once went skiing in the Lake District with a group from the lorry yard after I retired.

Right, I just wanted to go through a bit of history with you both before bed, okay?      What kind of history?      Is it about dinosaurs again?      No, this is different—sort of. Today we’re talking about how some people in the past treated others very badly—and why that happened.      Like a long time ago?      Yes, a very long time ago. It involved something called "slavery," which was when people were treated like things instead of humans. Can you imagine someone deciding another person is not even allowed to choose what they do with their lives?      So like… you belong to them?      Exactly. People were made to work for others, and they weren’t allowed to go home. It was in many parts of the world, including America, and even parts of this country. They didn’t get paid and they were forced to obey people who told them what to do.      That sounds like wickedness. Like, why would someone choose to be mean like that?      It’s a real good question. A lot of it happened because some people wanted to make money from the work others did—but they weren’t generous with their wealth, and they made rules to stop the people being slaves from saying no.      But what about wars? Like, why did people fight each other?      Oh, there are unfortunately a lot of reasons people start wars. Some are about greed, some are about wants for more land, some are because of disagreements over people’s rights or beliefs. I mean, there was a type of war the Roman Empire had where they fought to take over new lands and make more people their slaves.      But didn’t that stop at some point?      Yes. Slavery was eventually made illegal in many places. People started to say, “This isn’t fair, you can’t just own someone,” and there were brave people who stood up to say that everyone should be treated with kindness and respect.      Like, like heroes?      Exactly—heroes. There were people on both sides of the world who worked so hard to make sure that system of slavery ended. But it took a long time—and wars were one of the ways people tried to fix big problems.      So those wars, like… were they better than slavery?      Hmm. That’s a very thoughtful question. You have to understand that no one wants war, but people sometimes think that war is the only way to make things right.

Right, I just wanted to bring up the whole thing about that new series on iPlayer,  Only Lovers Left on the Bus , have you all seen it?      Oh yes, I did, it was funny. Very British, and kind of low-key. I think it was shot in Kent, if I remember right.      I watched it too! It’s not exactly a comedy but I found it quite touching in parts. I mean, it’s basically about how people end up alone in their 40s, which is pretty relatable when you think about it. I feel like the writers sort of reflect real life—no big drama, just the small, awkward moments.      Honestly, I haven’t even watched it yet. Too much on my plate with the business and whatnot, but I’ve heard it’s good. I did hear it’s based on something from Austria? Or was that another one?      Yeah, kind of, it’s an adaptation of a German play, I think—and then the TV version is based in the UK. But tell me—personally, what struck you about it? Because honestly, as a nurse, I found the way it showed people’s loneliness… well, it kind of mirrors a lot of what I see in the elderly patients. Not often do you see young people portrayed like that on TV.      Oh, absolutely. I think it was beautiful how it didn’t make it look like they were in a crisis or anything. It just sort of said, “Yeah, here’s where we are.” Some people just don’t find a partner and that’s it—end of story. No drama, no big romantic arc.      I don’t know the show, but I do know most young people now don’t even want to be in relationships! I mean, it’s all moved on to the internet, like that lot just playing on their phones all the time. Back in my day, we had proper conversations and didn’t all rush off to find someone online.      That’s true, Dad. But honestly, the show also shows people with pets, right? Like that woman with the dog?      Oh yes! She and the cat man— terrific  bit on the bus about the antacids or whatever it was. Still chuckling about that.      Oh, I loved that part. The way they just dropped in the weird little quips, it was amazing. It really added to the charm of the show.

Right, who’s putting the plates back in the cupboard? I think they’re still in the dishwasher.      I did it, I did it! See, I put the forks in a line and the cups all neat!      Oh well done, Flo! You sorted half of it out, didn’t you?      But I wanted to do it too! I found a spoon with jam on it!      Oh, right, that must be from yesterday’s toast. Make sure you put that in the sink to clean later.      Can I make a cuppa like you, Mummy? When you wash up?      Not quite yet, you’re not having tea this early! But you can help me sort the cutlery into the drawer.      Wait, Mummy! Why do we have a robot that puts the cups back? Is it like a wizard’s spell from  Harry Potter ?      Well, that’s a fun way to see it! But it’s not magic, it’s technology. Kind of like how trains work. You know who invented the first steam train?      Who? Was it Dumbledore?      No, no – Mummy told us about a man once. His name was…      George Stephenson! The Father of Railways, they call him. He made the first proper steam train system. Before that, they just had horse-drawn carriages and things!      Oh! Did he use a broomstick to fly there?      No! He used a man!      A man what?      A man who rode on the tracks!      That’s not exactly right, but it’s creative! He actually worked as an engineer and tested the steam engines.      So he sort of invented the train rush like  The Hogwarts Express ?      Yeah, kind of! Although I think the Hogwarts Express has a bit more magic around it than George Stephenson’s early engines.      Why don’t we go on a train sometime?      We can, if you want! I can get tickets on the phone. Would you like to go to Norwich one day and see where your cousin lives?      Can we have snacks on the train like Mummy has on the telly? Like crisps and little sausages?      You can have whatever you like, as long as you don’t drop it on the floor or make a mess!      I’ll be the best passenger ever!      I want to be a train driver like George Stephenson!      Well, that’s a respectable dream! And if you work hard at school, you never know – one day you might get to drive one for real!

So did you beat me in Words With Friends last night? I was literally trying to spell ‘sapphire’... got the ‘air’ part wrong, obviously.      Oh, yeah! Got 553 points with ‘sapphire’ as the last word. And you put ‘pear’? That’s passive-aggressive on a whole new level.      Yeah, I panicked. A lot. Like, I had a rack full of vowels and no idea what to do. You’d think a graduate would be better at this. Didn’t even want to play with you after you blocked my three-letter jumble!      Okay, okay, let’s not get in a  letter -storm. You’ve both got spelling levels high enough to be Oxford editors. Now, who wants to talk about how I’m opening the café at 7 a.m. every day this week for breakfast, and I’m already regretting it?      I hear you, love. Prep, ordering, cleaning, and then the customers like to order  espresso martinis . Not a crime, I guess, but I’m like, “It’s  eight in the morning .”      Sounds like my parents. They’d have a spot of tea, a knife and fork held with two hands, and then boom—full Prosecco at 3 p.m. and calling it ‘post-lunch refreshment’.      There’s a food group missing in the UK—afternoon wine. Should be a button on the calculator.  Calories: 190. Afternoon Wine: x1.5.       Not today, tiger. We’re eating healthily tonight. Spelt lasagna I made from scratch. My new supper club idea is that people bring one dish and it becomes a  full experience . Jokes, cocktails, napkins with actual guest names on them.      Sounds like it’ll be full of lawyers bringing canapés and suing you for gluten content.       Nods solemnly.  “Legal repercussions of mislabelled pasta”—hmm, I’m taking notes. Definite  HBO doc .      Anyway, talk of my day—the man at the food market today tried to flirt with me in French. I had to be like,  “Je suis barista, pas romantique.”       You’re in Australia-born barista mode again. You gave a man a latte and changed his Instagram bio to  “#latteislife”  last week.      Guilty. He started sobbing, but it was probably the almond milk.      Love the vibes here, honestly. Yeah, we’re eating lasagna, having cake for dinner, and then resolving world peace via Words With Friends. Perfect.      Exactly. And once you finish that cake— I’ve got a backup plan .      Which is?       More cake.

Rather skip the queue and just bring my own lunch most of the time.      Oh, I don’t mind waiting—that Italian bolognaise down there, it gives me a sense of familiarity, I must say. Back in Tomsk, we had a very unique take on it, but it’s not the same, of course.      You still miss home food?      A little—nothing beats a good borscht or a home-cooked pirozhki. But you know, I also love finding new things when I get the chance. You ever try the new Russian place down in Newmarket?      No, can’t say I have. My boys are more into burgers and crisps. Teenagers—what can I do? I try to sneak some veg in, but it’s like playing Whac-A-Mole.      Oh yeah, I’ve been there with a few friends. The pierogi are incredible, loaded with fillings—cheese, potatoes, mushrooms. It’s quite hearty—perfect for weather like this.      I take it you’re a big foodie then?      I would say so. I love cooking at home too. I’ve been trying out some sushi rolls recently—it’s not perfect, but it’s a fun challenge. Keeps my brain awake after work, you know?      You work with IT, right? Must be different from being in an office environment.      Yeah, oddly satisfying. You fix things, people are happy. It can be stressful being online all day, but I like it. What about your job, then—being a cover supervisor must be the most exciting office job I’ve heard of so far.      Haha, well it is a bit like herding cats most days. Different every day, always something new happenin’. But honestly, I love it. Keeps me busy and means I don’t have to grow up completely.      That’s good—don’t know if I’d have the patience with teenagers, I think I’d probably have left the room.      Then again, if you told me ten years go that I’d be supervising a group of seventeen-year-olds, I’d have said, “Nope, not me, I’m off to Russia.”      I can see it—coming in one day and making those pirozhki for the kids to win them over.      Mm, now that I wouldn’t have minded. I did try to get our cafeteria to make it, once, but let’s just say patience is very much needed for that process.

So do we go back past the traffic lights or up that road? I’m just trying to work it out...      Oh, I think it’s up this road, past the roundabout where we saw the ducks. You know the one, Simon?      Yeah, I saw the ducks, I don’t think they were   real   ducks though. Looked like fake plastic ones. A bit tragic if they were real and just got stuck.      Haha, nah, they were definitely plastic. But what’s the point, no kids about to feed em... like, who even puts ducks in a car park?      That’s what I’m asking. Anyway, keep going straight for a bit. The shop should be on the right-hand side after the next set of lights.      So if it’s the same place we went when we moved in, I think they’ve got a good range of blankets. I saw some oversized ones that looked really soft.      Yeah, we need like ten of them. Moving house is so expensive. I still can’t believe we’re not staying in Manchester. I only started sixth form.      Well, we’ve been offered a good price for the place – even though the survey said the roof might need fixing.      Yuck. I did not want to have to deal with building stuff again. Still, at least the walls in this new place are in good nick.      That’s the main thing. Some houses had all this weird   stuff   in the walls when they were inspected. I heard one place had like a dead cat blocked up...        Ew  , no way. That stuff only happens in horror films.      Well, if we run out of water, we can always put baked beans in it.      Haha, well don’t let your lecturer hear you say that. I hear your college is waiting on a new wave of students from Lagos and somewhere in China.      Yeah, the whole place’s gonna go international next year. I think they opened a new wing by the old staff room.      And if you don’t get into university, you’re just going to drop out entirely and live in a van somewhere, right?      Fat chance. I’ve been revising, I tell you. Unlike certain people I know, who’ve been doing wine studies or something over in Madrid.      That’s your   aunt Sally   you’re talking about, and she’s doing wine studies because it’s interesting, not because she’s avoiding adult life.

So do you play The Legend of Zelda on your phone, Nan? I know it's not real Zelda like on the Switch, but they have a version that's pretty close!      Oh heavens, no. Not since I was your age, love! I wouldn't know where to start with all these buttons and controls. I’m more of a   crosswords   and   bingo   sort of person. A bit too slow for me!      Don't knock it, Mum. It’s actually surprisingly low-key if you set it up right. It's like meditation with a bit of mystery. You get lost in it—literally and metaphorically.      Yeah like that one dungeon where you have to figure out the puzzle before anything makes sense! I had to Google what the symbols meant, and I   thought   I was good at psychology for understanding the human brain!      Psychology? Love, you're off in another world! I didn’t get much past sums, shapes, and the odd biology lesson. I remember once, I nearly boiled the frog, thinking it was part of an experiment I read in a magazine!      Haha, that sounds like my gran—except she tried to measure a cat’s heart rate with a tea cosy! Anyway, back to real life. So, Hannah, what do you want to do after university?      I’m not sure yet. I liked the psychology module the most this term—but I'm thinking maybe   neuroscience  ? It just feels like it's got so much potential, you know? Or maybe   cognitive science  ? I don’t even   know   what most people do with those degrees.      From what I can tell, they just tell you things like   "Your brain is barely aware of it, but it loves chocolate cake,"   and you give them money.      Mm, and then you suffer the sugar crash a few hours later and wonder why you paid for them to scientifically confirm what your tummy already knew.      Haha! Yeah but seriously, I think psychology helps with   understanding people  , even if you can't fix them by yourself! Maybe I can work in mental health one day. I’d like to help people.      Well that’s a noble ambition, love. You’ll be one of them clever people with post-it notes and questionnaires, and I won’t understand a word you’ll say—but I’ll nod like I bloody do!      On the other hand, maybe you’ll go all   tech   on us, Han.

Right, so today we're talking metals and fabrics, okay? Because I was explaining it to you when we were playing Minecraft and it got me thinking about how things work in real life, too. Let me start with metals first. Do you remember when we talked about what things are made of?      Mm-hmm. I remember that you said   iron   is important in the game.      Exactly, and in the real world, iron is super important too. It's one of the metals we use to make   tools  , like hammers, pots, or even parts of bikes and cars.
