But there's even   stronger metals   like   steel  , which is actually made by mixing iron with other things like   carbon  . Steel is what they use in   skyscrapers   and big bridges!      Do you have to melt the iron to make steel?      Well done, that’s a very good question! Yes, kind of, you heat it up a lot, then add   other elements   to change its strength or how it bends. But here, maybe we can start with what you have in Minecraft — like   copper  ,   iron  , and   gold  . In the game,   gold   is shiny and feels valuable, but in real life –?      Gold is actually kind of   soft  , isn’t it?      Very clever! You're right. Gold is   very malleable  , which is just a fancy word for bendy. If you made a sword out of gold, it would bend out of shape very easily. So in the real world, people make   alloys  , which is when they mix metals together, like   brass   or   bronze   . Those are better for making things that have to be tough.      Oh! So that’s why Minecraft has   iron tools   being better than wooden ones?      Spot on! Now, what about   fabrics  ? You both know about cotton, right? That’s what most clothes are made from.      But sometimes clothes have   spandex   in them and they stretch.      That's right! Spandex is a   synthetic fabric  , meaning it's made by humans in a factory. Natural fabrics like   wool  ,   silk  , and   cotton   come directly from animals or plants. Silk comes from   caterpillars  , by the way, and wool from   sheep  .      Wool feels softer than stringy things like cotton.      Yes, and wool can trap   heat  , which is why it’s good for winter. Cotton is cooler, so used in summer clothes. But now, in the Minecraft world, we were introducing a   new resource   called   legend  , which is like a   mistake from history  , a kind of   invented legend   that looks real!

Right, I swear I haven't seen anything bad on my feed since I blocked that last account. But like... every time I go out with the group chat, I feel like someone's watching      Aye, honestly I don't even know what you look for on the internet anymore. Got eeny weeny passive rabit on my twitch and that's it.      I mean yeah, but I still get the creeps sometimes. You remember that thing last year with Dan’s place?      Oh for god’s sake, don’t start with that again. He needs to sort it out, not us.      I only say because some of us are kids, like, under 18 and stuff. It makes us scared, y’know?      Yeah, but he’s sorted most of it by now. Probably better than when we started college. Look at us now, alright?      True, we have been through a lot together. Still, I miss when we were just like, doing outdoor things, smoking under the stars and playing shuffleboard in the bar.      Aye, remember that time we went to that little festival by the river and then lost our way back to the village?      Yeah and ended up getting lost in some creepy woods and found an apple orchard?      And then we collapsed at your place, and your mum was all “What are you lot doing on my floor?” like it was a full cosplay or something.      So much gin and apple tea that day.      You still have about five old Steve Roses taped all over your room, still haven’t changed them.      Guilty. Not like I've got better taste now, anyway.      True story. Speaking of, you passed that music theory exam, mate.      Oh yeah! Was easy, but I only scraped a B.      You’ll get an A next time.      Aye, if I do the next class, which is delivering something around this bar. I told the tutor I go every Thursday on your back if you don’t mind      Finally, someone that will teach me the box thing      It’s called sumo technique, seriously, why are we not in rock n roll band, I mean we have this to produce slots      We do have to practice more. I’m trying to get all the chords for “Your Love is My Drug” done, but it always feels like I can’t get the pace right      Aye, you got no rhythm, but then again… you’re much better at DJing, babe.

So did you lot hear about the EPQ project deadline? Like, it's in, what, two weeks?      Yuck, yeah. I haven't even started mine. I was thinking about doing something with humanitarianism or like, fighting extreme poverty. Just like a general thing. Got eeny ideas yet?      Mine is on vegetarianism in developing countries. Like how plant-based diets can save money or reduce food waste and help people who are really struggling. It's interesting, actually. We’ve been to Montenegro and stuff, and it’s wild how different things are over there.      Oh, no way, we went to Montenegro summer before last and like, the food was amazing. I remember this one guy who cooked this huge stew, and it was all homegrown, no meat. That’s the type of thing you’re talking about, right?      Yeah, I mean, like, I used to live in Wembley and we didn’t get to see many of those places. My family would never have considered a vegetarian diet unless you were being healthy or trendy.      But it’s not trendy anymore. It’s like, genuinely a global movement. And also, like, it feels like the only sustainable future. My nan’s been vegetarian since the 60s, and she used to say it was because of the war, but now it’s different. She still thinks universities should give more vegetarian options. Like, someone at my school is doing their EPQ on that.      That’s hotter than my project. I’m just doing something on university courses—compared education systems in the UK and America. I mean, I’m not even sure why the English system is different. It just is.      I’m doing something even weirder. Like, the history of juggling, and how it was used for education in the past. Like, people used to use juggling to train brain coordination or something.      No way! I could see that from hearing you talk about it. You’re always flipping around with your keys or whatever.      Yeah, well you try delivering a presentation with three balls in the air and see go. But I think it’s cool. If it gets me an A, even better.      That’d be something. Anyway, after half-term I’m going to Cambridge for a week with my cousin. We’re pretending to look at uni open days but we’ve got a plan for sneaking into the best food places and everything.

Honestly, I don't know how anyone can live in this kitchen. The sink's full of dishes from like... last week. Someone needs to do the washing up or I will murder someone.      Look, don't start. That's the same thing you said like five minutes ago. And I'm the one who last used the dishwasher, so   technically  , it's all self-cleaning.      Ay, that's true, it’s easier said than done though, pulling dishes out of a dishwasher is still like sorting through a graveyard of pots, don't get me wrong. I like to think of it as  archaeological excavations  every time I open that thing.      Archaeological excavations? You left your week-old bottle of rum in the back of the fridge, that was a   treasure trove  , not an excavation.      I heard that, and I will say for the record, I don’t usually leave bottles of spirits lying around, even if I have to store them in the kitchen because that man of mine insists on keeping all his inappropriate photos in the drawer next to the cutlery.      That’s wild. You live at home, how are you even allowed to put sensitive content in national service – er… flat storage? I mean, I barely store  toothpaste  without being yelled at by my mum.      Oh, don’t talk about your mum. Our parents all think we're geniuses because we made it into this place, but no one tells them that yes, this is   university  , and no, I will not be  home-schooled  in domestic responsibility.      I know right? I had this conversation with my mum literally yesterday and she said “Oh love, I left the handle of the kettle onཀ that’s just a  very  wet lesson for you.”      Wow, sounds like a modern-day parenting survival guide. I mean, I tried using the kettle when I first got here. It didn't  start a fire , but I fried two eggs in the kettle and it whistles now like some kind of demonic toaster.      Okay, the kettle is cursed go back to the pond it came from.      Can someone explain? Why are you all yelling in the kitchen? I just came from bed and you people are talking about  kettles and demonic appliances  like it's some kind of horror movie.      Oh, over here, we've moved on from missing socks and the ghost of whoever last used the toaster.

So did you get the turkey sorted for Christmas yet, Nana? I know it's still October, but... you and Grandad always start planning early.      Oh, I did last week, love. I had to drive up to Torbay Market at seven in the morning to make sure it was organic and free-range, like you both insisted!      And let me tell you—it didn’t come cheap, but your dad got a bit grumpy when we had that sad-looking bird in 2020.      Didn’t your dad get the smallest one ever? I was three or four and couldn’t believe it. I thought someone must’ve accidentally given Grandad a baby turkey.           Oh yes, you flew into the kitchen shouting, “Grandad, is this a   chicken?  ” It was darling, honestly. Made better memories than most turkeys, I’d say. Anyway... I’m thinking this year’s theme should be “travel fairs and family quirks,” since it’s your first real Christmas with us over from Lisbon, yes?      I mean, we land a week before and spend a few days on the coast, but yeah… watching us try to remember where we put all our Christmas traditions. Back in Portugal they have “Noche de Roldán,” which is basically a big dinner and dance before Christmas Eve, and it’s wild. I’m already foreseeing a massive culture clash when I want to dance at the dinner table!      Oh, just don’t start a tango in the middle of our dining room and I’ll be happy. Can’t have the floorboards buckling because of a flaminco fit.      But honestly, it’s lovely you’re bringing a bit of your life here. I love hearing about the school you teach at, by the way. My, you've made quite the leap from Torquay grammar to giving grammar lessons to 20-somethings in Lisbon!      I know, mad, isn't it? I tutored at home as well, but once I went abroad, I thought “why not do it properly?” And it's brilliant—my students come from everywhere. Last week, I had a Brazilian guy who asked me if “phrasal verbs” were made of cheese. Imagine that!      Oh, bless him. Must’ve heard you mention “cheese” somewhere!      Well, you know, Lisbon is lovely, but I’ve missed the hills, and the cold, and honestly, the weird little traditions. Like... my partner tried to make a mince pie and thought it was just jam.

Dad, I can't believe we're finally sitting in your car. Two years, Dad! Two years. I got used to not seeing you after I moved to Finland.      Aye, it's been a proper while. Look at you—tall, broad-shouldered. Got a bit of a  broad  look about you. Still got your sense of style, though. Looking clean. A university teacher, now? Proper professional. I’m proud, lad.      Thanks! You’d be surprised how hard it is to teach people how to say  proper  quantifiers. Russian students think  some  is plural, and Italian ones just scream when you correct their  present perfect .      Ha! Yeah, I used to do bits on the phone—customer service, mostly. I’ll be the first to say, I was far better at giving advice than taking it. But then I had a bad back... doc said I needed to slow down.      You always had a back problem. Did you ever see a physio or just, like, grit your teeth and shuffle about?      A bit of both, lad. Tell you what, this area used to be quieter. Suddenly, all these young folk moving in—start-ups, new cafes, even a yoga studio on the high street. You'd have been in the middle of it all!      It’s changed? I mean, in Finland someone said Crayford was suspiciously posh for a place just outside London. I said, “Well, is it not in London?” and they said no, and I had to Google it at 2 in the morning.      Hah, typical. You always were a slow learner when it came to geography. Not that I blame you. The problem is, all these new folks, they don’t know the rules. There’s more speeding, more people driving without licenses. You know they told me last week there was a van driver caught without a valid one—some dodgy European kid, he was.      Oh great, add that to the list. I took the flight over, you remember, after I nearly caused a diplomatic incident with an American guy over  Game of Thrones ?      You’re joking. What’d he do?      Called Ramsay Bolton a  “man of principle.”  I looked him in the eye and asked him if he’d had belly surgery. He still sent me a Christmas card over Zoom.      God bless the internet. Speaking of, did you get that new phone I sent you?      Yeah, very smooth.

So did you manage to sort out that public relations meeting with the student societies?      Yeah, I sorted it out with the president today. She seems keen—said she wanted to put a student perspective in the university brochure or something like that.      That sounds promising. I think having more student voices in the marketing material could really make the university feel more accessible.      Definitely. I just wish more of the admin team saw it that way. Last week’s session with the PR department was full of "we always do it this way" stuff. Utterly stifling.      I know, it's the same in the arts faculty. I tried suggesting more informal lectures, where students could bring their own music and discuss the art scene in the city. Darcy, the head of marketing, turned me down—said it was "unprofessional"!      I mean, everyone has a different view of what professionalism is. I remember when we used to have flashlights and laptop speakers in the lecture theatre for that "vibe".      Oh yes! I can still hear your terrible 80s mix when we did that session on postmodernism—it was basically a DJ night in a classroom.      Hey, that was iconic, and I know for a fact some of the students still dance to those tunes when they study at home.      True. Anyway, did you do that shopping for the houseplants I mentioned earlier?      Yes, I did. Found a nice pair of snake plants and a couple of ferns. I had to wait a while because most places were out of stock—Turns out “indoor jungles” are in.      Perfect. I love the idea of making this place feel greener. I feel like every time someone comes over they comment on how light and alive it's starting to feel.      It's all the talking to the plants, isn’t it? I’ve started to talk to them every morning as though they’re colleagues trying to network.      Now if only they responded, you could get a grant for it. I told you the psychology guy's always on the lookout for bizarre studies.      Yeah, he came to me with this idea about plants reacting to music. He wants me to stream all my worst Spotify playlists to the ferns and measure leaf growth.      True experiment. Just don’t let “80s Throwbacks and Tears” near the plants—remember what happened to that cactus last time?

Rather annoying isn't it, this thing.      What's annoying?      This shower curtain. It's see-through and I can't see the shop where we got it to swap it.      Oh that's a problem. We could buy a new one if you liked, we’ve got some spare cash this week.      I’ve been thinking about it. I actually wanted this one because it had these little flowers on it, which match the bathroom tile.      Didn’t it look a bit… kitschy to you?      Kitschy no, it's the décor, don’t you think it’s well done? Just a bit too much jelly to the shower curtain.      You're telling me, and I think the kids might be laughing at it too.      I heard them whispering this morning. "Look Mom, there’s a flower in the shower again!"      Well maybe we can replace it with something less see-through and still have flowers on it?      That’d be great. I’ve been knitting a new bean bag too, in blue—it should go well.      Excellent. Looking forward to it. But first, let’s actually make the supper tonight.      All right, what do you want? I’ve got some chicken thighs and we can make a quick pasta.      Sounds good to me. It just needs some sour cream on top and a bit of cheese.      I was thinking about that too. Maybe add some garlic and about half a tin of tomatoes.      We can mix it up a little by adding some capers. Not too much mind you, just a little for flavor.      I like that. It will make it a bit more interesting.      You know, I once had a recipe that used capers and olives together. It was a bit of a weapon of mass destruction.      A bit of a bomb? Was it good?      Actually, it was brilliant. Just go easy on the olives if you don’t want it to be too briny.      Right, I’ll bear that in mind. Can you chop the garlic while I get the pasta and start the chicken frying?      Of course. Do you want some chips with this too?      I’m not entirely sure yet. I’ve done chips often lately and I thought I’d try something different, maybe baked sweet potato wedges.      That’s a good idea. They go well with pasta, and they’re much better for you.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You think when you get old they’d just leave you be, but no, still got to fill in forms and make phone calls. This pension business is a right muddle.      Oh, I know what you mean, dear. I was trying to get through to the NHS last week about my medication and it nearly gave me a heart attack. All these automated systems and no real person to speak to!      You’re not the first to be frustrated. We’ve all got to get used to the way things are done now. Efficiency over compassion, I’m afraid. Still, at least you don’t have to deal with supply chains like I do in my business.      Supply chains? I thought you just ran a shop from the high street.      Pretty much. It’s a little gift shop and coffee kiosk. But no—there’s this company in Manchester I get my novelty mugs from, and they keep getting delayed, ordering online’s a nightmare. They tell me it’s international shipping, one thing and another—my stock’s running low and I can’t keep telling customers “I don’t know when they’ll get here.”      Sounds like quite a task. Mind you, I remember when I used to childmind, people still used paper cards for birthdays and thank yous. Now it’s all emails and message apps.      Everything’s been modernised, but not always in a good way. Let me tell you about the time I tried to order a pair of shoes from the internet. It said three days delivery and they never came. Eventually I got them, but it took nearly three weeks!      That’s the other downside of automation. It’s efficient for the company, but not so much for the customer. Mind you, I can’t complain with the business I’ve had since the weather’s been nice. People seem keener to come out and about these days.      That’s lovely to hear. I hope you’re enjoying it as much as you can. It’s always been a dream of mine to run a place like that, but I never had the courage.      Courage’s not the word for it, love. Planning and organisation are key. But I suppose I’m not the one that runs a business—just sit around on the sofa these days with a cup of tea and watch the rain.

Right, I just texted the supermarket to request a delivery for tomorrow. That’ll save us a trip on Christmas Eve and give us more time to get ready.      That’s a good idea, Lucy. Though we do need the mince pies from the deli in Rochester — the ones on the shelves there just don’t cut it for the family.      Oh, I’ve ordered extra online. They deliver to the door and I’ve had good service before.      You can’t just order the same stuff online — it’s not the  same  as picking the actual mince pies! Dad still thinks no one makes them like Mrs Reynolds’ shop.      That’s because they don’t! Mrs Reynolds is magic. Maybe I should persuade her to take on an apprentice and open in Ashford?      Honestly, forget the mince pies. I’m more curious about everyone returning after their little Christmas adventures. I hear the Smiths went to Barcelona to see family.      Nancy, I think you do tell, don’t you? Lucy, their daughter, refuses to speak a word to her aunt and only pretends to like her cousin.      Oh, that’s got to be dramatic — denying your aunt and pretending to like the cousin? I wouldn’t have the guts. I’d just stay in and write haikus about the coast.      Ha! Now there’s someone who could publish a book.      Maybe one day. I’m working on something for a new client — wants to launch a tea brand called  Cultural Infusions . Insane name, about half as interesting as the actual tea.      It’s tea — what more could you ask for?      The twist is it’s marketed as “ethical” for hipsters. I’m supposed to make it sound like drinking it will save the world.      Tea saving the world — I’ll believe it when I see the profit margins as  ethical  as the branding!      Grumpy one today, Nancy?      No, I’m just saying — the world is still goin’ on with or without your tea. Still, at least it’s not in the news that  everything  is ruined this week.      So, have you made the Christmas cards yet? We need to collect those off the printers by next week.      I did mine last month — green cards with snowflakes and handwritten addresses. I got so bored writing "23 Ash House, Ashford, Kent, UK" for 58 times.      You’re bribing your friends to let you send them by hand next year, aren’t you?

So do you go out often on Sunday mornings      Well it's such a beautiful morning I got up rather early this morning went for a run down by the sea then had a quick shower and then thought why not come up and knock on your door as you were staying near the place I was staying and saw the place from the outside the other night and thought I'd like to try it      A lot of people would      And then you turn into a coffee shop like it's just you know it's got like this old outside bit with the pot plants and the stones and everything but it's brand new inside      What is it like inside      It's got this really modern seating and like bursts of like bottle green paint on the walls and the lighting is all very low but it's very very cozy you feel like you're in one of those breakfast clubs in old London except this one everyone has a beard in it and they all wear the oversized lumberjack shirts you know the kind that make them look like they're wearing pyjamas over trousers      Oh right      But as to the food and the coffee well it's quite different in here      Oh yeah      My latte came with a cinnamon stick and some kind of star anise powder on top and the apple muffins they have here have like a chocolate drizzle and some orange zests on them      That sounds nice      It does but oddly sour at the same time      What else is here      Well in the evenings it becomes a kind of live music bar where the same biker types come in and then have wings and burgers and things and some local cabaret acts you know the kind of thing where the lead singer puts the mic in her wine glass and pours wine into her glass and then drinks it all and shows her cleavage it's a bit too much for me      You mustn't come too often then as you're only being asked out once in a lifetime lunches      That happened last year with Ann's sister and a couple of other people like that the dinner was intended go out of my way to be something special      I see      And the box was delivered on a Monday your actual birthday was the Tuesday

Rather skip the new bar and go to our usual spot.      Yeah it's like... What was the name of it.      Erm The Lanterns or something like that.      Was it in the Grand Hotel.      Yeah I think that's right yeah we used to go there on our days off.      I remember that.      Yeah this new place it's quite a few blocks away from here isn't it and we walked past it the other night.      Mm looks grim.      Yeah it looks dead.      Yeah and another thing is the beers that they serve are four quid each.      Tenr I think.      Yeah and I think the food is up to an absolute nose.      Yeah it is yeah.      Hmmm in fact at the end of the day we thought, you know, spare a few hours and why not go for that.      Yeah.      I mean if we're not going to go to The Lanterns, what are we going to do on a Thursday night.      So is that what we decided then.      Yeah because the other bars around are the ones you dance in.      Yeah.      We might as well carry on in this walk at full pace to get back to the hotel.      Yeah definitely.      I just hope the pollution doesn't get too bad.      Erm it might about now actually I think I can smell it from here.      Mm what's that.      Erm the smog the air pollution.      Yeah I can feel it already.      Yeah and it's been a bit of a problem this week.      I know when I went out this morning to buy a coffee I came back with a sore throat.      Ugggh the same with me. My voice sounds like a smokers.      That's because go out of the room and you suffocate straight.      Yeah it is yeah that's why we were thinking of going to cafes near your place instead of the Grand Hotel.      Yeah I think that's a good idea maybe even take a walk to the park we saw the other day.      Yeah the one with the green lake.      Yeah the one where we saw the old woman throwing things in the lake.      It was kind of weird.      Yeah it was but I liked it.      I would've gone up to her and asked her what she was doing with the goat bones.      Yeah and her goat was practically looking at you the whole time.

Right, I just took the chicken out the oven — anyone fancy a bit of extra mint sauce with theirs? I got the recipe from one of those old cookery books I found at the charity shop. Proper classic stuff.      No, I’m good thanks — although now you mention it, that does sound nice. I’ve been living on toast and cereal this week. My fridge’s been completely empty since I’ve been working from home so much.      Oh, you should’ve seen my lunch today! Just a sandwich with the crusts cut off and no filling. I was too busy rewatching that series again,  Peaky Blinders . God, I’ve only watched it eight times now.      You left your laptop on the table, by the way — I almost spilled the gravy on it. Honestly, you spend more time with that show than you do with breakfast, don’t you?      I’m not too far behind you, Elaine. I’ve rewatched it at least five times. That Cillian Murphy—charming and deadly, all in one. Although, I have to say, your chicken is distracting me from grief of the show. Tell me you’re not watching it during dinner!      No chance. I already missed three seasons while I was in school, so I’m trying to catch up. But seriously, Sarah, your chicken is  amazing . What’s the secret? I swear, yours never turns out like this when I try!      Honestly, just let it rest a bit before you carve it — it’s the little things. And mint sauce is like the  chef’s kiss . You can put about five different meals to shame with that.      I had mint sauce a few days ago at this little café in Southport. It was so unassuming, but that sauce... wow. Burgers, chicken, grilled meats — it goes with everything. I reckon we should open a business just selling mint sauce.      You’re just saying that to make me not hoard every jar I see. I've already got a new one from the Co-op in the cupboard. You think I'd risk a mint sauce outage?      Look at you two, deep in a food conspiracy. Anyone taken photos of the food? I’m being a bit of a perfectionist about it. I want to post it later — maybe get some compliments on my lack of ability to burn chicken.      True to your word, Sarah, every day a new miracle.

Have you heard about the new bus route?      No, what’s that about?      It’s this new bus that goes directly from the city centre over to the Kettle’s Yard side of things. Supposedly, it’ll save like thirty minutes for people heading between the city and the university area.      That actually sounds useful. I’m always missing that last tram when I’m trying to get back from the Press bookshop. It was packed there last week.      Oh yeah, I’ve been in there a few times too. I went in last week and just spent ages browsing. Have you read  The Philosophical Investigations  by Wittgenstein yet? They had a new edition.      I’m not reading philosophy books on the side anymore. If I turned my head to the left for about a minute at work, I get accused of being 'distracted'. Haha. Though at least I’m not getting treated like a student anymore.      That’s something, I suppose. At least you get sent on proper training courses and not left in a lecture room repeating the same thing for six hours. Honestly, I’ve been at three different universities by now and been taught the same way. How do they even call it innovation in education?      Honestly, the only real innovation I've seen is in the protests. I saw this one student at the science faculty who dressed as 'King Charles' but in protest about the tuition fees. That was chaotic but hilarious.      Ah, yeah, I saw that on Twitter. Made the local paper as well. They’re getting more creative about it. I think a lot of people are just frustrated that the real issues—like funding for research and proper mental health support—are still barely mentioned.      That’s just standard for us lot, isn’t it? All the shouting, all the posters, and by the time they’ve sorted anything, we’re already graduating or gone.      Exactly my point. It feels like being shouted at by the system with no plan for the long term. Speaking of, do you think you’d be happy moving around with another course if the system crumbles in the next five years?      Not personally—no. I’ve got that secure engineering job with a bloke who’s already your age and you still don’t know what the water conservation bill’s going to do.      It’s a contrast, innit?

So did you manage to book the table at Elsie’s? I’ve heard her crumpets are like... legend.      Yes, actually I did. I called first thing this morning and got a spot for two o’clock. Beaten the queue, like the pro I am.      Nice one, Bibi. I reckon it’s about time we all chilled a bit. A lot’s been going on since this year, honestly.      For sure. With three of us, I keep thinking what the hell did I get out of school? I used to talk about growing up and  not  worrying about where the next bit of mental stuff will come from like that My turkey on Christmas Day! Ha!      I know right? I mean, I feel old and I’m only thirty-three. Living with mental health is harder than working full time when you’ve got kids and a partner. Honestly, I used to live for the weekend and not in a, you know, wine and Instagram kind of way.      That’s the truth. Speaking of, how’s your boyfriend? Adrian, is it?      Oh, we’ve been on three dates now. He’s a games developer. So far so good – very kind, smiles a lot, and actually remembers to  wash up  the dishes. He’s not Irish, though. Silly question, I suppose, but I keep expecting him to reply in a funny accent.      Aye, and here’s the thing. Accent’s not everything, is it? Or at least… it’s not  nothing . I used to be in love with a fellow with a Geordie brogue. He ended up stealing my credit card and spending a week in Spain! Going “Where are you now?” and me going “Should be in Spain, probably, ‘cos I can’t afford it.”      Oh no, that’s a slap in the face. Sounds like a bit of a fraud. You must’ve been crushed.      Let’s just say it’s the first and  last  Englishman I ever took seriously.      So, are you two coming with us to go over Christmas on the coast? It’s going to be just us and my mum in the caravan, but we could go further afield if you wanted your own space.      Yeah, we’re thinking about it. We’ve never gone to the Lake District to celebrate, and I’ve been over this – why not? A bit different from the usual Belfast-to-Birkenhead dash.

Rather skip the car and take the walk.      That’d be mad if it was raining, but I’ll take my luck now.      Yeah, least we get some fresh air. Not like I’ve seen much of the city in recent times. Sat in my house eeny weeny passive voice all day.      You’re tellin me, I’ve been transcription all week. Not once have I said a full sentence out loud. It was easier when someone said “the cup is full” instead of “hot chase” or “cat’s fold” or whatever the hell they said.      Oh God the American accents still give me headaches. And that one chap, I’m not even sure if he’s saying “what” or “boat” half the time, and then I think he turned round and started speaking in proper English. Cats and boats. I give up sometimes.      I used to listen to the stuff and marvel at how they can even do it. I mean, why would you choose that over driving? At least if I had a car, I’d be stuck in traffic somewhere. Still, I’ve never owned one, and I’m bloody fine with it.      Me too. I mean, who needs one when you can walk, bus, or just skip?      It’s not just the cost, it’s the hassle. The insurance, the parking, the never-ending repairs someone always seems to get. And don’t even get me started on car-washing. That’s a crime against nature.      Anyway, look at all the landmarks we are passing by. I did not even know there was all this here.      Yeah, it’s quite something. Going from that Woolwich side to the O2–the transformation in that walk is like going from one city to another.      The views at the O2 would be stunning. I think I once used it as a landmark for when I was doing a Google map rush as to how far I’ve gone.      It’s one of the few places I’ve actually wanted to go to for a nice evening out with the kids. Of go there with my parents and if you ask me, they appreciated it as well. Finally, they had somewhere they could go with big enough food portions.      That’s funny, I’ve never thought of it that way. I mean, even the portion sizes there confused me. I remember asking over this one coffee, and the barista said they serve it in “cups” and they were the size of my head.

Honestly, I could just cry. I tried to get my phone fixed today and it cost more than it was worth. Just another shower of rain and now I’m down a phone and £70 poorer.      £70 seems like a lot for a repair, love. Maybe it’s time for a newer model? I don’t use one much these days, but I still get on alright with a basic one.      Oh, I got a new one last week. It came in that little pink box with the cloud on the front. Didn’t even want to spend that much either, but the old one had stopped working altogether—literally wouldn’t turn on.      Ugh, what’s wrong with technology these days? I left mine in the back pocket, didn’t drop it, didn’t push buttons—just gave up on me. It used to be harder to break things back when, you know, things had real switches and buttons.      And speaking of things that give up on us—it rained again today. I tried to take the kids for a walk, and within five minutes, both their nappies were soaked.      It’s deadly for mums in this weather—it always has been. I remember when I got married in 1989 and it rained, and I had to borrow an umbrella from the vicar. It was so long he nearly drowned trying to hold it over both of us.      Haha, sounds like my grandad’s wedding. Anyway, have you thought about doing a swimming lesson? They’d love it. Or at least get a ‘build a bear’ for your little one?      I’m thinking about the bear. My little one’s had this obsession with fluffy stuff. She even sleeps with her old toys that barely have ears left. I think she believes that the bear will ‘protect her’.      Aww, that’s sweet. My grandkids would sleep holding any bloody rag I stitched up and call it ‘Mr. Blanket’. We just nod and smile.      Honestly, I’d kill to have that kind of imagination now. I can’t even bear to remember my childhood bear—it got lost in the laundry somewhere.      Anyway, enough about bears. Sports day is next week and I’ve got that to prepare for. That bloke on the council said they’re going to put in a new surface at the park—so we might actually get to play football dry for once this year.

So, I’ve been doing a fair bit of thinking about where we’re at. We’ve got this house here in the outback—quiet, beautiful—but I don’t know how long we can keep this as “the forever thing.” What do you think?      Honestly, I’ve felt the same. It  is  beautiful, and the time here has been good for us… for me. A bit of a break from the whirlwind of my job, school, everything. It was what I needed. But now we need to think about what comes next.      Exactly. I like to think of life in phased adventures. This was our “off-grid, reconnect with yourself” chapter. But what’s the next one? I’m thinking of starting a new branch of the business—maybe something sustainability focused, given how I’ve been seeing the local markets here in Australia. What about you? Your postgrad studies—maybe you want to go back into teaching in a new system, or maybe something completely different?      I’ve been considering that too. I mean, the education system here is very different from the one I left in England. I did do some online teaching during the pandemic, which gave me an idea—it would be nice to design a blended learning program, something that supports teachers in remote communities with curriculum resources, maybe even virtual support. It’s not the typical teacher job, but that’s what I want.      That sounds incredible, and it's something that contributes in a real way. And you know me—I like to build things. I could see us combining the two—maybe a community-focused education startup, focusing on rural and remote areas in both Australia and New Zealand.      That could work! But what about our personal lives? I’ve been thinking… if we’re going to make a long-term plan, we should also consider the family piece. I’d love to start planning for kids. Are you on board with that idea?      Absolutely. I’ve never looked at them as waiting till I “arrived” in business. I believe in doing things  with  the people you love, not just after. I do think, though, we set a tone around them growing up—staying grounded even as the business expands. Balance matters more than ever.      Completely. And I’d like to go further than that. I’ve met some amazing local teachers and Indigenous leaders here, and I think there’s genuine value in those connections, maybe even for future trips to include the kids in cultural understanding programs—learning while we travel.

Right, I just texted my gran to see when she’s coming over to her house tomorrow. She wanted to come and pick some apples from the tree at the bottom of our garden, apparently she saw a bunch of birds eating them and she’s not happy.      Apples? Why not just go and buy some from Costa then? Not like you haven’t got the money to do that?      Yeah, I mean this is the same gran who thinks you’ve to put a coat on if it’s thirty degrees outside. She doesn’t chase trends, she chases comfort.      Still, I reckon she probably fancies a walk out in the woods. It’s like that My Name Is Earl bit, you know, the bit where the bird steals the nut from the squirrel or whatever, and then the squirrel chases after it. It’s like that every weekend at her place.      Fair. I bet she clocks the whole lot, the apple pickin’, the bird-watching lot. Also, I once saw her throw a stale Waterford biscuit at a magpie in the garden. I mean full-on flung it like a ninja and missed by two inches.      GIRL. She’s taught me how to do that too – but I’m better. I got a pigeon once off the kitchen window.      You’re like the Silly Stones of the village aren’t you? Only, they never managed this.      Just because you live in the village doesn’t mean you can throw biscuits at wildlife, though. That’s real bad manners, I reckon. You’d be in so much trouble at Appleby with that.      Oh come on, Appleby vibes be like  Wait, you threw a biscuit at a bird?  And the student be all  But I found it on the floor!       So true. I reckon you’d get it in your Comfort score too. First-years always get docked for little stuff like that. Not to mention you’d end up being asked out by the groundskeeper.      Okay, but the main thing here is, are you going with her tomorrow? She’s gonna need goin’ with. She doesn’t like going up the hill alone and I’m sure as hell not driving.      I might. Yeah. It’ll be nice to get out of the flat for a bit. I’ve been cooped up all week doing audit stuff. I feel like I’m either at the Fitbit office or the Costa.

Rather skip the newfit and go to the original.      Mm, they’re like... What was the word she used?      “Gloriously chaotic”?      “Gloriously chaotic,” yes—exactly.      She’s beginning to sound like the kind of woman you find handed over to someone at the Royal Free.      What, if they think she might be a threat to herself or others?      Or just to the sanity of the people around her. But, no, she’s not mad... Not mad in the traditional sense. She’s just a bit... What’s the word?      My turkey came out undercooked last time though.      I’m not surprised.      I think I turned the timer off thinking I was about to put something else in when, no—fool me once, shame on me.      That is a tragedy, Ken. You have to get that under control. Or at least invite us over for puddings.      Yeah, I’m with Aunty Brenda. You might need a kitchen shepherd. Someone there in case you misfire.      That way we can at least have something besides cold mash and tepid sauce.      You weren’t there. All that turkey juice and the heat was beautiful. And the gravy! I made a good attempt at gravy.      Yes, but it was a bit blue.      Only slightly—there was a red streak as well.      I don’t know how you two have about five decades of conversation between you and not the other one’s watching the other.      That would be because I know when to step back. You don’t.      Oh, I like arguing with her.      And I prefer to argue with you both. It’s like three very intense witches in a pot waiting to happen.      What I’m curious about is whether the two of you plan a new big project next year.      Still trying to get around this idea of a manor house in gothic details on the coast if you don’t mind.      Ken, I’m not even going to begin to imagine something like what your head’s coming up with. I can hardly cope with this kitchen’s chaos.      Just because it’s a manor house in your head does not mean the real one has to be that grand. I can see it being quite creaky.      Listen, if it’s on the coast and comes with a garden and isn’t used by any academics, it could be just the escape we all need.

So did you talk to your uni about the whole module drop thing then?      Yeah... I did. But they’re just like, “You could still take it, you’d only be a year older!” Like, I don’t care about being a year older. I just don’t want to feel like I  have  to be there all day.      Yeah, I get that. I mean, I’m doing this foundation year, right, but honestly, I don’t know if it’s for me either. I just keep thinking, what if I’m wasting a year doing something I’m not even sure I want to do?      That’s how I felt like last term. Just sat there in lectures, thinking, “I could be working, or volunteering, or just lying on a beach somewhere in Cornwall.”      Oh, wait, Cornwall’s not even near Falmouth anymore? I’m confused. I grew up thinking I was the  most  south-western person I knew. But then I met someone from Land’s End and I just,  [personally falls silent] . I mean, Falmouth’s beautiful though. I used to go kayaking in the estuary—it was the only time I ever went without falling in.      No falling in, and actually kayaking? Sounds like a miracle. In Liverpool, I did all my ‘water adventures’ in the local canal. My grandad had this tiny old rowing boat full of fishing gear. I’d paddle around like I was doing some massive expedition. Some pigeon had the audacity to crap on my head once through the ceiling of the shed he kept it in.      That pigeon was  trying  to ruin your childhood. [Laughs.] Honestly though, your name—you know that was like some big family drama, right?      Yeah, like, my grandad wanted to call me Mavis. And my mum was like, “Absolutely not.” So it was this intense debate, and my little sister was born after me, so they had to do the same with her. She’s called Janice and wears cardigans with opals in. My grandad lost a bet.      Oh no go—opals? My nan had a clip with an opal in it once. I tried to take it and it sliced my finger off. I had to go to A&E. I was seven and looked like a serial murderer with my hand bandaged up and all this blood on the way.      That’s horrific. Is that true?

Oh my god, it’s been ages! I can’t believe we haven’t done this in like, what, over a year?      Blows my mind, honestly! Life just gets busy, doesn’t it? I’ve been buried in work at Pearson, like all the time. Campaigns, social media, the usual madness. How about you?      Yeah, I’ve been swamped too. Project management is a beast, honestly. Constantly rushing between meetings, pulling spreadsheets, and trying to remember to eat. Ugh. But Oxford? This place is beautiful—we used to wander around here as students.      Right? I still can’t believe we went to the same university and only met late in the second year. Remember when we both had to present in the same lecture hall and I spilled my coffee?      Oh wait,你是ש breakfast, no—maybe I'll just go for a drive in the evening."      沉默 for a second? Are you Chinese?      No, no, I meant "sprinkle"! Bah, my French is so rusty. I only speak it when I binge-watch French films on Netflix now. But it’s such a struggle—I want to keep my language skills up, but I’m still figuring out the best way.      Oh, you know what might help? I actually went back to Folkestone a few weekends ago just to visit my sister. We had such a calm, laid-back catch-up over sourdough bread and herbal tea. I think getting out of the city is so essential for me right now.      That does sound heavenly. I miss living near the sea. We were talking about thatched houses the other day—you know that place you told me about with the ivy-covered walls?      Oh you mean that cottage near Bexhill with the wild garden? My mum used to take us there as kids. We’d always hide under the little willow tree by the shed. Those were the days.      I’m a little jealous of your childhood memories! My parents never really took us to anything like that growing up in the West Midlands. I remember one visit to a manor house though…      Which one? Hopefully not Littlestone—my dad hated that place.      No, I think it was in Buckinghamshire, near where I grew up. There were these old stables we used to explore every summer. I always imagined they were haunted.      I love that! Kids often do love the weird and spooky stuff.

Right Aaron, I've just done my weekly sorting of post. A few bills, a couple of coupons—nothing much to worry about really. You've ordered more than I'd ever thought someone would want, though. Five boxes came with your name on 'em.      Yeah, most of it’s from Amazon, I think. It was all handed over to me by my mates last week—they let me have their accounts for a while before they deleted their socials.      For 'a while'? You mean you’ve been ordering stuff from people you don’t even know now? That’s like asking for a heap of mess when they sort it out. What did you get?      A bunch of stuff really—a jellycat plush, a starter bottle of aftershave, and a few bits of gaming headsets. They said I can take whatever was in the Amazon ‘Delivery for You’ boxes while it’s active.      Aftershave and gaming kit? You look after them both equally so I suppose. But you still need to learn how to shop, luv. eBay’s not too bad if you know what you’re doing. Did you know you can bid as well as shop on there?      No, I just press ‘Buy it Now’. But I’ve seen my mam bid on stuff on there. She once got an apple pie tin for next to nothing.      That’s the secret—look for what someone’s selling and ask yourself if you’d pay that much for it second-hand. I buy bits for my kid at home. Or I try to. The problem is, half the time people are selling stuff they made about five minutes ago.      Like what?      There was one lot of 'vintage-style' mugs. They were so new that the smell of glaze was still on them. And they passed them off as 'hand-painted by a local artist'. If you asked me, they probably stared at them for five seconds with a stick while saying “never fear… art’s here!”      That sounds like one of the fake Etsy muggers. Still, I got a nice headstamp on the gaming headset one go. Worked for a fiver. If I go wrong, I just chuck it in the bin.      You’ll learn your limits with time. I’ve been doing it for years and still manage to get the wrong size, or even the wrong type of item sometimes.

Rather a lot of changes in the world these days, ain't there luv? Felt like when I were young, the world changed slowly—longer to find out what was what.      I know what you mean, Grandad. Some things move so fast now you can hardly keep up. Work is like that—last week I was managing production on paper, and now they expect me to do it all through some app. Not exactly intuitive.      Haha, yeah, pulling teeth with those gadgets. I was trying to set up the bloody internet last week and gave up after half an hour. Told me granddaughter to sort it. Bit cheeky the way, mind you. "If you don’t want to keep changing, you should've left it like it was," I said.      [Laughs] That’s the grandparent comeback of the year, honestly. But honestly, I envy you a bit. I mean, you had time in your life to just be part of a slower rhythm, didn’t you? I feel like I'm always on the go.      Oh, I didn’t say I liked it, mind. Left to my own grief when I were younger, too. Long-term unemployed, never proper work, and then all the way to retirement without much to show for it. Sometimes, I think it would've been easier if the world didn't keep shifting so much.      I never thought about it that way, Grandad. You've got stories and experiences—those don’t die just because time moves forward.      Yeah, but some of us don’t get remembered through TikTok or Facebook! Most people are out there trying to get noticed, and we're the ones living the past.      Well, you can always write your memoirs. Type it up and have it printed up for family to read. That’s got to be easier than sending texts!      Haha, yeah, I’d still probably have to ask the grandkids to write them for me. I could stick the bits about queens and that—"Elizabeth gave me a bit of a slap for something once," that sort of thing.      [Laughs] Then you're already halfway there with the content. Look, I’ll tell you what—I’m going to give you a laptop one day, no excuses. We'll go through it together, slowly. Maybe we'll make you a blog about life in 1960s London. You could talk about pubs, markets, your dad’s old collier bike...

So do you lot reckon we should fly on Christmas Day or do we try and get the train through? I’d quite like to chill out with a drink at 10,000 feet over the Channel and not be sweating with a backpack full of auntie’s knick-knacks.      I thought  you  were the one who said airplanes make you panic about all the fake eyelashes you’ve glued on by mistake?      Well, easier said than done when I’ve got to be in my nan’s kitchen at 9 am for the stuffing. She still thinks “veal kidney stuffing” is a delicacy. Someone’s going to need heavy casualties to get out of that.      Just bring a casserole and left it in the back of the car – I’m not cooking anything this year. If I turned on a hob, I’d probably blow up the flat. I still haven’t recovered from the time I tried making Yorkshire puddings and the smoke alarm thought it was the apocalypse.      I’ll bake Christmas cake for you—no bones about it, it’s going to be good. I put in extra brandy. But you’re supplying the brandy. I’m not going out on a limb for extra festivities this year. I only have so much limelight left in me.      Yeah, no worries. Mate, you know I always carry a bottle or two in case of emergency. Like, if there was someone who needed cheering up— but not my shift at the café.  I start at seven on Christmas Eve, and it’s a madhouse. Between tea-latte-muffin-Tuesday customers and actual humans who understand how a milk frother works, it's touch and go whether I'll be standing by midnight.      So you’re telling me it’s a  full-time job  just making people over-cappuccinated and under-confident?      It's not just the drinks. People come in mid-January waiting for a “cinnamon latte as in the middle of  Christmas ” or with lunches delivered  at 9 am . I took the omelette workshops  seriously , man.      Anyway, back to the flying thing. If we're going to fly, I'm going in separate. Last year, we tried three blokes in one car and all we ended up with was a flu pandemic and a roadkill deer in the middle of the M3. You don’t want to see the state that car was in.

Right, so we've got about 40 minutes before we have to meet her in Chester. You sorted with the WhatsApp group, or shall I ping her again?      I think we’re good, don’t worry. I’ve seen her driving—she’ll take the scenic route, probably end up in Cheshire by accident. Or somewhere very 'posh' as she calls it.      Aww, but that's one of the cool parts about this trip, right? Like pulling her out of her comfort zone and forcing her to drive through cambridgeshire.      Yeah, but it's mostly just because she still thinks everything south of Manchester is still Manchester. I've had to explain to her four times that Bicester is not actually a town in Birmingham, and I still don't know why she thought that.      It's funny, isn't it? She doesn’t have a clue about this area. Honestly, I’m not even sure she realises Cambridge is a real, full university city and not a small village like she once thought—after one visit.      Oh, I laughed when she thought the Bridge of Sighs was the real Bridge of Sighs in… Italy. I tried to correct her then, but she just looked at me like I was being dramatic.      You weren’t wrong. I mean, don’t get me wrong, the Bridge of Sighs in Cambridge is beautiful, but she said it was ‘big improvements on the original’. I said it was a bit of a stretch.      Also, I think the fact she doesn’t ‘do accents’ helps make it worse. She speaks in a very neutral way, like she's trying not to offend the Queen or something.      Oh, you know that’s because she left the north when she was like nine to do her A-Levels. She picked up that BBC voice at grammar school. She used to open her mouth and do a posh voice just to annoy her sister, I think.      She did that to me once as well. Her sister called her 'posh little bird' and now it’s an inside joke. Still, I think she’s growing on it, though. She go to a few pond life improvements and stuff.      I just love the way that she's always explaining things in such detail when what we all want is to just have a laugh and not over think it. Like, when she comes to us with all this technical analysis on accents and phonetics.

So did you lot see the new Billie Eilish track that came out this morning?      Yeah, she’s barking mad, isn’t she? I was like, what even is that at first. But then I played it again and it started growing on me.      Same, I don’t think it’s for everyone, but I’m all about that sort of weird synth vibe now. Like, I’ve been putting it on loop in my study blocks.      You mean the ones where you get zero words done, but the beat is banging? I’ve totally been there.      Guilty. I had to go back to theitunes version 'cause the YouTube one kept buffering. My phone’s a bit slow sometimes, to be honest.      Oh, you should check out my uni brother’s Spotify playlist. He’s got, like, loads of this experimental jazz with a bit of electronica. It’s the vibes!      Yeah? I’ll ask him. He’s always on about NFTs and black holes though. Like, I don’t even know why he’s still alive if he spends all his time in there.      Honestly, when he told me that stars are basically just balls of gas held together by gravity, I just thought, bro, that’s somethin’.      Oh, it’s wild, but physics isn't just all stars and gravity — there are like, everyday things. Ever seen a video of a tennis ball bouncing on a super stretchy surface? It goes like,  blop ,  blop ,  blop . Insane. I showed it to my dad the other day, and he said, “So what’s the point?” and I was like, “You’re missing the point, Dad.”      Yeah, like, you can tell your grandkids you understood basic quantum theory at 16. It’s the dream. Speaking of, I tried watching that Marvel movie with the time travel. It had like  five  endings. I ended up trying to draw the timeline on paper and had to stop myself from going back in time and delivering the ending to the director.      That one was wild, yeah. I think mine was better though — the one where they’re stuck on this alien planet and the main guy has to sing to the plants to survive. The music was so kinaesthetic, I was headbanging by the end of it.      Sounds like you bought the silence of the lambs and the  Guardians of the Galaxy  soundtrack at the same time.

Okay, so today was Balanceability. You remember what that is, right? The jumping and balancing on beams...      Yes, like when you jump forward and then you jump over me!      I fell over and got a gold star for trying again straight away.      Oh, that’s brilliant, mate! I’m proud of you both. Your teacher said that Aimee actually got the best score in her group.      She jumped over the red beam and was like "I’m the best in the world."      I did too!      That’s very bold of you both.      So what’s next week? Are we doing the pool again?      If the weather is up to it, yes. But Mummy better wear her floaty hat again. I mean, no one wants to be a soggy bottom again, do we?      I liked being a soggy bottom—especially when the puddle dog came in and splashed us.      The pool water is green sometimes, like the garden pond.      Well, that’s just chlorine. It’s for keeping it clean, okay? And speaking of water, Haylie’s mum said that her family’s new house has a manmade waterfall. Imagine that! You don’t see those every day. Like a real-life castle.      Like a fairy castle?      Yeah, something like that. But real and with fish in it.      We can have a waterfall at our house too.      We’d have to dig a hole and buy some rocks. But maybe we can draw one first.      My friend Lucy said her big brother once jumped into the garden pond and broke his leg.      You shouldn’t jump in anywhere, like when you go to the pool. We have to wait for the yellow line to say it’s safe.      Exactly! That’s why the teachers always say you must never jump in unless it’s a proper depth.      But if you jump in gently like Mummy does, you can go all the way to the bottom.      Yeah, but only if you can swim and know the depth.      I want to go to Japan to see the cats.      Oh, do you mean National Cat Day? You know that’s not a real national day in Japan, but they do love their cats there.      My cat, Mr. Whiskers, can jump over me, just like in Balanceability.      Can he do backflips?      No, but he tries to climb the bookshelf every day.      Maybe we should teach him how not to fall.

So did you go for that cycle ride weekend?      No, it rained like...  shook head dramatically  I was already feeling down about missing a gym session, and then I see it’s pissing it down. Was not happening.      Haha yeah I saw the forecast, I thought about it but didn’t feel like getting all muddy and then not having a clean pair of trousers for work on Monday. Proper Yorkshire weather, innit?      Oh you! You and your Yorkshire attitude. “Getting muddy” – don’t make me laugh too hard, I’ve already bruised my ego enough this week with my takeaway-only diet.      My bad, my bad! I swear though, I did do a spin class on Saturday. Wasn’t too bad, I think I rode 12 miles in there while arguing with my bike instructor. She said I was “relying too much on the lights,” and I was like,  sheets , I can barely see my own hands in the dark.      That’s because your gym is in a derelict warehouse two streets from a train line. Did you tell her, “LOL no, I’m not risking getting run over in the dark just to burn 50 calories”?      Something like that. But I’ve had a rough week. All that event planning and phone calls? I’m already foreseeing a massive breakup, just from misreading someone’s calendar invite.      Agh, don’t start on that drama again. Also, have you seen Connor recently?       Sipped coffee  Only at Appleby’s birthday last week. He brought round the most insane Mexican takeout—like they had  chips with mole sauce  and dip. I’m still dreaming about it.      Okay, I need your guest list for that. And cut me in on the next invite.      Only if you start exercising. You can’t expect your knees to handle 12 tacos followed by 3 hours of trying to find the right Spotify playlist while balancing the chips on your head.      Fair enough. But speaking of relationships—did you really get asked out by that guy at the work function?       snorted  Yeah, bloke turned up in a kilt and asked me directly if I wanted to “take a tour of his highland cow farm” in Yorkshire. True to life?      Oh my God, did you say yes?      No, I said, “Well I’m not remotely Scottish but if you need a cow coat made, I could knit it.”

Right then, George—eat up before it goes cold. I’ve had enough of heating it through in the microwave after you pick at it for half the evening.      It’s good, Auntie Kate. Real cheesy. You don’t get this sort of crust at school pizza night.      That’s because we do things properly 'ere. Full cheese, full chilli flakes, a clean conscience. Now, your Uncle Rod’s told me he’s taking you out for fish and chips next week to celebrate the Domino Drive. I hope you're going to behave, or the man won’t show you another shop window again.      Now, now. I’ve only shown her two window displays that one visit, and I’ve already explained to her how a qualified haulier knows the difference between a DHL and a Fed-Ex van. You’re welcome to learn, lass.      I don’t need to learn about vans, I need to learn about motorbikes. There’s this new one at the shop—and it’s not like the ones Dad rides.      Oh, it’s not the one I drive, no. I’ve still got my bike in the shed, but it’s a proper trail machine, not some flashy thing from the showroom. Though if your Matey here wants a real ride, I might just pull it out. Let’s see if he’s got the knees for it.      And bring your riding sense, George. Last week at Dominoes, you dropped a cheese-and-pickle sandwich on a lady’s lap. Some Christmas spirit, that.      That wasn’t  my fault ! The conveyor belt wobbled and I swear I saw something shiny fly off the edge! She said it was “the most festive slip-up of the year.” Proper laughs.      Aye, but that’s the thing ‘bout Domino Drives. There’s always chaos, food, and someone’s trying to win the raffle. I nearly won last year with that novelty bacon sandwich waiting to happen. We lost to Ian and Dawn. They’ve got a shelf full of those lunches now.      Now, the next thing you tell me is you’re trying to get into the Domino CEO raffle. That one’s life-changing, or at least gives you a year of dentists, holidays, and maybe a motorbike.      Yeah, but I need 100 vouchers. I’ve only got two. And I can’t just ask people at Domino to buy them for me.

Rather annoying isn’t it? I swear I put the kettle on five minutes ago.      Well, I’ll tell you something, I’d much rather wait a few extra minutes for a decent cup of tea than rush to some pub like I used to at uni. No offence, but student pubs are all the same—loud, sticky floors, and overpriced.      Oh I agree. A lot’s changed since we were at uni, hasn’t it? I’ve not been into that bar scene since we moved to Cambridge. Everything here is more chilled, don’t you think?      Yeah, definitely. I mean, pubs here are nice—cosy, quiet, and they usually serve turkey on toast. Still, I miss the chaos a bit. Remember when we used to try to get into the place off campus because the bouncers were doing a dress code? We turned up in fancy dress and then spent half the night trying to find our friends in the crowd.      Oh god, I remember that! We came as Mary Poppins and Michael Caine, if you can believe it. And the guy in full pirate gear said he was going to spit-roast us for being too mainstream. It was disastrous—and hilarious.      Absolute legend. Even Mateo showed up in a superhero outfit, because he’s  that  charming.      Speaking of which, have you seen the latest press about him? He’s doing some charity food festival in Spitalfields—sounds boring, but I reckon it’ll be oddly fun. You’d probably like the vegetable stall. Or the celebrity chef being their usual snarky self.      I did see that. Honestly, the guy’s the most exciting vegetable he’s had in years must be kale—he fails at it. But you’re right, it is a fun idea. I do miss going out for proper meals rather than surviving on toast and muesli. I’m trying to become one with a bag of kale at the moment.      You’re doing what?      I’ve taken to pretending it’s my personal trainer and it whistles at me if I eat chocolate. Still, I’m halfway through it. I think it’s got goitrogen in it or something. Not sure if it’s trying to kill me or motivate me.      You’re mad. But your research is about obesity markers, right? Maybe you should just eat one normal meal and start writing something?

Right, I just shouted "dancing" and they gave me five looks like I'd grown a second head... What was I thinking? I’m not even halfway down my clue path yet.      You were probably overthinking it. Look, when you shout random stuff like "Deer dancing"—do you mind?!—it kind of breaks the moment. But if it helps, your "fluffy dog with no legs" is starting to worry me a bit more.      Let me guess—was it "animal in the snow"? Because that could’ve literally been a reindeer. You just... didn’t add enough rein.      Look, the real problem here is that some of us are more experienced than others. I’m still waiting for someone to give me a clue for "sand castle" that doesn’t end up in the world of pirate-related anagrams for about 20 minutes. I still haven’t recovered from that.      Oh don’t get me started. There was this one time back in the 80s, I was in a Waterstone’s shop, and I played this with my cousins. I gave the clue "house in the water"—and for  45 minutes , they didn’t get it. We literally had to look it up. And remember – no internet in those days! So I think it's important to support each other.      And what did you end up doing then, Bryn? Did you pay the bill for the someone who found it for you?      It was Waterstone’s. They didn’t sell the dictionary. It was a bit of a hill I had to climb with a horse and cart, most likely about forty miles through the heather. But the point is: take your time. Clue-givers: be clear. Clue-takers: be patient. And  definitely  do not laugh at someone who says "pokey man in the tree".      That was me. And it was "Peter Pan." I tried to be subtle.      Subtle as a rhino being gently herded through a London museum, yes.      I love it when people think they're being clever with their clues and the rest of us go straight into the pond of confusion. This one time – and I swear this is not fake news – I tried to go with "box on head" and they spent ten minutes guessing “bunny” and “hat” and “boxer” and never once thought of “bowler hat.” I was devastated.      Or "baker." That’s got a hat and a box and they often wear them kind of tight-fitting, like, on the head...

Right, I’m just saying, I do not understand how you manage to know all the cards that are left... every time I play this bloody game, I feel like I’ve blindfolded myself and thrown a dart at the deck.      Ah! C’mon now, it’s not that difficult if you  pay attention ! You know, just like teaching—when you actually listen, a miraculous thing happens: information sticks!      No, but seriously,   Speaker_1  , you haven’t even looked at the cards this round. Just kept staring out the window like you saw a ghost or something.      Look, the real ghost here is how stressed I get when Myra keeps winning. I’m a teacher, not a magician. I can’t predict the future or read minds, and I certainly can't predict what cards you lot are about to play.      You need to  engage with the game , Jo. When I was five, my nan taught me to play Whist so I could stop driving her mad by taking over the telly, and it worked!      Well, your nan was clearly a  disciplined  woman. Unlike me… I live by my own rhythm.      Ha! You know what, Jo, last night, I was making dinner and I thought I’d set the oven to 200, and I ended up putting 2000 and the whole cottage smelled like smoke and my bottom half was on fire in a metaphorical sense. So maybe  you  should watch out for what you're doing and be less surprising!      Oy, Nana Myra, you once burned the bannister trying to roast a potato. And I  saw  you. Don’t you dare gaslight me.      That was  one  time! And it was an  overheated toaster  at 6 a.m., not any fault of  mine !      Right, so while Jo and Myra bicker like they’re in a soap opera… anyone up for explaining what "go fish" actually is? Because I’m still learning these American card games!      That one time you played Go Fish and seriously went to the woods to “fish” for cards was genuinely one of the best moments of my life.      I  assure  you, Gary, I was hours away from retrieving some belly of a fish to complete the deck, metaphorically speaking.      I’m not entirely sure if I like that visual.      Honestly, it always makes me think of that one summer I went to stay with my uncle’s family in Powys before I met Jo’s husband, and this little boy— six years old —shouted that he saw a trout in the back garden and tried to cook it on the BBQ with a stick.

Okay, so I've just watched this whole series of "Bridgerton" and it's so good... but honestly, half of it is made up isn’t it?      Haha, totally! But who cares? It’s like a fairy tale for adults. And it’s nice not having to watch something  too  real for once, right? Especially this time of year… not after a week of Aunty Beverley coughing every other word.      I know! She came round and nearly gave me the flu for Christmas! I literally can’t afford that now – I’ve got three audits to finish before New Year and no flexible hours. What’s worse is my boss said I’m doing the turkey on Christmas Day because I’m “the most reliable one” – I’m not even married!      Oh no! That’s so bad – you’re only 17, you don’t even have to do that! Mum says I’m not allowed to cook anything ever, says I'll burn the kitchen down. Also, I got an email from the uni admissions office earlier, and I think I might actually get into Imperial for medicine!      No way! That's massive, Alice! I didn't even know you'd applied. Becca got rejected from most of the courses she asked for. I mean, I barely finished college and now I'm stuck doing basic support work with Mrs. Thistle’s dementia group. Not that I’m not grateful, but I just wonder what else could be out there.      It's one thing doing a job out of necessity, but it's another if you want it. I mean – I  literally  got my degree in about five years doing engineering for the navy. It’s not easy, but it’s progressing.      Oh that is so impressive, Tom! You're up there in that secret world, like on submarines or whatever. Geo, you passed your A-Levels and now you're a student  and  a part-time assistant in the high street shop. You must be doing all the boxes right?      Yeah Alice, you've got to keep the whole whack of things going – grades, volunteering,  and  a nice headshot! I tried to get goody photos on pond life from the park and it looked like a zombie had been in the pond before I even got the camera out!      Ha! You could have been The Creature from the Black Lake!

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You can’t even get anywhere without people cycling in front of cars like it’s the nineteenth century or something. I’m more than happy to take the bus, where are you off to today? Not to Cambridge Market, I hope?      No, we’re just going to that new park they’ve got on the edge of Trumpington. I wanted to see if I could do the full walk with Dad before the weather goes again.      Full walk? That sounds a bit arduous, don’t you think? I can’t imagine wanting to walk that far. I mean, even just going to the corner store makes me sweat like a hippo in a sauna.      Oh, you lazy lot. I used to walk everywhere, didn’t I? Drove the pick and mix stallholder up the wall with my coming in every week with cracked heels and aching legs!      Mum, I’m not lazy. It’s part of my training, you know, for the long weekends. I actually like it, taking time over it, seeing the countryside, taking in the air. I think cycling is a bit overrated, honestly. It's fine as long as they don’t cross the road like it’s their own private utility.      I don’t mind the cyclists, it's the drivers who are the real problem. It's not as if they have to go that fast, is it? I mean, they never go out of their way to drive slowly. Just because they’ve got four wheels and we haven’t got any doesn’t mean they have a right to be unpleasant.      I don’t know how you two put up with it. When I was your age, I didn’t have this choice. I just walked where I had to. Car was a luxury I never had. These days, I'd rather just go for a little cycle myself if it’s not raining too much. Though I have no idea how it's done any bloody different to riding a donkey!      Dad, you're such a drama queen. It’s not that bad. And honestly, I think it's better than driving if you ask me. Still, I did run into a bit of a problem the other day. I had to share a road with a man driving at full speed, line in the road, no lights.

Rather skip the talk and take a walk in the gardens, do you reckon?      I got the seats sorted out ages ago, you're not getting out of it like that.      Not quite my idea of a thrilling alumni day — spending three hours listening to someone called “Professor Fiddlesticks” talk about linguistic drift in   Old English  .      You might be surprised by how much you enjoy this stuff. I mean, you are into   language research  , right?      Ah, you're both discussing semantics now. You know what I like to talk about?   Sport  , particularly   Rugby  . When I was at Cambridge in the '70s, I played for the University XV.      Oh right? D’you pick and mix in the   Basque Country  , by the way, or do they only breakfast on peppers and walnuts?      Actually, the   Basque language  , that's   Euskara  , is fascinating. One of the few language isolates in Europe, you know? No proven relation to any other language.      You're only saying that because you've never been to   Wales  . I remember when the   Welsh national team   ran rings round us in a friendly in 1978.      All that   Cymraeg   and no one speaks a word of English, huh? Our co-ordinator in   China   once got stuck trying to order   pan-fried sour cabbage   with a chef who preferred classical   Mandarin  .      China's a good contrast to Basque. I mean, Mandarin's used by the   state  , but then you've got a thousand different   dialects   and   tones   and it's a whole other level entirely.      You young ones should visit more often. A bit of fresh air, a football match or something — all that time talking about   linguistics   must tire your brain out.      Is there anything to see in   London   on the way back? I do love a good   market  , maybe something a bit different like a place where the   locals   really get stuck in.      There's a   Chinese market   in Spitalfields that's amazing — you can pick your ingredients and get them all stir-fried for you on the spot.      I had belly-aching to a friend of mine once and overheard him offering food to his kids like   >  Object   The lasaurus. >  Subject   Who? >  Object   The lasaurus. >  Predicate   To dinner he want go. >     Classic parent speech, right? I've got a notebook full of examples for my thesis.      You really do live in an academic bubble.      Everyone has their thing, I guess.

So do you remember the last time we all saw each other? I was still in high school, right?      Oh yes, you were still wearing those awful tracksuits every day!      Charming, Karen. Some things never change, like Andrew’s terrible fashion sense.      Hey, they were   casual  . I’ve actually been working a lot since uni, so I don’t have time to worry about what I wear. It’s easier to just chuck on a jumper and call it a day.      Still, you'd think the job as a language teacher would allow you to at least look the part, don’t you? You know, the cute button-down shirts they all wear in the movies.      I’m not aiming to replicate Parisian cinema, Karen. But fine, I’ll dress smarter eventually.      Good. Now, are you finally filling in your university application, Andrew?      I have been! I just got stuck on the personal statement. I keep trying to sound impressive, and it ends up sounding like a corporate ad. “I am passionate and driven,”  please , that’s boring.      Well, just be yourself. Let them see your personality. You could always start with the time you tried to do the ice bucket challenge on Facebook and somehow got your cousin Silas sentenced to three minutes in a fish tank.      Yes! That’s a   story  . That wasn’t just a viral moment—it was family legend. Also, I   still   can’t believe you washed your phone in the sink in the middle of it.      I was trying to   rinse the ice off  . I panicked, okay!      Either way, it’s classic Andrew. Look, just write like that. Maybe you’ll get in if they’re looking for people with at least a bit of character.      I tried to apply for your school, Andrew, but my GCSE results were just enough to get me here: with a conditional offer and five years of waiting to do the same work I did at 17.      That’s rough. I remember your A-level exams though—you aced your French literature paper in, like, 30 minutes. You wrote something like 12 pages.      Yeah, and then you went out and taught your mother how to make  proper  French omelettes for two days after. Only to find out she’d been making the “proper” version her whole life.      That’s one of those memories that just captures the whole madness of us, isn’t it?

So do you not just take the coffee machine with you, or do we have to get it professionally removed first?      Oh, I think it would be a disaster if we just tried to move it ourselves. Not only do they have those fiddly bits you can’t see, but it’s probably got piping connected under the counter somewhere.      And let’s not forget the clean install on the other end. That’s a whole separate cost right there. You don’t just dump it in the new kitchen and hope for the best. Didn’t your old house have a gas line specially fitted for it?      Yes, goodness, the last time I had it serviced, they said it’s like a machine from the future—it runs on gas, water, steam, and who knows what else! I’d say it’s the most expensive piece of equipment in this whole house apart from the breakfast table.      Honestly, I’m just trying to calculate the total removal and storage, you know, before the estate agents start drilling holes in your ceiling like they did with Mrs. Pembroke’s Persian cat statue up the road.      Ah yes, the “vibrational clearance process” they call it. Leave it to estate agents to sound like they’re moving rocket ships when it’s just a chesterfield and a chandelier.      On another note, have you been keeping up with the Labour situation? I’m just trying to wrap my head around it. It feels like every week there's a new reshuffle or a new scandal hotter than the housing market.      Honestly, I don’t even trust the Prime Minister to count about five people in the room without glancing at the wall.
