We were doing statistics and probability in my last class—you know that data you get skewed when it starts snowing on your timeline. That’s where politics is now.      And let’s not forget the idealism. Young people think they can fix the system with a smile and a little bit of hope while the rest of us are still fighting to get a waterlogged email with a response. Idealism is good in theory, but let’s face it, delivering a single clean policy these days is like trying to go viral on a pond life streaming platform.      I just wish someone out there had a plan that actually worked—like a real one, not one made at 1 in the morning on conference notes while everyone was high on complimentary canapés and low on coherent thought.

So do you think we should go through our usual routine for Christmas or maybe try something different this year? I know you and Grandpa often have a massive party, and I know I say I’ll come every year, but it feels like we do the same thing over and over.      Well darling, traditions are there for a reason. It was the same when I was your age — "Mum, I’ve had enough of this!" — but now I see it was easier than having to deal with pulling everything together. We’ve had the same people for what feels like forever, but the formula has always worked: chips, mince pies, too much wine, and enough awkward family stories to last another year.      Yeah, I guess you’re right. I just feel like life is changing so fast now, with work and my new flat. This might be the last year for a while that I won’t be on a plane or working overseas for Christmas. I’d hate to miss it, you know?      Oh I know, I know. That’s why I’ve actually been thinking we should maybe book something a bit more up your way instead — somewhere a little more relaxed. I’ve seen some beautiful little cottages in the Cotswolds, nearer to Oxford, and I thought it might be nice?      That sounds actually amazing. You mean like a proper holiday sort of Christmas? Tree, log fire, mulled wine, no in-laws? What, is this you going soft on me in your old age?      Haha, no, no — you just need to have a break from real life being an adult for a few days. I’ve seen you at home, trying to juggle TEFL work, the landlords, and your chaotic social life. You deserve some rest.      Okay, fair enough. So we book the cottage, just us two for the first few days, then maybe bring others in for the weekend? I’d like it to be something fresh, but not fully isolating — you know, I sort of miss the chaos too.      That’s a very grown-up plan. I’m proud of you. And while you’re thinking ahead, have you thought about what comes next after your contract in go? Work-wise, life-wise?      Honestly, I’m not sure yet. I might go back to Spain or something, or try to settle down in London. I’m seriously toying with the idea of applying for those online teaching jobs full-time, so I could work from home or from anywhere really.

So did you lot hear about what’s going on at Waterfields then?      Yeah, I heard they’re expanding again. I’m more interested in their sausages though. Their Richmond sausages are £2 more than the rest, but worth it, honestly.      I went there last week to pick up some buns for the weekend. Proper queue of old folk with handkerchiefs. One of them was snoring halfway through the queue. Imagine!      You mean like, full-on sleeping?      Told you! Right in the middle of the queue, dead to rights, eyes closed, head on another old bint’s bag.      Sounds like the start of a comedy sketch, to be honest. D’you think they were in cahoots to take over the queue or something?      Nah, just happened. They had their own group at the front, and then these two fella’s puffing on fags and arguing over whether sausages need ketchup. One of ‘em was waving a bottle of it like a sword.      Hah! Tell that to my gran—she’d say any sauce on a sausage is suicide.      True. I mean, I’ve seen some weird stuff in the pub, but in a bakery? That’s something else.      I went to Waterfields for a birthday party once and they weren’t serving. Instead, a bloke at the end of the counter made a toast out of a bun and gravy and told me I was a good lad.      I mean, I wouldn’t have brought a man down for that, but man, he had confidence.      Speaking of which, have you heard from Jacinta? I texted her for the meeting last week and she never replied.      She’s probably off with Mark again. He snored through half our history lecture when he was doing his GCSEs.      No, he didn’t snore—he whistled. Not the same. Snoring you can deal with, but that sort of man-whistle? go straight to the pond and throw your handkerchief in.      I reckon it's genetic—her bloke’s from near your place, Shaw. I heard he’s got a bakery in Wigan. Or was it Rochdale?      Dunno. But I overheard him saying he was going to start up a café called ‘The Arrhythmic Bun’. Blokes love puns.      Right place, wrong name. ‘The Slumbering Loaf’ would do it before that.      I’d take a seat on their premises for tea and scones with that lot on the menu!

So did you get up at the crack of dawn again this weekend or did you finally manage to sleep in like a normal human being?      Haha, I tried, I really did! But no, the sun came up and I followed it. Got up early, had a quick walk in the fields, and checked on the hens. You know me and the hens.      Aww, hens and spreadsheets — that’s your life now, isn’t it? I know you said you were going to take the weekend for yourself, chase some sunshine or something. Were you planning a lie-in?      A bit, yeah. But I found myself thinking about the tenants needing that new turkey coop sorted before the weather gets too wet. It’s just habit, I suppose. You get into these roles and you think every patch of grass needs tending, every egg needs collecting.      Fair enough. I mean, I get it — it’s not like I haven’t spent my weekends stressed out about deadlines and budget spreadsheets over the last few years. I do envy you a bit, though. My idea of a short break is a walk to the shop and back.      Oh, come on now, work is a little part of life. How are things at your new job? I know you were swamped the last few months. You managing okay?      Ugh, I’m surviving. It’s not been the smoothest of starts. The client keeps changing their minds about everything from fonts to workflows, and I end up juggling ten things at once. It's like Russian roulette with project plans. One wrong move and someone gets excluded from the email chain.      Blooming typical! Sounds like something I’d have thumped on the desk about in another life. Still, I take it you're up for that dinner next weekend, like we planned?      As long as you promise no hen stories over the starter. I was told my tolerance for talking about farm animals is fairly low unless there’s a reward of good gravy.      Deal. And with that, I think it's time someone asked if the kettle in your bag is going to come out and boil the car with us cruising down the A12.      Haha, only if you promise not to ask me about budget projections with a cup of tea in your hand. Been there, done that, lost 300 hours in spreadsheets.

So do you ever miss teaching kids?      A bit, yeah. I mean, it’s got its moments, but honestly, now that I’m doing more admin, it’s just me and spreadsheets 24/7. No one to shout at over missing homework.      Right? I can't imagine that. I teach teenagers and if one of them isn't speaking English by the end of the week, I lose the will to live.      It must be tough with the older kids. I taught Year 1s for years—you get the most basic tantrums, like, "I want a  red  pen," and you hand it over and they’re fine.      Haha, you’re lucky. Teenagers are constantly dramatic, and half the time, they don’t even know what they want to say in English. Sometimes I’ve got to interpret for breakfast, homework and existential crises!      I envy your language skills. I can barely get my kids to say “hello” in anything other than English.      My parents are both Spanish, so I grew up bilingual. But honestly, as a language teacher, I wish  everyone  tried a bit harder—it would save me a lot of red ink.      Mate, I want to learn, but I barely remember how to count to ten in French anymore. All I know is bonjour, merci, and oh no—we might be in trouble.      That’s the spirit! Come to me and I’ll give you a crash course—unless you’d rather just teach your baby Spanish and be done with it.      Haha, I did just that. Anna’s the only one singing nursery rhymes in “proper” English.      Oh that’s brilliant! I’m jealous. My student moved back to Spain last month and realized she couldn’t form a sentence in Spanish anymore.      Are you serious? That is bloody depressing.      I know, right? She said the only words she remembered were “bien” and “agua.” I told her to join a language group if she ever comes back.      You know what? Maybe I’ll set one up. I mean, if you’re there to shout at people.      I will. And if you ever need help with your little one’s French lessons, just bring her over. I live for roles where I'm both teacher and babysitter.      Sounds like a dangerous combination—baby meltdown and language confusion. But I’m game! You up for it?      Bring the baby, the chaos, and the patience.

Rather annoying really, putting up all those bird feeders in the garden and they still don’t come when we want them to.      Oh Blimey, I've found where they disappear off to—there's a sparrow’s nest in the shed. Just like the one I had when I was a lad, under the eaves.      Oh isn't that adorable? A whole family in your shed!      No, it's not adorable, it's a mess! All the seed I put out doesn't stay in the feeders, it ends up under the floorboards of the shed.      What d’you expect? Birds have brains older than you, son. They know who to feed themselves best.      You're both too picky. If I had little creatures flapping around, I’d be very pleased. I still remember when Winnie the Pooh had a little beehive next to his house.      Aye, that was a time, those puppets on the telly, didn’t we all listen to the radio version in the 50s? Did you know real bees don’t like lavender in the country? They prefer thyme and borage.      I stopped listening the minute the actor tried to sound posh. “Oh, somethin’ to eat and somethin’ to drink,” and you know that made sense in the 30s but not now.      Oh, don't start on the radio again. Also, have a slice of cake and be quiet. That’s all I’ve been doing since breakfast—making about five different ones. I thought you’d like it, Alma, this one with thyme in it.      Aye, it smells nice, lass, but be careful ‘cos I’ve watched your blood sugar level go up about three notches since you woke up.      Terry, I am being careful! You don’t have to mention my diabetes as if I’m being stubborn.      I think it's partly the company he's with. The more sugar, the more stories we get told about the old days.      Aye, and you don’t find better company in the world than between two retired gents and one retired lady who can still make you feel like you’ve made it to the top of the world.      You two are both like a forgotten generation, full of stories and opinions nobody wants to hear.      Arrr, and they certainly don't want to hear them all at once, so don’t you go rushing off now, we need to talk about the weather, and before that, we need to find out where the cake went.

Rather skip the salad and just go for the main straight, do you reckon?      I got to go with the chicken and the salad, don’t fancy being stared at again by that table by the window.      Be as frightened as well. We haven’t been here eeny ween, but I swear one of 'em tried to speak to me in Turkish not five minutes ago. A lot of shouting and pointing at this lot.      It is interesting place to be in N. Cyprus, don’t get me wrong. But I still say we shoulda rented the villa near Kas rather than this—what’s it called again?      This is that Myra place, yes, you know, left it on the map by mistake. But the main point is, the place is lovely, the food’s reasonable, and for about a month of the year, it’s practically prime real estate.      Aye, you ever looked at the property prices down here now? I mean, not like the south, but still—there’s something in the air, you know. I mean, puts your mind in a different space.      Good for healing—good for getting over stuff. Be it emotional or physical. My brother-in-law was in fairly bad, and he came down here last summer. Barely spoke to anyone for two weeks and then started trying to learn to count in Turkish!      Hah! Spoken to him lately? Is he still going on about his  shaman  out in the hills? The one who wants to talk to his ancestors through a pile of goat bones and a chicken leg? I mean, I’m not knocking it, but talking to my dad this morning and he said his cousin—he knows you know her, right? Sukey—passed last week.      Oh no, Sukey? Poor thing passed years ago. That’s Vivian’s sister-in-law. But he means Linda.      Linda? Linda’s still about? Thought she had that breast thing.      She did, but she’s been clear since ‘15. Still, it comes around again, like a queue. Don’t go in details on the phone if you don’t mind. Not in public anyway.      Fair enough, I can see that. But all this talk of spiritual stuff, I suppose, it makes you think about things.      It certainly does. And it’s not just over here, either—back home, half the women I work with are dabbling in dowsing, crystal stuff.

Mum, I just wanted to say sorry about last week, I know I was supposed to pop over when Dad had his check-up, but with the site manager from the new project being on such short notice, I just couldn’t get away.      No worries, love. We understand. It’s just nice to see you more often, that’s all. Both your dad and I have been talking about you and Alistair. Are you two thinking about moving in together soon?      We’ve talked about it, yeah. But at the moment it’s too much with my work schedule and the fact that we both want to save up for a house. We’re thinking maybe another year? But like everyone else our age, I guess!      Ten more years and you’ll still be living in a poky flat! I’m just messin’, darling. But seriously, if you’re looking to settle down, this house of yours... I’d throw a few grand at the place and get it sorted. House prices are still a bit low, I reckon.      Dad! You’d say that if I put in a swimming pool as well!      Well, a properly watertight roof would be a good first step. You want to know – Mate of mine got a chap in and he said the damp in the back bedroom’s somethin’ to do with the old stone wall and the lime mortar. Still, if you carry out the works properly, the house could be a real beauty.      Oh, let’s not talk about renovations now. I just finished the apple crumble – I thought I’d get it out of the way about half an hour early so the turbinado sugar can crystallize on the top. Nancy made some custard yesterday, shall I bring some over?      That would be brilliant. Burgers and crumble sound like an odd combo, but honestly, I could eat a whole plate.      You always say that! You must take your father’s appetite. He and his mate Ivan from work went to this bar in Stratford the other day—stayed till the 10 o’clock slammer. They had steak and chips and a go at a game of darts. Not that he hits the board, obviously.      I hit the bloomin’ board plenty of times when I was at the pub quiz! 3000 in the pot once—lost by half a question. But I had a cracking pint of Foster’s, anyway.

So did y'fit watch the Catfish episode last week? That lass was cranked mad when they showed her the truth, innit?      Yeah, I did! That bloke was pretending to be this proper model or somethin’—what a twat. I mean, I get messin’ about on the internet, but that’s just tacky.      I’ve only caught bits. I’m more of a Jeremy Kyle girl, y’know? I like the ones where people go off and shout. Gave me a laugh last week with that big row over a frozen baby or whatever it was.      Oh the baby debate? That was mental! One minute they’re all kissy-fish, the next it’s like Ten Commandments gone wrong. You'd think they’d just say what they wanted and be done with it, innit?      Yeah, Jeremy Kyle is a proper circus though. I like it when people leg it out the back, you know? Cos they can’t bare to actually see the bloke or lass tellin’ them what a mess they’ve made of their life.      Honestly, sometimes I wonder if people go on those shows just for the extra attention. Be like “I want national news – here’s my sob story!” But still, it’s bonkers entertainment. Better than somethin’, eh?      Aye, and don’t even get me started on people pretendin’ to be who they ain’t. Catfish is just like real-life cosplay. You think you’re gettin’ a best mate, and it’s some random trying to make a quick buck or make a TikTok.      I had a friend who got conned once. This "sparkle influencer" was talkin’ her up and up, then up she popped to do a haul ‘cos she was like 2000 miles away. Bled her dry on gifts. She still thinks he was love.      Oh bless her! Honestly, the internet is a minefield. I’ve seen so many people with weird stories. I mean, I’ve got enough drama with me fam without fake friends on a screen!      Exactly. Though I do think it’s wild how everyone’s so keen to open up to strangers, innit? Like we go from total strangers to “will your catfish come to dinner?” in a week!      Well, it’s all well and good as long as you don’t lose your ‘moan’ when it all turns out different. Or worse, go all Arron Ap Rhys Jones on them.

So do you speak German properly?      A little bit. I learned it when I was in Vienna. But I haven’t used it much since I moved to England.      That must be quite sad. I mean, being from Vienna, like the capital of Austria and een all that. I’ve always wanted to go there. I reckon it must be full of painters and music and cafes with all these big serious intellectuals in the corner, nodding sagely and sipping coffee.      Well, maybe once. But now it’s changed. Still lovely, though. I went there with my brother when I was a girl, before the war, and I’ve never managed to get back since.      Wait, you said you were born in Vienna, but what about Italy? Why do you say you’re from Austria but born in Italy?      Oh, that’s just a mistake. I was in Vienna at the time, and I remember we used to go to Italy a lot—Venice, Verona, Florence. I suppose people often get it confused. But yes, I left Vienna when I was seventeen to come to London.      Wow… so did you move over on a boat or something?      Not at all. I came by train, actually. It was the late '30s, just before the whole war broke out. There was a woman who ran a correspondence course in painting. She offered one-year scholarships for young artists to come and study here. I had a letter of recommendation from my art teacher. So I packed a bag, got a ticket, and here I am!      I’m doing a module on the Renaissance at university, and I’m really into all that Greek and Roman stuff. Classics. I find the language side a bit tricky, to be honest, but the ideas—democracy, philosophy, all that—it really hits home.      You know, I once had a professor at art school who was convinced the Greeks had already discovered the Fibonacci sequence. He said they were always trying to find perfect ratios and proportions in their architecture.      Yeah, I’ve read bits like that. That must’ve been so inspiring for your own work?      Oh, absolutely. I think that’s why I’ve always loved working with bees. They follow patterns too. It’s like nature has its own kind of Greek idealism.      Wait, bees?      Yeah, I used to keep a few hives near where I lived in Cambridge.

So do you think we should’ve left London earlier? It’s already starting to rain, and the traffic is...  ugh .      I don’t know, love. I thought we’d get out before the rush. Besides, the SatNav said it’d take three hours. Can’t be far now.      It says 'two hours and 12 minutes' on my phone. But I wouldn’t trust that lot. SatNav isn’t what it used to be. I got lost once in Northampton and ended up at some animal feed warehouse.      You what? That’s wild! I mostly just use Google Maps, honestly. At least I can see where I am and if the roads are closed. Still, Dorset traffic’s a nightmare at this time on a Saturday.      I think it’s because of all the holiday traffic. Everyone’s heading to the coast, no doubt. I hated driving when it rained in my day. Visibility was non-existent and people driving like lunatics for the sake of the sun.      I know, Grandad! I saw a老爷 up near Guildford yesterday who almost did a wheelie going over a speed bump. Horrendous driving—it wasn't even a bump, it was just a small hump.      I wouldn’t mind that myself. At least he had a bit of spirit! Still, careful driving’s more important, love. You don’t want to end up stuck in A&E with a sprained wrist or something. I’ve seen it too many times at the care home.      So, Nana, what’s the plan once we get to Dorset? Are we about to spend the whole day trying to find the right antique shop?      We’ll pop into that little place in Wimborne. The one near the church. The owner is a retired academic from Oxford. Lovely man. He told me about his time studying Elizabethan furniture. I think he was on about it for two hours.      I hope he doesn’t start up again. He’s got a way of quoting Shakespeare at random times.      I love it, though! It’s something different. Plus, I’ve been looking into gothic architecture for my degree, and some of those old building features—like the timber framing—you see around here are amazing.      Oh yes, you’ll be pestering me for history on every postbox we pass, won’t you?      Only if you promise not to fall asleep halfway through!

Rather a damp day, isn't it?      That it is, Henry. Feels like the whole of Norfolk’s turned into a puddle.      Aye, I was out with the spade this morning, trying to sort the drains again. You’d think after all these years, the ground’d be friendly, but no. Still stubborn as ever.      Spare a thought for your old joints, love. No shame in letting nature deal with it for once. You’ve done enough digging in your time.      Tch. Necessary work, is what it is. Can’t let a bit of rain flood the front path. That’d be a state, wouldn’t it? Crying shame if I tripped and knocked myself out – who’d tell them all the stories I’ve got saved? Half the village doesn’t know the half of it.      Now, now, Henny. Don’t go looking for the headline again. You remember the one about the old man who chased the postman with a ladder over the puddle? That one nearly got you up on the local paper.      And deservedly too. That cheeky postman thought he'd trot through my garden like it was nothin'. – Baptiste: Typical city chap, no respect for the land.      It was a  shallow  puddle, Henry. Barely knee-deep, and he's just doing his job.      That's the trouble nowadays, folks do their jobs without a clue what it's all about. Take these ‘phones – I’ve had one in the house for years and about half the buttons do the same thing. One touch and you're on the news. Another and you're ordering bread. Ridiculous!      Maybe I’ll have a go at teaching you the lot of it. Though I doubt your patience would last more than a minute. Last time you got all fired up talking to that delivery driver about  "this mobile business,"  you had him halfway to tears explaining how a carriage clock knows the time better than the whole whirring invention he's got in his pocket.      Because the notion is utter gook! You wind it up and it does its work. No flashing lights, no whistles, no nonsense. These boxy gizmos are far too fast for their own good. The world feels smaller, and yet we're further apart.      Oh, come now. Look where you are – right here, with me, sipping the tea I just poured, warm and buttery. No batteries involved.

Rather annoying this wet weather isn't it? I was supposed to get the veg patch in the garden done up over the weekend and now it's just one big mud bath. Not a good look if you ask me.      Tell me about it. I was going to take the dog for a proper walk, and now I’ve resorted to twitching about on the pavement for ten minutes. You don’t even get a decent sniff of damp earth in this lot. Still, at least we’ve got some time off to do nothing and eat these ridiculous portions of pasta you've made, don't we?      Bless you. I mean, I throw a plate of something vaguely green on the table for appearances' sake, but honestly, I’ve just been crafting lasagne like it's art or something.      Qualities I respect. A little indulgence never did anyone any harm. Though if we’re talking indulgence, I've been re-listening to The Cure’s greatest hits. Mega oversized headphones, loudly, to the ire of the entire flat. I miss those early 90s anthems—personally, "Just Like Heaven" never puts a boot in.      You’ve still got the classics on-loan mentality, don't you? I got into that lo-fi – jazz hybrid recently, fairly chilled, and way more predictable than trying to figure out what your PhD is about these days. You phone me up and go, “it’s going okay, just trying to make someone care,” and I’m like—develop a bloody conclusion already.      Fair point. Also, it's a bit of a minefield at the moment. I had a meeting with my supervisor today about structuring the third chapter. Turns out the problem wasn't the chapter itself, but my obsession with footnote citations. She said I shouldn’t be worrying about whether a 1934 text should ‘officially’ be quoted or paraphrased.      Well, if it's a PhD, you can afford to be a little too careful. I envy your stick-to-itiveness, really. Though being academically-trailed with lunches of sandwiches and lukewarm tea doesn’t sound particularly romantic.      You're not wrong. That's one goody of my parents—the man runs a builders' yard and has made me a kingsizeike study bench. Complete with box files and a reading lamp your age would call 'antique'. I seriously question why he’s not in business making those things.

So did you watch The Lion King musical on iPlayer last night then?      Yeah, I did. I had no idea how much music was in it. I've seen the movie a million times, but that show was pretty intense. Some of those songs wouldn't be out of place in a rock concert.      Right? I reckon Elton John must have been on a mission that week. I mean, the soundtrack from that movie has brought me through more emotional phases in my life than I can count. And now the version on the West End, or the Broadway one – I can't even remember which one they showed – is like a full-blown rock opera now.      It still managed to hit all those same childhood feelings, though. Probably why they keep bringing it back. But I was thinking about the whole thing about backstage royalties and all that. Cats is still running, isn't it? I wonder how much money that's pulling in at this point.      Honestly, I wouldn’t be surprised if it paid off the original Waterfront Stadium by now. Mind you, I was thinking about that in contrast to your PhD. You’re supplying the real, non-musical brainpower to the world, while I’m out here just managing research teams and – no disrespect – mostly just making sure people don’t forget to submit forms on time.      You know what? There’s a certain nobility in making sure people submit forms on time. Without people like you, my PhD wouldn’t even have been approved. You’re the administrative heartbeat of it all. What I want to know is – if all research money in the UK is being spent about half as fast as it's supposed to, how the hell are we supposed to get a foothold in anything?      Exactly! And if we’re going to pay 27k per year to go to uni now, are we really meant to be told to become a researcher just for the love of it? I tried to apply for a grant last year and the form had 847 sections. It took me two weeks just to fill in the first half.      That’s a serious problem. I had a student the other day go off about how they wanted to do a masters, but at that rate, even before they start, they might be in a job that doesn’t exist anymore.

So do you think I could publish this?      Publish what, sweetheart?      This book I’ve been working on. I’ve been drawing all the pictures and writing little stories about our family. You know, like the one Grandad told about the two brothers in Glasgow and how they went different ways in life.      A book about the family? That sounds lovely, love.      That’s amazing, Mia. It’d be a treasured keepsake for the family. What makes you want to publish it?      I just think it’d make a good gift for Dad’s birthday. You know, since he left and now that Myke lives with us sometimes, I thought it would help him feel more connected to the rest of the family too.      That’s an excellent idea. My old school would’ve loved it—children love pictures and stories.      And I love the idea of telling our stories to Myke. He doesn’t know much about your Dad or his side of the family—personally, I think he might feel like part of a real family for once.      Exactly. I want him to know we’re a big, messy family. Not perfect, but we love each other. I mean, look at  us —my brother and me don’t live together, and you and his dad aren’t together anymore, but we still try to make things work.      That’s real life, isn’t it, love? Some folks make it work, some don’t. But being kind and loving matters most.      I wanted to include our family tree too. I found these old photos online—your wedding one, Grandma, and even one of Grandad with his two brothers. The one up in Glasgow that was a teacher like you.      Aye, William. He was me brother. I used to telephone him all the time when I was working. We had such a row one day about whether you  had  to feed a horse when you were riding it. He said you had to, I said you didn’t.      That’s the kind of thing I love including in your book, Mia. Those little real stories—they make the line of names on a family tree mean something.      Yeah. I’m also adding a few bits about why people went different ways. Like how Grandad never had children of his own but ended up with me and Myke, while Dad and my brother went separate ways.

So did you go and sort out that weekend job yet? I’ve been trying to get mine sorted for like ages.      Yeah I did actually I got a few messages after I put a little thing on Instagram. You should try it I got like three replies within like an hour.      Oh yeah I’ve got an account but I reckon it’s not as easy up here. I’ve only had one message and that was from my cousin’s boyfriend.      That sounds dodgy. Maybe just put a bit more info in your post or tag a place or something? I did that and it helped.      What did you say exactly?      Just said I’m looking for something flexible for a few weekends over the next couple of months, ideally near the city centre. And I tagged a couple of cafes near Cambridge uni. Got a bit of traction off that.      Yeah I’ll give that a go. I’m just not sure how to word it so people don’t think I’m a solicitor or something.      Haha I put short and sweet. Left it vague enough but serious enough. Honestly, people just want something easy.      Yeah I get that. Anyway – speaking of things to do – have you actually started shaving yet?      What? Why would I? I haven’t grown it out that long!      I mean not full-on, but I’ve got my legs a bit longer than usual so I’m thinking about getting it done before Christmas. You know, being festive and all.      Oh right I do like Leg Day every now and then. But honestly, I don’t mind going a bit wild for a bit longer. I’m trying to be less uptight about it.      Oh yeah I like that. I’m trying too, but sometimes when I’m going out it feels a bit messy otherwise.      I get it – but I swear to god, when I first stopped doing it every week, I felt like a new woman. Freedom!      Still, I’m a bit old-fashioned in the bathroom. I go every other week usually unless I’ve got a party or something coming up.      Mm yeah, I can see that. But if you ever want to have a lazy Leg Day with me and leave it out for a bit, I’ll vouch for your right to be uncivilised over the holidays.

So did I! The alphabet game’s a classic, innit. I was cracking up when Sarah said  zithers —haven’t heard that one in years. You need a specific kind of vocabulary for this, don’t you?      You bet.  Zithers  is good, but I went  zygote  the other day and got some looks. Classic pub quiz crowd. You’ve got to keep your niche words in shape if you’re playing with academics and former teachers.      True. Although I nearly.Fatalf  ed it when I said  zigzag —obvious but easy enough. Anyway, speaking of sharp vocab, how’s the PhD going? You stressed about that  zygotic mitotic  stuff?      Ten out of ten, thanks for asking. But hey, I’ll be fine. Just had an in-person seminar the other day. You know, the old debate about whether early embryonic development is affected by maternal stress. And the lecturer says, “Don’t fret—it won’t affect the  zygote .” I was like, “Excuse me, sir, I’m not the one splitting!”      Oh, deadly! You should’ve been a stand-up comic. But seriously, when are you publishing that paper on –?       Zingberg’s parallax theory ? Don’t set me off, love. Anyway, enough of that. Let’s talk about your weekend, huh? Our barista said you were up in Newcastle for boxing night?      Yeah, went with my mate from work. It was wild—full place, fights every fifteen minutes. We were at ringside and nearly about to fall off the bar stools when our man took the Mexican fighter down with a  zuave  left hook.      Suave, not zuave. You’re mixing your dance moves for the ring.      Tut, cut me some slack. I’ve been busy. But bloody entertaining it was. I tried a pint of that new ale,  Zealot’s Dawn , though. Rather good—sessionable with a nice  zesty  finish.      You’re trying to alphabet around this, aren’t you? Don’t go there. I remember your old man always warning about “bloody kids these days and their fancy pints.” He’d hate this.      He’s in Bournemouth with the bingo and his new best mate, Jimbo. Not a lot he can do about it now. Besides, that ‘fancy pint’ held me through a ten-round bender and my cousin’s birthday dosh for  zero  chemical enhancement. Water, wine, and willpower.      To your detox regime. But listen, while you were scribbling down  zygote  and  zoology , I had a bit of an odd moment.

Rather skip the new bar in town. You know what they do. Spend a ton, and they don’t care if the building’s five hundred years old. They’ll chuck in a modern bathroom and say job done. I was looking at the old mill the other day—  Laxton’s Mill  , if that’s the one you liked—        Laxton’s?   Oh yes, a beauty. A listing Grade II  if I’m not mistaken. Timbers all over the place, interesting beam work. But you’re right, the modern stuff never fits in, does it? You won’t get the grant without a sound proposal. They want   historical integrity   and a plan that shows some real   community benefit   these days. I remember an application last year, tried to put in a bakery, café, event space, and I think a climbing wall. Blimey, they got rejected for trying to do too much.      Precisely. And don’t get me started on the bidding process, the way they want the budget split. I spent three days arguing with the Heritage Foundation about whether the   cat tile removal   impacts the grant. Like it’s not a bit of tile off a gable, but they want to know how it affects the   list of sensitive materials  . It’s all bureaucracy hiding behind verbosity.      You’re not wrong. I’ve been trying to get   grants under the Local Heritage Initiative  , and you need to connect the project to   local tourism  , improvements in   heritage awareness  , even   sustainable energy use  . Funny thing—  one of the buildings I redid   had a   16th-century hearth   and they wanted a carbon-neutral   stone-revival stove  . I ended up building it with   reclaimed oak  , and they thought I was wasting resources. I gave up trying to please them all.      That’s the lesson, really. Pick one goal, stick to it, and present the minimal amount of benefit you think they’ll buy. For Laxton’s, I’m going to propose a   heritage learning hub  . Workshops, guided lunches, a little gallery with archives. Not too big, not too flashy—  but sustainable   and community-focused. That way, the work is on your own terms and keeps the building real.      That could work. And if you box in the costs with what your team can actually afford, you’ll get better results. I had one developer come in with a   £500k budget   but didn’t have a   single archaeologist on staff  .

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You think when you do a PhD you’d get time off but he’s got to go to some conference in Oslo next week and I’ve asked him like three times if he can bring back some £20 pastries like they do in Scandinavia.      Right, so  this  is what you want from me? You just wanted to tell me about a paper I haven’t written yet or the pastries I’m not even interested in.      No! You said you like the ones with the runny centre and the bergamot cream... like, literally last week you  promised . Now, while the kettle’s still on, can I bounce something off you? I’m writing up some new stuff for a panel on sociolinguistic mapping and accents in the north and I’m trying to find a way to make it about identity and place better.      So you want to link regional accents to emotional attachment to place? That actually sounds really interesting. You working on the dataset from Newcastle? Or something more recent?      Yeah, some of the Newcastle recordings and also quite a few from Manchester and Middlesbrough. I’m trying to map out how people describe their rhythm and then how they describe themselves. It’s funny though: often the same people who say their accent is “unfancy” or “ugly,” they’ll still fight for the right to speak it when it comes to dialect policing. Like this one forty-three-year-old guy from Gateshead who said, “I sound like a magazine wrapped with string, but at least nobody can mock me and be right.”      Oh, that’s a good quote. I hear a lot of that from the people I interview for my vibes and affect thesis. It’s like there’s this duality between self-perception and social perception. You know, like ‘ I  like the way I talk, others might not, and I accept that’ versus ‘Damage is being done to the English language by people like me.’      Exactly! It raises so many questions about regional identity in the digital age too. Like, people do so much online, but when you ask them where they’re from or how they speak, it becomes so immediate, rooted in place. It’s almost like two different versions of the self, innit?      You could frame your research around that. It’s not just about speech patterns, it’s about belonging.

Right, so today I just got through the post the latest info about the school dinner options, and it seems like we need to send some extra money in for the term. I need to know if you two are planning to have school dinners or bring packed lunches again this week.      I don’t want to have school dinners, Mummy. Not like   he   does.      I like the chicken nuggets. Not the sticky rice stuff, though. And sometimes they make pizza, which is nice. But you have to eat the salad first.      Mummy won’t fetch frozen peas out of my hair  again , no, thank you. I had to sit in the clinic like that for five minutes before anyone saw I was crying.      I had peas in my hair once too, and I told the teacher and she gave me a brush.      Well, no doubt about that. Look, here’s the thing — if you’d rather bring lunch again, that’s absolutely fine. All the other mums do it too, so it’s not like you’re being left out. But if you want to keep going for dinners, I’ll sort the money, deal?      But what if we don’t want to eat? What if we just look at the food and feel, like,  yucky ?      It’s not yucky when you use the plastic fork and knife. I use the red one. Like a sword.      Just trying to be a bit of a celebrity warrior at school lunchtime? Also, about later in the week — it’s the school tennis tournament on Wednesday, so make sure your sport kits are ready. That includes the clean pair of socks, William, because last time they said you looked like a   clown  .      Clowns are fun! I saw a proper clown at the fair once. He had big red shoes and his face was painted like a rainbow.      He threw a balloon at you and you screamed, Beatrice. It was a  lion .      He was not a lion! He was just a balloon man. And you took ages to get around.      Yeah, go Mummy on your own if you don’t want to run.      Alright, alright. Battle of the balloon facts another day. But yes, you two are both entering the tournament, so practice with the ball against the wall after dinner. And not in the hallway like you did last time.      Mummy! It wasn’t the ball’s fault!

So did you go see that film, the one at the cinema last week? The one with the historians and all those debates?      Yes, I did! That was an interesting one, wasn’t it? Divided quite a few people I heard later at the dinner table.      Right, which one was it again? I didn’t get out as much as I used to with a busy day job and all.      It was the one about how we should teach history in schools. You know, the big one that came out during the Cambridge education summit last week.      Oh yes! The debate is still going strong in the papers, actually. Some people think we should focus more on British history, especially post-WWII, while others argue for a more global or critical perspective, including colonialism and modern issues like Brexit.      That sounds better than when I was at school. I mean, I learned all about wars and monarchs, but not much about how history shapes the kind of policies we have today. Or how that even affects business.      I think that’s one of the frustrations teachers face as well. The national curriculum in England is still quite rigid in many ways. I tried introducing a unit about the history of advertising in the modern era once, but the principal wasn’t sure it was “historically relevant” enough.      That’s funny, coming from you, Mark. Still, isn't the past of advertising someone’s businesses and how they sell ideas a key part of history?      Some people seem to think it's a stretch, but it’s surprising how much historical research goes into brand identity and marketing today. I actually ran a marketing campaign inspired by the Renaissance merchant classes once—cringe, I know—but it worked.      I’m trying to push for more cross-subject projects, like linking history with economics or ethics. For example, when we studied the Industrial Revolution, the students did a project on the ethics of working conditions and then how modern companies still deal with supply chain ethics.      That’s a good idea. I remember when I was at school in Reading, the history class was just remember dates and regicide. Nothing about the context of how people actually lived then.      That’s one of the big points in the Cambridge debate, isn’t it? Higher education—and even what your A-levels cover—should focus more on critical thinking and less on memorisation.

Rather annoying this wet weather isn't it?      It's been nothing but rain and mist all week. Never thought I'd miss the dust of London!      You’re missing the smog, love. That's not what you call missing.      Well I won't go that far, but this constant mizzle is doing my head in.      I think it's doing this house in, too. The ceiling down there in the hallway is softening again.      Blimey, the damp. My mother used to spread newspapers on the window ledges so the cold wouldn't bite into the walls.      You know, I was just thinking about the war the other day. I had an uncle who was in the Eighth Army. Never saw the man again after he sailed for North Africa.      Aye, I knew some folk from Costessey who joined up. Only one came back, poor lad’s spine was shot through. Sat over there on that stool of yours, looked like a tree branch in a wind up.      Did you live in the house back then, George?      For twelve years, from fifty-two. The walls were paper-thin, could hear the school bus outside singing  Land of Hope and Glory  on the way to pick them up at half past two.      It’s strange, this. The war and everything—how it shaped everyone’s lives. My brother came back a different man. Just didn’t have a laugh in him anymore. Still, at least he had a laugh when he started working in the grocers.      Oh the grocers were the lifeblood of the neighborhood. My sister sold eggs and plug rho dishes and things.      My father had to put up treble guest bedrooms after the war. Parents were doubling up with their kids. Whole families in one poky little room.      I remember one time my father had to go to the police because a neighbor’s goat was wandering into the yard and eating the turnips. Served it right really, after the price of turnips the wartime ration gave goats a break.      You mean pre-war? Wait, after the war, food wasn’t so scarce any more.      It was only in the immediate aftermath, though, after ’45. I think people were still grumbling about it into the sixties over meat and bread queues and things.      The police back then, they were more about foot patrols and helping old ladies cross the road than doing dash cameras and stop and searches and all that modern nonsense.

Right, so we've got about 20 minutes before we get to Dad's place, if that. Traffic’s moving a bit slower than usual this side of Blowsden.      Yeah, it's funny how things change, innit? It used to take us ten minutes from your mum’s to my place, and now with the new roads and traffic lights, it’s like half an hour.      I know. I never thought I'd be driving into   Northamptonshire   and still calling it the "last trip" to your place, but here we are.      Still, at least you're not learning English the hard way now, like I did back in the 70s. I swear, left-right, red-light-green, the lot. You're a far better driver than I ever was.      Yeah, but I'll never live it down if I run a red light or drive in reverse across the road, ever again. You told Grandad that for a week after the test.      Fair point, fair point. I still say he laughed harder than me. What with the tea and the corn on the cob, we were in good spirits.      Speak of the devil. Looking back at the house, I can almost still smell that slap-up dinner we had the other night. It was brilliant, what with the sausages and the rosemary potatoes. Nothing like those fancy supermarkets’ frozen stuff.      Aye, and your mum’s sourdough—piece of toast is a feast in my world. But you know, I’ve had your grandmother’s lamb stew once and I still dream about it.      Well, I'm going to take what you taught me about budgeting and try and cook something like it. No promises, though. My idea of chopping is just "cover my hands in flour and cross my fingers."      You’ll get there. Just like I tried to teach your little sister, but she ended up with a   mortgage   of a mess in the kitchen.      That happened last year. I think you remember, something involving fire and a saucepan with the curtains goin' on.      That one was made into a PowerPoint, mate. You're in the box slide under "Disaster."
