Right, I just wanted to go through the plans again before we get the menu set in stone. The first thing we need to decide is whether we’re having more of a traditional meal or something a bit different this year for Nanna’s birthday.      I think traditional is better, just in case there’s things she doesn't understand anymore with the dementia. I reckon it’ll make her feel more at home.      Fair enough. I was thinking maybe a roast? Chicken or beef, easy to carve and serve. Less messy than salmon or something fishy when people get the spoon mixed up.      Fish does smell a bit strong, doesn't it? I don’t think she’d like that. And honestly, I’ve already got my hands full trying to remember where I put the knives.      I’ll be the one handling the knife assembling, don’t worry. I’ve done it enough times. But this time, I did rearrange the cupboards, so the oversized carving one might be in the spare bedroom by now. Good job I’m reliable like that.      You’d think someone would have put a sign up.      It’s not like I hide it in a suitcase. I just rotated it in with the best of them. Anyway – about the table plan. I’ve managed to seat the cousins on either side of Nanna. It’ll be good for them to engage her, chat about the photos I’m going to put out from this summer at the lakes.      That’ll be nice. I brought a few out last week, and she did a double take and say “Is that  you  when you were ten? You looked about five!” Her memory’s all over the place, but she still remembers the vibes.      Exactly. And I know she loves the Great British Bake Off, so if we do a cake for her, it’d be good if someone picks a recipe that reflects that. Maybe a technical round showstopper style thing.      I can do that. We could do a themed tray of mini bakes instead of just one big cake, keep the conversation going while the tea’s cooling. I’ve set some candles in the window by the way, the soft blue ones that smell like lavender.      That’ll set the mood perfectly. Just don’t go overboard with the scent or she’ll sneeze and lose track of the story I’m telling about how Uncle Gary tried to mix up the birthdays by mistake.

So do you know yet when they're taking your tooth out? mine came out last week and it was like... agony, I’ll be honest. I’m still got a hole in my mouth      Aww that doesn’t sound nice I had one a couple of months ago it was alright but I had to take a week off uni      Yeah I had to miss lectures on a Thursday but I had a test on the Friday too so I had to tell my teacher what was going on      Did she take it seriously?      Yeah she did I went to the nurse first who phased everything and then I went to the dentist in the uni block      Oh right I’ve never been to the nurse in mine yet      D’you know how I think it turned out? my tooth actually was breaking the wall of the back one, so they had to do a bit more... surgery in there      Oh that sounds even worse      It was, I was like really nervous cos I thought maybe it would be easier but the nurse put two injections in one go to numb my whole jaw      Oh wow      Yeah then it got taken out and I just felt it vibrate cos I could still feel it      That sounds really strange      It was I could feel the suction as well and the vibrations and stuff      I’m glad I didn’t have to go through that      Also, I had to stay overnight and be collected in the morning      Oh right I did that as well      Oh really what did your parents say?      They were alright with it I mean it is a student loan but I had to go back for follow up      I did too on the Tuesday after to check it was healing      I wonder if you miss your tooth or just stick to one side as you eat      Yeah I’ve been a little bit one-sided with eating      I was the same with mine like I just couldn’t even go near it on that side      Yeah it made my denture wobbly too because I had a big gap on one side      That sounds really annoying      It was also so weird when people looked at me to smile cos it was just a big hole in the middle      Aw I can imagine I probably wouldn’t be able to smile without being embarrassed

Right, so today is Chinese New Year weekend, and I thought we could talk about it and maybe think of a couple of fun things to do. I’m thinking lanterns, maybe something with red envelopes, or even doing a small act of kindness as the tradition kind of says. What do you two think?      I don’t think I want to do acts of kindness. It’s not very fun. I don’t want to give money to homeless people. They might take it and go and get sweets or something.      Sweets aren’t bad, Livvy. You could give them like, a chocolate bar! Not like pennies and stuff.      That’s a lovely idea, actually. You don’t have to give money, you could share food or write them a nice note, pick up litter in the park? Or even take in a neighbour’s cat for a weekend if they’re feeling ill?      I don’t want to touch a cat! They scratch you and puff fur everywhere.      It’s called petting, you goose! You can’t just pet them forever if you’re not a cat person.      I’m not a cat person! I’m a banana person.      Well, let’s focus on the Chinese New Year part for now. We could make some kind of decoration to put up in the house. I saw a template online for lion heads, they look fun. Who’s in?      I’ll help if we can use the draughts pieces as money for whatever game we play after. I’ve been using them as money in a fake economy at school about how rich people walk around with gold coins but it’s actually just shiny black and red pieces.      That’s barely a fake economy, George! Maybe we could do something proper like Burgers and Banjos or Loans and Loans.      Alright, any activity with coins sounds fun, but let’s just focus on today. We could also talk about what we want to do with our hair this year. I’ve been thinking of going back to blond but going back to normal is a bit boring. Maybe some streaks or even blue goop?      If you go blue, I’m going neon green. I had green before but it bloomed into pink and your hair was like radioactive.      Oh no, we don’t want radioactive parents. I’m staying natural unless I can talk you into something over the top.

Mummy, did you know that Alice in Wonderland is supposed to be a real place in Oxford?      No, love, is it? I thought it was just a fantasy story by Lewis Carroll.      Well, kind of! The Alice is a real person. She was a friend of his, and the place they had tea is real too. I read it on the internet.      That’s interesting. I remember reading Alice when I was your age, but it’s been a while. I liked the Mad Hatter the best. Do you know why he’s like that?      I think it’s the tea, right? Because Alice goes to a mad tea party. Oh, Mummy! When’s the last time you felt truly mad like the Mad Hatter?      I was about 16. Wait breakfast, no—maybe when I found out my car was in a minor accident, thanks to your Nan’s shopping trolley driving.      What happened?!      Nothing serious, I promise. She went to pick me up one day to go to the chemist, and as we were going out of the supermarket car park, she hit a seagull. Poor thing just flopped onto the roof, and I had to drive to the vet the next day with a bird on my bonnet!      That’s the funniest thing I’ve ever heard. Oh no, what did you do?      I took the bird in, the vet said it was just bruised and scared. That seagull looked at me like it knew I was guilty. I think I still have a photo of the car with the seagull on top.      Could I see it?      Maybe. But first, let me ask—what’s your next topic about Alice? I have a feeling there’s more where that came from.      Well, I started reading a while back about queens and how they dress. Websites mentioned corsets and layers of tulle and frills. I thought the costumes in Alice looked really magical. Then I saw a play the other day in Hastings that had a man dressed up like the Red Queen. He looked absolutely bonkers in a bright red hat and a wig with big puffy cheeks.      That sounds amazing! Theatre in Hastings has come on so much in the last few years. It gives your dad a chance to reminisce over proper musicals from when he was younger.      I like going there too. My teacher said the costumes are made from things people don’t usually think of.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You think they'd do a bit more research before putting up these turbines in places where they’ll just look like great big gadgets ruining the view. I've been over this with that little group up near Cheltenham and it’s such a maze.      That’s true, and we’ve got the same sort of problems here. They wanted to stick a wind farm just outside Ramsgate last year. Of course, it was going to be right by some lovely old sand dunes and nothing was taken into account. Didn’t even look at the effect on the migratory birds, as far as I can tell.      Aye, and it's like that all over the North. I’m still waiting to see a proper plan that takes the environmental impact into account. But the way I see it, the local planners are either too scared of the powers that be or too keen for a bit of Government funding to actually challenge the big energy companies. And the appeal process is maddeningly slow.      That’s exactly what I told the Cheltenham group last night. I mean, we did a bit of digging and found out that, for every pound they give local authorities for research, they’re handing out tenfold more in subsidies to the energy companies. No wonder they’re pushing for these things.      Now don’t get me started on the subsidies. I understand the need for renewable energy, heaven knows I want to see less smoke in London, but they need to sort the storage problem out. You can’t just fling solar panels about and hope the energy doesn’t go to waste when the sun sets.      That’s right. I’ve had a man down the office lot who fancies himself a bit of an inventor. He reckons we’re missing the trick if we don’t start investing properly in storage solutions. If the Government gives that sort of money to energy companies, why not spend a bit more on research? It all adds up. You’ve got protests on one hand, pro-renewable companies on the other, and the planners stuck in the middle.      And don’t forget the politics of it all. You try getting a development control committee to listen to goings-on on the ground if it's not going to give them some shiny line in the budget report.

Rather skip the new driving course eh, love? Thought you said you’d had enough of theory.      I have! I just need more practice, not another week of sitting in a classroom. I’m not getting any younger, Dad!      Now, darlin’, een’t rush. You’ve plenty of time. Your father here he tried to drive all of two roads before he let the clutch slip and nearly put the boot through a telegraph pole.      That was one time! And I were twelve months younger than when I passed.      Right, because now I’m  this  close to learning from the people who only teach people to drive like everyone else’s a criminal. I’m not going to start trembling every time I hear the starter motor.      I think he turned off the engine at a roundabout once. Made the car judder and then stoke out in front of a queue in traffic. People were honking so much we wondered if the car’s dead was a national emergency.      That was because I had a cold. My foot went numb in the clutch.      And that, Dad, is why I want to take it slow. I’m paying all this money so I at least know what I’m doing. I still think it’s bonkers that I can’t learn on my own somehow.      It weren’t like that in our day, dear. Our parents just tossed the key to the bonnet and said, “Drive careful, love.” And off we went.      Not helped being taught by Margie’s elder brother who spent more time waving at about five cows than staying on the road.      I get it. I just wish there weren’t so many rules. I mean, it’s a  car . You press the pedal, move the gear stick, look out the window.      And slam the horn if a cyclist tries to zip across with no regard for you or your passing station. We had to learn that.      Look, I’ll be fine. I’ve just been waiting for the lesson with no delays for  weeks , so this week or next, I’ll get goin’. I just pray if I ever pass, the insurance is affordable. Thought it was enough that I’m paying the course, let alone getting arrested due to a premium.      You think that’s bad, wait till you fall in love with someone else to insure you.

So Dad, I've been thinking about moving to Brighton once I finish my degree. Do you think it's worth it?      Brighton? Now that's a lively place, I must say! It's a world away from Gillingham, that’s for sure. But you’ll be in for a shock if you're not used to the cost of living. Back in the 50s, a clean suit would last you five years, and a cup of tea was under a penny. Times have changed, let me tell you.      Yeah, I know the price of rent up there is through the roof. Still, I like the idea of being near the sea, and there's more of a social scene. Just wish I didn't have to pay so much for parking! I heard you can’t even find a spot without a permit anymore.      Parking? Back in my day we used to park practically on the beach! Course, that was in London at the time, and not many people had cars to begin with. Still, the memories I have from that—village fetes, a nice cup of tea and a biscuit in the garden.      I'd kill for a decent cup of tea sometimes. I tried making it myself, but I swear it's never the same as what you serve. How do you do it?      Simple really. Three spoonfuls for a strong brew, no less! And never use the wrong water. Our tap water back in the 50s was tough on a delicate palate. I had a kettle with hotter water—served fresh, and brewed in a proper pot, not that leaf stuff people are into these days.      I prefer the leaf stuff! But yeah, I get what you mean. Maybe I should start making that better tea and biscuits for the kids. At the moment I'm just feeding them on toast and whatever takeaway I can afford. I feel bad sometimes.      You’re doing your best love. I remember when I was raising your mum, we lived on two pots of soup a week and eggs out of the food bank. You keep the kettle whistling and the kids fed, that's what matters.      I try! Honestly, it’s tough being a student and trying to save for a deposit in Brighton. I’ve taken a part-time job in a café, but it’s not all that regular.

So did you watch The History of England on iPlayer yet? That episode on Shakespeare—the one they said was all sarcasm and innuendo?      Not yet, but I saw a clip where they were talking about how he probably wrote  Hamlet  drunk at like 1 a.m. on a Tuesday. Sounds about right if you ask me. I reckon his nickname should’ve been “Shakespeare the Drunken Bard.”      Haha, yeah, but think of all the  kills  he could’ve gotten in if he’d golfed during the day before. Like, “To golf, to cluck—a swing and a miss!”      You’d have to change the putter to a quill, probably. “Drive left, lawyer—what a swing!”      Roaring. I think he’d have made it an in for the uni golf league if he was still around. You know I mean, with a bit of rep at the course, and all.      Honestly, he could’ve beaten us both off the bat. I still can’t get my drive past the 9 iron. You, though, with that long back swing of yours, you could probably get on the PGA Tour if it wasn’t for that stupid habit of yours.      Which one? Swinging way too hard and topping the ball into a hedge or telling people to “get their head out of the sand already” during every shot? Both seem fair in this group.      Fair. But man, if Shakespeare was here, I guarantee he’d make the pro shop a nightmare with his witty comes at the green fees.      “To golf, to pay—and suffer?”      “Thou dost charge most thievish for this round.” Definitely that one.      You sound like you’re quoting him, mate. What’s your surname by the way? I’ve called you Hancock since uni, but it’s still not stuck as a nickname.      You’re getting your sarcasm from the wrong time. My full surname’s Smith-Thorp, but no one uses it unless I’ve had too much. My grandad used to call me “Thorp the man with the short game,” which I think he meant as a warning.      Yeah, I’m just “Dave,” the one bloke who’s always one off par but two behind in the bets.      That’d be you alright, Dave. You might be a graduate, but you’re still over here pronouncing “caddie” like a Sassenach.      Hey, I pronounce it fine! It's just, I don’t do side jobs.

So do you not find it a bit weird working at an event where they know your full schedule?      Which one? The poetry one or the one at Ely?      The Ely one. I mean I had to dress up, like full smart-casual and all that. But yeah, the organisers knew my   whole   schedule basically.      I don’t find it weird at all! I mean, I work in production, so it’s like that. We’ve got to log everything for the timeline. But, don’t get me started on my shift boss—he thinks I’m  promising  to attend every after-shift pub drink.                Ten more, yeah? I mean, I’m not used to being paid for doing nothing. It’s like breaking muscle memory at this point.      Fair. I feel like in my job, I’m non-stop. I mean, ordering chairs for a venue? That’s like,  calm . Then there’s the panic when someone changes the start time three days in. Like, “right, change the   whole   colour scheme because they want something ‘more corporate’ now.”      Oh, my shift boss is like that. Last night, he just turned to me and said, “It’s not enough to be efficient, Lee. You have to   lead with flair  .” I said, “Sir, I just label boxes. I don’t lead a cavalry charge.”           What’s the   worst   bit?      Not being about to actually save any money. I’m the   only   one in my mate group not doing Airbnb. I mean, I’m paying barely more than housing benefit does, so I just pay rent, eat, and that’s it.      That’s rough. I know it’s a bit ‘get off my lawn’ but I did manage to start saving when I moved to Cambridge as part of my job. Even if it’s just lunches—  I’ve tried to do  , but the veganism thing just  kill  me.           Yeah, I tried going vegan for two weeks and my dentures just came out.      You went what!?      I made it 14 days, then I was down the local café with a £15 lentil casserole and a side of regret.      S’all my faults I got so bored of cottage cheese and toast. I once accidentally licked my hand trying to brush my teeth and taste my finger and it was just like, “Nope. Yeah. Definitely needs cheese again.”           What’s that supposed to mean?

Rather skip the newfit and go through the garden, see what’s what.      Oh, come on in, come in. I’m just watering the herbs. I've been trying to get this little patch of veg to do reasonably well.      Oh, it’s doing good een! That there, the mint runnerin’ all over the place again, I suppose.      Aye, but I’ve managed to keep it in check this time. It was quite a battle last summer! Put in some edging and whatnot. Although, the bamboo’s taking over the corner like it owns the place! Not sure what I was thinking when I planted that.      It’s a useful plant if you know how to manage it. I’ve read about some good clumping varieties. But this one I think is the invasive type—might need a fence sooner or later.      You need to put up a fence for that lot? When’s the last time we thought we needed to fence for anything? I thought we had more important things—like defending the telly licence!      I don’t watch telly as much as I used to, but someone still has to watch the news for the neighbour. She’s always moaning about it. Poor old Baptiste—he got a fine last week for it.      Yeah, the TV licence has got tighter than Silly String these days. You don’t even need to be watching it just someone at home!     By the way, did I show you the new owl box up by the cherry tree? I thought it might be a decent idea after we heard the tawny owl about last week. Seems peaceful up there.      Oh yes, I like that idea. The local wildlife people mentioned that owls are becoming more common in gardens now that the woods are so overgrown. I always thought it’d be lovely to see one up close.      Aye, I once had a sparrow nest on the roof beam in the kitchen. Tiny little things. Though I’ve seen more space than birds recently—watching “Cosmos” on YouTube the other night, you remember that programme? All that talk about the beginning of time goin’ on in your living room.      Oh, yeah! I remember that programme. Sue Perkins, wasn’t it? Anyway, all that talk about black holes and big bangs. Mind you, it did make you wonder, didn’t it? If we’ve come from a bang and swirl, imagine the food at the banquet of existence!

So do you reckon The Whitgift is still any good? I’ve not been in there for like a year.      Yeah, I’m more than happy to take your word for it, as long as we don’t end up waiting two hours for a table. Remember the last time?      Oh, yeah, that was an absolute   mare  ! I swear they put us on a playlist that only played jazz. Not the best vibe if you’ve had a long week.      Well, we’ll just pop into The Priory pub first, get a quick pint and a snack, then head over. I mean, is it much further from the car park?      It’s a walk, yeah, you know the traffic’s a bit of a mess on Mondays. You either risk getting stuck in the queue or you brave the 30-minute walk across town.      I’d say braving it is better than getting stuck in a car for ever. I hate driving in the rush hour. Also, the bus is full of blokes in overalls, if I book one of those seats I might have to legislate.        God  , don’t remind me. The last bus I caught practically reeked of fish and chips. I swear it was a new seasoning they hadn’t tried before!      Yeah, but don’t forget, if you phone for a taxi it’s like you’re paying for a prime minister's motorcade. Spent £50 to get from here to the bus stop last week. Madness.      So, if we hit it off at The Priory, we can continue the vibe at The Whitgift. I hear the nouvelle turbot is   legend  . Course, I can’t remember where that even   is  .      The Priory’s in that old market square, near the Cathedral. Got that new gastropub vibe. The food’s alright, the music is a bit too nice for a Monday, but it’s peaceful.      As long as we can’t hear the busses outside trying to catch speed bumps.      Some people like the soundtrack of a city.      Some people like actual goon rock on the jukebox.      You’re just in the mood for some proper noise.      Proper noise and a proper sandwich. If it’s too posh, we can always poach those cheese scones from the nearby manor farm shop. Know where they are, anyway?      Yeah, I think it’s off that cobbled lane. Just past the red-bricked house with the crooked tower.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? That bird at six o’clock every Sunday, squawkin like a lunatic. I often think it’s me ne’rbor’s dog, but no, turns out it’s that parrot of theirs, somewhere in the garden. Just like an alarm clock. Got een beginning to forget me own name if I keep gettin woken up like that.      Oh Ayn, I know the one! I heard it last Sunday too. Imagine keepin a parrot. Who taught it to shout like that at the crack of dawn? That’s a right griddle for anyone near it. I mean, I like a bit o’ bird song, but this is like a posh turkey on a bad day!      Ten to one it was the same one. But I was thinking of gettin me own bird feeder in the garden, tryin to see if I can actually tell what birds are about. Hears a lot o’ chipping and chirping but never can tell if it's a sparrow, a starling, or some fancy-pants tit.      Oh I can try and help ye with that. Did a little bird-watching course once in Chester… well, more of a hobby group, really. You start off with the basics. Little bitty chap with cheeps that sound like a cash register? That's a goldcrest. And if it's a big ratter one that screeches, it’s probably a rook.      Rats! That sounds advanced to me. I do manage to identify the seagulls mind, and let’s be honest, they're all the same in me opinion. Grey, about to steal y’r chips, and the lot of them. I had one thievin’ my toast yesterday. Proper cheeky!      Maybe you’re not feeding them the right thing. If you put out anything with butter or jam on it, they'll hover. Try a few sunflower seeds and peanuts, that way you’ll get the finches and the tits. Those are the cute little ones.      I might give that a go. I’ve also been having a bit of a run with my nose lately. Keeps bleedin goin on, usually when I get up in the morning. Gave me dentis’ a right laugh. He were more interested in y’r mouth than yer nose. Said something about flu and nose bleeds and the like.      Oh, I’ve been warned about that too. Gets worse if you’ve got them dry heaters on.

Victoria! Oh my goodness, look at you! You haven’t changed a bit. How long has it been? Five years?      It’s  Vicky  now, Andrea. And yes, it’s been far too long. Look at us—last time we saw each other was probably at eenie-meenie’s graduation party. How’s she doing?      She’s a trainee midwife now. Got her NUS card back in November. She’s into all that social media vlogging—constantly posting videos of her shift experiences. Apparently, she’s got a following of nurses now. Horrible photos mostly, but apparently it’s inspiring someone.      That’s brilliant! My son, Ollie, who’s left London and moved back up North to do landscape gardening, for some reason thought I should be the one to take an interest in his TikTok gig. I get it—relatable content—but mastering greensleeves videos in my early 40s is not quite my dream project.      Good for you for trying—viral or not, it’s all part of this new world we never expected to live in. So, how are you, Vicky? You looked… lighter. Happier. Something in the air?      Changes. Big changes. I split with my husband three years ago, but the real big move was after that—into social work. I left the corporate sector, did my conversion, and never looked back. It’s slower, more soulful. Less climbing a ladder, more climbing a mountain one day at a time.      Oh, darling, that’s so  you . You always had a heart about you. I finally pulled the plug on the school last year, too. Not for a new career—that fails—you know that was my rho factor and it cruelly failed IVF twice. My sister’s got two, and yes, her twin passed on a scratch on the floor and got all  I’ve disappointed my grandparents . Ridiculous, honestly.      I’m so sorry, Andrea. That must’ve been so hard. But I’ve got news too. I’m adopting. I’m halfway through the course and the social media thing go hand in hand now—sorting out risk assessments, managing online interactions.      Oh, bless you. That’s wonderful—and I’m your biggest fan. So, have you made peace with all this? The career change, the IVF?      I did talk about it in a blog I started—just a bit of therapy. You know my writing days back at uni?

I can't believe the weather’s still this bad in March. I swear it was colder today than it was in January. Aye, it’s not doing me body no favours, that's for sure. I had to cancel my walk with the dog yesterday — wouldn't even come out the house. Poor thing. It was raining proper hard. I kept thinking about my kids — I’ve got A-level students starting revision soon, and I don’t envy them studying in this weather. Aye, the schools nowadays, always stressing 'bout exams. Me, I came outta school, didn’t even know what a GCSE was, and I turned out right guid. Course, that’s what you think when you're young. I suppose! I teach English, and I always feel like these kids have more pressure now. Back in your day, did you ever have to do project work or present things to the class? No more’n being asked to read a paragraph out to the class and the whole room laughing at me for mispronouncing the word "hypnotic" — still gives me nightmares. Oh no! Did you say "hymn-otic" or something like that? Aye, that's the one! I was ten, I think. My teacher just sat there like she didn’t have a clue whether to laugh or help me. That’s pretty funny — sorry! Honestly, I'd have apologised for the class making you feel like that. These days we’re always on about mental health and creating a safe space. I wouldn’t have appreciated that then, mind you. I about cried I was so embarrassed. I just kept talking the whole time after that to stop people getting bored and looking at me! You handle it well! Maybe that’s why you found time for reading the newspaper twice a day now. I read it on the iPad, to be honest — I assume you still get the paper delivered? Aye, I do, good as it is. Let’s face it, trying to read on a little screen with my eyes like this is a no-go. Gave up trying with t’technology years ago. I get it! I tried to get my parents to help me set up my password, and they just looked at me like I'd asked them to speak Martian. It’s like fluency in tech is a new language now. Tell me about it.

Right, so we've got this thing on at the weekend. A few people from Cambridge and Peterborough—basically the usual bunch—get together now and then down here at Jon's place. It's a proper foodie sort of night. No takeaway, no microwave meals. Just like a proper Sunday roast or een Italian banger if the mood's with it.      Oh nice, that's a change. A lot of the times when we meet up, it's just pizza and chips and some dodgy kebab left over from the night before. Not that I'm complaining or anything.      Yeah, truth be told, I've been cooking a lot at home, actually. My partner and I are trying to be a bit more healthy. Though last week we tried to make lasagna from scratch and ended up ordering a takeaway anyway. A bit ironic really.      That doesn't sound unusual. I've been into meal prep for a while though. It’s the only way to keep some sanity when working shift rotas. One time, I thought I was making chilli, and it turned out to be vegan shepherd's pie with no seasoning. It still tasted like cardboard.      Meal prep—it's the circle of life in the admin world. I’m more of a cereal-for-dinner chap, I'm afraid. Hay, speaking of food, have you seen the new Jamie Oliver documentary?      No, but I heard he’s trying to convert someone into full-on sustainable lifestyle. Probably not a man like me who's been known to buy out the entire jar of marmalade from the supermarket once.      Yeah, there's a scene about how food waste is a global issue. Interesting talking point. We were just looking at a graph the other day at work that showed how much food the UK throws away every year. It’s mind-blowing. Like, if that was a city, it'd be the size of...      Bristol?      Manchester, actually.      Blimey.      Honestly, it makes me think I should join one of the “zero-waste” communities you hear about these days. Though I’m not sure I can go that far on the DIY front. I once tried to make my own deodorant, and I ended up with a box of questionable yellow powder and one very smelly t-shirt.      Oh no, that’s a crime against fashion right there.      Speaking of fashion, have either of you seen that new Banksy exhibition?

So did you lot hear the weather’s going mental tomorrow? Like proper gale force winds and horizontal rain.      Oh no, poor kids at the football camp then.      Yeah, I feel bad for the coaches. They must be spending half the session just trying not to lose the ball in the wind.      Honestly, I’ve been thinking about going to that new gym by the train station in Cambridge. I’ve heard the roof is  supposed  to be hurricane-proof. Maybe it's the only safe place outside of a bunker.      Right, because gyms make  perfect  places to shelter from the apocalypse, don’t they? You’ve got the turkey on the treadmill, the dodgy left hook in the boxing ring, and the guy who thinks he can replicate deadlifts he saw on TikTok.      Fair enough. But honestly, if I have to be stuck indoors for a day, might as well work out. I’ve been ordering way too many salads lately and not actually doing  anything  to burn it off, apart from walking to the fridge twice an hour.      Same. I’ve started calling it the "Netflix bodyfarm" lifestyle. You work out in theory all week, then Sunday comes – sushi, chill, repeat.      Oh, I’ve tried all the apps. You know what the worst one was? The one that gives you that creepy, robotic voice in your ear counting down. It’s like a fitness cult leader. It just goes:  "You can do it, Karen. Five more reps and you will be... powerful."  I  literally  threw my phone in about five minutes.      Haha, typical. I had one app that used to play failsafe motivational music that you  couldn’t  skip. No matter how much the 2000s pop star guest rapping about protein bars was grating at me.      Oh, I once travelled to Australia and tried to get into a gym while on holiday. Ended up in a full-body spandex suit trying to do bicep curls with rocks. Not only did it not work for my arms, but I caused a sand-based workout stormout in the room. They threw me out after I destroyed the parallel bars.      Sounds brutal. I tried a rock-climbing gym once and spent half the session just planning escape routes to the kiosk for snacks. My arms were vibrating by the end, but I still had the energy for two hot dogs.      Honestly, maybe the problem is all of us are going into gyms like it’s a war zone.

Rather skip the half-time ads eh?      Aye, just in time for that first half update. You’ll not miss it, I promise. This football’s on fire tonight.      Yeah, honestly I only came in for the pie and the dip you made. But it’s alright, the game isn’t bad either. Which team is he on again?      That’s Ake, he’s on West Ham now. Used to watch him play for Palace, pulling off little flicks and nutmegs like it was nothing. Still, the lad’s made it to the big time.      Aye, admirable. What’s the score now? Two-nil? That’s a good start for them.      Yeah, but I’m watching the match, not the result. I think the structure of this game is actually really interesting. Tiki-taka doesn’t really cut it any more, everyone goes a bit in behind now. It’s like chess in boots, you know?      Good one, Sam. You nearly sound like one of those BBC commentators there. Though I’ll take short, sharp passing over their hyper-analysing any day. Reminds me of watching films with my nan. Ten minutes of the opening credits and she already works out who dunnit, and none of the other characters matter after that.      Haha, yeah, I get it. You don’t need the homework to follow the story. Same with football. If the crowd’s buzzing, the rush of emotion is enough. You ever think about it? Watching sports or films as a sort of emotional escape?      All the time. I mean, I’m a research manager, the job’s all about data and vibes. But on nights like this, it’s good to just shut the laptop, unplug, and just feel something.      Definitely. And Easter will be about the same. Just me, a Cadbury’s Creme Egg, and maybe a DVD if I can be persuadable enough. You good for Easter? You going up to see your family?      Aye, I’m heading up north, you know, the usual. Mummy wants the house to look gothic with fake ivy if you ask me. But at least I get to spend quality time with the nieces—bit of an outdoor Easter egg hunt, maybe some rabbit inflatables, you name it.      Sounds like fun, though I’m not sure I’ve ever been to a proper Easter egg hunt. We used to dye eggs at school—remember my missus did that with her class?

Rather skip the new films and bring us out to the old cinema. I know her nan would kill us if we got her out of bed for something like that.      Yeah, she might not even make it. Not to start with the film, mind you — just getting through the entrance queue.      I used to take the older ones to the cinema when they were tiny. The dark helped keep them quiet, but now the old woman’s got to squint at a screen as if pulling teeth to spot one of their faces. They were always the chase ones, the kids with the bikes — hell frozen over without a sound!      I remember going to the fair in south London once, like, when I was ten. The carousel, the balloons, the scary guy who ran the ring toss. Made me go red the way he talked at everyone, like a clown but not funny. But Grand nan, she hated the fairs after she saw a donkey’s leg chopped off in one, or so Grandpa told the tale. Good ones, those stories—settle into the dinner table for them.      Fair or no fair, it’s the memories that live on. Like that time in Iceland—what was it? The Westfjords? The kid lost the power cable for his iPad and spent the entire walk to the waterfalls muttering under his breath. All that snow and the phone’s on airplane mode, and he’s shivered like a leaf in a storm.      And you didn’t have time to run up to the village with the kid—had him clinging to your coat and being mute as a ghost all the way back. Poor lad didn’t even make a face until he caught sight of the hotel lit up green like an elf’s house. You could almost forgive the lack of plug adapter after that.      I do wish, though, we took more photos back then. The only thing he has of baby me is a Polaroid where I was all red and wrapped in a blanket, stuck waiting for someone to come out from the shop and take a professional one. Next to me with a puzzled face and a whispy coat—right, no smile for ages after.      The baby photos are goonie on your own, you know. That one at the marathon, you in the wheelchair, cheering like a banshee while the runners went past your legs.

Rather skip the new book till we've finished with the old one.      But like I got the audible version so I can't skip backwards and forwards cos it's like fixed.      So we'll just have to wait till you've finished.      Right and there's the kind of print one as well if you fancied reading as well.      I think I'll stick with my knitting, much easier.      Oh do you fancy knitting the next one for us?      You know what Ma needs to knit a scarf for each character so we can keep track.      You like that idea?      Ooh I like that.      D'you know Ma I think you could sell them online you know for storytelling props and stuff.      I've been doing some odd bits in YouTube and what not you ever looked at that?      I have once or twice but I like the tactile thing more, maybe try some of those knitting apps I can show you.      And then we can still chat about the book on the way through.      Excellent.      And I can read on because the other day I was cooking and couldn't read the actual printed one and couldn't even tape it together so you had to wait till I finished.      Well I was trying to make a plum cake for the weekend.      Ooh plum cake sounds good.      We can have it for tea today about five thirty.      Oh the plum cake is for Saturday tea not today thanks.      Erm and it is plum cake not something else.      Yes plum not black Friday fruit cake.      No it's a proper plum cake it's very different.      Erm.      Let me tell you how we used to play with the big whistles when I was a kid.      You're going on the toys now Ma go back to the plum cake if you like.      No I was making a point about the plastic box we had on the wall your dad used to knock it off sometimes.      Oh I remember those plastic ones I had one as well with a farm in.      We had them as well I used to keep my marbles in that and they were the only kind of thing you had.      Yes and then there'd be the kind of elastic bands and string you could make slingshots with.      And the jacks and stuff as well.      Yes and the skipping ropes, oh I remember that.

Rather skip the newspaper today. Rather difficult when you get glue sticks and markers in it.      Never mind Harold. I’m more interested in what you’re having on your sandwich. Got me a cheese and pickle with a bit of Branston on the side.      Mm, I’ve got a truffle and brie if you don’t mind. Bit fancy I reckon. A lot too expensive for what it is. But it was on special.      Special! You mean the “aged for centuries” special? Or the “look at me I can afford to pretend it’s gourmet” special?      Aye, well, I like a bit of luxury now and again. Besides, got nothing else to spend money on. Children off their money on cars and holidays I hear.      That’s the problem with the modern world, no doubt about it. Spend all your life saving and then they take it off you as soon as they can drive.      That’s right. I was over at the village fete the other day—had one of those donkey rides. They still sell them little glasses of lemonade for a fiver. Makes you feel like it’s 1948.      I remember those. My mother used to take me to the Harrow fête. All those car boot stallies trying to sell you a VHS with your name on it. “This is your life in 101 minutes!”      [laughing] They’d better have a red carpet these days. Still, at least the birds are alright, eh? Not nearly about as many as they used to be round the area, though. I used to see a house full of robins in that cherry tree outside the kitchen window.      That tree’s overgrown now. Got a boy out here last week with his chainsaw trying to sort it. I was holding my breath the whole time.      Aye, you didn’t want that bird sanctuary of yours cut to ribbons.      Exactly. Some people, no respect for nature. Mind you, it was a man with a leaf goiter he had. One of those antiseptic soaps in his pocket.      Antiseptic soap? You sure what your man was carrying wasn’t something else?      [laughing] I never asked, Harold. But I did talk him into keeping the top branches. At least the robins can have shelter from my overgrown geraniums.      That’s the spirit, love. Listen, did I tell you that neighbour of ours used to have that German shepherd before?

So did you get the birthday present I sent to Fran? I raided the charity shop in Chester for that typewriter frame and everything.      Oh yeah I did! I've got it on a shelf in my kitchen now. She was so happy, mind you — wouldn't stop pretending to type out postcards and stuff. I think it got twitchy at one point.      Oh I saw that on Instagram, bless her! Such a show-off, but Fran deserves it. It's worth every penny. Speaking of presents, I got.Fatalfanstay called when I tried to book a car for my weekend to Malton. The bloody thing wouldn't go through. What’s up with that? I managed to get MyFavCar instead, but it smells like someone’s tried to lit incense and then burned the remains in the aircon.      Oh dear, that’s a classic! I once hired a car that had this weird linen scent... I only found out later it was the driver's hides, you know, those vegan ones? They reek like wet socks after a week.      I’m not vegan I don’t care what anyone says to me. I only took veganuary as a joke in like 2019 and it was all just way too much. My dog would have laughed at me, and I take that really personally.     Speaking of pets, mine has started trying to run through my legs during walks. Like, she thinks it’s someone’s birthday and she’s the DJ. I swear she picks the busiest days to do it — you know the one where a cat wants to cross and she’s charging like she’s chasing it, but it’s not about the cat. It’s about showmanship.      Poor vibes. I’ve been trying not to worry that she’s copying my step-mum. She’s got that same... strut. Burgundy hair ribbon and all.      Aha, no way. I'm told it was all very affectionate and no amount of scheming will break your bond. As long as you stay positive and say “yes” to the lunches and keep the biscuits coming.      Exactly, you don't question it. You just feed the beast and hope for the best. But enough about dogs — how are you two in the love line? I’m still figuring out if he lives in the "mate" box or the "maybe" box. The man sends emoji and then messages in full capital letters so I don’t know where I stand.

Rather skip the new bar across the road.      That's it, they said first floor got the seats, but no luck, they run out within ten minutes, sure      Yeah, £20 seems like a lot for a pint, but the place was doing good on opening night      Yeah,   Voldemort   is not as evil as most people think      That's a bit of an understatement      Second floor is just private wine and clubs, and third floor is just elevators and glorified car park      Yeah, I've been a couple of times, but only when we have block of tickets at work, cost free obviously      But Harry doesn't do half the things Darcy does in Pride and Prejudice      They’ve got to put something breakfast, no doubt      Haha, yeah, the gingerbread man is 4,000 years old so that’s why      I do like the way it is though, not too fancy, short bar, not as much noise as the old one, old-school design      You'd expect a little from the way it's been built      Yeah and actually it's not affected the local shop, no staff cut      Should I read the books or watch the movie      Who cares, just get on with it. read books? rush to finish it so you can watch the movie      I thought it was better movie      Haha most people do      I prefer the movie      Overall a good outcome and not too bad for the area      No, but to be honest, I prefer reading the actual books, well most of them      Are the books really long?      Yeah, you know when I started reading one while my kid was sleeping I ended up doing a word count      They told me the same thing when I started volunteering      Mummy! the printer is still goenvironment friendly on the toilet paper      What else is going on?      That bloke on the trains, all them anti-social stuff      Oh that’s not good      You don’t see it on the news or anything over here, but it creeps up like that      I’ve done some talks on it in lectures, you know, always see it as a symbol of fear mongering      Yeah, and it's no wonder, we have issues of our own here, you don’t need to bring that up.      Yeah, and the lectures have to be pretty chilled out in that department      I heard your class is popular      Yeah, it helps that I never fail the work, not for me      That no good

Rather skip the new school meals system entirely. That’s what I do – just pack a proper lunch in a Leithen tin with some home-made sausages and boiled eggs. I know Joan over at the Village Shop always keeps an eye out for the school fairs and the Harvest Festival bake-offs, but it’s all a bit  bland  these days, don’t you think?      I couldn’t agree more, Phyllis! The other week, I had a parent meeting and some woman proudly said she wasn’t going to heat the school dinners up for her child because they were vegan and gluten-free. It’s enough to make you long for the meat pies and the wartime supply of spam we had in my day.      Ha! I remember your stories about the war, Sylvia – the bread lines, the occasional piece of black pudding saved for Sunday. It must’ve shaped a lot of how we breakfast, don’t you think? My Brian still insists on frying his breakfast on the Aga as if we’re reenacting Churchill’s Britain.      It’s in the blood, you know! Speaking of which, I’m thinking of taking a trip to Nepal this spring. It’s something I’ve been planning for a while. I’ve got quite a stash of old clothes from my EFL days in Istanbul and Athens that should still do – just a few new hiking boots and a better camera.      Oh, what a wonderful idea! I’ve been to India a few times, but Nepal sounds like a breath of fresh air. When I took my language students on an exchange trip to the Czech Republic, the youngest of them still remembered it at their university open day years later! You’ll have about five decades of anecdotes to add to your memory bank.      I hope you take some good photos. I’m still trying to get my head around sending my first grandchild gluten-free sandwiches for school. I mean, how do you even know what’s  safe  these days? Last time, I brought in some Farm Shop mini sausages and he started sneezing like a dragon.      Ah, allergies were rarer in the war – unless you happened to be allergic to rationed sugar, of course. My dear Mary told me the most fascinating story of her mother-in-law fleeing from Siberia to Africa during the war on a freight train that had to stop in the middle of the desert for days because of supply issues.

So did you lot hear about the new project at work? Sarah’s promising it’ll be ‘a bit like a proper office rather than spreadsheet prison,’ but I’m not holding my breath, you know?      Oh don’t start. Look, I’ve been in meetings like that since I joined my current job. Every  new thing  is ‘revolutionary’ until it turns into something that needs a flowchart just to undo it. Honestly, I’m just waiting for my coffee cup to scan me in next.      Wait, are you saying you already have flowcharts? I swear my office is like, literally, one giant flowchart. I get assigned tasks and then accidentally reassign them to myself like three layers down. It’s mental! The interns left last week muttering about how they wanted to play D&D, not ERP.      Haha, yeah, I can see it. I mean, I love working in events. At least I’m not sat at a desk five days a week, you know? I get to shout into a mic, chase caterers, and forget things, and no one thinks it’s weird. I’m a  co-ordinator , not a glorified spreadsheet shepherd like you two!      But don’t write that on your LinkedIn. You’ll never get a new job! Listen, actually, I was thinking… are you two up for maybe doing that weekend away? Maybe something near the coast? Just the three of us, no husbands, no work WhatsApps. Just fizzy drinks and complaining about the Wi-Fi?      Only if the Wi-Fi’s  selectively  bad—so we can check emails when we feel like it and ignore them when we don’t. And you’re the one who’s currently on furlong 40 of some document you’re ‘proofreading.’ You can’t unplug for two days. My sister texted me four times yesterday about her toddler's grammar.      Ha, I’d take any break from my own life, to be honest. Work’s getting a bit too eventy—there was a corporate themed escape room last week with 'team-building' foam swords. One guy took it so seriously, he constructed a shield from scrap bits of paper and tried to rally the others. I think he was more stressed than everyone.      I would’ve offered to teach him the box office move… knight takes your employer’s title. It’s a classic.      Okay okay, you two are never going to stop talking about work.

So did you read the letter from the council last week about the library?      Yeah... I skimmed it at work. Something about redevelopment and "shifting community needs." That’s a lovely way of saying “cutting corners.”      Exactly! And I’ve had eenough of it, honestly. I think we need to start a petition. I’ve been thinking about a way to get people engaged.      You mean like a Sign Petition website or posters around the town?      Both. But first I want to speak to the librarian, Sarah. She knows who’s been using the library, who the real heart of the place is. And if the council thinks kids don’t use it, they’re wrong. Ten kids come everyday from the primary school next door.      That’s brilliant, yeah. And you’re better at breakfast, aren’t you? I’m up at 6 in the morning with the shifts and by 8, I’m looking for a second cup of tea.      At least you get weekends off. Mine start at 10, finish at 5 and then I’m off again at 8 on Sundays… plus transcription at night. I swear, if I don’t get at least one proper meal with you this week, I’ll forget how to swallow.      You’re mortal and you will forget what porridge is. I’ve been trying mnemonics this week at work. It’s part of a brain training thing they’ve started.      Ah, yeah. I read an article about mnemonics – the  Method of Loci , where you visualise places to remember things.      Oh yeah, I use a version of that! I imagine that data forms are laid out like park benches in the local park. My brain’s got better, anyway. Doesn’t help much when the council tries to play me with all the jargon.      That’s what I’m mad about. We’re not hearing straightforward answers. They say things like “community consultation” but we keep getting redirected from one form to another – it’s like a maze. You know what it really means? They don’t go out of their way unless someone  stirs them up .      And that’s what we need to do then – stir them up gently. A petition with proper data, names, statistics, and maybe we get a council meeting.      Exactly. I was going to start this weekend anyway, and I was thinking we could go to the community centre to talk to people there.

Rather annoying lot, those Jehovah’s Witnesses aren't they? I swear they pop up in the garden when I’m trying to read the paper on a Sunday.      Yeah, they are a right pain in the neck. I told the one feller off last week. "Deary me," I said, "if I wanted leaflets, I'd get them at the supermarket."      A lot of people just think they're a bit odd, don’t they? I mean, you go to the door and they’re practically holding your sins in their hands before you've even said hello. Not to mention, they won’t take a no for an answer half the time.      My son still talks to them, though. He’s one of them now, the lot who married into them, bless him.      Oh dear, is that his cousin Jenny we’re talking to at the village fair next week then?      Aye, and she’s always ordering puff pastries and tea for everyone like she’s paying—never mind the fact she’s got four kids and a mortgage I don’t think she can afford to feed herself and the whole village.      Makes you wonder why she doesn’t just vote “none of the above” then, with all that charity work. At least the council wouldn’t have to sort out parking problems if they sorted their own first.      Parking on the coast? Oh, someone should put one of those big boards:  "Intelligent parking only—don’t do the three-point turn in the supermarket car park."       That’d be a bit much, but I did see a man walk into the sea trying to park the other day. Poor chap thought it was the car park because it was easier to get out the back.      My, my! And I thought  I  was eccentric. Still, at least I remember to go to the dentist. I’ve got the tooth I tried to save myself when I was your age.      Let’s not go there. I’ve got a new bridge and I’ve got to be careful not to set it off with a nice tuck into the Sunday roast.      Oh nonsense. If it was good enough for my dentures, it’s good enough for you, Arthur. You just need your soup thick enough to hold the spoon in it.      Well, speaking of food—Andrew, remind your wife we said we’d pop over this week.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You know, having to talk about logs again. I've been on mute all weekend and now she's after us because she thought I'd asked for the fudge last week and I hadn't.      It's her way. She'll make a mountain out of a single bar of fudge. You know your mum-in-law. I tell her not to worry about it, but she still ends up sending me a photo of the log pile and asking what I think of it.      Oh, never mind the logs or the fudge – what did the headmistress from Edinburgh say when she heard you were thinking of outsource the work to India?      Oh, she was most particular. She said, "You're not the type to risk the quality of the school just for a bit of cash, now are you?"      He's not – but he has a budget to stick to. It’s the headmaster’s new policy to look for cost-saving measures. And I don't mind taking the calls, really, but it is tiring when the next-door neighbour puts out a log to their back gate and calls it an issue.      You'd think in their day they wouldn’t have worried – but they do now. I mean, who does that these days? Just gets a log on your doorstep and starts making a phone call?      It's the world changing, dear. In our time, people minded their business. Now? It's all logs, fudge, and logs again.      And what about this new restaurant that's come up near the antique shop about half a mile from us? I fancied trying the cuisine, but your mother said it’s too posh for her. Something to do with the mashed potato being ‘too chunky.’      Oh, that’s high praise if anything. The only place she'll go is if she can have all the courses with a bit of meat on the side.      Anyway, moving on from dining etiquette – you've heard of the new academy system? They're trying to set it up for the kids where they can travel like they're in Tokyo or go out of the country for a week or two.      Oh, I see. Well, I was a headmistress, and all I ever wanted was for the children to focus on their education, not on where they're going next year for a supposedly enlightening trip.

Rather annoying this new tax they’ve brought in, isn’t it? I was just reading about it in  The Norfolk Chronicle .      Oh Blimey, what’s it called this time? I don’t even know what they’re taxing us for! I wouldn’t be surprised if we end up paying for the bloody moon if we’re not careful.      It’s that “smart meter tax”, love. They’re charging more from those of us who don’t use them. Seems a bit unfair if you ask me. I don’t see the point when it’s the government taking more from those who’ve already had it hardest.      That’s just it, Jo. It’s like they think you still get free TV licences when you’re retired, or that you’ve still got the spare money for these silly new levies. I’m up to my neck in bills as it is.      You and me both, Jack. I only moved in next door last year and I thought, “Right, I’ll get a place where I don’t have to worry about the bills, and I can just sit and shuffle my knuckles with the cat as it knocks things over.” Hah! Tell that to the local council.      Speaking of houses—I’ve been helping my niece with a new place out in Horsham. It’s huge! She’s got nearly half an acre just for the garden. If I’d got that when I was younger, I wouldn’t still be sitting in an old bungalow with a dodgy boiler and a garden full of weeds!      Aye, and I thought being a civil engineer I’d make enough in my life to live in about five places like that! But you know the problem, we had to retire early. I suppose you could say I know that house you’re talking about, Jo—the one with the green gate and a ‘No Parking’ sign twice as big as the others.      Ha, it is a funny place, that Horsham lot. Everyone there thinks they’re the expert on recycling. I had this chap at the recycling bin once trying to tell me how to flatten a can. I took the liberty of telling him  he  looked like a tin can the way he stood goin’ on.      Oh Charlie, your face when you said that—you looked like you’d seen a bloke in a zimmer frame try and jive.

Right, so the laptop’s still not working, is it? I’ll have a look tomorrow if that’s alright with ye.      Oh, thank you, love. I’d be ever so grateful. I don’t know what the problem is—just freezes every time she tries to watch her eeny weeny video of the dolly duck.           That one from  Peppa Pig  where she bumps into a horse?       Giggles  Moo-oo!      That’s the one. Aye, we can have that sorted. It’s probably just one of those driver issues or a failing hard drive, but I’ll run the check tomorrow. Easier in the mornin’ with no phone calls and all that.      Oh, God bless ye, Jack. And don’t mind the mess in here—my day didn’t go the way I’d planned.      Nonsense, it’s fine. Toddlers are chaos incarnate. What did he do this time? Painted the wall again?      Worse! He was playing with “the spices” – somehow managed to knock the fajita sauce off the top shelf and created the mess of the kitchen.      Oh no! Is that the orange mexicany one? Our geography teacher at school always said it looked like emergency stuff or something.       laughs  That is it! So toxic you couldn’t swim in it – but  thankfully , there’s not nearly enough to make a pool out of!      Aye, th’ kid’s got some idea of what looks like fun. I remember me lad up in Dublin—same with bleach. Burgundy hair for six weeks.       Giggles  I’d love to see that!       Sounds like a spoon clattering from the next room       Oh, lunches ready! Grilled cheese and crispy chicken fingers – you want any of this, love?      Yeah, go on then. But let me ask ye—were you at the rugby yesterday? I was watching that between jobs. Ireland did alright until the 70th minute.      Oh, I didn’t watch it. We had a birthday party for Harry’s cousin’s son—like, two over in宜昌, or whatever the hell it’s called. I think he’s got five mums now.      Exeter, right?      Ah! So anyway, she’s just got back before midnight.      Aye, those DJ nights in Exeter are wild. Was that with the mates from uni who run the lectures in the morning?      Yeah. I met one of the lecturers once. She mentioned something about a linguistics module, and I thought I’d get an easy one for my GCSE.

Right, who’s up for helping me cut up the peppers for the pizza? I reckon it’s time we had a weekend treat, what d’you think, love?      Yes! Pizza is the best! We can make the fairy garden fairy pizzas too, like the little ones in the box!      I wanna do a handstand on the table! Then I can grab the pizza before it’s cold!      No, no, you can’t do a handstand on the table, Josh. You might knock the bowls over or the bread rolls – specially if you’re thinking of fairy pizzas  and  Loch Ness Monster-sized ones! Rather a lot today, wasn't it? That case dragged on far longer than expected.      It was rather, yes. That one poor chap looked absolutely exhausted. I've been in this job long enough to see how these things can wear on a person.      I admire how you stay so calm, considering the pace of it all. I think being a teacher actually helped me with a bit of discipline, but this—this is a whole other ball game.      Discipline's a good thing, no doubt. And for what it’s worth, I still find being up to date on the changes in the system is a bit of a learning curve. I had to go to a training session last month, which was interesting, especially how they’re starting to prioritise more restorative justice for minor cases.      That sounds like a good step in the right direction. From what I've read, the justice system is trying very hard to reduce reoffending rates, especially for first-timers.      Yes, and not just that—there's more pressure than ever to get people into support groups, housing, or even job schemes if that’s their issue. It’s not just punishment anymore, is it?      Absolutely, and I suppose that's one of the big differences with the younger generation in general. There’s more of a focus on support rather than just consequences.      Aye, and don’t get me wrong, I’m not against consequences. But I also think there’s a lot of room to give people a second chance—especially when the law feels a bit too harsh on people who perhaps didn’t mean any harm in the first place.      That makes me think of the climate change protests I’ve had to teach a little about this term. Young people are so keen to stand up for things they believe in, even if it means facing the law. It's fascinating how much they care.      You say they’re facing the law—do they get charges for demonstrating?      Not always, as long as they stay peaceful. But if things turn chaotic, or if someone gets hurt, then the magistrates usually step in. I think it’s a bit of a minefield for the authorities really—they don’t want to risk suppressing free speech, but nor do they want violence.      That must be something to see from the outside.

Right, who wants jelly and ice cream for pudding?      Me! Me!      And me too! Me more than her!      Okay, okay—both of you! No need to argue. We can all have jelly. One, two… go on then.      One, two…      One, two, three, four! I’m good at numbers, mummy.      Good for you, darling. Now, do you remember when we sang that song earlier?  If you’re happy and you know it, clap your hands!       Yeah! I know it!       I  sing it better than Lucy.      No,  I  sing better!      Alright, alright, let’s not compare. Now, something to think about: do you know what being rich is?      Having lots of money?      Right! But do you know what being happy is?      Smiling!      And having lollipops!      Yes, lollipops are fun. But happiness can be as simple as holding your mummy’s hand, or hearing your sister laugh. Sometimes, having a little bit of money and a lot of love is more important than having a  lot  of money and  no  love.      So… are we happy?      I think we are. How about you?      I’m the  happiest  big boy in the world!      I’m the happiest ever, mummy. I have you and Daddy and lots of toys and a cat and a dog and a jelly tree in the garden and a castle in my bedroom. I  love  my castle.      Well, that does sound very fancy. But even if we had  no  castle, and just had each other and a small house, would we still be happy?      Yeah, because we have each other. That’s what you said, mummy.      And that’s rhymes too!  Other  and  mummy  go like the songs.      Exactly! So even if we didn’t have a hundred pounds, just the three of us can still be the happiest people in the world.      Then let’s never ever spend all our money on ice cream, because we need to be happy with  love  as well!

So do you reckon I should go into engineering or software stuff? My dad says engineering's solid ‘cos like... you don’t get replaced by robots or whatever yet.      Nah, I reckon software is the future. I mean, like, what if you create some app or AI or whatever and then you get  billionaire  one day. I reckon Bill Gates did all that from his kitchen with a cow or something.      Haha, no, he was in a lab or a garage or something. Anyway, what about you? You want to be a programmer or what?      Not sure. I thought about inventing like, you know, some kind of robot dishwasher turkey thing. You know, like a machine that automatically makes and opens cans of Monster Energy and dispenses them in your hand in the dark?      What? How would it know when you want it?      Oh, just a sensor. Like infrared or motion, you know? Or maybe a shout. Like, you shout “Monster Water Time!” and it does it. I could patent that. Imagine if we did a patent to China and sold the idea and then they make a billion of them and sell it back to us for like fifty pounds.      True. I heard they copy everything and then put huge stickers on it saying “Made in China.”      Yeah, man, I’m always like—this is mine. This chicken Tikka Masala recipe is my design. I mean, they’re doing 5G and stuff that we can barely even get handle on.      Yeah, for real. If you put your money into some robot tea-making Chinese company, man, it’ll just zoom up. I mean, I tried to buy some shares on my mum’s laptop, but it was too complicated.      Yeah, I think it’s all about tech and the future. Even like, delivering stuff around with drones or electric cars or whatever. I bet in five years, if you don’t get into one of those fields, you’ll be selling burgers.      Nah, your burger-selling future could have a robot that hears your ketchup needs from two miles away and brings it with like, a tiny drone on a hoverboard.      That’s the spirit.

So did you manage to book the snowshoeing tour for tomorrow yet? I think it’s the first thing available and I’d really love to do it before the guides get too busy.      Yes, I did! Anyway, after snowshoeing, I was thinking we could grab a coffee in the village and maybe pop into that new little gift shop we saw the other day.

Rather annoying when a string’s snapped, isn't it? I was promising one of the secondary school mums I'd lend her my racket for the weekend match, and I can't even play now.      Aye, seems like I break strings at the worst times. Over twenty quid een time if you go to the pro shop they'll restring it. But I've been trying a bit of a DIY method, actually—      No, really? Go on, tell me. If it's cheaper and faster, and doesn't chase me out of the garden court every Sunday...      So, I bought some heavy-duty cable ties, the sort you use for electrics. You know, the ones with a solid plastic bit and a clasp. You wind the main string around the broken piece and tie it off with the cable tie in the middle. It creates a bit of tension and keeps it working enough for casual games or for a student at the primary using it as a practice tool, even if it's not perfect.      Oh, clever! Might get me some of those—      What did you say your grief was for, by the way?      Wait, who was that?      Apologies, I sneaked in while you were talking and gave you the wrong cut on the side—there’s a whole stripe in the hair and one earlobe might be a little shorter.      Well, you're a retired EFL teacher, not a barber! Some students had the same problem with a ruler and a bottle cap once—      Haha, I did just that years ago! Although I tripped over the stool and cut my thumb off a little too—that's how I ended up with barely a left lobe.      Makes you wonder if the "fleet" of racket users are all cut up and tied together by the time they’re done being reckless!      A little macabre, but accurate! So, if we're doing a business here—badminton string repair via DIY—how would we market it?      You're onto something, love. Imagine goin' on the  Dragons’ Den  or one of those shows. “Budget Badminton Solutions,” the box might say—and picture the one about secondary schools. It's cheaper than mats and cleaning supplies and one less thing to chase after broken items in the PE cupboard.      Sounds brilliant, but we’d need a catchy slogan. Somen’ like  “Keep the game going, even when strings don’t!”       Or  “Stop the snipes and string snapping.”

Rather nice to have you all round for a bit of a chat. I was just admiring that picture on the wall again. Never had much luck painting myself, but I can tell a decent one when I see one.      That one? That’s a print, dear. A few years ago I saw the real thing at the Tate. Not many people know that, but I’ve actually been on a few day trips to art galleries over the years. I used to collect postcards, you know, back in the days when we had to buy stamps and pop them in the postbox.      That’s interesting, Mum! Art’s something I’ve been trying to weave into the students' assignments lately. It helps them look beyond the textbook sometimes. I got a bit of pushback, to be honest—some of them think art is frivolous compared to ‘proper’ subjects like science or history.      I actually include art in some of my lectures too, though more from a modern perspective. Show them some pieces that have shaped culture—like Banksy, or even Yayoi Kusama if we're going abstract. They get into it if you land it in the right way.      Oh, I remember watching a documentary once about Kusama. She looked so frail, but then they showed her installation with the dots, and it was beautiful. Like being inside her brain. All that repetition and depth.      You don’t say. I wouldn’t have thought someone with her style could get so much out of just a few simple shapes.      That’s the genius of it, though. Minimalism allows for so much interpretation. My students found it quite touching, actually. One even tried to make a room full of polka dot balloons. It didn’t quite work out—you know how university labs are!      Maybe they’re not built for that kind of creative chaos. I had a student once who tried to make a 10-foot-long sculpture out of wooden spoons. I tried to stop him when he started hammering the first one, but… well, academically speaking, it was a mess.      Some people just want to be  artists , dear.      Yeah, go on then! But it was educational in its own strange way. You learn just how hard it is to make something that looks  easy .      So all this talk of art, but how many of you have actually seen one of those big museums in person?

But now it's 8 o'clock in the morning and you're staring at a screen again and I'm making bloody tea and then feeding the dog.      Yeah well most people work from home now, but I still have this obsession with routine.      You know it’s just you grinding the gears of your mind again. You always say that.      I mean I do, you know, going out with mates or I’d be with your mother. But since she moved back in, it's like there's something watching us at all times. Okay, but you do drag your Aran out every time you feel like sulking over being unemployed.      I haven't told my parents yet, but let’s not set off a panic around here by bringing it up.      They'd be more worried about me than you, though. You're the man, you're supposed to have all the answers. I can get away with being all hot and cold and emotional. You know, they often say in those so-called liberal circles, like in the trendy women’s media, that men are the problem, but it’s just not that straightforward.

Rather do this than drink tea eh?      Aye, it's peace ‘n’ quiet, and I’m not about to let you run out on me again by disappearing into your PhD headspace for a month with no update. Look at this—get a load of the pattern I’ve started on this scarf. I’ve been watching one of those   YouTube tutorials   again.      Aye, love watching those! Got one from a lass in Dumfries she does, easy as pie. Knitter to the bone. You get the chase when it's the Olympics on the telly like, but truth be told, I can't tell a short track sprint from cycling if my life depended on it.      Ha! You left it on the telly, didn’t you? D’you pick a country to cheer for? Or are you just there to eat and giggle at breakfast-time coverage?      Aye, I like Spain and Italy, ever since I went on that field trip for the art dissertation. Absolutely lit up the night.      Real passion, eh? I still think it's bonkers that you had a whole PhD in   art history  , and now you're analysing knitting cables for fun.      Aye, but it’s also   easter  —time to unleash my creativity. I got some fluff from this market in Cambridge and started this here ‘castle motif’ thing for your grandmother. She’s gonna have about five heart attacks when she sees it, but she’ll adore it.      You and your   castle   plans. Last year you sent her a ‘knit to the theme of ‘knurlington’’ guest list card. I swear to God, if it wasn’t for knitting I’d be watching   celebrity   gossip all day like you, getting worked up by some silly man’s divorce or goings-on on some lake in Nova Scotia.      I do not, I study it. Celebrities, I mean. You might call it gossip, but I track it like it's statistics—  a cultural barometer   of broken relationships and vanity, mostly.      Perks of being the ambitious pair from the north and midlands, I suppose.

Rather than chuck afit of the vapours, I said. A few more hours in the ‘bus and I got to see some proper sights. That’t more than I can say for you, love, stuck on that 53 all afternoon. Told me to go and wait at the next stop. Fifty minutes I waited in the rain.      Right, well, I couldn’t be arsed with that. Took the train into Euston and made my way to the Museum of London. The new Imax is there now – I didn’t know you could get films in 3D there. They showed one about the Great Fire of London. The flames looked like they was going to leap through the screen.      I didn’t go to that one, didn’t I. I got the wrong time, sat in the shop for twenty minutes, and by the time I got up I missed two bloody shows.      It wasn’t that fancy, but it gave you a bit of a rhythm in your day. You’re not used to doing much besides reading the paper, and now it’s all museums and Imax and 3D nonsense.      If I’d ‘ad a proper job, I wouldn’t be out here at the mercy of the bus system. You’d think they’d run a few more damn routes for folk looking to have a day out. Not when you’re doing it. But when you’re seeing it as 3D flames and falling bombs, aye, it’s fairly educational if you ask me. Still, I did run into Margaret from the church. She was goin’ on about how she got a standing ticket for the Crystal Palace open day. Imagine that,  after  the Palace bloomin’ disappeared thirty years ago.      I might’ve been there if I’d had the hours to spare.

Rather skip the turkey and just bring a load of dumplings. I’m telling you, it’s been like... What, eight years since we went back for Christmas?      Yeah, gotta be close to that. I can't believe how peaceful it is out here. You don't get this kind of quiet in London, do you? No way. It's completely different. Even on the quietest days in London, there's always a car horn, a siren, or a street performer playing terrible clarinet. Ugh, I miss the birdsong out here. It’s like they don’t even have to try—they just sing their best every single morning. It's one of the things I always loved about Norfolk. The countryside here is so open, but still peaceful. You don’t often wander far enough to feel lost—just like you're in the middle of something ancient and steady. Yeah, I’ve only been to Norwich a couple of times, but the villages here are what really impressed me. I think the world should be more like this—tiny communities with everyone knowing each other, no rush, no hustle. The hills don’t look like much from a distance, but when you walk them—and I mean properly walk them, not like I did with my sneakers on inappropriate socks—you start to see how the land changes. I love that. Small details like the way the light hits the thatched roofs in the villages. You can’t really see that kind of stuff unless you’re walking, you know? Yeah, it’s not just the view—it’s the feeling that the village has been there for hundreds of years. Like this walk we’re doing now—someone might have made this path five centuries ago. And still walking it now. That’s real continuity. Unlike in cities, where nothing stays the same for more than a decade without being redeveloped. Exactly. We were saying the other day—if we could afford it, we’d like to find a small house near here, something that’s just big enough for the two of us and maybe a garden. I could picture it. A small library, wooden floors, maybe a stone hearth. You know, the kind of place that feels like time just slows down a bit. Yeah, and with the hills just outside the door. Even if we never did run marathons or anything, we could go for regular walks and see if the sun moves higher or lower in the sky each day, just like the farmers. You know what your hobby would be?

So did you watch The Martian last night?      Yeah, it was solid. Thriller with a bit of science peppered in. He was delivering solar panels, and the kerb was too uneven to pull over properly, so he was wedged in a bit, and some老爷爷cyclist in a helmet said “I might be early for work, but I won’t be if you don't move!”      Hah!
