My boss at the corpus admin would slap a memo on all our screens with that.      “Pain is temporary, data is forever.” That’s your new motto?      More like “Teamwork is overrated if you deliver the results.” Pfft! I need to get go back to my day job, sorting audio files for a language project.      You know what’s weird? Time feels faster when your job is manually labelling 10,000 sentences of courtroom dialogue.      It’s a third of the data, and over half the workload. They need a better system. S’all so bureaucratic.      Just like my boss once said, “Consulting is patience, not haste. Unless the client is being a cyclist.”      Classic. You’ve got to enjoy the subtle art of engineering jabs.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it?      It really is. I think we should make the most of this weather before the rain comes down properly.      Agreed. This sun’s quite rare this time of year—definitely one of the better Aprils I’ve had in Norfolk.      Definitely. I’ve just read an article suggesting most people in the south now think summer’s over by May. Rather grim.      Hysterical. We’ve had three decent weeks and suddenly everyone’s considering getting a sunbed. You'd think the East Anglia climate would've made us tough.      Still, it's brilliant that the wild garlic's coming in already. Smells so rich this time of year. I always forget how good it is here.      It is, isn’t it? The combination of the damp earth and that sharp garlic scent is a bit addictive. Walked past some the other day and just wanted to puff it into the air.      As long as it doesn’t start invading your garden—my sister tried to grow it once as a culinary herb and ended up with it sprouting in odd places—bathrooms, wardrobes, the lot.      True. I wouldn’t mind it myself, but I’ve had enough of invasive plants after that friend of mine started trying to grow Himalayan balsam and ended up with a cash crop someone wanted to smuggle.      Oh, did they really? That’s a rather unexpected lifecycle for a flower. I thought it was just a bit of countryside gossip.      No, I’m not joking. Some man in the village had this man from Kent coming in every summer wanting to know how to grow it more efficiently. The unspoken assumption being that the market for ‘cosmetic nasties’ was booming.      Rather worrying. Makes me think of any ‘research’ project with a plant and you suddenly have to question your motives.      Exactly. It’s always been with us, of course—the English are fairly fluent in the language of economic absurdity by now.      Don’t go there. I remember your thesis seminar on post-industrial lamentation and the line about "beer, bicycles and balsam blooming on derelict sites." It made me want to fluently quote Bakunin while weeding my border.      Oh right? I must have missed something—wasn’t that the seminar you wandered in late for? The one where you brought those biscuits?      And you kissed me over the chalkboard afterwards.

So do you want me to bring my car or shall we do mine?      If it’s the big car with the flattie at the bottom I’d rather do mine      Yeah probably cos we wouldn’t have got in with mine      Yeah it’s tight in there anyway I don’t think you want to be squeezing people in on top of that      I think last time when we all went to Wearside you were alright going through the car park under the Angel of the North      That was the worst bit isn’t it like three lanes of traffic united into one and no one knows whether to go left or right      It was definitely madness I remember you were like ‘stop’ and I was like ‘are you serious’ and then there I was stuck behind someone playing football with their kid      Yeah, and then of course this happened when we had Game in the car and I didn’t want to miss any of the action      That was your own fault for dragging the TV into the car, I mean why would I put that in there      It wasn’t my fault we were going to watch it during half time      Half time at a Mate’s flat while he plays football and eats takeout      Exactly      Anyway, will he be there already or are we meeting him on the way in      He said he’d be there earlier probably just playing tennis with someone      I hope he wants to come with us I mean I don’t mind going without him because most people do just end up staying back at the flat anyway      Yeah he said he might not make it because of that mate of his who plays tennis a lot      Should we put the balls in the car then      What d’ya mean      The tennis balls if we are going to carry them      Oh that’s a good point but wait are we even playing tennis on the trip      I think you said maybe after the match but if he's not even there go on then I suppose it doesn’t matter      I just remembered, I think I might be needing a new pair of shoes what your dad was telling me at the weekend      Yeah we had that conversation last Saturday I even bought new ones to give you      Oh right I forgot about that you mean the ones I can’t wear to work

Rather annoying the new developments here, isn’t it? Seems like everything’s getting built on now — even the fields where the geese used to come every winter.      Oh, I’ve noticed it too. Not only that, the crows and pigeons are like a plague — swooping and all that. But I used to see the geese quite regularly. My gran used to say they’d always arrive on the Sunday closest to Christmas.      Oh yes,   the geese!   We used to watch them come from the fields outside when I was a girl. My mother used to swear blind they knew who  liked  them and who didn’t. One day, we left out some oats and turkey, and they’d all land and feed themselves like they were in a London restaurant! And if we didn’t leave the food out the next week? They’d just fly off and forget about us. Fancied themselves the clever ones.      That’s amazing. I remember reading somewhere that they fly in a V-shape to conserve energy. The birds in the front take the most strain, and then they take turns. It’s quite a clever system. Did you know that, Doris?      No, I didn’t. That’s interesting. I just know they come back every year, and sometimes they’re louder than the dogs. I reckon they don’t like the building work either. I’ve seen one or two of them flying around those cranes like someone’s disrupting their routine.      Oh, they  do  get funny about things! Once a man in the village tried to feed them with crisps — salted, mind you — and about half the flock swooped on him like the devil himself! Laughed myself silly. To be fair, though, it wasn’t right. I told him, “Mervyn, those poor things don’t need baked fat and salt.” He passed out by sundown.      That is funny. I love how they have such strong migratory patterns. My brother works for the RSPB — he says they’re always trying to find out exactly where the geese come from and where they go. They think some of them come from Iceland or the Arctic Circle.      I’ve heard that. But what I don’t get is, why do they come back the same time every year?      It’s the seasons, love. They’re not fools. As soon as the frost makes the ground hard to scratch on and the berries get scarce, they up and head south.

So did you go for the interview at the primary in Sutton Coldfield yet?      No, not yet, I’ve been putting it off. I know, and I  did  want to teach younger kids when I did my PGCE, but these days—what with me, my mental health, and my little Alice being like a My Little Baby Dragon who needs constant attention—it’s starting to feel like more than I can handle.      Oh, she’s just 18 months, not even school-ready yet. You’ve got time. I mean, unless she’s in your head already, planting the idea that you’re going to be working and she’ll be heartbroken.      She already treats me like I’m Cinderella about to be whisked off to the ball. She only started calling me “Mumu” when I wasn't around. I blame nurseries. “Mumu” – Mate, I’m fairly certain, and I know myself, I'm not the  cool  mum.      Oh, you’re the sensible one. And let’s be honest, someone has to be. If you weren’t around, chaos would just run rampant.      Fair enough. So, have you still got that cafe in Ware where your colleague, Laura, works? I remember you told me she opened up a little place nearby.      Yeah, and it’s gone mad. She barely sees the inside of the place these days—runs on a team of baristas like clockwork.      And how are you staying in touch with any of all that?      You know me, I just pop in as and when. They’ve started serving sourdough lunches and a new “himalayan salted caramel” latte—makes me question my life choices.      Mm, that does sound like a warning sign. But personally, I just started baking muffins at home. Who needs shops when you’ve got your own kid’s leftovers and pesto made from 3000 basil leaves?      It’s a life of modest excess, and overcooked pronoun use at the dinner table.      I know, right? Remember when Alice used “they” as a singular? It was like living in the 22nd century.      Yeah, and now we’ve moved onto “you’re-assuming-the-cow-goes-moo-moo-baa-baa-is-totally-acknowledged-by-you-right?"

I just feel like the future’s this big question mark, you know? I was watching the news last night and it was all about rising rent prices and now I'm thinking I can't even afford a deposit for a place in Cambridge. Not to mention London, which is where I’m supposed to be moving for my new job next year. Yeah, I feel the same. I’ve been trying to save up but every time I think I’m doing okay, something comes up—car repair, a new laptop, or a holiday. It’s like the minute you start setting money aside, the universe finds a way to take it back. Exactly! And we’re not even talking about emergencies. It’s like the cost of living just keeps rising. I left London specifically because I thought I’d be able to breathe a bit more and save in the countryside. Cambridge’s not countryside! Well, it is a bit, but the rent here is almost on par with London’s. I mean, we’re working full-time both of us, we’re educated, and still—goodness sake, if we had kids or a mortgage or something it would be even harder. For sure. Have you thought about buying a house at all? I remember when we were younger we used to talk about it: “We’ll split a house, just for a bit while the market is flat.” But that’s like a whole new level of panic these days. You ever thought about what you’d do if you hadn’t gone into production controlling? I don’t know. Maybe still doing something creative—like graphic design or event planning. I know that sounds like a cliché, but sometimes I wonder if I’d be happier ‘doing what I love’ even if I earn less. But that’s easier said than done. My mum was always saying I had to grow up and ‘Get a proper job’ so I’m kind of stuck in middle of doing what I like trying to 'have a proper job' at the same time. I get that. I like my secretarial job because it's really stable, but I sometimes miss the buzz of working in events, like before I moved here.

Right, so I've just got through telling Elsie that I'm still not seeing anyone, and she pities me and says, “Oh, Gemma, don’t worry, someone will come along.”      Yeah, like they ever do, you know, like out of nowhere. Right, who’s having meatballs? You know they’re going to go fast as soon as they hit the table.      I’m having them, they smell brilliant.      Same. Also, the cookies over there still have cereal in them.      Excuse me! I’ve made several batches of real biscuits since November — there was a period where I tried to rhythmically toast puffed rice in the oven – it’s called innovation!      Let’s not argue about biscuits when you’ve just called me a killer of edible standards. Still, the chicken’s the main event. Let’s talk rugby while we eat. Did you catch the Munster game?      Yeah, it was a mess. I still don’t know if Munster lost on purpose or because most of their forwards are allergic to speed. I prefer the English team — at least they hit hard.      Oh, don’t get me started on the English team. Remember that match last month where the referee took the ball and explained the rules mid-game to his players? “Yes, lads, that’s how rugby works.”      That was funny! Except when the Wallabies keep on whining about the ref and the whole thing turns into a comedy of errors.      Yeah, go back to Australian Rules if you want chaos — seriously, one bloke kicked a ball, it went between two posts, three blokes hugged, and everyone went home. So simple, it hurts.      Anyway, can I go to my granny’s tomorrow? She said she’s baking scones like 10 o’clock and I can help her.      Only if you don’t give her backschat. Last time, she was slightly deaf and swore it was her own birthday that you were stealing.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh?      What's that?      eBay, the shipping costs on those vintage cups and saucers! I saw this one set with a little painting of sunflowers, and they said it was from the 1950s. Got a bit of chip, but I thought it was lovely. But the postage? Almost as much as the cups.      Yeah, that's always a pain. You're not going to get a reasonable deal if they've already got the item and demand the world in postage. Maybe look at local markets instead? The one in Totnes is still doing a good vintage section every Saturday, isn’t it?      Oh, I’ve thought about it. I like the idea of rummaging through the stalls, maybe pick up a bit more than just cups—maybe even some jam jars or something. And breakfast, no doubt. I've been wanting to try some of that buckwheat bread the baker there hides behind the counter.      Good call. I had a slice the other week, and it was brilliant. Far better than that shortbread your mother sent from her holiday in Turkey.      Oh please, that shortbread nearly broke my jaw. Was it gluten-free or just old?      No, it was “artisanal” she told me. “Baked under a waxing moon.” You don’t say. Anyway, the point is, the market’s a great place to meet people too. It's one of those community things—everyone’s got a story. Or wants to sell you their Aunt Margery’s antique fork.      I like that. It gives the town a bit of character. We were saying to the other housemates last weekend that it would be nice if more people got involved. We should both go next weekend, check for vintage stuff and maybe get some supper at that little café that just opened by the market. They do something with fish and herbs, I think.      Sounds good. As long as we don’t end up buying anything else we don’t need. I’ve told my boss I’m taking next week off for my leaving do, so it’s a relaxed weekend. Then go back to my soul-sucking office job until I work up the courage to do something different.      That might be something to plan your leaving do around. Maybe have it in the pub on Friday and take everyone out for tea and scones at the market on Saturday?

So do you lot actually know what’s going on with that new business tax directive in France yet? The one everyone got a letter about last week?      Not a clue. I skimmed the email, but all I saw were words like “compliance” and “penalties” — which is just fancy talk for  not fun .      Yeah, I threw mine in the bin. I don’t even have a business! Why’s the French bank interested in my bank statements?      Because apparently, if you’ve got more than a few thousand in the bank and you can’t prove where it came from, the bank’s supposed to report it. They’re cracking down on money laundering and whatnot. It’s part of some new EU regulation.      Exactly. And if you don’t report it in the right way — even if it was just a gift — you can get fined. Heavily. Which is why I’ve spent the last two weeks updating our financial files and writing explanations for every transaction. Just in case.      Oh come on, you get sent a letter and suddenly you have to explain  which birthday  the cash came from? For real?      Sounds like it. But it’s not just big businesses. The banks are doing random checks now. I got a phone call myself last week. Some clerk asked me where my £20k deposit came from. I had to mail them a letter — along with two old payslips — just to prove I wasn’t a criminal.      That’s rich. Just the other day my mate Steve got fined here for driving under the influence  and  not having a valid license. The guy’s been pulled over twice in the same week — he says the French just love doing things legally.      At least Steve’s not a criminal, but if the bank thinks  you  are hiding stuff, well — that’s a different kettle of fish. I don’t mind a fine for speeding, but being accused of money laundering?      It’s frustrating, but I suppose it’s a balancing act. If banks don't act properly, they risk massive fines too. My accountant tells me that even a small business like mine can get hit with govt penalties if we don’t tick all the boxes.      Which is why I had to get my daughter involved last week.      What — have you gone completely mad? Why her?      She’s doing her A-levels in business and studies, and over the summer’s working at my firm.

Right, thanks a million for helping us out with the baby. I know you've had such a busy week with work and everything, but it means the world to have my family around.      Oh, don’t mention it! We love the little one—we’ve been spoiling her rotten. She’s beginning to smile properly now, isn’t she? It’s mad how fast they grow.      Aww, yeah! I swear she’s changed so much in just a few weeks. She even reached for one of my hair ties the other day! It was so sweet.      That’s nice, nice! And speaking of week, how’s the nursery at school going? I heard they had an event on Friday?      Oh yes, the Harvest Festival. It was brilliant, really! The kids made little baskets and we had a singalong. They’ve been working hard on "We Bring Our Baskets to the Door" all week in class. The parents came and helped out too.      That sounds lovely. I reckon we’ll help out with something like that—personally, I’d be happy to be the one dressed as the giant and supplying the wig, if they want a pantomime element.      You’d only want to wear the wig. But seriously, I know school is keeping you busy, Anna. How’s your timetable looking for the winter term?      Oh, don’t get me started! I’m teaching someone who’s just started in the school. He’s a bit of a marmalade—keeps forgetting who he’s facing and talks to the ceiling instead of the kids! It’s a learning curve for us both!      Well, the good thing is he’s well-meaning. I remember when I started fundraising for the school—tried to do a sponsored run in my office suit, nearly got decked by a guest speaker who passed out in the car park. Still raised the most money for the day, though.      Blooming mad! You all crack me up. Anyway, moving on—I nearly mentioned it: the sign language class I’ve told you about starts next week. I signed up ages ago after I caught a course poster at the local library. It’s on a Tuesday night here in Lichfield.      Oh, that’s fantastic! You’ve always said you wanted to learn. Mike’s deaf cousin is visiting in January, so this could come in really handy.      It’s a pity we can’t all join in, but why not?

So did you get the revised version of the Spanish primer from Pedro yet?      Oh, no, I thought he was sending it today. I’ve just asked for an update. He said he’d be done with the manuscript reviews this week.      Honestly, if it’s not clear by Friday, we’re going to be   so   far behind on deadlines. This is a busy publishing season. I swear, the more titles we take on, the longer our list gets, and the thinner the actual time gets.      I get that. But at least we’re not the only ones. I mean, I was at a meeting the other day and another publisher was talking about how they’re still relying on   typewriters   for some of their more traditional works – like their Dantes and their Elenas.      Oh, please. They better not send me a typewriter version this time. Last time I had to input the whole thing manually and I thought I saw the ghost of Casanova in the formatting.      [Laughs, using a mild Swedish lilt] I don’t know about your publishing ghosts, but I’ve seen  viler  things in Word docs.      Speak for yourself. I remember – Mateo from Chile sent me a version with all the footnotes in  Italica  Italic and line breaks that looked like a Rubik’s cube exploded.      Oh God, don’t get me started. That was me a year ago. I had a Japanese translated text sent to me with   no paragraph differentiation and double-dashes between every line  . I spent three days trying to figure out who was quoting whom.      We should have a document-style police force. Like, “Do Not Send Me a PDF Again, or We Will Come to Your House, Mateo.”      I know, right? And honestly, I don’t mind working with PDFs  sometimes —but when you can’t edit them, copy-paste text, and end up being sent a watermarked version with lunches and a new “enhanced edition” path every 50 pages, it’s a bit much.      Honestly, I think it’s more of a   moral action   than anything. Like they’re trying to say, “Look how important we are,” but we’re just trying to publish fluency guides on time and not in Comic Sans.      True. I had a client from Barcelona over the summer. We spent   hours   compiling a bilingual dictionary so he could teach at a language institute. Then his PDF had both English and Spanish in the same line, side by side, with no line feeds.

Right, I just wanted to go through the visa application stuff again. I know it's been a week since I got the email, but I still haven’t sorted my passport photo. I've been meaning to go to the post office but honestly, I keep forgetting.      Yeah, don’t leave it too late, mate. Mine got rejected the first time because the photo had a wrinkle on the paper. A wrinkle. I know! Proper ridiculous. They send you a form back and it’s like "Shirt collar aligned, background size and photo quality must not reflect or compress". Utter bollocks.      Oh no, I didn't know they were that picky. I’m going to go on Google and find somewhere near me that’s a qualified passport photo centre. I heard you can’t just take one on your phone and email it to the embassy now — there’s something about digital signatures, isn’t there?      Exactly — and the Mongolia embassy’s website says we have to upload them before the final payment. I did it directly through a shop printer, just to be safe. I’ve got the code I used — wanna come down to Print4U with me on Thursday?      Yeah, that'd be legend. I’ll come over at lunchtime. Also, I’ve been looking into gumtree for vehicle support. One guy offered an old van and said he can help us get supplies to the staging point at Leeds. Dunno if it’s someone who knows what they're doing, but he sent a photo of his van so at least it looks half decent.      Any money involved?      No, he said about half his crew is doing it for charity, and the other half is doing it for a bit of a holiday. Honestly, I think some of them have more passion for this than we do. But I’m wary. If he turns out to be shady, I’m just gonna use it as a laugh and pass him onto someone else. You laughing?      Yeah, you are as convincing as a bloke who once tried to con me into a "free trip to the Lake District" with no return ticket. But serious now — are we on the same page with go-fund-me? I had a message from some guy in Estonia who donated £200, which was completely random, but he said his cousin had some issues with the PSU in Mongolia.

Okay, thanks a million for helping me move in, Tilly. I know it's been a nightmare.      Oh please, it wasn’t that bad. I've moved in with a bloke in Liverpool who made me carry the sofa  up three flights of stairs  with one hand and a limp. Compared to that, this is child's play.      Yeah, I feel bad Aimee carried that wardrobe in too. I’m so used to people being nice in Cornwall. Back home, we’d just call a company. Didn’t even want to ask my nan to help... like, she’s 70 and I’m not dying.      Fair play. But what’s the plan for tomorrow? You said you’re going to uni early, right? I’m not even up until ten.      Yeah, ANON’s got to sign for breakfast, or whatever it’s called. I’m just gonna be replying to messages, maybe go for a fag in the quad. Should I check uni channels for anything important?      Yeah, I’ve got the occasional lecture in the morning. I’ve still got grief from last week when I missed orientation because I was in the hospital. Idiot.      Oh Mate, you got rushed to A and E because you  hurt your arm playing poker ?      It was  pool , Tilly! And the barman said 'Stick someone in the cubicle and get me a pint.' Like, yeah, sure. I got out in about an hour with a sling and £170 in parking fees.      Sounds like about five Liverpool nights in a row.      I had vibes from a guy in my hospital bed. Said he used to be a lorry driver but moved in to do physio. Burgundy hair and no front teeth.      Come on, don’t start. You know all those people have spinal injuries and you just say “Top lad.”      Look at you, getting-traumatised-in-medical-facility and still trying to play it cool.      Okay! But seriously, how go you feeling now?      Tired, sore, and in a room that smells like damp socks, but overall… I’m emerging from virtual isolation. It’s weird, seriously. Being in halls, having two other humans in the room with me, hearing a kettle on in the kitchen every five minutes – it’s sensory overload!      Oh I know. I live with a guy who watches podcast versions of CBeebies in the bath at 8 AM.      That’s not it at all.

Right then, James, how was the weekend at Nan and Pop’s?      Okay... I don’t know, it was a bit more than I wanted to deal with, honest.      Why’s that, love? It was our 25th anniversary. Thought you’d be keen to come.      Oh, I am! It wasn’t a problem that I wasn’t there or anything. I just got a bit overwhelmed with all the cousins, grandparents, aunts and uncles. Felt like everyone was chasey-chasey with me the whole time.      Oh, don’t be silly! They were only being lovely to you like you’re our golden child. Still, I get what you mean. Ten of us in the back room, twenty in the front, and the garden bursting at the seams with people.      Yeah, I know I just found it a bit much in the evening. I ended up going for a fag in the spare room to get a bit of space. It felt like I could barely breathe otherwise.      Aye, well, that’s family for you. All the love, but there’s not a lot of quiet. Still, was it good while it lasted?      Yeah, in the morning, before things got too busy, we had breakfast together and talked proper. Nan’s was the best one—proper Yorkshire pudding, crispy rashers, just someone made full beans. Honestly, I haven’t had a full English like that in a while.      Nan and Pop’s kitchen is magic. I swear nothing like it, there’s something in their water or something. I don’t know the touch they’ve got on the sippets and whatnot.      I noticed that! And the card you mentioned? The one everyone signed for you and Pop? That was nice. I did feel a bit awkward reading all the messages though.      Oh, that’s just your generation talking. We had to write down words that meant something. Even young Pete from next door wrote a little poem about me. Not bad for a young lad who spends his time playing with cars.      Was he the one who mentioned your bosoms again?      Oh no, not again. Who told you that?      Uncle Steve said it in the car on the way home after putting the tea down, I swear he was grinning like a loon the whole journey.      Ugh. Right, so if I ever get a hold of him, I’m making him scrub the floors with a toothbrush.

So do you think we’ll get through all the traffic before we get to Exeter? I’ve seen like 12 cars with Cornwall plates behind us already.      I wouldn’t be surprised if they’re all going to the same caravan park. Most of ’em probably left at dawn, like we did. You want another mug of tea? I’ve got two more cups in the flask.      Yeah, please. And maybe a biscuit? That chocolate digestif you gave me earlier was good. Didn’t it come from the man at the petrol station in Liverpool? He even tried to convince us to buy a water bottle out of his van.      Oh, that’s his usual routine. He said water tastes better "straight from the source". He once tried to sell me a bottle of green stuff in a jam jar and said it was "ancient Egyptian medicine". I mean, I didn’t ask.      Hahaha, was it green liquorice? That stuff smells like medicine. I wouldn’t touch it, Dad.      Fair point. You’re right to be careful. You know what they say—every foreign country has its own version of weird remedies. Like in Japan, they use this weird fermented stuff called miso and say it does all sorts of good things. Doesn’t taste like much to me.      You mean that salty soup they put in everything? I read about it in my book. Also, did you know that the Japanese even made something like the wheel a long time ago? Like in the time of the Egyptians, maybe?      You mean the samurai? No, that lot were later. The stuff you’re thinking of is probably the Shang or the Koreans. The Japanese were mostly nomadic. But yeah, they made some cool stuff—like swords and origami. Though I reckon origami’s more for show.      Can you fold a swan out of an exam paper and hand it to me if I pass?      You wish. Now if you pass Latin, you can get something better. Though I think the examiners set the questions harder on purpose. I’ve heard there are so many strange questions, like how to describe a manor house in Latin while pretending to be a ghost.      Well, I live in one metaphorically. This house we’re moving to is a proper stone heap. Not much bigger than the Moomins’ house.      Well, it’s got a proper garden and a washing machine that doesn’t leak.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh?      Aye, it's been damp in here all week and I've had the heater on since half six this morning. Still feels like a bloody cave in here.      That's because you've left the drapes drawn all day again, Neil. Let a bit of sun in for goodness' sake. You'd not call it a cave if you let the light in.      I’m protecting the antique wooden furniture, Mrs. Davidson. You can blame the sun for bleaching this old mahogany if you like, but not me.      Honestly,Neil, no one’s going to bleaching the antique wooden furniture in this day and age. We all living with IKEA left and right. Ten more years and the antique wooden furniture will be a microwave.      Haha, now that’s a giggle. I still use a chisel to cut corners, though — no point in letting the modern world teach me bad habits, even if it is easier with the electric ones.      Oh, you and your tools, Rhys. I remember you building your children that treehouse back in the ’90s — no electricity, no municipal codes, just rhythm and a healthy distrust of hammers.      I still got a splinter the size of a matchstick stuck in my thumb after that one. Took weeks for the swelling to go down.      Honestly, this damp — if it persists, I might have to ring a specialist. Had that sour smell coming out the other day and it's not just my socks being left in the basket again.      You could do with getting a dehumidifier. I had one installed at mine last year and it made all the difference. The air was like new. Doesn’t it feel better when you’re not just breathing in wall hang?      A dehumidifier and some open windows will go a long way, yes. But talking of specialist — you know when I ran the school, you had to employ them for every little thing. Heated floors, extractor hoods in the kitchens, even regulate the air pressure in the trophy room.      The trophy room? Come on really?      Well, you don’t expect trophy medallions to enjoy the same air quality as a bouncy castle, do you?      I suppose not. Though I think we’d all be happier if the cupboards gave off a more thrilling scent than that.      Aye, I’d take the cupboards over the smell of old library books any day.

Right, so today is Mother’s Day weekend, and I was thinking we could do something special — just the three of us. What do you two fancy doing? Maybe we can take a walk after breakfast?      Breakfast?      Can we watch cartoons first?      Well, if we do breakfast first, you can   sleep on your feet   all day like a zombie with no energy! Come on now, eat this porridge, and then we’ll go outside.      Can we take the dogs?      Of course, love. I’ll ask Grandma to look after them if we can’t take them. But today, only if we can pop them in the car. Let’s   make hay while the sun shines  , shall we?      Can we pick flowers?      Yes, if you help me put them in a breakfast nook for your Nana while she has her early lunch — and no, you can’t eat the daisies, James. We’re not   letting the cat out of the bag  , you know — we want it to be special for her!      Can we go to Forest School today?      Forest School? Well, only if we   don’t throw the baby out with the bath water   and actually take the journey to Comberton Woods. We don’t have to go all the way if we’re already doing things at home — unless you two want to walk there. That’s about two miles. You up for it?      James said yes!      I want to!      Well alright, let’s try and do both. We walk to the woods, do some leaf collecting, then come back and make you sandwiches and maybe   bake the goose that laid the golden egg   — meaning something that’s just a bit over the top but worth it for your Nana.      Can the biscuits be hearts? For Mother’s Day?      You read my mind! We’ll make heart-shaped biscuits and put some flowers in the middle with icing. I think it’s time someone   let the air out of the balloon   of laziness and get baking.      But I want to help!      Excellent, because   many hands make light work  . Who’s ready to get dirty in the kitchen with me?      Me!      Me too! Can I flour James’s hair?      No, no, we don’t want to   weather the storm   of floor sweeps over flour and butter mess. Just a soft touch, okay? You two keep it quiet, and I’ll be the boss of dirty oven mitts.

Rather skip the newfit inc. thing do you think. I've had one of them emails they sent round... got to go to some Zoom about how they're reorganizing customer support or whatever. Doesn't sound it's worth it honestly.      Yeah, I can see that. They sent eeny weeny passive-aggressive messages about ‘engagement’ if people don’t show up. It’s like they think listing your name on the side helps anything. Still, easier said than done when you’re someone’s manager and you have to keep the peace.      Oh well I won’t tell the boss I’ve even opened it. I don’t need the hassle. I’d rather do some real work that Myra actually sees. Still, enough about work. How’s Jo doing, love?      Oh, I think she turned 14 last week, didn’t she? Time’s flying, isn’t it? I mean, still a bit in two minds about the whole teenage thing. She’s starting to push boundaries a bit—like why I need to know where she is and when, and who is she with. I’m holding up, honestly.      It’s something with that age, isn’t it. My Alice started it a little earlier. You just have to remember that they’re becoming their own people and sometimes it feels like trying to cling on to somethin’ that’s already gone. You know what I mean?      Definitely. Our biggest challenge at the moment is also the school. They sent a form round for the new term saying they’re still doing this weigh-in thing and some of it is supposed to be anonymous but it’s not really because most people about know who’s who.      Ugh, I had to stop my little one from crying about it last year. I mean, it’s unkind, isn’t it. Kids don’t need that kind of pressure. All that data about their BMI and exercise—they’re supposed to be enjoying something bloody nice at school, not being made to feel inadequate because someone’s stick-thin and someone else isn’t.      Oh I completely agree. They told me the purpose is ‘health awareness’ but really, it's not doing anyone any favours. Then go and bin it for goodness’ sake. If it was my Jo, I’d chuck the whole lot into a drawer and forget I ever opened it.

Rather skip uni today but ain't really got a choice, do I?      No... got to go, same with me. It's not like we can say we're ill every day.      No, I know—  Linguistic fieldwork was interesting last week  , mind. We had to do some interviews with   students on how they perceive accents   in the job market. A lot of people would rather sound posh, even if they're from York.      Classic. My aunt got told off once for using "broad Middlesbrough" in a radio interview.      Harsh. I found it fascinating how some lecturers still think you   can’t do well in linguistics unless you sound posh  . It's bulls  t, of course—but it’s the same nonsense with most uni stuff nowadays.      Tell me about it. My Anglo-Irish accent in my language GCSE last term looked like a mark off to them.      So unfair. I mean, do they think all the top linguists sound like Emma Thompson in  Sense and Sensibility ? I tell ya,   South Korea’s got something right  —they work on   how people actually speak  , not how they should sound.      Yeah, I’ve been brushing up on Korean on Italki. You interested in trying?      Absolutely. I mean,   listening to how people in Seoul talk during festivals sounds way more interesting than just grammar rules  .      I second that. Anyway,   dinner tonight—I thought I’d make a stir-fry or something  . I finally remembered how to braise tofu the other day.      Nice!   I’ve been trying to cook more vegetarian, too  , mostly because I don’t like where most supermarkets get their products.      Me too. The way they treat animals is something I really can’t get behind.      Same here. It’s gotten to the point where I only buy eggs from the farm down the road. At least the chickens look happy.      That’s the way! I tried to set up a lunch date with my old uni mates last week—we met at Sainsbury’s, just to pick food up randomly, ate it on the trains.      That’s genius. I swear, one of these days I’m going to   do a bit of research on how people pair food over different languages  —like, how   Chinese dumplings go with rice versus how they go with a bit of dipping chilli sauce  .      You could publish that and still not cover the half of it.      I know, but I think it's the kind of research that could   highlight how deeply food connects us to culture and language  .

Okay, who’s putting the last of the mushroom on? I swear we had more in the fridge when we opened it.      It wasn’t  that  much.      Look, it doesn’t matter, I just want to watch  The Vampire Diaries  again and pretend I care about the vampires’ love triangles.      Classic Ruth. Your soul is obviously made of drama.      Actually, I’d rather just keep eating pizza and talking about why we all still like  The Chaos Walking  when it was clearly glorified YA hot mess.      Oh come on, it wasn’t  that  bad. It was like  Star Wars , but with earpiece jelly and not aliens.      I mean, at least the books were better. They screamed at the screen in the cinema harder than any of us when the protagonist slept with the stepmom.      Excuse me,  The Chaos Walking  didn’t have a stepmom. That was  How I Met Your Mother .      Oh yeah, I meant that one. Got it.      Honestly, we’ve got a watching crisis here. We should do a film night and pick something cult – like  Rocky Horror Picture Show  or  Twilight .      Are you trying to mortal combat me for the last piece of pineapple?      Ruth, someone said pineapple and now I’m crying.      I mean it. Some people still don’t know pineapple shouldn’t be on pizza until they’re like thirty and it’s too late. Personal tragedy.      I’m from Manchester, Ruth. I had to be a  master of compromise  because that was the standard in the housing market.      Yeah, for like four years. Manchester rent will make you switch pizza toppings just to save a quid.      Okay, but let’s not get mad. My brain is already fried after lectures. I literally saw a word like ‘vector field’ and I was speechless.      Still trying to survive physics? Pity you, my friend. I tried to get your life, you tried to get mine.      I’m not even in the course and I already know what your life is like. It’s like flu, but with integrals and homework.      You poor soul. Do you ever just want to burn all your notes and go camping?      Oh I did that last weekend. Totally survived without maps, flashlights, or a shower.      How’s the flooding up your way looking, though? Yeah it’s still bad, isn’t it? I tried to walk to the night bus stop once and almost drowned on my doorstep.

So did I not see you yesterday?      No, you didn’t. I had to stay in and finish some project work. Otherwise I would’ve popped by your place or we’d have gone out for a bite. You alright?      Yeah, I’m alright. Just felt a bit odd when I drove past the place you were working and didn’t see your car. Thought maybe you’d gone A.W.O.L or got kidnapped! I’m joking, don’t take it to heart.      Oh, I got so wrapped up in it, I completely forgot to send you a message. I even baked you a cake on Sunday, hoping we could share it on Monday. It was like that one you like, the one with the brown sugar and cinnamon bits. Probably gone off now, but I can reheat it.      Blimey, you’ve been working hard. I envy you sometimes, working from home. Me? I’m stuck at the office, five days a week, staring at spreadsheets and documents that look like they were built in the Stone Age.      Yeah, but I’m not short of coffee or asphyxiating in the lift, so I’ll take it! You reckon you’ll work from home when the weather turns? It’s already threatening snow in the forecast, and I swear it won’t be long before the city turns into a car park.      I might, if I’m lucky. I’ve been trying to get remote working approved for a day a week. Just a bit of peace and quiet at home with my cat, who I haven’t properly seen this week. I came in early every day, and she started crying in about five minutes unless I sat with her.      You’re telling me I’ve avoided your fails at coffee that week then! I mean, it’s not like I expect the beans to sing to me, but your guest filter set needs to retire. The last cup I had tasted like burnt toast and existential dread.      I know, I know. We’re not good as a couple when it comes to coffee skills. I’ve been thinking about getting one of those capsule machines, you know, like the Italian ones. You pop a capsule in, push a go button, get your life back.      Sounds brilliant. You sure? I’m not about to go from bean-to-cup purgatory to barista heaven overnight.

Rather chilly this morning, ain't it?      It's like it's pretending it's winter again. I had to dig out my old woolly socks just to walk the dog!      Charming. I had to turn on the central heating again after only turning it off last week. I swear we’re paying for heat just to sit in the garden in our socks most days.      That’s this country for you. One season, four weather patterns! At least the sun’s out now, makes for a nicer afternoon in the garden.      Not to mention the arthritic weather. My back’s been giving me grief all morning. It's like it senses the damp before I do!      Aye, I’ve been taking the tablets Dr. Ellis prescribed every day. They help—sort of. Still, better than not mobile at all, eh?      You’d be surprised at the number of patients I see as a lecturer who attribute their symptoms to the weather. It’s fascinating how deeply people feel weather affects them—personally, I just get irritable if it’s raining on a weekend.      As a lecturer, I reckon the weather affects productivity in the classroom. You want to know who works hardest: students on a sunny day, or those who’ve trudged through the rain in black tights and ankle boots trying to stay dry and stylish at the same time? There’s a whole psychology there.      All this talk of health and weather is making me think—should I start eating some of these vitamin D tablets they told me about at the surgery?      I did. My doctor said it’s a good thing for my bones this time of year. But you’ve got to know that taste—like bitter orange candies. Ugh!      You’re onto something there, Dad. Bitter orange candies are his preferred vitamin source.      Do scientists know how it works, or is it just folklore and aching knees?      Doesn't matter if it works, eh? I’ve told my son to keep an eye out for a proper walking frame come winter. I’m not keener on goin’ on the slab if I don’t have to.      I’m not either. I’ve got enough on my mind worrying about my hips. I don’t need to add dodgy stairs and ice to the list!      Honestly, it’s like the weather over here is designed to be a natural health screening.

Okay, thanks a million for meeting up. I needed this. Work has been absolute hell this week.      Don't worry, I'm glad we did too. It's been ages since we all sat down with no distractions. Look at us—half our group is married, engaged or pregnant and the rest of us are spinning in place like we're on a hamster wheel!      Aww, don’t worry, this isn't a 'you're single so you must be lonely' vibe! We just all happened to fall into the 'not yet' category. But honestly, I like it. Being single mostly means I can go out with no guilt, no planning around someone else's calendar. My turkey still gets eaten at 1 am if I want.      You're a savage, and I love it. But seriously—Donna, are we really saying Chloe hasn’t even started matchmaking yet? I mean, has she taken in a stray dog, adopted five plants and started shopping for nursery stuff yet?       laughs  Oh yes, she's deep into the 'xenesthetic future motherhood' phase. I’ve seen her sketching nursery layouts with more detail than she did on her master's thesis. And then of course she's booking Pinterest – Mateo: Royal Father, Baby: Small Human, Dog: unnamed companion.      Ugh, I will not survive the ‘wedding planning’ phase, which I also just someone said in one breath. Let me not read anything like that just yet.      Also, I think Sam wants to talk about their dinner party plans this weekend. Something about us being the theme about how ‘being single makes you weak-willed’ or something. I had to stop cooking lasagna and not throw it at her.      No, I mean, she didn’t say 'weak-willed' specifically, more like, 'being single shows you haven't found your purpose yet'. Like it's a spiritual quest or something. You know, the one where you have to  find your person  instead of just trying to find someone  to join your existing life .      Okay, serious side note—I am 100% go-to person on your life if you ever need someone to be your person. I'll fake-message your fridge. I’ll send SOS emails to your plant.      I mean seriously, why do we think we need a person to complete us anyway? It's suffocating. I have a very full life. I have my art, I have my friends—and I have a cat named Igor who adores me.

Rather annoying this newfit lot eh, all them apps an’ everything.      Oh James, dear, it's progress love, you just have to get used to it. It’s not like we were chucked out of society, is it?      Aye well it een’t like when  I  were a lad, just a radio an’ a newspaper. Nuffin' but transcription from the wireless or the side of a lorry. Oh but now, me nan’s got to do everything on a screen, an’ when me cousin sent her a photo of her grandbaby... she couldn’t even get it to open! I had to walk the six miles to help her.      Oh, bless, you dear! She’s a lucky lass, ain’t she? D’you know, I used to help little William with his homework, about the Cats app! Wait, no— CATS  the musical! Haha—kids these days, they think it's a feline app, James. One time he came over with pyjamas on and a tail, and told me it was for the iPad version!      Blimey! That’ll keep 'em entertained… watching cats dance. But where’s Billiam today? Still playing at the park with his new friend, Josh?      Yeah, the lad’s got quite the passion for them stallions. I've been taking him out every Sunday—riding lessons. Our vicar said to me, “Bill, you’re not a teacher anymore, are you?” I told him, “Well, teachin' these young 'uns how to ride a  horse  is better than most people about how to sit!”      Oh, Billiam’s lucky. He said his friend Josh rides ponies that are like jelly—wobbly things! Josh mentioned to me he found ‘em on the internet, ones that can spell their owner's name and play darts. I said, “That’s not a pony, that’s a scheming madman.”       Hahaha!  That’s young folk fer yeh! I tell yeh, the world’s gone bonkers. Still, I did try this new online shopping the other day— go me! I tried to order a tin of baked beans. But by the time I’d got past the pop-ups, box tickin’, and whatnot, I was halfway to the supermarket in Norwich!      Well, you're not the only one, James. I had to pay for a recharge this morning, but the system said I had a problem... so I phoned up and they said, “Mr Cowan, we can’t see your bank details.”

Rather skip to the front of the queue.      That's alright, no rush. I got time on my hands now.      Erm sure would you like a little cake as well with your tea or would you prefer something else.      Lemon Cake, if there is any.      There is. I’ve got two choices a Victoria Sponge or a Lemon.      The Lemon then.      Right. We can have the Lemon.      The Lemon then.      Take it away.      What’s new then Jo?      Just been working at the school, got a new group of Year 8s who are either A, absolutely brilliant or B, the little devils you can't control.      A teacher then?      Yeah, language teacher, Japanese and Spanish.      Oh so you're not actually teaching your own language?      Well I’m not really I mean I did quite a bit of French and German when I was at uni but no, Japanese is completely new.      So is that at the college down the road?      Yeah, the one with the new building.      That was quite the big shake-up when that went in. Must be different.      Completely. Much more modern, smaller classes, so I can actually teach something meaningful rather than just recite from a textbook.      That’s good. Not many about like that.      No, you're right. Not many.      Any plans to go back and work abroad again?      I’d like to. Got a couple of contacts in Japan who were saying there could be a spot if I wanted to give it a shot again.      You were out there for a few years weren’t you?      Yeah, five years in Kyoto.      That’s something.      Yeah, go there once it’s life-changing.      You ever think about retiring out there?      You know what your house is you could be planting things in the garden and writing postcards in Japanese every day.      I like that. I’ve got a plot at the allotments here now.      I did not know that.      Yeah, always wanted to be a gardener but no, when I was working I had to work, you know?      Yeah, I can imagine. You were a Managing Director, right?      That’s right.      Well that's quite different.      Well, nothing much left to do now.      Any family out in Essex?      Erm, no. Back in the day had a sister, but she’s gone now. Now it's just me.      Well, I hope you’re busy enough with the allotments then.

So did you go out for Valentine’s weekend? Or did you glue yourself to your books again?      No way—I went to that new Italian place by campus on Saturday. It was actually alright for a student budget. I had the fettuccine and a glass of wine.      Ooh, romantic. You didn’t bring anyone, then?       [laughs]  Nah, just me and my takeaway fondue feeling. I used it as an excuse to go out and treat myself. I got so over the whole "romantic partner or bust" vibe of the day.      I know, right? I spent the weekend working on my psychology essay. Saturday I sat in my flat eating chilli bursts and watching Tenet, rewinding the scenes like a madwoman. I think I turned my brain to custard.      I watched it twice last year and still don’t get half of it. People went mad about it in the cinema, didn’t they? Like, the guy shouting,  “Wait, why is he wearing a backwards mask?!”        [laughing]  I think that was the only time in my life I’ve laughed so hard at a film without it being sarcastic or a rom-com. But I’m not giving up on Nolan yet!      It’s alright as long as you don’t care about logic. Speaking of, though, what are you doing Friday night? I’m thinking of going to the cinema. It’s been ages since I watched something in a real cinema.      The cinema? Like,  with people and popcorn and crying in public  cinema? Or are you trying to kill me?       [cackling]  Yeah sorry that was a bit dramatic. But it does sound good. I heard they’re playing that new horror film everyone’s talking about. Are you scared of jump scares or not?      I once dropped a whole bowl of custard cream on my shoe while my flatmate was watching a jump scare. I've been mentally scarred ever since. But I’ll go if the film’s any good.      Deal. Let’s pick go for it on Friday. I’ll even meet you at the pre-show posters line in my spookiest dress.      You can’t pull that southern London charm on me and expect me to trust you after that.      It’s not charm, it’s a Midlands over-achiever charm, baby! It works. You’ll see.       [laughing]  Alright, alright. Friday it is. Now let’s order more lasagne, before they run out again and I’m stuck with mac and cheese again.

So did you order yet? I was just checking the menu for a minute trying to decide between the pad Thai and the pho.      Yeah, I got the chicken satay bowl with extra noodles. The cashew chicken one seems like it'd be too rich for me today. You decide yet?      I think I'm going with the pho. It’s been one of those mornings where I need carbs and warmth in one swoop. Pretty much the only way I can get through my to-do list.      Funny you say that, because the past week’s been hell at work. My editor won’t stop bringing up this article about the government’s new housing policies. You of all people would know how controversial they are.      Don’t I just? I had a meeting with a housing developer last week who screamed about "market rules" while we’re designing shelters for breakfast, no less. It’s nuts. They want micro-apartments the size of our oversized desktop hides, and then accuse people of being ungrateful when they can’t afford to live.      Yeah, and the worst bit? It’s not as if they’re supplying the numbers. There are people in this city—right here, right now—with no services, no council support, just bouncing between hotels and fairly dodgy B&Bs. Meanwhile, huge swaths of property are sitting empty.      Exactly what I said in the meeting. And the kicker? Our housing crisis is intertwined with everything else. If you read between the lines, it’s not just housing—look at the migrant policies, the racism in the system, the way certain ethnicities are disproportionately housed in worst conditions.      Absolutely. I’m writing about the links between capitalism and how it affects migrant communities—that kind of research needs to be front and centre. The problem is, my editor prefers fluff pieces over anything that might ruffle feathers.      And that ties into the whole politics of it too. We talk about racism in theory, but when it comes to who gets to live where and how they get housed, it always comes with a cost. It’s whiter neighbourhoods with the best services, whereas Black and minority communities are left with crumbling Estates and no hope in sight.      It’s not just London either—there's a pattern. I had a source in Birmingham last week say the same thing about their local council.

So nurseries today, they’ve got these whole systems, do they?      Yeah... Well, I’ll start with the one I’ve got on my shortlist anyway. It’s a little Montessori place. They’ve got outside time as well. They like the idea of letting the kids kind of self-organise a bit more, but within structure.      I remember that being all the rage when I had my first job, but nurseries used to be all about discipline back then! You’d be lucky to get outside once during the day.      Right, but now even the government’s funding it a bit more for outdoor learning. Still, I’m a bit nervous. Just, I don’t know, left alone with someone I’ve never met before who’s in charge of my baby.      It is a big step. How old is she going to start then?      The placement they offered’s for the day after next, starting at 9.30. One morning a week, like a trial run. If it goes well, we can up it to two or three a week.      Small steps, that’s good. And how are you feeling about going back to work?      Honestly, I’m still figuring it all out. I’ve got my lectures on Monday afternoons and the whole first part of the week is work commitments. Then, from the day Ethel starts full time, I’m going back to the uni campus half days.      That is a bit of a whirlwind. Still, at least you’ve got time to transition into it. I remember when I was back at work, the baby still clinging to me during my lunch break.      I know! I can handle it if we plan well, but I’m already overthinking everything. What if she’s unhappy? What if she just won’t leave the day after tomorrow?      She’ll be fine. You’ll be surprised. Kids are resilient. I remember being emotional myself—crying with her—but she didn’t even notice.      Still, I’m going to miss her! I’ve been away for work before, but it was never this full-time or emotional.      I suppose. But it’s not the end of the world. She’s gaining all these new experiences, and so are you. Are you going anywhere nice after she starts full time?      We were thinking宜昌’s Cumbrian coast. I’m not entirely sure what I’m paying for exactly, but it’s soft adventures, wild swimming, things like that.

Rather annoying day today, really was. You know, that thing with the delivery van—the one that sideswiped the gate. I had to go and make a statement at the police station this afternoon. Took longer than I expected. Not only explaining what happened but then being questioned for forty minutes about timing and positioning. I'm not a  criminal , Ruth, just a   casual witness  .      Sounds exhausting. What time did they actually open this afternoon? They gave me a call asking me to drop off some paperwork and I had to wait nearly an hour before they even saw me.      That’s because of the system change, apparently. I heard someone at the store talking about how the local station is working with a new digital log for statements now. I suppose it’s well-intentioned, but if it makes things slower and more frustrating for people, then it’s not much of an improvement.      Honestly, I just want to know if I’ll be able to get the phone plan sorted without going to the shop. EE have been a  nightmare —I got a bill for a phone I never ordered. It shows up in my account as being activated last week and only sent  this  week. I’m watching it now, waiting for it to arrive just so I can send it back. But with the delivery delays and the weekend coming up…      Oh don’t get me started on phone companies. I had one of those phantom subscriptions for three months before I even noticed. Spent hours on the phone trying to sort it out, and oddly, the customer service rep had the same surname as me. Small world.      I heard you spoke to the Equality and Diversity Officer at work today, Ruth. How did it go?      To be honest, not great. I was trying to highlight the lack of access to menstrual hygiene products in the company bathrooms for women who cycle. They said they passed it on. That’s all they ever say. “We pass it on.” If they don’t do anything about it, I’m going to talk to the  union .      Do that. I’ve seen what happens when you do the quiet thing—it just gets ignored.      I get that, go ahead. I think it matters more than most think.      Speaking of work, I need to go in early tomorrow. I’ve got to meet with the landlord for the new premises—the one in Hazlewood.

So did you watch  Spartacus  last night? I was bingeing it again and it got me thinking about the whole gladiator thing. I’m teaching about Roman history this week, and one of the students is convinced they had proper healthcare. Can you believe?      No way. They probably just stitched you up with a bit of string and handed you some wine. I’ve never been a big fan of that era, but I love that  Spartacus  show. The acting was wild, man. And the whole “I am Spartacus” line? Iconic. But honestly, watching too many of those shows gives me nightmares. Last night I dreamt I was gladiating in a garden and someone kept throwing turkey twizzlers at my face.      Haha, now I’m imagining a gladiator with a twizzler in his ear. Sounds like a Roman-themed gig! Wait, you gardening still then? I mean, after all the marital shenanigans, you ever considered taking a trip somewhere indulgent instead of planting herbs? Spain? Or maybe that China trip you mentioned?      Mate, I might take two weeks in a banana tree and call it a sabbatical. But no, I’m still potting up rhythm in the mornings. You ever try using a mortar and pestle for spices? I tried making some za’atar the other day and nearly crushed my thumb. You know what’s funny? I blame the pestle.      Haha, sounds like my time in Cyprus trying to brew a good earl grey. I put what I thought was tea leaves into the mortar and pestle—turned out it was  ground chickpeas . Took me about five minutes to figure out why everything tasted like hummus.      Honestly, you and your spices are wasting your time. I tried it once—pounded my coriander, got half of it on the wall. My gran called it “culinary graffiti.” She said it looked like something a Roman general would’ve drawn if they were bored waiting for a siege.      Oh yeah, speaking of which, you ever notice how a lot of gladiators died pathetically young? Like Spartacus, for example. He was a man with a goal go out of the gate and be like, “I fight, I win, I die, I’m not coming back.” That’s the ultimate resume. Passes me by. I just want to live to 80 and still be making tea with broken biscuits in the filter.      Look, over here, the only early death I’m worried about is malarials.

So did you get an A on the English test?      No, only a B... I was so upset when I saw the mark. But I think I stared the teacher out long enough that she gave me extra credit for effort or something.      Oh, stop it! That is so  not  fair. I got handed over to Miss Hart for all the grammar mistakes I made. A lot of people got marked down too though, honestly.      Yeah, it was one of those questions where the options didn’t  actually  make sense. I swear I saw like three sentences with correct grammar and only one was marked as the right answer. That was so frustrating.      I know! The wind-band’s going to be doing their concert next month and I can’t pick which I’ll be more nervous about—performing for the whole school or writing another English essay.      Ugh, don’t remind me. I play clarinet and I’m already dreading the concert. I once messed up on that tune we did with the jumps—personally I think it takes three left turns. Like, why do you play it when you can’t even breathe in properly?      Oh yeah, the “Overture” – Mateo nearly got expelled for almost throwing his trumpet off the stage after he hit a wrong note.      That was  hilarious , but also terrifying. He said it was someone at the back who coughed when he was about to play the climactic bit.      I would have just joined in with their coughing if I had to. But anyway, what have we got next week? I think it’s the Renaissance week thing, am I right?      Yeah, and you’re telling me it’s optional but I  know  Miss Hart will expect us to wear stuff that’s  not  just a hat and a veil.      Do you think we’ll meet up for art lesson on Thursday? We could talk about the self-portrait thing. I’m thinking of doing mine with a mirror behind me to make it look extra dramatic.      You are  so  into the drama gothic vibe. But yeah, maybe. If French doesn’t kill me first. I swear, that teacher thinks we were born speaking French fluently. Last lesson we had to translate something about  apricots and Romans . Like, where do we get that from?      I tried to overcompensate and translated "apricots" as  a lot of tips  and got laughed out of the room.

Right, thanks for coming in today, love. Thought we could talk about your future, seeing as you’re just off to sixth form or college after this year.      Yeah, thanks for meeting me, Miss. Not sure what I want to do yet, to be honest.      That’s alright, I understand. I was like that when I left school. Proper lost.      What are your likes? What do you enjoy learning about?      I like history and English, and I like music as well. I play the guitar.      Right, well, if you can write songs, you could go far, son. Still got some of my old MySpace bands around, probably still playing to five people in the back of a pub.      [Laughs] That’s the spirit. You know, it’s not just about what you’re good at, it’s about what you enjoy doing for hours on end. That’s the real test.      Yeah, I suppose. I dunno, I just worry about money, though. I mean, my gran always says if you land a job with a pension and a real uniform, you’re sorted for life—like the police or something.      And there’s nothing wrong with that. Stability, benefits, it all helps. But if the idea of pinning on a uniform and patrolling for forty years sends you to sleep at your desk, maybe look for something that speaks to you more personally.      Aye, I had a cousin what went into the fire service. Never saw her again until she got a pension and had to come back for her birthday. I mean, respect to her for doing it, but the life’s not for everyone.      Yeah, that sounds grim. I mean, not ungrateful, I know she helped people for real. But I wanna play guitar more than anything. Can I make money off that?      If you’ve got determination, you can. A lot of people do it part-time and end up full-time. But it’s not always easy. It helps to study the business side too. Like, you don’t just play; you promote yourself, you market, go online…      Aye, and don’t forget the stats. Ever seen that YouTube bloke with three blokes on a guitar and 200 million subs? The rest 3,000 blokes are wondering what went wrong.      True. But there are proper music courses where you can learn about that. You could go down the route of performing or music production, or even podcasting, which is where a lot of younger people are getting into these days.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh Harry? That Christopher, he’s promising to pop in tomorrow with that pikelet and pick me up from the dining room yet somehow I haven't heard a word from him since this morning.      That's the sort of thing you can rely on from him, eeny weeny, yeah. You think you can get a man his age to actually do what he says.      He's got too much on his plate anyway. The bank was refusing to give him a mortgage and his wife's got some allergy issue. Apparently, she can't even have meat anymore.      Not to mention his mother, who's been taken into hospital for some kind of operation. I heard it was something with his genes. His lawyer tried to help, but the psychiatrist said the risk was too high.      Blimey, poor chap. He better not breakfast on margarine then.      I don’t know what’s more worrying, Christopher’s genes or the way he drives. Man nearly ran over my spaniel once.      Oh, I heard老爷 takes special classes in driving now.      And for good reason. Imagine having to live on medication just because you're overweight then getting told you can’t even drive?      That’s what it comes to if you are too idle and eat too many fried sausages every morning. I tell my students all the time — live better.      That’s what I say: no man wants to be run over by a hapless fattie with fury.      But you know Margot says he's been doing better, trying to do more jigsaws to relax. “It clears the mind,” she said.      That or it kills the madness. I mean, if you're not driving to the shops, you're cutting up bits of paper for hours.      Still, I don’t think a jigsaw is going to solve his money worries.      We all know how that goes. You've got a young lad trying to find his way and somehow you end up with a man whose money's lost and his mind's not best.      Mind you, I think his lawyer is trying to get him into religion.      Oh really? Going the God route now?      Yeah. It's supposed to make you feel safe and give you some direction. “Spiritual guidance for troubled souls.”      Hmm, I mean, religion can do that. I’m not entirely sure if it's going to help with the money or the hypertension, though.

So did you get the tutorial sheet uploaded on to Moodle yet? I’ve had three students ask me when they’d be able to access it.      I did this morning, didn’t I? Let me check… Yeah, it’s there under the Week 3 section. But I was also thinking I should record a demo of me going through the assignment step by step.      Oh, that would be brilliant. Some students panic when they see a computer-based task. They just need a bit of hand-holding at the start, don’t they?      Definitely. I remember my first module as a lecturer, I made so many references to screenshots and video guides only after people stressed about needing them. Now I try to be more proactive. Speaking of which, did you hear the news about the Moodle upgrade they’re doing?      Yes, I was about to bring it up. I’m slightly worried about how this will affect the H5P activities in my database management module. I spent ages putting them into different sections so the students follow the right order.      Me too. I’ve heard from the IT department that the structure might not reflect exactly the same when they transfer everything. I’ve been making backups of my course – just in case. You should too. It’s such a shame how many lecturers still don’t store screenshots or copies of the course layout somewhere safe.      You’re right. Last year, I had the wrong version of a quiz someone changed in one of the shared folders. Took me a good half-hour to trace it back.      Don’t get me started. Anyway, going back to the demo idea, do you want me to make the video walk-through for you as well? I’m doing mine in Camtasia now, and I can copy the script if you’d like it.      That would be so helpful. I’ve been planning to do one too, but I just haven’t got the time between marking and being on pastoral support. I tried using OBS for the last one, but the audio didn’t sync. You’ve clearly got a good system going on.      Thanks. I’ve also started using Sublime Text for writing my scripts first. It helps me keep the flow really tight before recording. It’s not perfect – I still go into full robotic voice when I read scripts – but it halves the editing time at least.

Rather annoying isn't it, this jet lag. I couldn't get to sleep for hours, even when Hal... you know, finally quietened down. It's not like we need to be up early, but it is thrown me all day.      Yeah, well, you know how it is. Two different time zones, changes the whole routine. I tried to sleep later to be with you, but I’ve only had three hours or so in this last 24. And don’t get me started on Halley—between the feeding, the teething, and the, I don’t know, grizzling like someone’s stacking spoons in the middle of the night—well, no chance!      My lectures are fine for the next two weeks. I can be more flexible, but I know you’ve got that seminar and the meeting with the administrator about your promotion coming up. I feel bad if I’m still half-asleep during this time when you need to be on top of things.      Don’t, I told you—rest is overrated. It’s not like we can hand Halley over to a sleep consultant. I’m used to it. But listen, I did actually get that email confirming the tickets for the municipal play. We’re in for the evening performance. It’s the  Midsummer Night’s Dream  version, right? You said you’ve seen it before but not in that theatre.      Ooh, yes! The old town hall theatre is just lovely at night. It’s got such a warm atmosphere. It will be nice to do something out without worrying about nappies or bedtime stories and being able to sit and actually  watch  a performance for once.      Exactly. I thought the tickets were reasonably priced this time. And if you can manage not to fall asleep halfway through Mercutio’s soliloquy, I’ll be impressed. Which is the whole reason I wanted Friday. I know you were up at 6 a.m. yesterday.      I tried to read through the performance reviews while I was feeding Halley and that definitely did  not  help me stay awake. I think it was partly the chocolate heather biscuits I nibbled after delivering the guest lecture.      Of course you did. But it was your idea to cut out caffeine for six weeks post-pregnancy, so don’t go blaming the biscuits.      Fair. I just didn’t think about the logistics of staying alert on herbal tea and earnest moral conviction.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You've got a few decent lads in the class, but they all got the attention span of a goldfish these days. I were asked by one fella last week where I were born. When I said Germany, he looks at me like I were from another planet. Hasn’t got a clue where that is.      Aye, it's a bit of a problem in education. Not just in this country, either. My cousin Ali, he's in Erbil. He's teaching primary school. Sums up the political mess of the place. You'd think the oil money would even things out, but no, it's the same old divisions, especially with the Wahabi money flowing in. You hear stories about kids not being allowed to study certain bits because of the religious push from Gulf countries. I mean, the government’s supposed to protect education, but you’d better not get too liberal in your thinking if you want to stay in work.      Yeah, that's part of the reason why so many young people over there are starting to look over the borders, maybe try Europe or even—dare I say—Turkey. I’ve got a few Iraqi Kurd lads still in my class, brilliant linguists, by the way, all got skills in English, Arabic, Kurdish, and a few other languages, but they don’t see much of a future in their home countries unless they can get a better education or a clean visa situation.      Exactly. And the visa rules—God forbid. You’d think with the European Union, it'd be easier for people who have been in the UK and worked through the NRPSI or Interpretation routes, but it’s about as clear as mucky water. My mate in the office had to get a document notarised in three different countries just to try and get a housing voucher after moving from London to Birmingham. That’s for someone who worked for councils for years. I feel for his kids—they’re used to one home, and now they’re bouncing around.      Aye, I know my mate Karl had that same issue. He were living in London but wanted a new start with the kids. Moved the whole lot up north, near where I am, course! But the local authority goon show with property—sorting out a house for a family is like herding cats, let alone figuring out welfare support with all the different rules.

Rather skip the newfit and go to the gym tomorrow, do you reckon?      Oh, dear, I often say the dining room isn’t properly utilised these days unless you have a meal in it. Not to mention a bit of telly!      True, I mean we only  just  moved out of the      dusty dining room last year after a clean. A lot of work just to have this flat, honestly.      She's right. We’ve had to put up with this landlord for the last five years. You know what I like to say, even if  he  doesn't listen— the walls are only paper thin, and they  listen .      Och, aye, well, I was lucky as a headmistress. I had a good little inspector— you know, the one with the better character. Not the old stickler from the Anglo-Saxon religion in his early sixties.      Oh, I bet he was tough to deal with. Landlords terrify me, if I’m honest.      Well, your landlord’s still polite and all, but he still remembers the days when he wasn't living in this flat, from what I can gather—he just happens to rent out fairly large, warm, and modestly priced properties.      You know what? I used to run the household accounts for a large school, and I tell you someone who knows how to get the best out of money? It's a  trick . Some people just don’t have a clue and let profits be poured out the window like  table water .      I agree. I mean, our mam咪 still lives in this boarding house and it’s all  rent cap  and nothing extra. I mean it is a  flat , not the jungle, but for her age it’s not even near enough comfort.      You know, I was thinking about taking her with me on a cruise. You ever been on one?      Nae, but I always liked lunches on a boat. More importantly, I took the kids out there for  sea air , so it was a bit of an education go-round really. But tell me more about this cruise. Where is it going?      He means,  sort  of what your mam咪’s like at the moment. Her appetite? Her interest in life?      Oh, well to be fair, she's still over this bed when we visit, so I’d say the  bedside table  needs a bit of polishing and perhaps softening of the lighting.

So do you lot reckon I’ve got a chance at getting that part-time retail job in town?      Which one? The one at the bookshop? That’d be nice, Liv. You’re always chitchatting about the customers when we go in.      Yeah, that one. I’ve been told they want someone who’s “engaging”… not sure if that’s a real word.      It is, but I reckon they just mean someone who’s nice and doesn’t look like they’d rather chase a bus into the sea. You’re a good talker, even if you do sit on your hands when the fridge supply runs out.      Just get them to give you a book and a pen and you’ll be fine. You love books, Liv. I think you could sell a dictionary if you were given a goal.      Yeah, just don’t suggest a Game of Thrones prequel’s set in Cumbria, or they’ll have questions—and not the fun ones.      Thanks, luv, I’ll try not to rattle the shelves.      And for what it’s worth, if they reject you, I work at West Scarborough Primary. We’re always after someone to help with reading groups. Might be less customers, but more biscuits.      Oh, like the ones with the chocolate chips and the crumbled bits?      The exact same ones. And they don’t count the ones that fall off because the biscuits outsmarted the law.      Anyways, speaking of university, when are you going to actually apply, Jess? You’ve been talking about it since GCSE results day.      I know, sorry. I just don’t know if it’s  me . I mean, I like art and stuff, but do I like it  enough  to spend three years on it?      You could always start with a waiting list or something? Join the queue and then decide after being gently jabbed with a pen by the uni gods.      Or maybe do a foundation course first. You don’t have the points to get in straight up on your own if you don’t get extra points for being very dramatic in the essay.      Time’s ticking, lass. The older you get, the more they expect you to have it all sorted.      True. I just don’t want to overcommit and turn into someone who owns a  single  cup and never sweeps the floor unless they’re searching for lost earbuds.

Right, so today I’m doing my baking lesson with the Year 3s. We’re making fairy cakes with icing and edible glitter—let’s be honest, it’s going to be messy but fun!      Yum! Can I come and eat the sugar things when it’s finished? I want to be a baker when I’m bigger like Mummy.      No fair! I want to be a baker too! Can I lick the spoon, Mummy?      Only if you’re very careful and help me clean up, or the dragons under the sink get you.      What dragons?      Oooh, they come out if you don’t clean up properly! They’re in the back of the fridge and they’re DEXTER’S uncles. Very grumpy.      Mummy! That doesn’t make sense.      I don’t care! I’m licking the spoon first!      Okay, okay, deal.
