But only one lick each, and then we need to listen properly while I make the mixture. What did you both do today?      I had a mini-birthday today! Well, it wasn’t really a real birthday but it was half-time! So I had cake and juice and Anna brought me a new Tomodachi Life toy!      Mine didn’t bring me anything, and I also had someone at school called Anna. But they said my hair looked like yogurt.      That’s not a nice thing to say.       laughs  Oh, come on, about hair like yogurt—now  that’s  good poetry! We can put it in a poem for your class. “My hair today was yogurt and it moved!”      That’s not true. My hair was lumpy.      Well, the yogurt hair was probably nicer.      I found your beetle book at Morrisons, by the way. You remember the one we got from the library last week and it told us the beetles lived in forests? Well, I saw it in the snack aisle, next to the goji berries. It looked lonely.      You’re joking!      Who lives in the snack aisle?      The book. It was on the floor next to some crisps and a Rubik’s cube. I thought it was in a strange adventurers' meeting.      Mummy, can we go to the library again today?      And can we get a book about yogurt hair?      Maybe, but only after your mini birthday cake is baked, and then you have to taste my terrible poetry to the class on Monday.      Deal! But I get to be the pirate in the poem again.

Rather annoying isn’t it? My phone just sat there for ten minutes trying to download the photo.      Which one? The one from your cousin’s birthday? I remember seeing it pop up on my end. Not quite sure why the rest of the family can't get past it.      Yeah, it's one of those   50MB   ones – "high quality." I’ve sent it by email now, in case they give up. Oh, and she was quite upset someone commented  "This cake looks tragic."       Oh dear. Probably some grumpy guy from Kent who baked a soggy bottom last Sunday.      Honestly, I’m not sure whether it's the cake or his spelling. The comment said "ratic". I had to double-check it wasn't a new word.      You’ve got to feel for breakfast, haven’t you? I mean, no one should be replying to social media five minutes after they’ve ate their cereal.      Or sat in traffic. I saw one of those posts from your dad—“changing lanes in the morning is as pointless as trying to tell my boss what to do”      Classic rhythm of rage. He only ever writes at red lights.      So, anyway, back to the cake photo—what was odd to me was that Silvia was the only one who commented at all. Most people just 'liked' it in silence. Maybe they’re trying to be considerate.      Or just waiting to weigh in after the weekend.      Maybe. Though, there is a conspiracy about how Facebook only shows us the photos our friends  want  to show. Not the whole picture.      That’s true. I had a student last semester who was convinced her ‘missing’ post about her new car was censored by the system. Turns out she had it scheduled for midnight on Christmas Eve.      You’re joking. So the algorithm didn’t like that she was doing something luxurious when everyone was asleep and lonely on Christmas?      Exactly. Still, I did run with it. I told her the algorithm golems were on strike that night.      You’re a better lecturer than I will ever be. That might have been the best excuse all year.      Well, when you’ve been grading 200 essays with "This is to certify that..." in the middle of comparative pronoun analysis, you learn the magic of the fictitious bureaucratic nightmare.      I can believe it. And to think I did my masters on medieval literature—went medieval on my poor students with Old English and scribal habits.

Right, I just wanted to get through the whole conversation first. I need to think it through properly before asking... What was the plot of Cloudy with a chance of meatballs again? I think I might’ve missed it because I was making snacks. Was it like those things that rain food?      Yeah kind of, but more like a town that makes machines to eat all the food because they don’t want to waste it. Like they put everything from the bakery to the chip shop into machines and it’s supposed to solve hunger... or was it the opposite?      Oh right, the meatballs like, literally, falling from the sky? I thought it was the dumbest thing when we first watched it. My uncle still quotes "Cloudy with a chance of cheese" constantly. I’m like, what the hell, Dad?      But then you actually watch it a few times and it doesn’t seem that dumb... I mean, like... some of the jokes are not even for kids! There’s, like, subtle stuff about how the town excluded the inventor guy—so maybe it’s, like, a feminist allegory or something?      Hah, tell that to my mate Alice. She said watching it reminded her of secondary school when all the “cool” kids laughed at her because she liked making stuff and fixing things. You know, like the film is saying don’t ignore people who do their own thing?      Maybe. Anyway, the food just starting to rain and everything—like, sounds like climate change or something. I mean, if everyone just had free food, would we even need money? Anyway, maybe I’m analysing it too much because it’s about meatballs... or meatball turkeys?      [Laughs] Meatball turkeys! Yeah, that was the highlight. I remember thinking,  how does that even work, like for the ecosystem?  Geo didn’t explain it, did she?      She told me once that scientists are talking about worlds where you can 3D-print food. She said it’s something to do with not having space or resources. I don't get it—my brain’s not working like that.      Geo’s a genius basically. She go to university on that stuff? Feminist inventor, real one, not the one in the cartoon? I don’t know, I just feel like what your teacher Geo said made sense. She made it seem like how girls and boys get treated differently in schools?

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You know, how they talk politics like it's some real religion. I got to Joensuu from the train station, and I swear half the cabs over here are plastered with UK election stickers. Still, I bet most of these cabbies haven’t a clue who’s running now, eh?!      Ha! You reckon I'd have a clue? I’ve only got time to watch the Merseys FC match, unless it’s a Premier League blockbuster. But politics—eh, that’s like the weather. Didn’t used to be.      Right, but back in the day—New Labour, Tony Blair and all that—there was some real buzz in the pubs, you know? I remember my German dad saying, “Football, politics—same game, same liars and fools in the end.” But he did vote for them, eventually.      Heh, I mean, what choice did we have at the time, mate? 1997, I was still working the docks, full on, and I was thinking, if this lot can give us more money for development in the North, as opposed to London and the South, then more power to 'em. But now it’s all about spin and who got which photo ops.      Exactly, and now it's all about the “stakeholder model” and funding lines and all that rhetoric. I teach English lit, so I see it—this political language that’s full of jargon. Just trying to sound like they’ve thought it through. You ever think about the parallels with sports? Like, the politicians—prioritizing clubs over communities, as it were.      That’s the thing, man. Football’s different. It’s a game you can  get  into. Not like politics. I remember when the Reds went up to the top, ‘cos of the treble, man—Blind Joe Friday would know more about that than most MPs. But bloody politics—eh, I tried once, voted when I was 18, didn’t vote again after being asked what I thought about the 'global economy' by some spin doctor.      Still, I think Tony Blair did some good, personally. He go me a grant for my postgrad studies, back in the pre-Brexit days, when the UK was still in with Europe. You know what your problem is, mate? You only ever see politics on the telly after match highlights.      It’s true, but I like that ‘dumbing down’—ain’t nobody needs to know the macroeconomic implications of tax reform unless they’re running a chemical plant.

So did you watch The One Show yesterday? That bit about the Maldives was cracking—the whales they filmed. I got so jealous, honestly.      Oh yeah, that was wild! I was doing a full “ugh” when the presenter said diving with whales is like the biggest bucket-list thing. Right up there with owning a pug, apparently.      Don’t get me started on pugs. I would  kill  for a pug. They’re just so wobbly and snorty and just... everything.      Oh, you know I saw like three pug photos in  one  LinkedIn post yesterday. It’s taken over LinkedIn. It’s like everyone’s promoting their pet now instead of their career.      [laughs] You're telling me. I’ve been seeing the same photo of a dog in a suit since 2014—still trending. I mean, no one cares about your marketing updates, Linda from Bristol! Show us the pug!      Speaking of which—did I tell you, I had to record a BNC-style conversation two weeks ago for work? You know, the kind with like, minimal context, and everyone says "erm" and "well..." just to sound realistic?      Oh, I remember that! You said it was the most awkward fun. I did one for a phone app a while back, and the director kept saying, “No, just someone being  boring  in a café.” I tried to order a scone and failed—job done!      Hey, while you two linguists are talking about BNC and LinkedIn, I just want to know: does anyone here know how to fly without screaming? I’m going to Spain next month and it’s the most terrifying thing.      Oh, come on! That’s nothing. My sister’s been flying since she was five and still can’t go on a plane. She once said the seat belt looked like it was waiting to strangle her.      Honestly, I’d rather live with that fear than the fact that I’ve been living in Wales for three years and still get lost trying to get into the city. Once I missed a funeral because I stopped to ask for directions and got distracted by a really good bakery.      You’re telling me. Last time I was in London, I made it to King’s Cross by following two pigeons—there was even a momento mural to commemorate it.      Oh, and don’t even get me started on my cousin who’s been living in Spain for  two years  and still claims to not know where Barcelona is on a map.

Rather skip the newfit incense. You know what, let’s just stick to the original.      No, no, this one’s actually quite nice. I got it from that little shop near Hackney. It’s got this sort of—      —is this about the incense again? You two have been going on about that for a week now. What’s the deal, is it a spiritual awakening or just a midlife crisis?      Both, probably. But seriously, I can’t stand the new brand. It smells like wet wool and someone’s fridge accidentally exploded.      It’s called "minimalist aromatic fusion." The description said it opens up the space for emotional clarity. But I thought I’d get the clarity of finally makingSpeaker_1 stop smoking that rose-saffron crap from last year.      Oh come on, you loved it! That’s what gave the spare room the vibe. You wouldn’t let anyone go in there without permission, like it was some sacred place or something.      Tell me about it. I tried it once and sneezed like I’d inhaled a ghost. So, while you two debate your aromatherapy wars, what are we having for dinner?      Just a stir-fry, really. I was just tellingSpeaker_1 here that I might actually try a new recipe for Christmas. I’m thinking something a bit more—dignified. Maybe a proper meatless pie? I’ve been reading about it all week.      You? A proper meatless pie? You once tried cooking lasagna and ended up with a cheese dip and a plate of cooked unseasoned noodles.      It was an  experiment . A  bold  experiment. And besides, it was my intern who dropped the cheese grater on the floor. My fault? No.      Websites mentioned it. Your lunches mentioned it. “The Intern Chronicles” took over your work feed for a month.      Mm, I wasn’t even working there, and I still got the line about the intern that “accidentally tried to microwaverefrigerated stock for two hours.”      Okay, that one was truly tragic. But I had to let him learn the hard way. Accountability and all that.      Yeah, accountability and also throwing a full meltdown when the soup went from golden to something closer to nuclear sludge.      So, how many interns before that one, huh? I’ve lost count.      Four. And one of them tried to type “soul food” into a menu, only to realisewe’re in London and it didn’t mean what they thought it did.

So did you manage to pick up those spice blends I mentioned earlier? I was thinking we could whip up something a bit more exotic tonight—maybe something Moroccan?      I sure did! I grabbed the saffron, cumin, and that warming cinnamon you love. Oh, and I also found a nice jar of preserved lemons while I was in the Middle Eastern shop. I thought it’d be a nice touch.      Oh! Preserved lemons are brilliant. It’ll add that tangy, salty kick to the tagine. Speaking of which, how’s the shoulder of lamb you bought frozen? I hope it defrosted alright.      Yep, it thawed in the fridge last night. I also picked up some new potatoes and a few courgettes to go with it. It all sounded very hearty in the recipe I skimmed online last night while procrastinating on writing an article.      Procrastination via recipe research—I live for that. Honestly, I thought I’d never find myself cooking so passionately, but now I can’t help myself. I’ve even joined that Zumba class nearby twice now. You should come.      I thought about it, but I was on a medication regime for a few weeks, and the movement made my back flare up. But I’m feeling better now, so maybe I’ll come next week. Would you want to go as a pair?      Absolutely! We could make a night of it—go to the class, get a coffee afterward, maybe a bit of dessert. I’ve been craving nutty-chocolate things. Or maybe I should be asking  you  where I should get a good croissant in Birmingham now I’m staying a while?      Oh, there’s a little French boulangerie just off the Bullring. It’s not too upmarket, but the pain au chocolat is baked fresh twice a day. I’ll take you there next weekend. And don’t you dare pass on the apple turnover with cinnamon—the way it’s made makes me feel like I’m back in Paris.      Perfection. I’ll add that to the list. Now, back to the tagine—should I start with the onions or the lamb first?      Start with the onions, definitely. Let them caramelise a bit, then brown the lamb before adding the spices. Oh, and your legs will thank you later for planning ahead.      Haha, you speak as though I’m planning this to fuel a week of gym sessions over this one meal.

So did you talk to James last night?      Yeah, he messaged me first. Said he and Sophie had finally sorted the childcare so they could come to the dinner next week.      Oh brilliant! That’s the last of our group. We haven’t all met up in ages. I’ve missed the old gang.      Same. You know, with everyone working in different cities now, it’s easy to lose touch. But I’m glad they’re coming. Sophie mentioned you and her had a chat when you met in Oxford?      Yeah, I bumped into her at the café near the university. We had a long catch-up. She’s doing the postdoc in Manchester, you know, and she says the teaching load is brutal there. You’d think they’d cut lecturers some slack after the pandemic.      Honestly, I feel the same. I’ve been swamped this term. Between prepping for the new module and marking, I barely have time to think. Are you over the grading yet?      Just about. Thank God for the weekend! Although honestly, I’ve still got a few essays on my desk. I was supposed to have a proper work rhythm in Beijjing, but somehow I always find something new to do.      Sounds familiar. I’m trying to remind myself that just because I have access to the internet and email doesn’t mean I have to reply in five minutes flat.      Hear, hear. Besides, we’re on holiday—well, as holiday as a Mandarin-speaking crash course comes. I still can’t pronounce your colleague’s name, Zhang Wenjun. I always say “Jen-Wee-jun” instead of “jung-joon.”      I tell him it’s fine, but he insists on correcting me every time. You’d think he’d have better things to do than play language police.      He does have a point, though. You know I’m already struggling to tell if people are being polite or annoyed when they talk with their hands. It’s one thing reading about gestural communication in teaching journals and quite another seeing it in real life.      I think it’s hilarious. And seriously, don’t worry about your toes, by the way. I saw your flip-flop’s edge lifting all day at the museum. You might want to invest in a better pair next trip.      True, but these were the only ones I packed. They looked super comfortable!

So did you watch The Late Late Show last night? Hugh Jackman came on and it was  so  funny. I mean, I love him as a musician and actor, but I didn’t think he had that kind of… I don’t know,  wackiness .      Oh I saw the clip online. He did that one with the piano player where he pretended to be completely tone-deaf. A lot of people swore that was a fake, though. You know, the usual tech conspiracy stuff—people say it was all AI-generated for the show. Apparently, the piano player has a different haircut in three different clips.      Honestly, sometimes the people who claim that stuff is real are the ones you should be concerned about! But I think it was real. He’s had enough years in the industry, he’d know not to look like a fool if it was staged. Cats would have been all over it if it was just a trick.      Maybe, maybe. I’m just not sure where the line is anymore between clever choreography and real magic—especially with the kind of technology being used in the media now. I read yesterday about a conspiracy that suggests the royal family actually  aren’t  real. Just a bunch of actors trotted out when the cameras roll. Can you believe?      Oh no, that one’s been around for years! But seriously, if that were true, who’s running the country? The universities? The BBC? There are people out there who think it’s also all a simulation. That the whole of Europe is a computer programme with programmed citizens walking around.      I’m not sure I need  that  much explaining when I have about five emails to deal with before I head to the office tomorrow. I had to cancel a meeting with a Danish client because of the weather. I mean it wasn’t  snowing , but the roads were like liquid soap. My driver nearly slid into a van on his way to me yesterday. I was told it was all because of a North Atlantic current collapse or something mad like that.      Oh gosh, I read about that with the Jet Stream and the polar vortex. Some say the recent cold snaps are part of something larger. I was talking about it the other day in class with my pupils, and one of them was convinced it was simply the Earth’s magnetic field flipping.

Dad, I’m really excited we’re going to Jamaica Inn! Have you been there before?      Aye, I have. Years ago, when I were a lad. Back in the day, it was more of a haunt for the film  Jamaica Inn —Deborah Kerr and eeny Robert Taylor, yeah? It’s got some good scenery out there.      I’ve seen the film! Like, the one from the 1930s? It looked so old-school. We watched it in English class and the teacher said it was based on a real inn. I like the red curtains and the spooky vibes.      Aye, that’s the lot of that place. Morbid tales and red velvet—it’s got a bit of a gothic vibe like Lewis Carroll threw a party and Sherlock Holmes dropped by for a dram!      Haha, I see what you mean. I read  Alice in Wonderland  once and it’s mad how Carroll made everything so confusing and yet kind of makes sense. Like, how real was Alice?      Well, I reckon she was written in a different land of logic to ours. Kind of like Morse code—makes no sense unless you know the code. Like a telegram from the land of fairy tales.      I know what Morse code is! It’s like the dots and dashes they used to send messages through the telegraph, right? Like in old Western films, they transmit in this funny code. But how does it work?      Aye, it does—kinda like letters have a rhythm. Dots and dashes make up each letter, so people can understand it even if they’re far apart. Just like you can read English here and someone in Africa or America can too.      So you’re saying language is like a code? I never thought of it like that. Like, words are like dots and dashes?      Exactly. Even Braille is a language—just with bumps instead of letters. You read with your fingers. It’s clever how that works.      Do people still use the telegraph?      Not really—technology’s caught up with it. Now we’ve got texts goin’ on smartphones, if you can believe it. Phones that fit in your pocket, no fewer.      Time machine, innit?      Aye, feels like it sometimes. When I was your age, I had to send a telegram to let folk know I was alive if I went away for longer than a few days. Now you just text them at 3am.

Rather skip the queue at the cinema. You know what they do. I was just in Chester and paid like eight quid for a child’s ticket now I think. I can take the kids to see that dinosaur film for less cash £2 or something like that in places round here.      Eight quid dear, that’s more than a twitch with your mug if you know what I mean.      Yeah, but I think that's just because it's easier to inflate prices now, not like it used to be. Back in the day when I served in the forces, a pound would buy you everything, even a brand new  Variety  cinema ticket and the popcorn supply’d go on for weeks.      Oh, you lot talk like it was the last century, but I reckon you're nostalgic, Dad. I mean, the kids now spend most of their time on tablets and phones. I see it every day at work—language has changed for goodness’ sake. I had to teach someone once how to say “I am eating a biscuit” in Mandarin, and they kept getting mixed up between “eating” and “biting”!      Ah, technology for you. Everything’s different now… but not the queues. Still a waste of time. I remember when the buses would stop at the same places and you could just get on and off. Now you need a phone to check if the thing’s even running. And the petrol stations! What a racket. When I worked at BT in my time, you could read the sign and just drive up. Now you need a degree to work out which pump wants your card and which one’s trying to make your key fob do a boogie!      Don’t get me started on the pump fob thang. My car fails to know that I’m even in the vicinity sometimes. At least in my old Triumph, you just put the fuel in and didn’t have to fight with technology. I remember once trying to get a filling at the garage and they said no, you can’t just pay cash anymore. It had to go on a chip or a card. What next? Jet fuel on demand with a selfie scan?      But you know what, Dad? The good news is go-karts on pond life are still pretty much free if you know where to line up, and that’s more exciting than a bloke in a gray suit fixing virtual fences.

Mum, thanks a million for helping me sort out the list. I’d have completely forgotten half of it otherwise.      Oh love, it's nothing. I’ve been through it all myself when I moved in here with your dad. Look, I’ve added a few things you’ll probably need that I didn’t at first — like a good pestle and mortar if you like spices.      Brilliant, I never thought of that. Honestly, I’ve barely stepped into a kitchen since uni catering.      Well, you’re going to run when you get the washing machine up and running like you’ve been told! And speaking of running, how are the jet lag and your back? You looked like the turkey on Christmas Day after you got back last week.      I still do, a bit. I’ve been taking the little walks to the shops, but the old gig is playing up, no doubt from that 12-hour flight and no sleeps at the hotel. I’m starting to regret taking the job in Casablanca. I miss your Sunday roasts.      Well, listen, I’ll make you a promise — as soon as you move in, you’ll have one every Sunday. You can't move out without a taste of your old Mum's chicken and dumplings.      Dealt! You know, while we're talking about food, did you ever manage to cook that weaver fish we found at that weekend market in Essex?      Oh, I tried. It was a bit of a disaster. I put it in the oven at 200 and forgot it for an hour. Looked like it had been there since the ice age. Steve finally pulled it out and made it into fish pie. It wasn’t a patch on your father’s cod and chips, I’ll tell you that.      That does sound like him. Always got a way out of tragedy.      He did. Bless him. Oh, love, have I told you about your Auntie Sheila’s engagement? She’s been going out with this landscape gardener from Essex.      No! Since when? Wasn’t she set on a serious romance with that bloke from the bowling club in Walthamstow?      Oh, he’s off in Australia now, I’m afraid. Anyway, this gardener, your aunt’s never stopped laughing since she met him. You’d like him — he’s quite the talker and not half bad to look at either.

Was it someone close?      Sort of. I can't believe it's been almost two years since I started university. Time really flies, doesn't it? It mentioned how he used his stories of the countryside and people he met as the basis for his work. I think I inherited that from him. That sounds just like him. Always had a real love for people and the places they came from. He always used to say that "everyone has a story," and he wanted to bring those lives to the canvas.

So do you know anyone at the uni in Lancaster?      Not personally, but my cousin went there a few years ago. She did psychology and I think she's working in Manchester now. Yeah, I remember when we used to do that. Burgers and board games at Danny’s place, remember? That厮 always used to win.      Oh man, that was them! My cousin runs a place down by Rotherham, and it’s not that far.      A what!? Go-karting at 19? 20?      Why not? You don’t get to be a kid for ever, mate. Only once a year!      Fair point. I might get changed out of my tracksuit once, then.      Just make sure to wear the helmet properly, or I swear you won’t get a ride with me.

Okay, I’m just saying, Joshua’s been acting way too calm the whole game. Well, if Myra keeps playing "balance the cube" like it’s Tetris, I’m terrified I’m gonna end up in Paris alone without a cure for anything. It’s too much pressure. It’s the capital of chaos and human failure.      Oh, let’s not go down the metaphor route until we’ve solved one colour. Then we can have a big debate about why this game’s metaphor is better than “The Martian,” which, by the way, we saw last week over wine and chocolate fudge.      Okay, I’m going to forget that was suggested. I need my focus. If we keep flapping like headless chickens, we’re going to lose the blue cure, and before that, we’ll have a helicopter in Tangier, and I  refuse  to be that helicopter guy who sits around doing nothing.

Right, so today is CBeebies day, and we need to make the most of it. The panto got postponed because of rain last week, so thank goodness it’s finally on today! I’m gonna be a dragon, Mummy. Like the ones in  Pogles’ Wood .      Oh, that’s brilliant, Mummy’s making you a cardboard one with wings! I know, and then you fell asleep on Daddy’s shoulder halfway through the credits. Right, as for this weekend—your summer birthday is still ages away, but we can start planning.      Are we gonna go to the park with Auntie Emma and her twins again?      We could! Maybe add in a stop for ice cream or a trip to the library for a World Book Day special. How ‘bout we do it on Saturday afternoon after we help Mummy pick up some new storybooks.      Can I read to Mummy on Mother’s Day too?      Of course, love. We might, but only if you manage to sit through the whole panto andBehaviour doesn’t go sideways!      I’ll be good, I’ll not kick the chair like last time.      Mm, let’s not talk about that. The chair is still creaking.      And can we order pizza for dinner after the panto? Like our usual?      Yeah, we can do that… as long as you don’t flick the pepperoni at the dog.

So do you lot reckon we’ve got a chance of anyone going back to London for a bit?      Honestly? I don’t see it. I’ve asked three times now. Everyone's “next month,” “when things calm down,” or “maybe in the spring.” It’s like they’re all stuck here now.      I reckon it depends on how much they’ve got here. A lot of people just got more jobs and social connections. You know, once you get into that rhythm, moving can feel like a step back. Didn’t you get that job offer in Bristol too?      Yeah, I did, but the pay’s nothing compared to what I could get up North. Just not enough to justify the hassle of starting over. Tenants, London prices, the commute—it all adds up.      It is a bit of a dilemma. I mean, I’d love to go back. My mum misses me like mad. But you ever looked at the rent in South London now? It’s not exactly affordable for a bloke in technical work, you know?      I know, honestly, as much as I loved the energy and everything London has, this place—it’s manageable. We’ve been out of the city so much more since we moved here, actually. More like normal people than finance bros.      Yeah, fair point. I went back once for a weekend, and I just felt someone out of place. Like I was trying to live a rush lifestyle when I’d preferably be out walking the dog at dawn.      What’s the dog’s name again?      Rex. Bit of a showoff the little fella, but friendly. He’s doing okay—he even met Sarah’s parents at the weekend and survived.      That’s quite the test. Sarah’s guest list can be a bit unpredictable. I once brought a pear tart to a dinner and everyone was wondering if I tried to make them gag on fruit.      Oh yeah, Sarah’s very specific about food. She says she loves English food but then gets confused when it's just meat and something green.      Honestly, it’s one of life’s mysteries. If it wasn’t for dating apps and the language work, I don’t know how I’d meet people. London was fine for meeting people, but here it feels more personal.      I never had to use dating apps much.

So did I tell you about the time I used to make cakes and they exploded in the oven?      No, no you haven’t yet. I’ve had my fair share of kitchen disasters, though—once I boiled a ceramic jug and cracked it!      Oh no! That sounds like a nightmare. Mine was one of those mug cakes—15 minutes in the oven and it just… erupted. Like lava, but with chocolate.      I would not be surprised if one of my kids has done that. Didn’t your youngest come home with a “potato cannon” from a school project, Claire?      Oh yeah, her and that child’s obsession with pyrotechnics! The head teacher’s office still smells like smoke to this day.      Oh, the little delights we bring into the world, right? Chloe, when you were younger, what sorts of toys did you get in Boston?      Well, you didn’t have the same selection as here, but we had trolls from Troll and Toymaker, some sturdy wooden things. I remember saving up for a doll with removable clothes and only realising when I washed her in the sink that the stickers wouldn’t come off.      Mate, I got a Tamagotchi that died because I forgot to feed it. Now don’t laugh, but I took it to the school counsellor! She said, “It's just a toy,” and I said, “She stopped breathing!”      That’s typical Peterborough upbringing—Tamagotchi and being told not to cry over toys. Though, there was a time I got a horse. Just not the living kind.      Oh a what? Another failsafe educational toy that you barely opened the box on?      That horse was made of balls of wool. All you had to do was tie it together to shape it. I was too scared to untie it in case I messed it up. Still in the shed, as far as I know.      That’s the kind of thing that happened when your parents were busy working. I remember my dad talking to me about his job in gothic details I didn’t understand. It was sales—that’s all I ever really knew, him trying to sell something he cared too much about.      I have to say, I’ve never had the patience for that. I did admin and HR, so to me, it was about fixing systems, not selling dreams to them!      Fair enough. I do numbers, so I kind of like both worlds.

So did you go anywhere nice on your trip, Nan? We’ve only just found out you were away.      Oh love, it was Blaenavon in Wales. Best kept secret, it were. Charming little town, all those old slate houses. And it was peaceful—no dogs barking, no telephones ringing, just good old peace.      I didn’t know you went to Wales, Dad! I thought you said you were stuck at home, pulling weeds or something!      Oh, shut it, lad. I made a proper trip of it. Nan even took me to that little Welsh pub—had real cwtch vibes, and they served the best lamb cawl I’ve ever had.      Cwtch? Is that some sort of dip?      No, no, silly. It’s Welsh for hug—Welsh cwtch, alright? The whole place was full of it. Everyone was chatting, sharing stories, feeding the tabby cat under the table.      You had a cat? In the pub?      Course. Name of Ellis, old minger but he’d come for the lamb trotters.      So – no estate agents, no dog walkers, no laptops?      No, don’t be daft. Silly place, no one rushing about. Though we did meet this old fella who told us to “hold on tight” just before the bus crashed into a cow.      A  bus crash and a cow ? That’s not peaceful, that’s a National Geographic documentary!      Haha! She’s not wrong. But it didn’t crash—that was part of his charm. He said the cow had a  right cheek , so he hit ‘er with the bus. Turned out it was a joke. Bit more drama than a pantomime.      Nan, you always manage to make your holidays sound eventful.      Oh, it were proper nice. And speaking of events, I took the dog. The road trip was something else. Pippa the corgi goin’ mental every time I passed a junction.      Pippa? You brought  your  dog? You said you were going alone!      Of course, love. Poor thing was hours with the cat in the garden. She needed a holiday too, and besides—travel’s not just about us old folks. You young ‘uns need to remember dogs get homesick too.      Okay, Nan, you’re a class act. But what about sports? You two playing any before?      Cycled down them little lanes on the Wales Coastal Path. Beautiful. It were on my bucket list, see? Nan decided to bring her backgammon set—endless. Took her six hours to beat me.

Rather skip the queue and just go through the side doors, do we need to take our coats off?      Maybe not yet, unless we find a bench to sit on      Look at that moon! No, I mean outside!      Yeah it's beginning to look a bit more autumnal than I'd hoped      Yeah, a bit      Got one!      What was it, Anteater?      Is that the one when he's chased by a hyena...      Yeah, that's it, we watched it last week      My turkey came out all right!      Ten more, ten more      Erm, no the gravy came out all right, the turkey was very very very breakfast, no doubt about that      The turkey came out looking like the Queen!      Yeah so I thought why not      She looked very dignified, I mean not the Queen I mean the turkey      It did, it looked proud of itself      Absolutely      How much does it cost to get a dog, like, does it cost a huge amount of money?      Not at first, the initial cost is quite small      They just cost in vet fees and things      Yeah, but it's not outlandish, is it?      I mean if you get a horse it's a different ball game      Right, the problem is my dad says I've got a house full of kids and it's not like I've got a big house      Yeah but that's the joy of dogs, they can live in tiny places and be perfectly happy      Do you want to get a breed you can train?      Like what?      Golden retrievers, spaniels, those kinds of dogs      But I don't know if I can get a dog go out of my house unless I get a house with a garden      It's not impossible but it's not particularly easy      So I have to get a special dog and then I have to go hours to get them and then I have to pay a vet and that's over      Yeah      Unless I got a cat      Right, they can always be house trained      They can, yeah they can      They're quite good in an apartment as well      But I don't like cats as much as I like birds      Birds can be pets too      Yeah I've known people who had canaries and parrots and stuff like that      Yeah but they're not as friendly      I don't know, if your room was filled with light and particularly warm things

So do you not find it funny that we used to grumble about the roads in Peterborough and now he’s got to adapt to roads with no one on them?      I dunno, probably is a bit eerie honestly. No traffic, no honking — just like the opposite of home. I mean, at least here we can complain about the bus routes and the potholes… that’s a kind of tradition now.      I heard it’s easier building a house there, or like, you can afford to build your own. Like, outside of the cities.      That’s true enough. I mean, I was deployed there once and the supply lines were nuts — like you had to plan a week ahead for everything. Fun for bursts, not for life, mind you.      Easier to get the decorator in then, I guess — if you’re moving out there, Reg. You need to get some tips from me in advance though. I’ve got opinions.      Yeah, so do I. I reckon Reg should go for one of those big l-shaped sofas — you can’t have that in a land where everyone’s still trying to get off their knees as a greeting. It’s not practical.      That’s so funny — my nan’s been bugging me to go visit her in Texas again. She keeps telling me “It’s not as dry as you think!” Like, no, it’s not — it’s just wet-ish all at once and then on fire.      That’s oddly literal. You ever think about following Reg out there? You worked in logistics before — could be a good fit?      I considered it briefly. I mean, living the dream, building systems in the middle of a desert where your SatNav is suddenly telling you to take the next right into a dune? That’s a whole vibe. Maybe not for my blood pressure though.      SatNavs are a joke any bloody place I go. I tried using them on night patrols once. We ended up 30 miles off route. No Google Street View with sand dunes and camels looking at you funny.      I’m saying this because I’m the one who got goaded into map reading by Dad as a kid. Just give me a compass and a greasy finger, and I’ll get you there.      Look mate, just take Reg seriously when he asks directions. He’s going hours off course otherwise.

Rather annoying I caught an infection last week.      That's dreadful, what happened?      Hope it wasn’t anything too serious, you don’t look over the worst.      No, I mean, it started with a sore throat, then it just kind of went downhill from there.      Did you see a doctor?      I did, yeah. They said it was a throat infection, nothing too bad, but it clung on for ages.      Did they give you anything?      Some antibiotics. I’ve been taking them religiously, but still, it took about ten days to clear up. I’ve been relying on herbal remedies a lot more since then to keep my immune system on track.      That’s wise, I’ve been into alternative therapies for a while—nettle tea, echinacea... I swear by them.      I’m not sure I have the time for all that, but I do try and eat more organic—personally I think it takes care of a lot.      It probably does. I’ve been thinking about changing up my diet. I’m surrounded by organic produce here in New Zealand but it's often fairly expensive, and I barely cook at home these days.      It’s all about trying to make it practical, you know? For me, I batch-cook at the weekends. It helps me not fall into the trap of takeaway.      That is a good idea. I’d be tempted to just heat something up every night, but it doesn’t do you any favours in the long run.      Honestly, cooking is one of the things I’ve struggled with since I started this business. No time in the day. But I realized I was feeling irritable, fatigued, all that. Signals you to take it more seriously.      For sure. I remember when I first started out as a communications strategist I lived on coffee and pizza. Took me a year or two to realize I was burning myself out.      So this entire trip—Stockholm, away from work—has been life-affirming for me. I think I needed to reconnect, not only with nature but with a simpler routine.      This place is beautiful, seriously. I was reading last night about the history of the gardens—do you know it’s been here since the 17th century? They’ve been cultivating plants for medicinal and agricultural purposes for centuries.      Oh, absolutely, it's like a living library of botany. I could spend hours here just walking through the different sections.

So do you lot ever notice how thick our accents get when we talk about childhood memories? I swear when I’m telling the kids at university about growing up in Gillingham, I sound like a caricature of a Kent person. Not to be rude, Dad.      Hey, don’t eeny mind me, luv. It’s all good. I’ve got an accent thick enough to hang coats on, haven’t I? Got it from my nan, who lived in Croydon, believe it or not! You sound just like us, poppet. Just younger and with less swearing.      Honestly, I’ve never noticed it much, but the other night I was trying to use my phone’s voice assistant, and it kept asking me to repeat myself. I said, “Open GoogleMaps,” and it thought I said “Open Krolle Maps.” Sounds like a biscuit to it, doesn’t it?      Haha! My phone does the same. I sound like I’ve got a lisp or something. Maybe I should just speak more like Mum and do it in a posh voice. Though I might lose two words out of every five and confuse myself entirely.      Honestly, I reckon the only reason it recognises me is if I sound like a dead man talking to a computer, and even then, half the time I just switch to typing. All that “Alexa, play Stones . . . oh no, it put on Stone Cold by Kreator!” Spent half the night trying to calm it down. Rude piece of tech.      Aye, and let’s be honest, most of us speak like we’ve got stones in our mouths half the time. My old missus used to swear at me for shouting at her over the TV and not realising that I was barely speaking louder than a whisper. She said I was just using ‘em like punctuation.      Oh God, I used to suffer the same. I was working with a couple of fellas from Basingstoke, and they told me I whispered like I was being followed by the council trying to catch me spending money on clothes! They asked if I always talk like that or if something had happened.      That’s because of my parents, if you ask me. Always shouting at each other about the bill or the kids. I just learned to speak quieter so I wouldn’t cause a row. Fat lot of good it did—got dragged into every argument anyway.

Right, lads, dig in. I've made a few of the usuals—lasagne, spaghetti bolognese, and some garlic bread. Oh, I also threw in a bit of roasted pumpkin and some mash. Not quite traditional, but I thought we might try something with a bit more veg for once.      Thanks, Mrs. Winters! Lasagne all the way for me. I don’t really like pumpkin, but this looks good. Is there any cheese on there, or should I pass?      Oh, there’s cheddar and a bit of gruyère spread out on the side. Feel free to go to town and make your own combo. I like to mix the turkey and vegetable ones in with the pasta left over.      I’m gonna risk it and try the pumpkin. My teacher at school said she was about to try something new for breakfast, and now she’s eating porridge with... I don’t know, ginger or something. Just thought I'd follow suit.      Porridge with ginger? That’s a bit of an experiment, but I say go for it. Like your Auntie Jess, remember when she tried making her own baked Alaska and ended up with a baked... banana? No one said it looked like a rocket.      Yeah, that was hilarious. I remember my cousin nearly choked on that “banana” at her party. She said it was the size of a microwave.      Tales of baked disasters: my speciality. But joking aside, I’m thinking about getting the kids involved a bit more in the kitchen—say, next time I’m hosting a Halloween party at home, you lot could help us decorate and make the decorations.      Halloween party? At your house? Properly like a big one? With a haunted house in the garden and punch bowls for the big kids?      Well, I’m trying to recruit a few other mums and their kids to pitch in, you know, team effort. We could make good use of that overgrown garden out there. Maybe some spooky stories too.      Yeah, but there’s that one time Uncle Matt told a story about his first job goin' on a recruitment trip and he kept using so many big words, like “stakeholder engagement” and “synergy,” everyone just fell asleep.      Uncle Matt does have a habit of earnestly launching into his life anecdotes like a TED Talk, doesn’t he? Remember the time he tried to explain discrimination in the workplace over lasagne?

Rather than a newfit, eh?      Aye, it's mad when you think about it, innit? Just went on autopilot after I got into it.      Aye, I remember when you first told me you were thinking about doing it — I said “You? Flying a plane? That’s you with your mug of tea and your cat on your lap!”      Yeah! I never thought I'd be one of those people who like to do something so daft like that. Funny how things turn out when you least expect ’em, like.      Oh, I know, love. I had no idea where I was now when Myra and I went back to New York last year either. Ten years I’ve been back and forth now, and still I think it’s like a different country in some ways!      I’ve been wanting to take you up for a trial in the summer. I’ve got a bit of flight time now, so they let me do it.      Oh, you get me up in one of them tin cans and we land in a field and you say “Right, that’s it” — I’ll have a proper trot off in a huff and come back at the house with a cup of tea, and Myra will say “Mum, relax.”      If I could get you out of your kitchen, even for an hour, I’d call that a success! That place is a museum, love.      Oh, is it? Well, I don’t see it that way — but your colleague, Neil, he nearly did trip over my walk-in larder the other week when he was here looking for a clipboard.      Oh right! I remember that. You said, “Don’t be ridiculous, that’s just the National Collection.”      Aye, well, it is a bit, innit? I haven’t eaten half of that stuff since the previous millennium, but you can’t just chuck things out! What if the lunches come up and demand what I’ve been feeding them?      You’re not feeding them! You’re just giving goody bags on your own if you ask me.      Well, I’m trying to keep up with the blooming refuse schedule, your lot. Every week I have to sort it all out and then one week I miss it and the bin men give me this look like “Sorry luv, over满了, we can’t take this lot.”      I know, and they don’t say it soft like you’d expect.

Right, I just played "unspecified" to get a few of the vowels out—the Scrabble gods owe me after the last round when I had to make do with "XQZ"      Honestly, Nick, do you have to use words that no one actually says in real life? I'm still trying to figure out if "unspecified" is even allowed.      Look, Aimee, he's got a point. The dictionary says it's a word, and as far as Scrabble is concerned, the dictionary doesn't lie. It's the coursework that counts, not the spelling.      Bullseye. What I found fascinating is how "unspecified" comes from Latin roots. "Specire" means "to look at," so "unspecified" literally means "not looked at in detail." Wild, right?      Yeah, I still can't believe I scored a triple word after playing "aardvark." That looked wrong but, apparently, it’s a word.      I mean, it is, but it is what it is. I don't think even aardvarks look at things in "unspecified" ways. Speaking of, how's your university course, Nick? You still surviving the linguistics part of it?      It’s huge. One lecture last week was about etymology and the whole idea of words evolving over time. We even had homework on the origins of someone being "pale." Turns out it comes from a word meaning "to sour," which kind of makes sense if you think about how pale and sour look kind of similar.      Kind of about like how I finally figured out "flabbergasted" is just an absurd word made up by someone wanting to sound fancy.      You're not wrong there. My grandma read us a story about a guest speaker who passed out after being flabbergasted by a giant chocolate cake. It was tragic.      You read children’s books while you're a  chef ? Is that allowed?      It's part of the job when you work at a café delivering themed menus. Plus, kids love their books as much as they love snacks. I'm still wondering how anyone got into A Levels to study classics and ended up with something like that. I think my least favourite part was the bit where Charlie finds the ticket and forgets to say thank you. That's the bit where I wanted to ring him up.

Rather a cold day we've had, isn't it, Doris?      Oh, bless us, it's been biter than a witch's kiss. I've nearly dropped my cup three times already.      Aye, aye. We'll be lucky if the radiators even kick in properly.      You think it's them gas bills? I’ve been hearing all sorts on the radio—something about supply shortages and all that. Makes me feel like it’s one of them years where the cold doesn’t chase when it should.      That’s the truth. I remember when I were a lad, the winters were long, but at least you knew what you were getting. Now you never know what’s coming. So did you watch The Lie last night? That Shakespeare remake they put out on iPlayer?      No, I haven't had time. I've been swamped with coursework. How was it? So did you just pop in from Cambridge?      Yeah, just drove through. Or just your carb addiction. You haven’t changed.      Touché. But in all seriousness, I’ve made peace with the fact that I’m moving into marketing management after this role.

So do you ever remember your dreams, love? Or is it like mine—gone the second I open my eyes?      I do, actually. Some of them anyway. You just unplug it and wait for your dream toast!      Logical. Very sound child logic.      I’m just waiting for my dream to come true where I don’t have to correct three hundred spelling errors in one evening.      Like, zero?      Yeah. A blessed few, preferably.      I had a dream I could fly, but only with a rocket on my back. It went  very  fast.      Next time you dream of fast travel, just imagine your lottery ticket.

Rather skip the new economy and go back to what used to do. That's good of you, Charlie. I’d be keen to hear what you know. Not that I’d take it all on by myself, mind. My back’s not like it used to be.      Aye, well the world's a funny place, isn’t it? I reckon go for it while we’ve still got our wits about us. Speaking of which, did I tell you about Sue’s nephew? He’s moving to Berlin to study environmental science.

Rather skip the starter and just go for the pie and mash. I’m famished, honestly. The pints got to me somehow.      Blows me away, how drinking in a pub can make your tummy growl like you haven’t eaten in a week. But fair play, it’s been a while since I’ve had proper pie and mash here.      Yeah, I remember that Aneurin Barnard character from  Happy Valley  always had that stew thing, pulling pork or something. And I’m not even emotional, but I was bawling by the end of the last series.      Me too, honestly. You need this pub’s kind of comfort in your life after that. Look at these hides, though — leather booths and a tinny chandelier. Someone thought this was fancy.      I mean, the stone walls and the landings as décor definitely sell it. I do—looked like some sort of red and black tumbleweed rolling towards Margravine. I spent the next two hours about five sizes smaller while I waited for it to dry.      And I thought you were being modest because of that scarf! I mean, it does sound like something that would be in  Happy Valley —poor man’s chaos. Still remember when you tried to tuck it back into the back pocket and it came loose and nearly suffocated you.      I tripped, I spilled a lager, and the cat ran out of the room.
