So did you lot actually manage to get anything done at work today or what?      I got the site sorted out by about ten o'clock and I’ve been sweeping up after the lads since. It were a proper nightmare. Look at me—get a load of the state of my boots and all the dust I’ve tracked in. Not exactly good form if someone important's coming round later, is it?      Yeah, I heard someone important _is_ coming round, which is why you’re cleaning and not me. You lot never chase when it's the blokes doing the fetchin’.      Aww, don't start, Jess. Rob's stressed and rightly so.      Stressed? No, Rob just doesn't see the point in things. He’d probably say "sort the mess later" if it was about him and forget it.      Alright, but still... I’m just curious what’s happening with this “big thing” at work for Rob? I thought he was just doing that warehouse revamp for the week—personally I’d be up for that if the coffee was as good as the grief.      Nah, it’s bigger than that. The council from Cambridge said they’re gonna come check it all out cos they’re pushing for that sustainability star or something. So he’s got to clean up, sort through the paperwork, and make sure the truckers are on time and all in line.      And you didn’t consider mentioning that before we left the house with our takeaway pizza and a moody Rob?      Look, it’s not like I invite people about to make them suffer. I brought chips to share, didn’t I? Not much cop on the restaurant front if you’re not paying.      Maybe I’ll start offering chips at my events. "Fancy meeting someone at 9am on a Tuesday with a side of battered aubergine"—I reckon I could sell them on that.      Like your speaker line-up of me and Simon Cowell lunches, right? “Cake tragics and acoustic sets with no audience.”      Cheeky. Don’t go getting all smug cos you’ve got a job managing other people and I just chuck bricks around. You don’t know how blokes feel when the client says “we want all the noise made by 3 and then leave it untouched till 7.” I had to stand there with a marker pen in the rain over yesterday, writing “DO NOT TOUCH” in forty places.

Rather do a nice cup of tea, innit? Seems like everything wants you to buy it ‘organic’ or ‘fair trade’ or some muck like that now. I mean, sure, where’s the tea bag gone? £2 for a single cup? Preposterous.      Oh come now, Fred, I understand the sticker price, but I reckon it’s not all that bad if you buy in bulk from the supermarket or the local co-op. Still cheaper than a takeaway latte, wouldn’t you say?      You lot are missing the point. Let’s be honest—we’re not here for the brand, are we? We just want our tea, a bit of warm milk and a bit of turkey on toast if we’re lucky! Me and Agnes back in Manchester used to chuck the Dandelion and Burdock in the kettle and call it an herbal brew by the end of the week. Strong stuff!      Honestly, I don’t know what’s changed. When I started teaching, the staff room had a tin of builders’ tea and that was it—no frills, no info on the bag. I mean, we all knew it was probably grown in the rainforest by someone we’ve never met, but it tasted like tea nonetheless. Now you have to read a mile of small print before you can even pour the water!      That’s the lot of us, Agatha. Too old to understand ‘ethical sourcing,’ and too stubborn to care. I just want my afternoon cup with two sugars and a spot of milk, not some sour-faced barista lecturing me on carbon footprints and plant-based creamers.      I do agree there, Fred. I make mine with a dash of milk from the local dairy, and I let it brew just long enough not to scald the throat. I mean, if you’re going to step up your game, for heaven’s sake, tell us how much caffeine is in that leaf, not where the farmer lives.      Here’s another thought for you all—do you remember the good old days when the only thing you had to worry about with your builder’s tea was whether the kettle had enough hot water? Now you’re delivering a sermon with your snack! I swear, even the sugar bowls have got life-sized carbon labels now.      Still, I do enjoy the occasional English breakfast with a splash of cold milk.

Rather skip the new bar in Norwich. You know what they do. I had her in for a drink once.      Oh God, I remember her. She asked me if I’d studied a little for the job interview.      You frightened her, like you were gonna turn her eeny weeny passive aggressive comment into a research paper.      Look, I don’t want to be accused of anything serious, so this is a top priority for me. It was quite interesting as it turns out we had the same flat once when she was considerably younger.      Get out, is that even legally possible?      No, no, another person with the same flat. It was a bit strange, but it left her a bit shaken up, to be honest.      I think the world is just strange most of the time. Cats on the internet breakfast, no doubt.      Haha, yeah. People’s lives are so fragmented these days, even the CRB checks have holes in them.      I tell you what, I applied for one the other day and the application form asked whether I had any tattoos or body piercings. Honestly, is that even relevant?!      It's ridiculous – unless it's for a job in a swimming pool.      Well, maybe they're trying to assess depth of commitment or something. ‘What’s the meaning behind your nose ring? Explain. In full.’      That's already half a page of unnecessary questions!      It's like applying for being yourself. Can I speak for longer than five minutes? Do I flinch at authority? I don’t know the answer to that, but I’m fairly certain I don’t.      I once had to do a CRB check to do something ridiculous like volunteer cutting bread at a guest house.      And? Did they believe it was a high-risk position?      I think the question was whether I had ever had a prosecution for fraud. I nearly mentioned the time with the incorrect change on the bus fare. Not that the bus driver noticed anyway.      Sometimes I wonder how we function as a society on the back of these checks. Any real crimes tend to be left out, but somehow your teenage snot box piercing becomes the most damning piece of evidence you could file.      Oh gosh, I'm not even going to visit that emotional minefield right now.      Speaking of emotional minefields, I’m not entirely sure what I think about circumcision.

Hey, thanks for putting the tea on. I needed that. I’m still in holiday mode, to be honest.      You’re lucky, then. I’ve been swamped. Work's been hell this week with all the reviews going on. But at least you had a proper lie-in after your flight.      It was ridiculous. I got onto the plane in the morning, a layover that felt like 12 hours, and got here last night. I’m still in my pyjamas and pretending to be awake. But worth it — the trip was brilliant. Tore through my reading list, had some laughs with Maisie, and ate way too much fish and chips. Again.      Haha, you always talk like it's the most exquisite cuisine. I still can't believe you pick fish and chips every single time. Why not try something fancy once?      Because I love it, and besides, after three days of tourists being tourists, the greasy hides the day perfectly. I had a laugh with Emily over it too. You remember her ex, the one who used to listen to the radio in the bath?      Oh yeah,  that  one. The one who thought the bath was his personal concert venue. What's he up to?      Apparently still doing that, but now he’s into deep-sea fishing. Emily swears it's a new chapter or something. Honestly, I’d pay good money to just see that in action. Deep-sea fishing? In a bath?      Some things never change. I suppose it’s better than being an ex who still pops up when it suits them, right?      Ugh, true. Speaking of — did Charlie text you again this week? He seems to know that your ex barely left the house, so he thinks he’s got a chance. Cute little stalker energy.      Ugh, honestly, leave the man-child alone. I’ve said it once, I’ll say it a thousand times: We are not getting back together. He’s like a bad vaccine — the first round didn't work, so the second? Probably going to make things worse.      Fair enough. I still go out of my way to avoid him. If I saw him in Sainsbury’s, I’d probably sprint like he was a bad smell.      So, have you made peace with your new job roles yet? From what you said, it sounded like your boss is a bit of a ‘dump everything on the new girl’ type.

I spoke to Anna yesterday. She’s not doing too well. Her oncologist says the chemo is starting to take its toll, and she’s really tired more than usual.      That’s awful to hear. I can’t even imagine what she and her family are going through. Has she had any good days at all recently?      A few, yes. She mentioned that she managed a day out with the kids last week, just a short walk in the park. It was cold, but it cheered them all up. I hope she can keep having those small moments.      Yes, I think even tiny things like that matter a lot when the rest of life feels out of control. I’m going to bring over some soup or something next week, maybe just a distraction to help her feel looked after, even for a bit.      That’d be lovely. She mentioned she doesn’t have the energy to cook most days, which I suppose isn’t surprising, but it is sad that even the simplest routine is disrupted.      I know—especially when it’s someone who always loved taking care of their home. Anyway, moving on from that for a few moments—did you see that there’s another house for sale in the village?      Yes! I saw it advertised on the realtor’s board at the village shop. The old Whitmore place by the stream? That one with the big garden. It’s gorgeous, even if it’s a bit dated. I think it could be stunning with a bit of a modern touch.      I was looking at it too. What I don’t get is why so many people are trying to develop the area around the stream. I know the planning committee just approved those new flats, but it’s going to change the whole feel of the village.      Exactly. It’s fine to have some modern development for local people, but it’s not like the area is underserved at all. You can walk into any nearby town in under ten minutes. I just worry that once those houses come up, we’ll start seeing more visitors or out-of-town investors with no real connection to the place.      Me too. I know the council says it’s about “affordable housing,” but really it feels like it’s about filling a demand from investors rather than helping the community.

Rather skip the queue and just go through the side doors, do you?      Yeah, I don’t get why they even let maintenance run down like this. I've seen dishes stacked up in the sink for three days and not one person in site says a word.      Right, like, I don’t mind the mess   so much  , but when it’s not clean? That’s when it gets to me. Proper stub my toe on a bin lid and slip over in a puddle of something you don’t wanna know what it is.      You’re not wrong. I had one girl in my building throw a mattress out the fire exit into another block’s yard like it was a bloody doorstep. I’m not even mad—I’m just confused.      Aye, and I   don’t like   the smell in the stairwells sometimes. Like breakfast, no—  not   the coffee, the   rotten food smell  . Someone leaves a burrito or whatever in the bin and leaves it to die, and that’s the one closest to my door.      I know, honestly, as much as I don’t like confrontation, I might go in and say something tomorrow. But it’s such a struggle. Half the kids just look at you like you’ve got three heads because they don’t see cleaning as a big deal.      Tell me about it. I don’t even like the lights turning off at someone else’s key. Go in to switch a bulb and the bloody building management system logs you out if you're not a   proper   admin.      Ugh, and there’s the people about   security  —I don’t like the   cheque-in-and-out vibes   in here. Someone fails to log their access badge and the next day it’s up on the main whiteboard like they’re on the most-wanted list.      Aye, and it’s not just the logs either. I don’t like how people   take liberties   with the security doors as if they own the place. Next thing you know, you’ve got someone whistling “Fortnite” in the corridor and a couple of students letting their mates in with a fake go-to-place map.      Honestly, I could write a thesis on things I don’t like in this blooming building. Lifts that don’t work at 10 am, cleaning staff who leave after two hours pretending they cleaned the   whole block  , and don’t even get me started on the complaints process—just a filing cabinet that never gets opened.

So did I really imagine it, or did I actually see that man outside saying “cheerio” like it was the most normal thing in the world?      No, you saw it! That is exactly what happened. I was behind you in line at the café. He looked like he’d stepped out of a  Downton Abbey  episode. I reckon he was on one of those budget European package tours—they all seem to speak in old English and never shut up about the Queen.      Honestly, we British are like ghosts abroad. We chase after each other like “Oh look, another one of ours!”, mostly just because we don’t want to die of boredom without another warm cuppa and a My turkey delight sandwich. I met an entire group in Antwerp last year, and half of them had shouted, “Blimey, the beers are even colder here!” by the end of the first breakfast.      That’s so true! I think it helps, you know, when you’re somewhere unfamiliar, to have a shout of solidarity over full English and custard creams.      I remember when I was young and we went to Herne Bay for a weekend off, my aunt tried to shop at every single market stall. She said, “If I don’t buy this cheeky fox hat, I’ll regret it for the rest of my life.” I reckon she still has that fox hat in the attic. Somewhere haunted.      There’s something comforting about that, isn’t there? Making a fool of yourself with your own people. I remember with my son—before he got too old to want being seen as a spectacle—I’d sneak in rhyming slang whenever I could. I told him the other day the doctor said my heart “crackles like a ton of bricks” because I was doing too much worrying. He didn’t laugh.      Oh, I still do that. My gran used to say that. I told my uni friend once that my professor was “a dead cert,” and I think he genuinely thought I was being sarcastic and not endearing.      Kids these days don't have the digestive system for rhyming slang. Still, I suppose it’s best to feed the rhymes to goers rather than your own children. Not everyone wants to be metaphorically kicked in the biscuit by their parents.      A bit of truth with a wink doesn’t hurt, though. I had a job in care where those jokes really helped people forget the pain for a moment.

So did you watch the news last night about Ireland and the vote on equality?      Oh yes, I saw it! That was such a big moment, wasn’t it? A proper change in the world.      Yeah! It was amazing. People who weren’t allowed to get married finally could. I think it was like… a big win for fairness.      A big win, yes! Some people said it was a blessing, others thought it would ruin marriage altogether. But you know what? They were wrong.      Were they? I didn’t think it even needed to be voted on. Shouldn’t people just be allowed to love who they want?      Oh dear, I can see your mother’s face if I said that at the last birthday party. She turned tomato red when you challenged her about the old ‘in sickness and health’ speech she gave me while everyone was eating cake in the garden.      Oh, didn’t I say the wrong thing? I just told her I was going to tell anyone I loved, even a girl if I fancied one.      And she said what, again?      She said I was being “pushy” and that “people have to be careful with their hearts these days.”      Oh don’t get me started. I swear if I weren’t so sensible I’d tell her she should’ve just gone back to being a nun.      That’s harsh, but fair—what did the nuns teach her anyway? Chastity and sprinkled sugar on your tea?      Something like that! Although I’m the one who’s had to mind most of it. Maybe next time you should be the one to take me to the shop, not her—she just fancies herself as the queen of tradition.      I will, but don’t let her catch me saying I prefer women, or she’ll drag out the Bible again while the cake’s going cold.      She’ll do it with the cake  and  the birthday candles. That woman’s got a serious side with candles. Last year she lit one go out because it flickered if you don’t mind. Said it was “disrespectful.”      I can see her already. “If you don’t have enough respect for a small flame, how can you respect those around you?”      Exactly! And that from the woman who bought me a fishbowl for a present  instead  of a birthday card.      That’s it?

Rather skip the newfit meat eh?      Aye, it's always a bit poncey, isn't it? You’d think with all that fancy packaging, you’d get something a little nicer in there. Still, better the bird than the frightened look on your face when you try it and find it’s rubber!           I’ve had that with a few of the supermarket economy packs. Got one from Tesco last week; it looked alright in the freezer but once you cook it, it's practically holding on for dear life, don't you think?      Honestly, I'd rather just go meat-free once in a while now. You know, like that Mycoprotein stuff. It's not bad if you cook it right. I made a stir-fry with it last week and not a single person noticed it wasn't real beef!      Hmm, I’m more of a sausage man myself. The ones rolled in breadcrumbs, roasted in the oven, you know the kind. Hits the spot nicely over a bit of mash.      Oh, I’ve got a recipe for that — quite a few tricks with the herbs and spices, gives it that extra kick. You reckon you'd like it?      Aye – long as it ain’t one of them fancy artisan ones with names like “herby somethin’,” mind you. I want a proper meaty taste, not that tat which’s all wet and soft in the middle!           That’s because it  should  be soft in the middle, you delicious old groaner! Now come  on  — there’s a bit about sausages and a hamster story from years ago that had this place looking like a scene from  Doctor Who  that I bet you two gentlemen haven't heard yet!      Oh for heaven’s sake, tell her that one — about the hamster? The one where it went into the microwave?      Ah, right — I’ll have you know, it was  Tom Fool’s  night in, trying to find his bedtime snack. He had the wrong end of the stick, you see, and somehow managed to get into the microwave by himself. We heard it whirring and thought there was something wrong with the plug. Then, out comes this poor little creature, all charred and wide-eyed, and you could  smell  it!           Blimey, sound like a crime scene! Or them war movies when they go in and all that's left is the mess.

Rather annoying the new bank charges, isn't it? Every time I go to take out money they charge me... It's beyond me why they're doing it more than once a month now.      I know. I only had to pay a £2 charge last week. It's one thing when you're dealing with a branch, but with online banking these days, it seems so unnecessary. You don’t even have to visit a branch now to get a free withdrawal.      It's interesting you should mention banks. When I was headmistress, we used to get kids who wrote backwards—we called it mirror-writing. One girl used to write all her exams in the correct orientation only when we stressed about it. My colleague thought it was linked to left-handedness or something. Tenacity, I say, is what it is.      Oh, really? I was about to say something about mirror-writing, too—there was this article about a cat in Canada apparently paw-writing on the keyboard and actually creating code, or something daft like that. One of those stories that spreads on Twitter.      Cats are clever creatures, I grant you. But as to writing code—outhouse, by the way. I taught three cats how to trot rhythmically when the staff left the building at the end of the day. Absolute delight.      Honestly, the real nonsense is trying to manage debt without all the high-street banks. You don’t even get a proper conversation any more. It’s just automation and suspiciously-worded customer service bots.      Some of them are better than others. I had one last weekend that managed to answer  every  question with “Your request about [topic] is being transferred to our Finance Department.” Repeating it five times. I just hung up.      Aye, it's a world turned upside down. My day had real handshakes and guest books. I remember when you had to wait for a month to get a telephone connection, and now we're waiting weeks for plumbing when our pipes freeze in the winter! At least I still do the crossword every evening. Do either of you do cryptic?      Me? Every Thursday, after the kids are in bed. They laugh because I talk to my pen sometimes if I'm stuck.      I started trying it last month. Honestly, it feels like learning a code your whole life and then someone just asks you for 3-letter Romans gods in two down.

Right, I just wanted to bring up something I’ve noticed. I’m not trying to be a nag—really—but the kids have been glued to the computer and tablets since they came home today. It’s not even that they’re doing homework or practising spelling. It’s all  Ninjago  and  Minecraft .      But Mummy, it’s not all the time! I’ve only been playing for five minutes before doing this colouring.      It’s not just five minutes! You’ve been doing the colouring  after  an hour of  Minecraft . I like to see you both reading  sometimes . Books are fun too! You know, you can make up your own worlds in a book, instead of just crafting them in a game.      But Darcy, books are sad. There’s no explosions in books.      Yeah, Mummy—there’s no fireballs. Only boring stuff in books.      Oh, come on! Some books have so much action. Have you read that new  Percy Jackson  book I bought? There are lightning bolts and monsters and a demigod sword and everything.      Real swords?      Well, not  real , silly—but just about. Plus, the best bit is, it makes you imagine everything. When you play  Minecraft , you see the whole world on the screen already built for you. But when you read, you get to build it in your head. That’s like a superpower!      But Mummy, it takes  forever  to read. Can’t I just download a game world and be in about five minutes?      I know, sweetie. It’s just a little different—that’s all. But learning to read is really important. You could even both make your own  Ninjago  stories and write them down.      Like a diary?      Exactly! Or a mini-book you can read to your little brother. Think about it. I’ll even help you write it.      Can we write about the time the dragon exploded in our  Minecraft  house?      Of course you can! But let’s do it  after  one more game session. Then, no screen time for an hour, and then we’ll read your story together at the table. Deal?      Deal!      Deal… as long as we get to talk about the explosions in the book too.      Now that I can definitely promise. Let’s get that game finished, and then let’s find a book to light up your imagination! Alright, adventure time—this time with real words and pictures!

Right, thanks for coming in today, love. I’ve missed having the house full again, especially with you two. You’ve both had such busy lives these past few months! How was your break, Liv?      Aw, thanks, Mum. It was good, really good. I booked a weekend trip to York with the store team. We stayed at this cute little B&B and had a cracking time. It was just what I needed before the new season starts.      That sounds lovely. I do hope you had time to take some proper photos. I want to see how you look in those new outfits you were trying to stock—those dresses you showed me the other night still haven’t left the folding chair!      Ha ha! Yeah, Liv tried to sneak them into the back of the wardrobe, but I found them. They screamed ‘Oscar-winner dress’ and ‘influencer envy’ in equal measures!      Oh, don’t listen to her, Nan hides my sparkly puff jackets and expects me not to over-dress! I was defending the fashion, not being inappropriate!      Bah, your mother as a child was  always  overdressed. I remember she’d show up at parents’ night in little Cinderella clothes while most kids were wearing gym wear! I let her wear what made her happy, and I’ll let her now. Bless that girl.      Bless you, Mum! Though, to be fair, this time I was just being honest. But speaking of fashion, Mum, did I tell you I’m attending a university fashion week later this term? It’s split between Manchester and London, which is a bit of a commitment, but exciting!      Oh! That’s brilliant news, Lacie. I’m so proud of you both. Liv has the shop, and Lacie has her studies. My girls are growing up!      Aww, cut that out, you'll go all soppy and cry, and then we’ll have to fetch the tissues again. Honestly, the amount of tissue we hoard in this house—enough for a small country.      Well, let’s hope you don’t get a cold then. Now, shall we set go over today’s plans? I’ve made a few extra scones, and I was hoping we could go for a drive later—maybe head to Tamworth and visit the museum. I know it's been a while, and I think those two historical figures deserve a little love!      Perks of growing up near places with royal ties, eh?

So did you watch The Last of Us on Netflix yet? I binged the whole first series over the weekend.      Yeah, I’m halfway through it! That first episode nearly gave me a heart attack — I had to keep stopping the film because I was laughing so much at how much it’s eeny different to the game.      I haven’t played the game… yet, but I’ve heard all about it. Is it too much like a horror movie? Because I can’t handle like, realism and zombies and all that. Is that what it is?      Sort of, but it’s not just about the dead. It’s got the humans, the relationships, the survival stuff. My uncle, who’s in the military, said it’s got some realistic bits about how the world would fall apart if something like that happened.      Oh yeah, and they talk about rationing and looters and stuff. My Mum actually got in a bit of a rant about it when we talked, comparing it to the supply problems in Ukraine. She said that if something like the Cordyceps mushroom happened in real life, it would be even worse than war zones she’s seen.      Wow… That does sound grim. I’d rather just stay home and eat a sandwich and watch Bridgerton, honestly. My cousin just brought back some Turkish sandwiches from her holiday in Istanbul and they were amazing. You know what I’m talking about? That mix of hummus, egg, and chicken in pitta?      Yeah, sounds good. I’m craving a decent chicken wrap now. Why can’t the canteen at school make something like that, instead of just bolognaise?      I know! Our headteacher is a vibes person — all into “wellbeing” and “mentorship” — but the food is still out of the 1990s. My sister’s in sixth form and she got made a prefect by the year planner bloke, all because he thought she smiled a lot. Doesn’t mean she’s the best at leading.      My cousin’s a prefect too. She wears the badge with pride, but let’s say you try to queue jump during lunch and she’ll basically report you go straight to the head. I think some of them are just trying to look important in front of teachers.      Time to reform the prefect system. Maybe we could have a monthly rotation to randomly select students who are kind and responsible, not just people who agree with the head on everything.

So did you watch  17 Again  last night? I was laughing so much in the car when we saw it on the way out of town. It's actually properly funny, right?      Yeah, I did! It was like, what even is this movie? Like, why is he in a body pillow and then a teenager the next day? But honestly, I snorted like five times in that car. My brother would NOT stop quoting it.      Oh, my mum said she wasn't going to watch it and then she called me halfway through the film being like, "Daniel, is it even  that  bad?" and I was like, no, ma, it's like a comedy turkey but I’m living for it.      I think the best bit was when they showed how sad every single adult is. Like, everyone was just a hot mess. Wait, does your teacher teach that chapter in English with H.G. Wells and the time machine?      Yeah, the one about the time machine, and that Mr Waterhouse guy? I don’t get it. My form tutor put two hands up and said to read it and tell her something smart. I’ve read it three times and it just sounds like a boy got lost in a forest and then panicked.      I just copied a bit from the film  The Time Machine  as like a metaphor for feeling old. She didn’t slap that. She looked at me like someone just put glue in her coffee. Like why do we have to read books that are  a hundred years old ??      I know! Like,  Jane Eyre  is just a sad girl who hates her aunt. I’m just trying to pass, I don't understand any of this. My sister is doing that school and she says it's even harder.      Oh yeah, like your sister’s in the grammar school with that geography teacher with the funny biscuits? The one who always mixes up longitude and latitude?      That’s him! He had that sprite of chalk written across the board with 'Longitude is the big one' written underneath it and then he said it  wasn't . My form tutor told me he got goonie on pond life if you don’t get it.      I remember when we had the surprise Geography test on ecosystems and your teacher walked in with a pestle and mortar and randomly asked who wanted to dissect a slug.

So, I just wanted to say, I am  so  jealous of you two heading out to Transylvania this summer. That sounds mental.      Thanks, mate. I know, right? I keep telling Lugh [Speaker_3]—get us a castle with a moat and eeny weeny  bloodsucking undead  just for ambiance.      Oh please, Dani, I’m running a  café . I’m barely balancing my own bank account, never mind financing a rom-com pilgrimage to the Carpathians. But when are you kids leaving?      First week of June—final week before exams. We figured, if not now, then never? My lectures are all online anyway, so I got nothing to do. Probably go to Bucharest as well.      Oh, that’s an adventure for sure. I’d have been all,  “We need to see Vlad’s castle and then grab a Cobb’s for five o’clock, yeah?”  But fair enagh. Good on you, bloke.      Thanks, Rhett. I mean, we’re not going to go  drinking real blood  or anything—despite what we’ve teased.      Hmm. Looking for Baptists in Transylvania, are we? Any Romanian  exorcists  on your itinerary?      You know what, no—save the sarcasm, Lugh. I just want to hike, get outdoors, not die of a heatstroke for once. I’m thinking about getting the laser eye surgery before I go. Any of you had it?      Not me, doll. I’m a glasses girl. But I heard it’s  cracking  if you can afford it. Rhett, you’re the only one with unbreakable eyes—being a barista for 10 years, no doubt. Rather skip the new tax increases eh?      I’m trying to get my head around it all, Dad. Around 70% of public spending funds the NHS, welfare, and education. Of course, it also covers the military, the police, and road maintenance, too. I did my placement with their marketing department and it was like stepping into a BBC drama—well, just someone who cast an actress who doesn’t audition.      Oh, let’s not talk drama, I just spent three days in a meeting room with a board  literally  made of foam and about five people asking me to "coordinate" the PowerPoint flow.       Burps  Going into that manager world now, huh? You're up for it?      I like the pressure. I like knowing what's on the plate. I don’t really want any surprises, like the time I tried to make my own madras and ended up with something resembling  earth sprite weapon of war .      That was your nan’s “low辣” sauce, you remember, after she caught you eating a pepper with the skin goin' on like it was your ex’s LinkedIn description.      Yep, I was like the box office bomb of the Indian spice aisle. But hey, have you made any plans for this summer? I’d kill for a proper holiday.      Thinking about going to Goa this year. Maybe do a bit of sightseeing—Dudhsagar Falls, Fort Aguada, and plenty of chilli fritters, obviously.

So do you go up often? Back to Birmingham, I mean. I know it's not that far from here, but I always forget how small the train network actually is!      Nah, not often. Not since I started the PhD. It's easier to stay in Cambridge than waste time on trains and tube journeys. But I do miss the   Villa  —still all concrete and grime though. A lot’s changed in the last ten years, honestly.      Oh you know, I’ve never been to the East Midlands. I literally can’t imagine what it looks like without like three colliery hills in the background.      [Laughs] Fair play. It’s not all that different, you know—it’s just a bit flatter, a bit less moody. But the people are good. Birmingham’s got its charm in a different way. Got better shopping.      Well, no shortage of shopping around here either, thanks to the uni and all the tourists puffing around the city centre. I swear half the students shop over the road, get told off for missing tutorials, and then never show up anyway.      That’ll be my experience in postgrad life too. But I suppose when you got publishing papers and research methodologies on your plate, messing around with cheques and cards is a bit low on the priority list.      You know what I miss though? The hills. Like proper hills. You walk down Spital Tongues in the morning, it's already like a trek. I remember thinking when I’d moved here:  'Okay, here’s the flat, here’s your key, good luck.’  I mean, I walk a mile every day just trying to find the nearest coffee shop.      Oh that’s grim! I grew up near the  canals , so I’m used to flatlands. Unless you’re near Harborne or something. But honestly, I don’t mind a flat life. I prefer not climbing anything when I’ve had a pint or two.      Right. And what about the music? You ever bring any of your Birmingham bands up here with you? Still trying to get a gig in the North?      I tried once, yeah. Got a friend from the band I used to play with that now produces stuff in London, he said I should ‘go back to the North and bring something fresh to the table’. I think he meant ‘chill out and stop overthinking it’.

Nana, why d’you think all them politicians ‘aven’t sorted out the cost o’ living yet? It don’t make sense. Y’know, prices goin’ up an’ wages ain’t keepin’ up.      Oh love, well I were brought up in a een time when we  shared  a toothbrush with me brother if we were lucky! Times like now—it’s just ‘cos too many folk think they  entitled  to more than they’ve earned, if you ask me.      But that’s not right though, innit? Like, like, even if some folk  do  waste money, we’re all paying for stuff we can’t even get. Like, I couldn’t even get a train ticket last week without paying extra for the platform or somethin’.      Aye, I was about the same age as thee when I worked in a factory, an’ we didn’t get no “platform fee” on milk! No, you didn’t have to pay extra for anything except maybe your bloomin’ bones if you stood up too long.      But what about all them big companies and the government, innit? Shouldn’t they be doin’ something about it all?      Should be, love, should be. But they’re busy arguing over the cheapest somethin’ to line them pockets with. I remember the ‘80s and the miners’ strikes, an’ I were just a young ‘un. Folks like us, down here, we got told to just “stand it”, or else we’d be “outta our jobs” altogether.      Yeah, I heard about the miners’ strikes in history class, but it didn’t feel like we really got the whole truth. Like, I mean, it’s not like we’re doin’  that  now, but it’s still bad, innit?      Aye, ‘course it is. I dunno what’s worse—having your livelihood taken from you as if it were nothing, or havin’ the prices of bread and chips whackin’ up every week like there’s some kind of invisible man tippin’ money into the govt’s coffers.      I think people are just ticked off, nana. Me ‘n’ my mates at school all talk about it. We were even discussing if we should start a campaign against high prices or something.      Is that right? ‘Course you should! We used to hold placards and sing songs so loud the parliament could ‘ear us. Though I doubt they’d be able to hear now, not unless we made a noise worthy of the deafest elephant.

So do you know what’s a blood moon, Granny? I was reading about it in class today.      A blood moon? Now that sounds a bit spooky, sure does. Là, where’d ye hear about moon things? Was it in yer textbook?      Yeah, it was in a history thing about full moons and stuff. They said it's when the Earth’s shadow makes the moon look reddish or something.      Oh, right! Like a lunar eclipse. We’ve had one of those once when you were small, but the clouds came in too thick for you to see much.      That’s correct, blood moon is part of a lunar eclipse event, definitely happens when the Earth passes between the sun and the moon, casting a shadow. D’you know how often they happen?      No, wait — the teacher said it happens every now and then, but not very often in each place. I didn’t get the exact number, though.      Ah, now that’s interesting. When I were a wee one in Glascow, I used to think a blood moon meant fairies were dancing on the hills. Good stories they told us, anyway.      Hmm, maybe – but it’s better than my mother’s stories. She once said the moon was a giant pinball machine that aliens played with at night.      Well, someone at least gave your imagination a boost. But seriously, it’s a natural astronomical phenomenon. Some people attach all kinds of meaning to it, but it’s just physics and geometry!      I did ask the teacher what causes the red color, and he said something about Earth’s atmosphere — like how dust and clouds are scattered to make it look orangey.      That’s quite complicated for someone still learning about how light bends!      Not too complicated, it’s actually a beautiful way our atmosphere filters light. Makes me glad to have studied planetarium software as well as IT.      So what are we having for dinner, anyway? Still trying to get around this idea of eating the same veggies three go-rounds on your plate if you don’t cut them up right.      You’ll be needing a spoon then, son. Pass the potatoes, would ye?      Ò, I think those dinner table manners are improving, aren’t they? For once, he didn’t try to chew and talk at the same time.      I didn’t do that! I was just asking about the moon!

Rather skip the new beer and go for the old one.      Yeah they passed first time got the seats sorted out.      Not a trouble.      A full £2000 and £100 bonus.      Right and now I've got the print screen and handed over to his wife's sister.      What is this policy?      Oh it's alright as long as you don't have to answer questions from the accountants.      You won’t get frozen but I had one who'd made sure no one could short the fridge supply only herself.      Yeah I did that too.      Probably I had the same as Darcy, he used to make a good little sandwich.      He better not breakfast, no doubt about that.      And she was looking for the milk again but he'd given it to the neighbor.      I mean I do tell you all the time I listen to the radio in short bursts.      It's not like today we go on holidays watching other people's holidays on Instagram then.      Mate it's got fairly radical, and now it's even more radical.      Yeah they want independence now for the first time in Scotland.      Our daughter says it's just another TV show.      That's because she doesn't really understand the politics of it.      That's all right she's only sixteen.      She'll catch up. Have you still got that job interview going?      Yeah that was today. I met up with a chap from Brighton to do the interview.      And how did it go?      I think I was too nice to the colleague I meet there.      Not to worry you can't be professional if you're always trying to be nice.      Some people don’t like you trying to be friendly with them.      Mm I remember someone from Brighton who had a real inferiority complex.      He always tried to be the best at what he did.      But he never was and he knew it.      It's a pity really because he could have been very good.      Yeah the problem is he wanted to be better than everyone else and in the end he failed.      Likewise with the other staff and the senior partners she had to manage it before it became a mess.      She was on the phone for ages, I thought someone would have to fetch the manager.      The manager just came and her and that was that.

Right Aaron, you've got your seatbelt on, right? Ann wants to hear the whole story about that hedgehog again.      Yeah, I can't believe you found one in your garden, Dad. Not every day you have a wild visitor!      Well it was a bit more  wild  than I was expecting. I reckon it just wanted to sample my herbs.      Honestly, that was a bit funny. You had us all running out there like it was a goldfish in the hedge.      Oh, it was not a goldfish. It even nibbled the basil. That hedgehog's got a taste for herb gardens!      You didn't get too close, did you? They can be feisty little things.      A little feisty, yes, but not dangerous. Just enough to give me a moment’s thought about why I didn't opt for ornamental grass instead of basil!      Well, maybe it’s time to start that wildlife corner you mentioned, you know, with bird feeders and bug hotels and all that.      Mmm, as long as it doesn’t attract the neighbour’s cat. He already gives us the evil eye – no need for new reasons!      Good point. Let’s keep the wildlife part to creatures who can’t knock on the window and demand snacks at 2am!      That’s the spirit! Anyway, what are we having for lunch? I’m starved.      I thought we might try that new sandwich place over near St Neots. I’ve heard good things.      Sandwiches? I was going for a full three-course lunch. This is the countryside! We should have steak and ale pie or something.      Steer that boy toward the sandwich van. The last time he demanded a three-course lunch, he insisted it had to come with a side of waiting staff!      What can I say? I appreciate good service.      Well, if he's going to be demanding, maybe after lunch we head to that place with the giant go-karts on the lake? Something about  world records  and driving into the water?      That might be something from the ‘70s. I’m not sure it's been safe since the dinosaurs roamed those waters.      I’ll take my chances. Sounds adventurous – especially if there's a photo at the end where my arm is out of the window like a passenger in an action movie!      Perfect. Just make sure when we hit the record books, I’m there to explain it to the photographer in my best  BBC weather  voice.

Rather skip the new drive route eh gran? That bit o’ A66 near Penrith gets p’d up on a Saturday mornin’. It’s not worth it.      Oh hush, don’t start. Look, I’ve driven over them hills more times than you’ve een to the shops, lass. It was fine thirty years ago an’ it’ll be fine now.      Fair dos, but I don’t fancy being tail-ended into a field of sheep by a lorry. Leeds to Carlisle at the best of times isn’t a holiday.      Still, if we can grab a break at the services, we can do some of that posh turkey and stuffing quiche they’ve grafted themselves into selling now. I ain’t eating sandwiches again.      Aye, an’ if it’s a nice day we can breakfast on the farm before we head in. They’ve got eggs fresh off the hens and milk straight from the cow. Still use a milking pail over there, I expect.      You’d think they’d have gone full robotic cow handlers by now. Modern farming’s all hi-tech, gran.      Eh, give it time. Robotic cows might come about, but until then I’ll still take a slap-up breakfast off a chippy plate with apple pie and custard. Silly lads.      Gran’s never met a pie she didn’t like. But seriously, why’d we have to drive up so early? Some normal folk’d be asleep at this hour.      Because  someone  insisted we make it in time for the 10 a.m. tour. She’s had this on her calendar for months. “Meet the sheep that are shaggable,” she says.      That’s  sheep shearing , you idjit. And yes, I did have me on the guest list for it ‘cos I once used to knit scarves for the Aran Goods Co. back in ’74. They sent me a brass thimble to keep the memories fresh.      Gran you once lived in a caravan by a muddy field with a goat goin’ on your nerve about the milk jug.      I’ll bet that goat was shaggable too, gran.      You watch your tongue, lad. That was a noble dairy beast. And speak to anyone who belly-flopped off a tractor in the ‘80s when they tried to modernise the farm. I reckoned I’d stick to wool.      Listen, can we get gran a telly guide while we’re at the farm?

Rather skip the newfit and go for a short walk in the garden later.      Oh I got the email from cathedral choir about the next music meeting I think it's probably after choir practice.      Charming indeed the choir practice as such.      Hasn't your friend Margot been asked to give an address at the charity summit.      I didn't know that I think he's doing this project helping to send books to schools in Africa.      Which is important I think and also the chase when he's talking about charity work reminds me of the time when I won the sportsmanship award at school.      You know I like that My turkey curry was a disaster I swear it left bursts on the pot.      Darcy, pick and I think he turned out very kindly with assembling it.      I see no doubt.      Hmmm in fact at his age, five o clock we'll have to leave for the concert in Kendal.      I do tell you yes we need to listen to the occasional orchestra if we're not going to be late and only be on time as we go on.      Absolutely and then from there we can grab a bite at the café before heading back, least way it won't be too much of a rush.      Perfect, and I've invited my cousin Liam as well, he’s just finished his placement at the vet’s in Penrith.      Oh, do tell what made him decide to go into veterinary work.      I think he was in love with the horses in about five at school.      That explains it then.      Maybe he could give me an opinion on my cat's digestive issues.      My, you've made the most troubling guest list.      And I'm sure the school will be mentioned at least once again with Darcy's enthusiasm for waiting till the last minute.      He’s doing a lot of calculations with his computer right now.      Wasn’t that you once, after all.      Oh away go.      It's not about calculations at all.      Hopefully it's not the boxset that's getting the blame this time.      Ah yes, and Father’s Day is coming up so I think we should do something to thank my husband.      Only because he cleaned the fish tank last week I think he wants to know if we're taking him somewhere next week.      Right, and we haven’t yet decided if the garden needs onions or just some chillies.

Right, so the teacher mentioned that Joshua is really coming along with his reading, which is such a relief. I was so worried after last term.      Yeah, I've been reading with him every night before bed. We do a bit of  Harry Potter  sometimes. He loves Dumbledore.      That’s fantastic. It helps with his vocabulary and his confidence. But… they were a bit concerned about your maths work, love. The teacher said it was quite inconsistent.      That’s because we had to do the circus homework instead of maths, don’t you remember? I did like the clowns better anyway.      Well the maths and the circus both have to be done. You still need to learn how to multiply numbers properly, not just throw confetti around like you're on stage.      Mummy! It wasn't about clowns — it was about the history of the circus!      Which is interesting, but you also need to finish sums, even if they're about elephants. One elephant, two elephants… Eventually you do ten, and it's not funny anymore — I promise.      I did five of them, didn’t I?      Yeah, and then Josh got distracted by the World Book Day parade at school. He dressed up as Paddington Bear again. I had to wear Roald Dahl, obviously.      I got extra crumpets for homework because of it. Mrs. Spilsbury said I was the best Roald Dahl in Years 1 through 4.      Well, I’d be proud if you hadn’t had your head stuck in a biscuit tin for half the lesson. Speaking of biccies, pass the tomatoes, will you? I can’t make rouladen without burning the kitchen down if I’m hungry while I cook.      What’s rouladen?      It’s German. You take a piece of meat, roll it up, and cook it in some beef gravy. We had to make it in home economics last year.      Yeah, and your teacher must have thought the meats were plotting against you, the way you made a mess.      So it’s like if you took a sausage and made it even more confused?      Something like that. But it’s what your dad used to make at the weekend. Speaking of which, we’re having some friends over after dinner. Just for a bit to chat about the parents’ evening stuff.      Is it that yummy lady who buys all the oatcakes from the bakery?      And the one who once said that cooked human flesh smells like burnt bacon?

So do you know what’s happening for Oisin’s birthday yet? I was just trying to think when he’s got it and what we’re doing this year.      Yeah, he said he wants it at Currie’s – you know the curtain shop where Cian works now. He’s real chuffed working there, likes the vibe, says the customers are mad funny. He wanted to have a bit of a ‘proper’ party for the kids this year, maybe bring in a bouncy castle?      Oh right, I like that. Didn’t Cian get the job under some kind of like, apprenticeship or something? I thought he was learning the whole décor side of things.      Aye, that’s right. He left the garage life back in Dublin to do it. D’you know, I think he turned down a promotion at the garage to do something ‘in character’ as he puts it.      Mu-ment!      That’s Oisin, isn’t it? He’s saying, “Not yet.” He says he wants to be a treasurer.      A real treasurer? Like for a shop or a club?      No, no. He’s convinced he’s been made a treasurer of like, the garage or something. “You know, the club.” He was saying to me the other day that he’d locked the coffee machine someone into the storeroom. Just because they hadn’t brought their tax receipt.      Ah, now mind, I worked with lads like that – all right when they’re small, but when they get older... “Tax receipts” my foot. It’s just a wee bit of fun he’s having.      Well, as long as he’s happy, I suppose. I just wish he didn’t sound like a funny man all the time. You know, like he got all his words mixed up from watching too much telly or something.      Oh aye, he’s grand. Kids do that a lot these days—mash up the words. Reminds me of the time my sister was a toddler and called the goonie map man “Mr. Grease-Shirt”.      Oh, I see it. He’s just got his own style. But yes, Currie’s is a big step up from the Ó Síocháin’s garden last year, where we had to talk him into not blowing out the lights on the deck because it would “attract wildlife.”      Wildlife? My goodness. They probably brought the whole of Cork with ‘em.      Ah, you’d be in for a few laughs.

So do you lot ever play word games? I’ve been trying to get people into it, especially when we're all together and it's raining outside and there's no option to go out.      Yeah, I quite like scrabble, or sometimes just making up words on the spot. Got a fave sort of genre of word game you like best?      Yeah, I love anagrams and stuff. Got a side hustle putting together puzzles for a language learning app as it happens. Keeps the mind fresh.      Anagrams, yeah? I love ’em too. Sometimes I just challenge myself to reword headlines from the paper to make them rhyme or form some kind of coded message. Just for fun, you know.      Oh, I like that, stealing news and twisting it. A bit of nonsense journalism if you like. What about you then, Dave, do you dabble much in messing with words?      Only if someone hides a bottle of something near the laptop and dares me to stay in the room until it’s done. Otherwise, I’m more the diagrams and numbers type. Got a crossword once, tried to do it with only synonyms from the Oxford Thesaurus. Took me a week.      Mate, you got a week, and I barely lasted ten minutes. I once tried to do a crossword with homonyms and phone messages. It ended in confusion and a shout about toilets and roast dinners.      Haha sounds like it wasn’t just a language game then. Some folks still need to weigh up the risks of pulling double entendre jokes in mixed company.      I mean, I once pulled a verbal gag on my boss: he asked me to document a new process and I said “Of course, I’ll get it down on  paper .” He just stared at me like I’d quoted Monty Python at him.      You know you’re in a different league once someone gets stared at for a little bit too long after a pun. Like when I said to my sister “I couldn’t find the right expression for what I was feeling, but it was  word -ly serious”      Oh yeah go me then I once said to my parents “I went to see a doctor today and he said I had a serious condition, called Time Poverty.” My dad just went “I could have told you that.”      Well you three are clearly in the top tier of word game enthusiasts.

So did you see the picture Laura posted on Facebook last week? That one from her holiday in Scotland when we were all still in university?      Blimey, what one? She put a load up—cats with beards, the view from some mountain... Was it the one of you three on the quad at Warrington College with the ridiculous hats on?      Yeah, that one! Aunty Beverley still messes that photo up with your face swapped into a zebra pattern or something! You’d be like a walking animal print by the end of the night at the uni ball.       laughs  I still can't believe people fall for that. I've shown that MySpace-era editing trick to my students and they’re like, “Is this real?”      Oh, I think Aunty Beverley's just making sure we never forget how we looked when we thought we were clever.      And how we were  actually  clever, if you remember the group presentation about the housing crisis we did for that Urban Studies module.      Yeah, and the one about short-term land use as it relates to grief. You were on fire that day. Still watching that TED Talk version on a loop from time to time?      No, I got banned from that for making jokes about “pent-up somatic energy.” Mrs Bellamy was not impressed. Still, got a first for that essay, huh? Our collective PowerPoint was full of memes and emojis.      That's oddly endearing now—look at the kid now, right?      Can I just say, though, Laura would’ve made about five TikToks a day back then. Imagine the chaos if she had a smartphone.      Definitely would’ve been streaming the time we napped in the lecture hall. My eyelids are like wet treacle that day.      And I remember trying to nap without a pillow. Do you know how intense that is? I had a chair full of crack from Professor Millhouse. He’s still out there, by the way—teaching management at some do-it-all-outside campus.      You're like a man with a grudge. But I get it, that guy once called my essay “a very modern take on sustainable living” and then wrote, “This isn’t what your parents paid for.”      Yeah, and then he checked out my barista blog?      Oh right! He gave you a D and said “creativity alone isn’t a sustainable career path.”      My  creativity  started paying rent two years ago when I opened that café in town.

So did you read the planning meeting minutes from last week? The application they had for the old school site—what was the name of it again?      Yeah, I had a skim through them this morning. I think the developer wants to convert it into a mixed-use building—flats on the upper floors and a community space below. It was called   Valewood Housing & Heritage Initiative  , if I remember correctly.      Yeah, that's it. And you think it was approved?      Not officially yet. The committee requested more information, especially about how the preservation of the original façade would be handled. They also had questions about the number of affordable units they’re offering in the mix.      Mmm, interesting. It’s a tricky one because the building is listed. But the architectural plans they submitted look solid. I suppose if it’s a genuine balance between conservation and modern development, then it might just about pass.      Absolutely. But I’m wary of the fact that property developers so often underplay the details on that—especially when it comes to affordable housing percentages. We should really check that the council’s legal team is on top of verifying the stats.      You’re right. We don’t want another situation like the one at Riverside Square where they promised five per cent and ended up with barely two. I’ve raised that in our previous reports as problematic for the council’s commitment to social equity.      Precisely. And with the new housing crisis intensifying, it's vital that every claim made by developers—especially in the public sphere—is thoroughly vetted. I’m going to suggest that the committee insist on tying the approval to a tangible binding agreement for the affordable units.      That’s a solid move. Maybe even recommend that it be included in the planning documentation as a formal condition for approval.      Exactly. If the developer’s not ready to commit to that up front, they might need to think twice before putting their proposal forward.      I’ll note that in my contribution for the next meeting. Also, we should probably take a nuanced stance on the heritage angle. Not all the committee members fully understand what a listed building truly entails.      True. A few of them are more focused on fiscal outcomes than heritage preservation. We’ll need to frame it clearly—maybe with a visual comparison of what proper restoration looks like versus what poor planning can lead to.

So did you watch The Crown last night? That episode with Margaret was bonkers.      What, the one she dumps Tony on the steps of the hospital? I was rolling. I told my sister it was like watching a 1970s slapstick comedy gone wrong.      Exactly! I felt bad for Tony, but he was basically asking her to fake a pregnancy with another woman? Come on!      No, but honestly, was it worth it? If he’d just taken the hint and called it off when he should’ve… Anyway, not my drama to sort.      True enough. What’s new with you? I’ve been swamped since Monday. I swear my inbox is like a snowdrift – I dig it back and then more snow falls.      Blimey, sorry to hear that. I get it though – your job does mean everyone has a micro-project they want done  yesterday .      Don’t get me started. I had this bloke from Marketing who wanted me to book a venue in Manchester for next week like it was a walk in the park and I'd magically found a place with availability… on short notice. I’m a coordinator, not a wizard.      Fair enough, and I know the feeling – some people come in all “It’s not a big deal” and then want to micromanage every single detail.      Oh yes, and meanwhile I haven’t had a proper meal all week. I’m surviving on toast and fury.      Don’t look at me! I’ve been better because most of my shift last week was spent trying to round the tea trolley like it was part of a mission.      Speaking of which, have you managed to cook anything that didn’t come in a packet?      I did manage that roast chicken with a bit of stuffing – was bloody stressful though. Bird fell apart mid-roast and I looked like a crackpot trying to re-jiggle the sides.      That’s what I’ve been reduced to. My takeaway bag is my best friend. Prawn noodles on a Tuesday because I didn’t have time to be a human cook.      I’ll make us something this weekend – maybe a pizza night? Proper one from scratch, with bases and tomato sauce?      Yes, please! I’ll even clean up this time.      You mean when I clean up  for  you? I so miss that version of you.      Touché. You really keep me on my toes, you know that?

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You think they'd do something about the housework by now.      Maybe if you actually told your sister properly, instead of just rolling your eyes and muttering under your breath.      Yeah, well, the next time she’s on the telly watching yet another advert for some ridiculous diet tea, I’ll try to have a word.      Fair enough. Honestly though, it’s easier watching telly and letting the ads run. Who’d want to diet when you can just chase it up with a packet of biscuits?      Lakelands is on telly tomorrow. I might actually go to one of those car boot sales, see if I can get a bargain.      Why not? D’you think there’ll be any good gee-gaws knocking about for my NLP stuff?      I dunno. Maybe a bargain in there. Blokes love the odd bit of bric-a-brac. Also, I might actually buy something that helps me with the job, maybe a new whiteboard pen or one of them fancy mobile phone stands to organise my teaching materials.      You know, I saw something on a news story today about dyslexic children being misdiagnosed as attention problems. It really bugged me.      Yeah, I’ve seen that too. I’ve had a few kids in my class where it was only picked up when they weren’t making progress. Should be picked up earlier, innit?      It shouldn’t be this hard. I mean, I speak to teachers and journalists all the time about how misinfo is spread about these things.      Honestly, I’ve seen some fails in education that are just barely accidental. Remember Steve at school? He was the bin man ‘cos they thought he’d always sit in the back and play on his phone.      Oh yeah! He used to do psychology stuff on the side, mind you.      Right, but if they’d just tested him a little more, he could have been doing more than that.      Truth. Anyway, I’ve go work on my report tomorrow about journaling and emotional processing. Gonna be a long, deep session with my cup of tea and bad music.      I’m planning to update my lesson plans and maybe watch some BBC crime stuff to clear my head. True crime’s a waste of time, but I still do it.      I get it. It's like those true crime people and those podcast addicts, it always feels like you could do better than them, but you still want to know what happens next.

So did you lot see the weather today? That was mad. I came home and it was like a penguin got out and started throwing bricks.      Erm, I saw that! Got soaked in the car trying to get the kids from football. The motor’s gone a bit soft again on the way home, I swear it’s twitching.      Yeah, it’s been that way all week. Rather skip the small talk and go straight in to what you do then luv.      Well, I trained as a Speech and Language Therapist back in Australia, actually. Poetic, really.      I have to admit, it was a bit lonely as a child there, but there’s a kind of richness in solitude. As a therapist, I came to see language as a lifeline. Especially for the children I worked with—learning to speak meant learning how to belong. Then again, I think the visual has its own language too, doesn’t it?      You’re not wrong, luv. Rather skip the talk and take a walk in the garden, do you?      Oh... Well, I thought we could check this out more. I mean, I've heard about this archaeo-language seminar before. Speaking of which, have you managed any   fieldwork abroad   recently?      I was at a   French excavation   site in Morocco a year ago. Now, the Berbers, you must know, they had a way with the   Arabic go-betweens  , if you take my drift.      That’s fascinating. We’ve done a comparative study on   Sino-North African   linguistic influences in Tangier. You ever see the street names? Half of them are   geographical mistranslations   made in the ‘40s.      Now that rings my bell. I’ve done work in the   Mediterranean basin   area, trying to place   Barbary pirates’ language styles   used during negotiation with European traders before 1800.
