Wait, wait, what’s breakfast, then? You don’t just have eggs or something in the North?      Oh, no, it's the full works. Brunch, more like. Turkey with all the trimmings, same as the main meal, but spread out. We might add a little ham, maybe some smoked salmon. It's like the Northern version of a Christmas all day.      All day? I wouldn’t mind that. We have huge feasts, but it’s more spread out. Like, first day is the big one, second day we’d have leftover lasagna someone brought in. But also, maybe a second dinner? It just goes on.      That sounds a bit over the top. Still, more food the better, in my opinion. Not many about with that much enthusiasm for the season these days.      It’s true. My lola, that’s my grandmother in the Philippines, she’d be in the kitchen for three days straight before the actual holiday. All the fruit salads, the ham and egg rolls, the lechon. Oh, man, talking about it makes me miss it.      Lechon?! That’s a word I remember with lunches back in the seventies! They brought it out with all that crispy skin, the rice with bits of meat, the coleslaw—oh my! My Thai friends used to get so confused trying to wrap their head around British Christmas food.      Aye, some of them still think pigs in blankets are a conservation charity.      I think Malaysians might think that too. For some, ‘mince pies’ means green pie filing. I once had one go all squint at a custard cream and say it looked like a turd in a handkerchief.      That’s rough.

So did you watch the new series of  Shadow Court  yet? I know it's not real detective work, but the episodes are tight.      I binged it all in one weekend! It reminded me of when we used to read those crime novels at uni—rip through a few in a night, then argue over the ending. Remember that?      Of course! You always thought everyone was guilty except the butler. Such a show-off.      [laughs] Hey, the butler had the best alibi! Didn’t even want to be there. You’re just bitter because I solved it faster.      Honestly, I found it easier to get into now that Myra and I have started cooking for the kids. It’s like crime, dinner, and emotional drama all in one place.      Living with in-laws is a crime drama waiting to happen—no TV needed!      I’ll second that. And speaking of crime, how’s the admin work going? Still printing out forms like it’s 1999?      Hah, I wish. Actually, I’ve moved to supplying transcripts for legal cases. You’d probably love watching it all—it’s rhythm and then abrupt drama. Courtroom-style.      I can imagine. It’s interesting how much of the process is hidden. All that legalese you use—do you ever miss writing proper prose? Like… well, what someone like me does for a living.      Sometimes. I had a poetry ambition in my 20s. Now I rewrite politicians’ words for a living! But it pays the bills and I do enjoy transcribing—especially the verbal brawls between lawyers. Reminds me of a good TV series.      I’d take it over unboxing videos any day. My sister’s on her third batch of guest speaker videos. Said she wants to start a YouTube channel. I told her it was called  captured moments , not  Get You Speakered .      Oh, I’ve seen those. She filmed me reading a chapter of one of my novels last week. I said it was a live version with uncomfortable pauses.      You really need to invest in a Kindle. They highlight typos.      I tried one. The box ate my highlighter. Probably some virtual anti-overhighlighting system. I’ve been writing notes in the margins with tea—very atmospheric.      Just don’t fall asleep over it. Last time, I wrote half a poem in green ink all over a draft. Only noticed the next morning.      That’s probably going in the next book.

Rather annoying this newfit of sorts. You know what I mean. The one where it comes through when you try to do something with tablets or something on the gadgets. I can't get the thing where you type in it doesn’t come up properly. Look like squares sometimes!      Oh dear, William dear, that sounds like the fonts aren’t installed correctly. You know I had that on my laptop once. A lot of programmes just needed updating. I got my Timmy to install a new programme which fetched it. He’s rather clever with the modern stuff.      Timmy? You mean Timmy Smith from Mary’s church?      Aye, that one. He’s My grandson, you know, he helps me out with the laptop and the phone. I’d never get on without him. I think he turned 21 last month, aren’t you proud!      A clever boy. Reminds me of my Reg. He would’ve been 45, if he’d have still been with us.      That’s very kind of you both. I’ve got that same problem with the squashed fonts. I only started using my tablet again a fortnight ago. My IT chap at Westgate put me onto it.      Oh, Westgate, that store in Maidenhead. They do have some good people there, don’t they? I visited them once for a broken printer. Lost the simplest jobs at that stage.      Aye, they’ve done well with the village shops in recent years. I mind the old days when it was just a few bobbies and a butcher’s. Not nearly about bright lights and smart tablets.      We were talking to the IT chap, and he said it might be to do with the language settings. Something about regional fonts. My device had been switched to US rather than UK settings. Said it can cause all sorts of strange glitches.      Oh, I tried that once. You switch the region by mistake, and you suddenly end up being asked to log in in French!      French? That’s a proper far cry from Costessey. Pah! I couldn’t even go to Lowestoft without losing my way.      I do wonder, William, if they ever update the old county names on the maps properly. Norfolk still doesn’t seem to fit right on the screen, does it?      It’s to do with the data, I imagine. The digitising company probably hasn’t finished.

So do you lot think we’ve got anything to worry about with the printers? I mean, they’re piling up and I don’t know if the maintenance guy’s even gonna turn up today      Aye, we’ve been like this all week! I wouldn’t rely on him turnin’ up if I were you. I told ‘im   last week   that we’ve got that next batch of cards to print by Friday or the bloody boss is gonna lose it.      Honestly, if one more thing goes wrong today, I swear I might just quit and become a barista... like, literally, even make  latte art .      That’s a brave move if you don’t know what   espresso   is. But I feel you, this is the worst week for tech support and I think the world might end if the deadline for the Horace printin’ doesn’t come in on time.      Oh don’t remind me about  Horace . They didn’t even say the print was going to be directly related to the project we’re benchmarkin’ for this month.      What did they say, like the original  Horace  stuff? The Roman poet?      No, no, no – this is one of those weird, like, graphic cards based on some historical poem and they’re printing it with   insect preservation   images?! I’m not even joking.      Who prints stuff like that? I mean, why do a whole set of language cards on an ancient poet and moths??       Horace  is a key figure in classical literature. Couple it with entomology and the beauty of preservation—there’s a whole aesthetic and pedagogical angle to it. I mean it is a  slightly  edgy idea.      Honestly, I just want to know if it works on the printer. I was holding my breath trying to print yesterday and I just got half a wing on the page. Like  what even is that .      Yeah and speaking of wings – have we organised the team  party  for after the print deadline? Because the printer is still goin’ on time or not and none of us are taking it seriously.      Well we were going to have it at the bar after work but I spoke to the bar and they’re kina full after 7 hours so maybe we’ll move it to a more unsociable time where people are wasted anyway.      You know my philosophy is that any event that manages to finish after 6 p.m. is a  late-night function .

Okay, I swear I’m going to fail maths tomorrow. I’ve literally done nothing.      You’ve done nothing? You told me you were going to revise on Sunday!      I  meant  Monday, and then it was  definitely  gonna be Tuesday and then I got distracted by TikTok.      You are  so  going to get that A  I swear.      No, I’m going to get a D because Miss Rahman’s questions are like the most random things. Like, today she asked us how to use the cosine rule in real-life situations and I was like, “Miss, no one uses this outside of like, MySpace quizzes.”      I know right?! I told her I’d use it if I ever tried to measure the height of a tree while being super dramatic. But she just looked at me like I was mad.      Oh my God, you’re not wrong though, you’d look kind of hot doing that.      I do like, get into character. Anyways, I actually revised yesterday. I did like, three past papers and everything.      You what? How did you do it? You’re like, the most chaotic person I know.      I used my mum’s new app. It’s got like a phone lock thing where it only works if you finish the homework first. Like, someone at Spacemans Anonymous must have made it.      That’s evil. Also, it’s unfair because I don’t live with you so I  can’t  use it. I did technically live with you for the entire summer but now the lock is on your vibes and not mine.      Well, I’m telling your mum to install it too. My sister’s got it and she’s actually doing A-level maths now. She says it works wonders.      I don’t know if I can take that kind of pressure. Last Saturday I tried to revise for English and instead ended up trying to draw Batman using the writing from "Great Expectations." Wasn’t a good look.      That is classic gothic Batman though. If you do it again, you should sell it at the school café. I’d buy it just to laugh.      Thanks. I’m planning to make a small fortune off of it next year when we all drop out of school and start selling commodities made in our bedrooms over Etsy.      I’m in. You be the one drawing Batman with "The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde" typography and I’ll write the descriptions.

Rather skip the starter, actually. I'm just not very hungry. I had a late lunch.      Right, no problem. I'll have the soup though, if we're going for starters.      Oh, fanny! I wouldn't dream of skipping the starter on a Friday night out. Gives the main course something to build on!      I know, I know, but I’ve been working all week, and honestly, I’m knackered. This place is lovely, though. Bit nicer than the pub last time.      Yeah, I like it here. Bit classier, don't you think, Mum?      Aye, I’ve been here once before. It’s a good bet. I had the fish and chips last time I came—fella at the table next to me nearly died of envy when I ordered it.      Haha, classic. People’s faces when you tell them fish and chips is classed as a main course over anything else.      Honestly, some of them Americans would be livin’ in a dream if they knew we could actually get proper fish and chips in a restaurant.      Speak for yourself. I remember my nan’s chips better than I remember school dinners.      Well, she had a proper chip shop behind the council flat, love. Not some posh kitchen with a fancy name on the door.      Yeah, but this counts for a bit of variety, right? Also, I think the wine menu is being generous. Margaux for十二条?      I mean, I’m not the wine expert, but the waitress said this place recommends pairing it with the salmon.      I’m not sure if we should be that precious with our food for £20 plates.      Aye, me neither. I’d just as soon have a decent portion of meat and two veg and not worry about what the sommelier thinks. Though to be fair, the salmon here’s not bad. Had it before.      Still, I’m happy with anything that’s not chicken tikka masala tonight. That stuff’s like our national identity or something.      I mean, we can’t all be chips and kebabs forever. We’ve got to keep evolving, don’t we?      Ay, that’s the spirit. Just don’t start ‘evolving’ into food that won’t give you energy to work on Monday. I’ve done that once.      And let’s not forget, you had chicken cordon bleu, and then swore it was slimming before midnight.      I was optimistic.

Victoria, thanks so much for helping me tidy up today. I appreciate it more than I can say with everything that’s going on at the moment.      Anytime, Andrea. That's what friends are for, right? No need to thank me! Besides, I’d rather be in here than out dealing with some of the folks today. Honestly, I reckon half the people in town couldn’t tie their own shoelaces if policy said so!      Laughs It's not just that. We’ve had the worst few weeks at work. I’m juggling three big clients, my teenager is causing enough drama, and now I’ve got to plan the upcoming hospital appointment for my surgery. Being older than you, I seem to be gathering problems left, right, and centre!      Surgery? What’s it for?      They’ve found something unusual during a routine scan—maybe cancer, maybe nothing. I’ve been told to have an operation to remove a mass, so we’ll see. I’m trying not to stress too much about it, but it's challenging being the one arranging all the childcare in the meantime. You know how teenagers are—asking for space when they should be on their knees thanking us for remembering to cook!      Oh no, that does sound stressful, and I know all about trying to organise the kids. Now don’t laugh, but when Silas was younger—about fourteen—had detention for three weeks for failing geography.      Detention? At a time like that? For a subject he flunked?      Exactly! Made him so angry he drew all over his geography teacher’s car with permanent marker. I don’t even know where he found it! The poor woman had to walk home!      I can handle the school stuff, but I do need to plan for the time I’ll be out after the operation. Parents’ evening at the bank is one thing, but being confined to bed with a sling and painkillers is another. We’re already hearing about planning that building work in the backyard.      Aye, the building society’s going in there for some kind of extension. They say it's all about improving the mortgage deal on your home if you tidy it up properly. But I swear to God, they only understand technical stuff—no bloke on the street can get them to speak plain English!      I know, it's so infuriating!

So did you get the tutorial sorted for tomorrow? Or are they still making you jump through hoops like last week?      Ugh, sorted. I just had to send a reply to the admin person because they thought I registered under the wrong name—typical uni shenanigans. But yeah, all good now. I just wanted to study in here for a bit before it gets too crammed.      Fair enough. Honestly, I’ve barely stepped into a library since I started working nights. We’ve been so busy at the bar. Looks like the season’s well under way already.      No way? I thought summer wasn’t out yet. Wait, is it like that at the bar already? I remember you said last year it was just picking up in July. You must be knackers. I mean, I’m up to my neck in assignments, and I still can’t see the light at the end of the tunnel...      Nah, it’s rough, you know? I love the tips, but I’m knackered by the time I get home. I’d rather be up half the night with a pint in the pub and a fag on the balcony than in bed… but not tomorrow, I’m telling you. I’ve got Sunday off for once.      Ooh, what’s the plan? You finally going out for that weekend in the Lake District?      Yeah, actually—well, just someone said there’s a cottage near Keswick they might rent out for a couple of nights. Just needs a bit more sorting. I’ll let you know—might come up if I need someone to save my soul after about five days of walkies in the fells.      I might be doing my summer projects by that point. I’ve got to finish a presentation for my finals. My brain’s fried already.      Well, here’s to surviving both of our respective hells. What about you, then? Got a decent work placement sorted yet or still being fobbed off with temping academies and waitressing firms?      Ugh, temping… that sounds  so  unappealing. I applied for an internship in Manchester with one of those marketing agencies. If I get it, I’ll be in the office Monday-to-Wednesday, four days a week. Financially it’s not much, but I’ll kill two birds with one stone—get hours in, maybe even make some contacts to help me after studies.

Rather skip the queue and just go through the request button, do you?      Oh aye, I’ll tell you something, I had this one student from Galway who thought we were all doing a fancy dress party one Monday in October. He turned up with a green leprechaun hat and everything!  Where’s the trinket treasure?  he kept saying!      A lot worse things have happened in this library, honestly. Oh, and once there was a guy dressed as a superhero demanding to see the philosophy section. Told him the only heroes we had were Dewey Decimal ones. Still,  plenty  of holidays here to keep us busy, wouldn’t you say? My turkey still hasn’t thawed.      Probably still in the back of the larder and I’ll be the one serving it at Christmas again. My old man better not breakfast on it again or I swear I’ll give him the chop like a posh charcuterie! No, you didn’t hear that from me.      Ah, forget the turkey—personally I’m just glancing forward to a dram of something to wash away grief of real life for a few hours. Me folks always fancied trotting off to Tenerife. Not much for me though, with the blazing sun and fake tan slap jobs everywhere. I prefer a sombre little black Irish sweater and a pub with a fire.      Fair enough. Our bunch usually just pots about up in the Peak District. Trek a bit, have a sourdough with nutty-choc—only in the real deal here, not the supermarkets’. No, we are fully committed to home about here. My partner pulled the same story the other week: had this job looking for a house in Manchester. Going “Sheffield’s barely two hours away, Rob, luv—give her a  break .”      Ah, here we are at it again. I remember a time when all I had to do was smile, wave and serve a doughnut while my kid played  alphabet soup  of Websites and space weapons with his computer. Now it's "Can you do the simulation again, Tom?" and "Is this virtual course any good for my credentials goenvironmental map?" Honestly, sometimes I think I work at a technological dent in the head, not a library.      Pass some virtual scrolls to someone bent on fluency in emoji and you’re in business!      It's a right laugh alright. Know where we are at the end of them?

Rather skip the half-time take-away this weekend, I think. My back's killing me after that lab visit yesterday.      Oh yeah, that sounds brutal. You saw the lab where we're doing that follow-up with the Oxford team?      Yeah. Ten floors up in that university building and no lift. I felt like an old lady just walking up the stairs—three times!      I bet. Got side tracked and got to wonder why you don’t just get a taxi to those meetings.      Funny you say that, but the bloke responsible for transport needs to sort it out, apparently. I had to email three times just to get a confirmation for the lift breakdown.      So what are you going to do over half-time then, lie on the sofa and rest?      Something like that, yeah. Rather than have Domino's, I'm thinking I'll just reheat last night's spaghetti hoops. I'm over greasy food, honestly.      Are you now? I thought you were over the spaghetti hoops a decade ago.      Bah, nostalgia! It’s comfort food and only ten pence a portion from the local shops. Doesn’t work for Domino's. That lot is like £18 for a burger and chips, and none of the buns actually fit the burger.      Fair point. You know what I miss though? That mexican place in the city centre. The chicken one. It cost me a week's wages but it was oddly satisfying.      Oh yeah, the one with the neon green walls and the guy with the ballet shoes?      Yeah, that’s the one. But I still haven’t forgiven them for the "vegetarian burrito" that had bacon in it. I nearly had a stroke.      Should've gone with the veggie lasagne at home. Still, I reckon me and the spaghetti hoops are better off focusing on the match.      You’re making me crack up. So what's the player doing out there now trying to catch the ball like it's been chased by a beehive? Looks like a cartoon character.      Yeah, go on then! But let me warn you—if he scores, I’m demanding a drink, no excuses.      Deal. And what if we lose?      Then I’m blaming the spaghetti hoops and the hours of lab reports I’m planning to read tonight. Same outcome, different excuses.      You're a legend. I might just sit here, support you, and try to remember which of us claims to be the balanced one out of us.

Rather skip the new one haven't I?      That's it, that's it... got to pick the good ones. Otherwise you're down the shops again, same time next week!      I'll have a fiver says he watches it all anyway.       laughs  Yeah, you know me and big blockbusters... they're not for a man who works all week.      Still, easier watching films than me trying to cook something. Know me and the kitchen—light's never come on yet!      That’s because you don’t  try . I reckon with a bit of effort you could do something besides pasta and heating turkey on Christmas.      Well, fair play, I was the one who shouted, “Blimey, this is a proper meal,” when you brought out the sausages, Mum.      Haha! And don’t forget you ate it twice that night, didn’t you?       grins  I do like my meat. Speaking of, I’ve got that shortbread your nan made to go with the tea, yeah?      You cheeky trot! That was from the tin she left at the back of the cupboards—she still doesn’t know it’s gone.      Oh, don’t you dare touch what’s already left! That’s been in those tins since someone was in the Queen’s Army!      That’s not a surprise—look at the date on my birthday cake from last year, I still hadn’t  eaten it .      Ahh, but you did the talking for it, didn’t you? "Top of the range!" you said.      So, while we’re all reminiscing like old hippos, what about your work? How’s the project going? Still stressing the hell outta you?      Ah, it’s mad. Got a team of 12 that can’t agree what day it is, but we keep the budget on line. Not bad for a Manchester bloke trying to speak properly with a posh man watching the KPIs.      If it was anyone else, I’d say, “Flog it,” but you blokes in suits always get all worked up.      You know what’s worse than that? Grandson never had a proper bike to ride on the road, ‘cause he was too busy fancies his pushes up a hill in the park.       laughs  Right, Nan, I see you trying to make me sound like a posh Manchester ridge rider. I just like it before it goes flat and then I walk.      Still, better than me.

Right, who’s ready for pancake day tomorrow? I’ve got the batter made already, and I even found those pancakes in the shape of bunnies from the shop!      I want to flip the pancakes like you showed us, Mummy!      Okay, but only if you  help me  with the mixing first. Both of you need to put your hands in clean water, though. Washing before eating!      I watched a clip about someone flipping a pancake and it hit the ceiling! Didn’t it, Mummy?      Yes, George! And when I flipped a pancake the other night, it went  straight  on the turkey. Lucky I had melamine! Speaking of, you boys – I had the school assembly on Friday, and one of the kids asked me what “melamine” was. Mummy nearly snorted her tea out of her nose!      What was melamine again, Mummy?      It’s not actually anything to do with food – it’s the table we have in the kitchen! I think that puts your points as to how much you’ve actually  eaten  in recent days.      Be fair, Gemma. We – weren’t – that bad!      Oh, are we talking about the apple muffins? Or the whole grain flapjacks? You two literally made the recycling bin proud.      Well, maybe next time I’ll have more appetite when we do the  Green Knowe  story. That was way more interesting than flapjacks.      Yeah, about that – I think I know what “spectral” means now. It means… like… ghosts and stuff?      Exactly! And if we ever visit that old house, like the story says, I will not go into the attic. Not unless I have a torch and a friend.      Can we read it when we’re older? Not now, Mummy.      Yes, but not right after breakfast – unless you're going to finish your  one  bite of banana. Mummy’s not kidding about tooth goop. You two need to brush after  every  meal, or I will not let you go to the Festival Hall with me this weekend.      Festival Hall? What’s happening there?      There’s a junior orchestra concert this Saturday, and it’s only five quid if we book online. We can go for lunch too – I know there's a great little bap shop next door.      Can Uncle Tom come? He said we can go to the Science Museum with him before Easter.      If we arrange it, yes. But for now, you two need to focus.

Okay, thanks a lot for this. You know, six people’s worth of Chinese food and it’s like... barely any left.      Haha, typical. I was half-expecting a takeaway for 20 based on how you advertised it.      Hey, if it’s good, it deserves more than one plate, right?      It’s not just a plate. A lot of this is  metallic  isn’t it? Like, what was in the duck? Copper?      You're just jealous your prawn fried rice has no meat in it. That’s not even  rice —it’s shredded marble.      Alright, well Myra, if you’ve got enough to feed a dragon, maybe you should start calling yourself the dragon wrangler.      Oh ha-ha, funny. But seriously, what’s breakfast, lunch and then dinner this early in the week for?      Mega oversized takeaway hides a massive indulgence. Casually working the week away, Sami—vibes.      Oh, I’m working full-time land remediation from this couch and only real news since November is that England bowlers are still getting trotted out when it’s raining. How are the Baptists of Zimbabwe funding cricket, I ask you?      Yeah, seriously. All that rain and they couldn’t even win the one overcast day.      They just don’t know how to bowl with a sly one. Raining like that, you need floring tactics, not whatever the lads were being told.      Yeah, or maybe just a flamin’ kettle to warm the pitch up.      Alright, okay, what else is going on? Any funerals or accidental outings to Bob the Builder?      Should be the usual. My sister’s expressing passed tragedy about her cat. He meows a bit less these days, so I think he’s tired of her scheming.      Ugh, that’s what  my  cat does with me. I think it’s resentment. He took the remote last week.      Pfft! Maybe he was trying go viral on TikTok. I saw a clip of a cat in Scotland who just started building houses out of crumbs. People were  thrilled .      I have news. Found a new bid writing job in Cambridge. Inherit the project team like, supposedly. Still on the same company.      That’s proper work. You’ll have so much money to invest in those "200 sqft apartments with CB Radiators" you dream about.      Or at least enough to finally buy you a bid writing certificate and then mock you properly.      I would take that personal.

Rather skip the new house and go back to the old one. I miss the garden—the peace and quiet. It got too big, didn't it? I remember when we first moved in, we thought we'd never need a bigger place.      Aye, things do change, don’t they? I remember when I used to drive you all about when you were little. Proper roaring around on a Sunday. A lot’s happened since then.      Oh, Grandad, you were always the one to give the best rides and cause the most speed camera fines. Still, I don’t suppose you remember that.      I remember them very well, thank you. Just wish I had my wits left when the police pulled me over.      I used to think it was funny. Now, I’m far more nervous behind the wheel. I heard there’s driverless cars coming soon though. I wonder if they’d be safer than people like my dad-in-law.      Driverless cars—now that’s a big one. I’d listen to the BBC news and think,  is this the future or the Ministry of Silly Walks?  But imagine never having to take a trip without the risk of someone else being a bad driver.      Risk’s part of life. I flew planes quite a few times in the Forces. Still, I never trusted a pilot more than I trusted the coffee I had first thing in the morning.      That’s oddly reassuring. Or terrifying, depending on your view. Speaking of flight and being scared—Rosie’s house over in Staverton had a complete refit. They pulled the entire floor up and found all sorts of critters living under what was once the kitchen. Properly grim!      That’s not the first time I’ve heard of hiding things under flooring. I remember when my parents converted the garage into a studio—only to find all their old bills and Christmas cards from ten years ago. My mum was furious.      It’s always the bits of paper people think are gone! My experiment last week with the students was all about memory recall. We had them place random objects in a room and then come back after an hour. Only half of them could name six of them. đáng tiếc.      Memory your lot study—there’s something about it that feels dodgy to me. I remember those days, never had to worry about a third of it.

Right, who’s ready for Chinese New Year? I’ve bought some red paper for us to cut out decorations. What do you think—dragons, lanterns, or maybe even something like a phoenix?      A dragon! We did one in Art at school, but it looked more like a lizard! I want mine to look proper with loads of spots and big horns.      Well, let’s see if we can do better this time. Maybe we can draw a picture first, like you did with Mrs. Johnson in Year 2 when you made that dinosaur out of sweets. You remember?      Yeah! I did a dragon with glitter and markers, and it had eight legs like a spider turkey. Ooh, Mummy, can I draw mine on the wall?       laughs  I think the paper might be a safer bet for now, Mummy! Wait until you see the dragon I helped Dad paint for Hattie’s birthday. It was five feet long and looked like it could breathe fire!      Did it really? I want one of those! Can we hang it up next to the planets poster?      Sure thing, love. As long as you don’t confuse it with Jupiter when you’re doing your homework. Speaking of homework—is your astronomy project finished? I saw you scribbling something about the gas giants on the kitchen table.      It’s almost done! I’m calling it “Blue Giants vs. Red Spots,” and I’ve got a chart of the order of the planets. Oh—look what happened at school yesterday.  [She hands a drawing of a dragon biting the planet Mars.]       That is excellent! You’re the Picasso of Comberton. I can see you doing this at art college when you’re older. But while we're on space, did you know that China has their own space station now? They call it Tiangong.      Tiangong sounds like a spaceship with a gingerbread house!      Not bad! Now, how about we talk about food? What do you think of Chinese food? Would you like dumplings, sweet and sour chicken, or maybe some Peking duck?      Dumplings! But I want to learn how to fold them.      I can teach you—Dad showed me when I was about your age. It’s like making little pockets of happiness. We can do that on Chinese New Year’s Eve, along with some tangyuan for dessert.      Tangyuan… yummy. I had some of that at Nana’s.

So do you lot stay in the same area or are you scattered all over Rome for AirBnB?      Oh, we're split. I’m in this cute little flat near the Pantheon with some mates from uni. Jamie and I—     —yes, Jamie and I booked together, but we’re both in the same hostal near the Colosseum. I’ve been waking up to this view of the Via Appia every morning; it’s wild.      You lucked out. I’m just outside the Trastevere. No view, just three decent-sized bedrooms and a shared kitchen. I’m bunking with two other students. It’s like a dorm, but definitely cheaper than hotel.      And I’m the farthest out. I landed last night in a converted palace up in the EUR district. My flatmate is an Italian, and he doesn’t speak a word of English. The other night he’s like,  “Ciao, buona pizza,”  and I’m like,  bless you?       Oh老爷! I can’t believe your flatmate doesn’t speak English. You must’ve gone full immersion on him.      He’s got no idea. I tried ordering food one day and said,  "Dove è il bagno?"  and he looked at me and said,  "Here’s the bathroom. And the kitchen’s that way, and the coffee is always here."  I thought I was trying to be a romantic tourist, but I definitely failed out of the gate.      Anyways, speaking of food — what’s the plan for dinner tonight? I’ve been surviving on the coffee here, and the pastries taste like vibes and regret.      I know! I tried this gelato place last night that was recommended, but it was just… ice cream. Boring. So basic. I’m open to suggestions. Anywhere not too pricey, though. I’ve already spent my grant on getting here.      Jamie’s doing a pizza night. She’s taking a couple of us to this little place near the Spanish Steps where they do something called  pizza al metro .      You mean like you get measured for your slice?      No, it's like you order how long your pizza is — 50 cm, 100 cm — and then they stretch it out for you, right in front of you. It’s beautiful.      That’s wild! It’s like the Italian equivalent of lasagna, but for pizza?      And to think I baked for a living back home. Now I’m drinking espresso and asking how to say  "where’s the loo?"  in Italian.

So do you two actually know what’s on for the hen do yet?      We had a WhatsApp group, but no one’s properly sorted anything yet! Ali’s been super vague about where she wants it. “Romantic and cozy,” she says!      Yeah, I mean, that could mean anything. It could be   Villa Romanticus in the Lake District   or a wine bar in Bristol.      She said something about a “girls-only baking session.”      Oh for god’s sake. That means we’ll all have to bring frozen scones and make  visible  mistakes with Pavlova, and then Rob will grill us about it at the reception.      I’m not sure I want to be the one who burns pastry this time. Last year I managed to make an Edible Paperweight out of a chocolate breakfast roll—Ali actually kept it in her house for  weeks .      Honestly, I’m ordering puff pastry. Just thick slabs of it directly from the shop and pass out the rolling pins. Who are we kidding, it’s a baking day as much as it is a pretense for cake consumption.      But it’s about the  atmosphere , isn’t it? Lights, cinnamon, and way too many mugs of tea. I reckon we could just go to Rosie and Ali’s place and do it at home.      They just got a new house in   Gloucester  , right? That’s oddly literal.      I mean, if we want it to be romantic and cozy  literally , there’s not many about. I’m picturing the same living room where the mice had a party last year and Ron left a damp sock in the washing machine.      Maybe we’re overthinking. Should we put up a form or something? A proper survey with tick boxes? “Craft corner,” “Baking afternoon,” “Policy meeting about the amount of icing sugar anyone gets.” We could run it as tight as a professional event.      I think it’s partly about   friends  . Like, you don’t  technically  need a man’s wedding to go out with your best mates, you know?      Yeah, but it becomes  everything . Who remembers arranging the hen do, and who forgets to bring something, and who cancels and then shows up hungover hours after the venue had closed.      I still can’t get over the time we tried to do a balloon-filled Macaron Arrangement at   Embark  , and the venue had to call an ambulance because one of us spontaneously created a dangerously spicy glace cherry-topped flan.

Right, I just texted the hotel in Bath — they said everything looks booked for Saturday. Should be sorted.      Sweet. I’m just glad I agreed to cover for you over the weekend. I don’t mind the explaining part, but I bet you picked one of the weirder ones again.      Shut up. Not all of them are weird. Okay, maybe they are a bit. A lot of them just think that because I’m an artworker, I’m going to know someone famous. Once this one was like, “Can you chase Tracey Emin for me to send her my portfolio?”      Oh come on, that’s the best one yet!      My point exactly. Anyway, I’m just cooking up a bit of food, in case I’m too ill tomorrow. I’ve been feeling this little sneeze coming for about a week now.      You need to look after yourself a bit more, mate. I know the deadline for that billboard you were working on is tomorrow, but why did you stay out past midnight eating fish and chips and reading inappropriate things on the train?      Because it wasn’t  that  inappropriate. I was just on a Substack article.      That one which says “10 Ways to Ruin Your Life in 2025,” was it?      It was inspiring! Anyway, what am I supposed to do? Give homework to the people at work who think TikTok makes them artists?      That’s not a point—look, the sooner you rest, the faster you’ll be better. I’ve had your curry powder in my fridge for about five years. Use it while you can.      Alright, alright — what you got in there?      It’s coconut-chili, but I have some rice. Burgers and treacle scones passed their expiry date last week, by the way. Don’t assume I eat microwave meals every day.      I don’t. You just seem like that type of guy.      I  am  that type of guy, but also I like sashimi.      Don’t derail the go-to plan on your own if you start getting seasick at the thought of me in a hotel room by myself.      I already said yes. Look, I’m planning to stay with you and manage the homework while you rest. I’ll even clean your desk to make you feel better.      …What? Is this a trap? I’ve been hiding one of my mismatched socks in the drawer for three years, haven’t I?

Rather annoying isn't it, how birthday cards always get your age muddled up. Someone gave me 68 last week and I'm not even 60 yet. Honestly, what were they thinking?      Oh, I know the feeling. I got a card once that said "Happy 81st Birthday!" I was so confused I read it three times! But I suppose it's just a bit of transcription error by the machine that prints the inside. Still, you’d think they’d get the numbers right. We’ve had better things to do than double-check a card's script, haven’t we?      Tell me about it. I've been meaning to get those calendar fobs for this year. You know, the magnetic ones you stick on your fridge. They’re handy to keep track of what we need each month. Shopping lists are always getting lost if I just scribble them on a bit of paper.      Yes, I agree. And don’t forget the ever-useful shopping fobs to hold spare keys or a small pack of tissues. It’s all practical, really, and it keeps things in place. I remember in the old days, when I used to teach, we’d use bits of fabric and safety pins to make key holders in our art and craft classes. Back then, we made everything by hand, and now it's all plastic and magnets. Children didn't waste things back then like they do now.      Absolutely. I remember the old hockey boots at our primary school—proper leather. They’d last ages, and we’d mend them with tape and shoelaces. These days, they're through in a week if the soles are slightly worn. I do miss those times. I sometimes wonder if the kids still do art and craft properly. I suppose some schools have gone digital with everything now.      Oh, they're still using glue and paper, I promise you that. Though I heard about one school that’s trying to blend it with digital art—scanning drawings onto computers to annotate them. You’d think the kids would rebel, but apparently they love being able to see their work with special effects. It’s whizzy, if you ask me.      I can imagine. I sometimes get interested in the sound recording courses at the university nearby. If I was young again, I'd love to do that. It sounds fascinating, recording voices and music.

So do you like it here yet?      Aye, it's different, that's for certain. I thought I'd be comfortable in a new place by now, sure I've been there before, but… it's quiet. That and the garden! I wouldn't say it was in good shape, mind you, but I’m startin’ to enjoy the bit of digging in the evenings.      I think that's one of the best parts of this area, really. It’s not as busy as you might be used to, but that’s the charm of Holsworthy.      Oh yes! And the neighbours. I met Mrs. Armstrong at the postbox on Tuesday. She’s a delight. You know she still mends her own clothes and grows her own veg right out the back? I was quite in awe.      That’s a nice touch. I must see if I can get her recipe for stewed apple—she mentioned it’s different from what I used to make in Southend. Also, the train station, mind you—there's not much of a timetable, I’ve noticed. I don’t fancy waiting half an hour for a few minutes off to town, but I suppose I’ll get used to it.      It's lovely for a weekend walk, actually. There’s a path just behind the pub. You can see the river from there, and the whole countryside seems to stretch out for ever. I’ve been telling the others at work that the skyline is practically suspiciously peaceful.      I had a bit of a chuckle at the local hardware store yesterday. I asked where the outdoor lighting was, and the guy behind the counter about did a double take when I used “indoor” and “outdoor” properly. I think he thought I was drunk.      Aye, lingo changes. My sister ‘phoned me the other day. She passed on a funny poem about Southend vs. Devon—“Bread brushed with butter, or brushed with jam? You mustn’t stick to one good side when you live in Devon, young man!”      That one’s been going around the school staff room for ages. You know, it’s funny the little cultural adjustments you have to get your head round. I mean, I appreciated the cold, hard facts of tax return season more before I moved here—now it’s just part of the scenery.      I think the one I had the most fun with was the local pub.

You’d think the internet’s fast enough these days, but no. I had to wait twenty minutes for my Deliveroo to show up on the app. It was ready at twelve-thirty, and by the time it got to me, it was stone cold and half-melted.      Typical. That’s why I’ve switched to Amazon Fresh. At least if it’s not delivered on time, I can just take it back. Not like that Deliveroo lark where you eat soggy chicken and pretend you like it.      Soggy chicken? That was the  chicken katsu bento ! One of their best ones. I paid extra for the garlic sauce!      My bad, I’m just being sarcastic. I can smell the takeaway, though – I’m gonna have to pick something I can microwave and not regret. Maybe I’ll just eat cereal for dinner. breakfast, dinner… doesn’t matter.      You live on that stuff. I remember you told me once that you once ate Cheerios for  three  days straight because you forgot to buy food.      I take full responsibility. But as it turns out, cornflakes with a side of regret… it’s the circle of life.      True. – Mate, have you actually finished your online course yet? You said you were going to finish it by the end of January and now it’s April.      Give me a break, I work forty hours in my part-time job at the Hair & Beauty shop, I’m at school all day, and somehow I’m still studying between the bus rides and scanning the shelves for expired products. This is not a winning situation.      I know right? I mean I haven't done a  single  job since I graduated. Three months in and it's a classic case of "being in limbo for the foreseeable future."      So you're just gaming 24/7 now? I saw you on Twitch again yesterday, you looked like you hadn’t slept. You good?      Yeah, just trying to catch up a little. But I do have an interview next week, you remember? I got this virtual course setup gig with a company in Manchester. I think it’s legit.      You’re going in? I’m proud of you.      I’m nervous as hell. It’s been over a year since I’ve spoken in public. Last time I gave a presentation was at university and it made me break out in hives.

Rather skip the new coat of paint for now, what with the heating still playing up. I’ve been thinking... got to get some proper storage sorted before you start putting things in.      Oh, we were just telling Julia about the DIY shop in Exeter – they do these cheap-and-cheerful shelving units. Might do until you get your own style sorted.      I’ve got a mate who’s done that too, got a flat for a couple of months, dump everything in and just live in the mess. But when you start moving, suddenly the place has a flow... like, without even trying!      That’s the plan then, mess for a bit and then magic happens. I’ve already sketched out the room layouts. Probably need to start with the kitchen. Still, no point in getting the heavy stuff if you can’t heat the place properly.      I know a fella... not in Exeter anymore, but five years ago he told me to always buy a laptop and a fridge secondhand. The rest will hold out, if you know what I mean.      What about the heating system? It doesn’t look as dodgy as the others.      No, no. The boiler – that’s been replaced fairly recently, and the venting’s decent. The problem’s the thermostat. All these old houses have their own little quirks.      There’s also this walk I’ve been meaning to take you both on... a bit of a coastal route through Holsworthy. Sorted out some maps, and I thought it might be a decent idea for your new place – make it a proper settling-in weekend walk.      Oh, I’d love that! We can pack some lunch. I’m trying new dishes these days, unashamedly healthier. My sister’s over here every other week, cooking up all these quinoa things. I told her the only way I was giving that up was if I ended up in a cult.      Sounds like that’s going to be a bit of a lunches-to-go operation. But hey, if we can’t feed ourselves for once, where’s the fun in that?      I’ll see if I can get a picnic table for the garden. Need to do that shopping trip we were talking about last week – what with all the furniture. I’ve been looking at benches and tables and one of those striped awnings, maybe even a couple of outside lights.

Rather annoying to be honest. I had a request from a colleague to review this paper, and they sent it to me in a PDF with no track changes.      Again? That’s a bit lazy, isn’t it? Did you not review things like that before things went digital?      Oh, I used to print it out and write on it with a red pen. Now I feel old just thinking about it. Much more efficient to use highlighter and margin notes, though, interestingly, those still work in the digital age for some reason.      You’re a child of the old school! I still can’t get used to the idea that people can do entire journals like that without ever meeting in person. I swear my last meeting week was just three calls to parents who didn’t understand why their child couldn’t be the class president because their name was spelled wrong on the form.      Now  that  sounds exhausting. I don’t envy you the day job one little bit. How’s the laptop working? Still over-heating?      Not today, thank goodness. Though I might have short-circuited it last week when I took it on the train and left it on my damp coat. I blame the weather. You’re okay at the uni though? Still fairly sane?      Oh, I’ve had my moments. Three funding deadlines next week, and I’m still waiting for a response from the hospital trust. Our ethics committee took four weeks to get back to me. At this rate, I’ll start a parallel career in project managing chaos.      Sounds like my week – chasing feedback from teachers, chasing forms from parents, and chasing respect from a child who thinks the word “no” is an exciting new phrase. Maybe we should start a support group. Call it “The Overworked and Underappreciated”.      That’s got promise. I might actually join that. Just kidding. You know, I was thinking the other day how weird it is how quickly things have changed. We’re both 38, and yet academically speaking, the world we’re in now is almost unrecognisable compared to when we started university.      Absolutely. When I got my MSc I never imagined I’d end up using spreadsheets for attendance logs and not for research stats. And you—psychology postdoc? I always saw you as the biology type.      You misjudged me. I just never had the stomach for animal dissection.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You know, me being left-handed and her being right-handed. We’d be making a cup of tea and one would be trying to get a grip on the handle and the other would be trying to open the tap, and we’d end up knocking things over. Happens all the time.      It was the same with me and my mum as well. Though I reckon that was before I learned how to hold a knife properly, so we had a right old mess in the kitchen. We used to be doing the school dinners when I was younger and the lad at the meat saw everything, jokes about it,  “Oh no, here we are, double left-handed people trying to put a sausage on a plate.”       Left-handed! I’m right-handed as well, but I used to make a real mess of cutting clover for my grandmother. She kept shouting,  “Charlie, look at you! You're holding the shears the wrong way round.”  I told her to mind her own business and that I was doing it that way for a reason.      Honestly, I always thought that was quite a rude way to treat your grandparent, Charlie. Imagine saying that to her. I mean, it’s only a humble piece of clover – surely it can't be that hard?      She was the one who set me off, mind you. She used to call me ‘Baldrick’ for heaven’s sake. I couldn’t help it. I’m not a calm man in the kitchen.      Well, the kid now, he wants to cook and he’s got a pair of left-handed chopsticks because he’s about half-chinese. I don’t quite know where the genes came from but I thought cooking with chopsticks would be another way to avoid me having to handle the ladle for once.      Oh, left-handed chopsticks? That’s actually really thoughtful. I remember when my dad used to give me all the wrong tools, like trying to hand me a screwdriver with the left side as the dominant hand.  “It’s fine, Jules, you’ll survive.”  Not really the best advice when you’re a kid trying to fix a lamp.      I remember being left-handed and trying to use a sewing machine as a teenager. Imagine that, stitching left to right with a machine that’s already biased to go the other way.

Rather skip the newfit meat eh gran?      Well you’d think it'd be like mince and I thought I'd bung it in the stew, but then I found out it's like pork substitute. Not quite right for the casserole.      Honestly, it’s all the same to me. Just as long as it’s edible.      Oh aye lad, but when you're trying to make a proper Sunday lunch, you don’t want some sort of fancy processed fiber pretending to be meat. It doesn’t chase the hens.      Yeah, I mean I’m  trying  to go for more plant-based, but I wouldn’t die of hunger if turkey came around. Still, you’d think they could make things more, y’know, like them, if they’re trying to pass for meat.      Mm. Wait a second—did you say this happened  last week  in Paris?      Yeah, my office was looking for a few weekends in Europe for team building, so I went with the gang—personally I’d rather be in the pub with a pint than in some high-tech team-building workshop with fancy sandwiches.      You work in a place that gives you weekends in Paris for team-building? I’d have done something smarter with myself at that age. Though I reckon I was more interested in making sure the phone was working properly and cables were plugged in the right places.      That’s what retirement’s for, Grandad. Besides, we had a tour—went to the Louvre, sketched some of the architecture, had a few  very  overpriced pastries about five times a day.      Sounds nicer than this job. I just sit all day marking clauses in contracts and trying not to accidentally delete the whole database while I restructure something.      What do you do again?      I’m a Corpus Administrator. Basically, I wrangle with huge sets of text data and make sure the language models run properly. It sounds exciting but 90% of the time I’m just looking at commas in massive XML files going,  “Why are you here?!”       I bet it doesn’t beat plugging in a few extra cables in some call centre in Manchester in 1982, though.      Can you two sum it all up for me? I like the bit about commas.      It’s alright gran, we like you.      On the flip side, tell us about Paris—how did you feel walking round the cobbled streets in loafers, trying not to trip over your coat?

Okay, so I've got this seminar on postcolonial theory next week, and I'm trying to think of a way to make it more interactive than just me talking at them for an hour. Any ideas?      Hmm, have you tried using case studies? Maybe pairing the theory with contemporary examples? That way they can discuss how the ideas apply to modern issues.      Yeah, I’ve considered that. I was thinking of using  Homegoing  by Yaa Gyasi as a supplemental text to complement one of the primary readings. But I don’t want to overload them with reading.      Maybe split the seminar into small groups and give each a different text to tackle? That could encourage deeper thinking and reduce the reading load for everyone. Or even a panel discussion format, where you act as the moderator and pick one or two students to lead parts of the session.      That doesn’t sound bad. I’ve been wanting to encourage more student-led input. I might also add a film or documentary to break up the reading—something like  The Color of Fear  or  13th . That’d give them a visual way in, especially if they’re struggling with the theory.      Definitely. Visual media can help a lot of our students who find it hard to grasp theoretical concepts from dense academic texts. I actually had the students watch a film the other week and then debate whether it reinforced or challenged colonial ideologies. The discussion was amazing.      Oh, that sounds good. What did you show them?       The Last King of Scotland . It’s a controversial choice, but the moral ambiguity in the film really got them talking. Some of them were about to throw tomatoes at the screen! Laughter in the hall is always a good sign.      Definitely. I think I need to liven things up a bit—being in China for over a year has made guest lectures harder to arrange, so I have to do more on my own. But I don’t want to lose the academic rigor.      Of course not. Maybe include a mock critique or short presentation from the students on a piece of theory related to the reading? That would give you a chance to give them feedback and stretch the higher achievers.      I like that. I was also planning to schedule a review session two days before the seminar—maybe a flipped classroom approach, where they do some pre-reading and I post a few discussion questions online in advance.

Rather than chuck the entire coffee machine out, I suppose we could get it cleaned. But it’s so pitted with rust and half the parts don’t even belong to it! Honestly, I think it might be more cost-efficient to buy a new one, even secondhand.      I don’t want to start another  project , Ruth. We had that mug storage thing last week—three of us trying to fit thirteen mugs into one drawer! Why do we even own so many mugs?      We’ve been removing things for weeks now! If it wasn’t for the charity shop donations, I swear this place would already be a skip. I’m surprised the walls are still holding up with all that  emptiness  echoing around.      Well, I’m not paying £300 for storage, and I’m definitely not doing that storage company with the dodgy-looking man who asked if I liked Bucks Fizz!      That’s not his fault, Ruth. You walked into the room looking like a woman who’d just discovered her pyjamas were glued to her, and then immediately asked, “Do you take short-term landfills as payment?”      Honestly, we’ve got bigger problems than the storage prices. Have you all got a minute to talk about this Labour business? I’m not sure I can watch any more of Sir Keir being “unified,” “decent,” and “positively grounded.” It’s like watching a prime minister in a PowerPoint.      I don’t know, maybe they need someone with a bit more flannel—someone who can  do  the politicians while they  do  the talking. You know, someone who can make binding commitments while still leaving wiggle room! Someone like a maths teacher.      That’s it—I’m running! I’m becoming the unashamedly green, beanie-wearing, baked-bean-leftover idealist who believes in tax breaks for dandelions. Provincial politics is giving me  grave  spinal tiredness.      We’re already hearing about  policies  from a ragged union with lunches delivered by pigeons and a policy document written in invisible ink. Still, maybe something will shake it up! Maybe someone will come in and say, “Let’s redistribute risk  and  cake,” and become the leader of the left by genuinely being the left.      Now that’s what I call planning. You’ve got to start small, then go for the earnest moral altitude bit, and end with a modest slogan that sounds like a prayer.

So do you lot ever just go out on a canal boat or anything? I mean, it’s not like we’re right in the middle of the Thames, but there’s got to be some decent routes round here.      No, I mean, I’ve never really considered it. Why? Has someone got a boat?      I reckon it depends on your pseudonyms, really. If I had a floating café, I’d be doing it every Sunday. “Sally on the Serpentine” sounds way posher than “Layla’s Latte Lane.”      That’s true!  laughs  I’d call mine the “Sourdough Schooner.”      You know, in Australia we’ve got this whole thing with the Murray River and whatnot, but no one calls it the Murray. Everyone just says, “We’re boating on breakfast, mate.”      Haha, yeah, over here you’ve got to be careful, ’cos I think the canals might actually be regulated by like Waterway Watch or something—personally I’d start up a boat full of strong Italian food to see what they say.      Oh, I’d board any boat with a decent caprese salad. Kosher?      Why?      No reason. I was just trying to remember if my cousin Silas was the one who converted to kosher law or if it was his girlfriend. Either way, they’ll judge me if my antipasti isn’t up to scratch.      So, if you want mouths full of premium mozzarella, your key condiments would be balsamic reduction and—      Chilli oil. Always.      Yeah, that and extra basil. Doesn’t it feel like the more expensive the food, the more herbs you’re allowed to put on it?      Tell me about it. My last lunch was three sandwiches, one with pesto, one with prosciutto, and one with both. I’ve never looked so fancy with lunches.      Now if only our lunch spots weren’t empty. This restaurant is like a ghost town.      Maybe if you piped some jazz in and made posters like “Chike’s Café—Now with Less Money,” someone would notice your microwaves.      You think? I tried putting my hours up as “Monday to Monday” to see if it would scare people in, but the only one who came was my nan. She buys all the scones.      That’s romantic. Concentrated baked goods, serial visiting.      So, just to recap before someone changes the subject—I’ve been trying to get out more, but I had a bit of an incident at a club last week.

Nah, I swear I ain't even opened Tinder in weeks. I’m just not in the mood for it no more. It’s all the same, innit?      Oh come on! There’s some good ones on there. Look, I’ve swiped a few times and I’ve met eeny weeny decent people. You just gotta filter out the mad people.      I’ve been on it too. Honestly tho, too much crying, too much swearing, too many questions about whether you're a feminist or not. It's like a bloody exam, innit?      Yeah, it’s mostly just blokes asking me to send photos or wanting to go straight to the second date. It’s not for me either. I left it on ‘just friends’ for ages, and then I deleted the app altogether.      Honestly, it’s harder than uni! Wait, no—uni’s hard enough already. I’ve got tutors bad at the minute. One of em hides behind his notes the entire time and mutters to himself. One bloke I went out with, he had a uni degree and still couldn’t explain the difference between as/des. I tell ya, it's dodgy in there sometimes.      Be fair, some modules are alright – but it's mostly just trying not to fall asleep in the lecture. I miss sixth form. It was proper social then. At least I knew all my housemates at home. Now they’re all just someone who eats my leftovers and doesn’t clean up after themselves.      Oh yeah, housemates is a whole nightmare. I live with two others now – one’s always in the shower when you need to use it, and the other’s always arguing with the landlord about the council. It’s like chaos and not in a fun way.      I live with my boyfriend. My sister’s over every other weekend, so it’s like a mini-family. But at least I know it won't culminate in me trying to grow a beard from stressing out about someone’s dodgy habits.      Is he nice? Does he do his fair share of the washing up?      Oh, he does now. He had a couple points to learn goin' on. One day I came home to a sink full of unclean plates, innit. He said he was bloke enough to do ‘em but forgot. I said, “Well, clearly, you’re not.”

Rather annoying this new eligibility criteria eh?      Aye, it's a real mither, isn’t it? I had to apply for more documents than when I got married the first time! Got me checking my £20 note for clues, mind you.      Ha! I'm telling you, I sat down with the application and nearly had to use the darts board for a yes/no vote on each question! Got so infuriated I had to watch a couple of episodes of Ant and Dec to calm me down again.      Oh, don't say that – reminds me of the time dear George couldn’t understand his pension letter, and the pen rolled across the table and off the edge. Poor chap, I had to chase it like it was a bottle rocket or something.      Always was a bit slow with paperwork. Blamed it on the government eventually.      He was always clever at evasion! Haha. But back to the benefits – it's getting ridiculous, the way they're expecting people to prove they need help. I mean, do they think we've just applied out of boredom?      It’s like they don’t believe we’ve still got bills to pay. I’ve got electricity, gas, and the utility bill from Lady – no, wait, that was last year, it was Harold’s birthday. Anyway, you see my point.      If I had a quid every time the TV’s said 'unemployment at record low' while I’ve been filling in a form to say I can’t buy toothpaste without looking at the discount in the supermarket… I'd be a wealthy man.      Not nearly as wealthy as Steve from the street who picked the right numbers on the lottery. Not that I’ve ever smoked! Swear that was just a metaphor.      You’re all just making up for the time you didn’t play bingo properly.      Well, the TV these days is scarcely fit for company. I tried to watch some politics on iPlayer once. It didn’t like that. Prevented me from watching by crashing. Told me it was "geographically restricted." Sarcasm set on maximum.      Still watching the weather go bad on my telly, though. If it can’t give me news on benefits, at least it’ll give me a forecast that tells me what to wear. Although half the time it’s wrong anyway.      As long as it gets the belly of the storm right, it’s a good day in my book.

Rather skip the newfit meat again, love. Thought we’d have something nice for a change.      Never mind, it was just more of a budget kind of day. Meetings, meetings, meetings—haven’t stopped explaining since the morning.     Deer, it’s beginning to sound like you don’t like the job. Still got that letter about your back-up? I remember that Aneurin bloke in the garden shed mentioned it last week.     Shh! Not in the house for that. If the wife of the bloke next door hears, she'll think I've been knocking on his door with baited breath, only to find out he’s older than me by ten years and still smells of left-over primrose.      Oliver, you know very well what Aneurin means. He was at the old school with me when I was younger. I've been wanting to ask for a while—are his dreams about the Great War as vivid as the ones I had when I was growing up, or was I just over imaginative?     Well, I don’t rightly know about that. But what I do know is that today’s bloody exhausting. You would not believe the time I was put through by that mother at the Baptism Centre with her forty-piece family, all wanting to be in the same photo and not quite willing to suffer mortal injury at the hands of the one poor photographer at the back, huh?      Sounds more suspicious than a conspiracy to me. Trying to get a decent meal out of you’d be like herding marshmallows with tea bags under your nose!     It about did me in. I mean, I know it’s my job to pacify and stuff, but some people—you know that manager at Boots who treats it as a calling? I bet she’d laugh at that lot.     She did once. I was in there the other day picking something up, and the moment I tried to ask about waiting times, she said, “You know what I do to people who misbehaved with lunches, right?” She told me the story of the man who tried to fake a queue around the tills and the look on his goon’s face when he found out.     I like that, yeah. You don’t meet many blokes like her. Pass the gravy will you?     Don’t want it poaching those off-odours like newfit meat does?

Rather annoying isn’t it, this weather? One minute it’s sunny and warm, the next it’s like someone’s turned the showerhead on upside down.      Yeah, I mean I get it — spring in Poland can be… temperamental, but I wouldn’t have minded a bit more of a warning. I’ve got a bad back and these sudden changes really play havoc with it. Though I suppose that’s just life.      Oh, love, are you still taking those tablets? The ones you said were from the clinic? Didn’t your doctor say they’d made a difference?      Not anymore. I stopped them last week, actually. Went for some kind of therapy session instead, you know, the holistic sort. The one where you visualise your pain being washed away. Ridiculous I know, but somehow it helped. I’m not saying it’s better, I’m just saying it’s… happened.      That’s interesting. I remember when I first came back for Mum’s funeral. Everything was just so raw, you know? Like, I had to choose between staying in England or coming back out here. And I didn’t even know  why  I chose this… country.      I know what you mean. My nan used to say that you’re never really at home anywhere if you’ve moved a lot. It’s why I stayed in Tarnow after the flat became mine. It just felt… right. Less someone else’s idea of what I should be.      Oh, I think you were always better at finding your own way. I look at you and I think, she’s got her own thing about her. I’m not trying to be the English lit major or the “main character.” I’m more like… whatever happens to be on sale at the market.      That’s not true. You’ve got your own rhythm, your own way of doing things. You know, I was looking through old Instagram posts the other day, just waiting for a student who was running late, and I came across one of you sitting by the river here a couple of years ago. You had the sun in your eyes and a smile so wide it nearly touched the horizon. That didn’t look random to me.      Well, I do try, don’t I. Although I’ve got to say, the one thing I  didn’t  expect was how much I’d like teaching again.

So did you get the email from the uni about the postgrad funding yet?      No, and I’m starting to panic now because my part-time job at the survey company is only a temp gig until December. I’m not going to cover rent on my own.      That’s rough, I feel for you. I remember when I was doing my undergrad, trying to balance work and A-level stuff. Honestly, I was a mess half the time.      Oh, I can imagine. I don’t know how people do it. I’ve been up to 2am submitting survey tests just to make sure I get the bonus at the end of the week. It’s like working a full-time job on top of my course.      I know what you mean, but hey, at least the tea here is decent, right? This place is better than breakfast clubs and universities if I’m honest.      Amen to that. I’m just not sure how long I can keep this up. I need something more stable. I spoke to my cousin the other day, and he’s raving about his job as a junior copywriter. He said it only took him three months to get it.      Oh yeah, copywriting is one of those fairly accessible creative jobs, but you do need some experience. I actually got mine after doing freelance bits through uni. If you’re interested, I can give you a few tips for portfolio work — maybe even a writing challenge to test out your voice.      That would be amazing, thanks. I think I’d be good at it—I just need to get the bug out of my system of being afraid to put my work out there.      It’s all about confidence. Trust me, I used to panic every time I submitted a draft. Now I just hit ‘send’ and keep calm. Honestly, most editors just want people who aren’t scared to write.      Okay, that’s encouraging. You know, your copy is everywhere now—those posters for the tech start-up always make me want to keep browsing their site. They have such an easy-going voice for such a serious product.      That’s the idea! They wanted to make it feel friendly but professional, and I just leaned into that vibe. It helps that the client let me run with it after the first two drafts.

Rather annoying to be woken up by two people jumping on the bed at 6 in the morning, don’t you think?      It wasn’t my fault! I was just doing cartwheels and then   he   joined in!      I like doing cartwheels! I saw a lady at the weekend do one on a   trapeze  ! Proper circus skills!      I think your trapeze lady was on a trampoline, sweetheart. But who am I to argue with circus dreams? Just don’t do them in the house.      I want to juggle! Not like that silly lady with the flamingos, though.   She   made everyone laugh!      The flamingos were the best bit! I made her wear safety goggles!      Fair enough, I suppose if she was juggling hot sauce bottles she might need goggles. But I think we’ll stick to toast in this house today, thanks.      Do we have any of that Australian toast? The one that says “G’day, Mate”?      I think that’s a souvenir from last time we visited your grandad. You’ve probably got it in the cupboard. I saw it the other day. Though I’m not sure it’s safe to eat.      I’ve seen a somersault! On   Jimmy the Silly Man  ! He somersaulted three times and then did a handstand in one hand!      That’s not a handstand, that’s a   freakoutstand  !      That’s not a word!      I just made it up! Just like “flipping butterbrick” is a word!      Let me be the first to say: it is not a word. Now, do either of you want proper breakfast or do I have to feed you both slices of bread with a teaspoon of jam on it?      Proper breakfast, please. I want mushrooms on toast and a   double yellow sprite   of cereal!      That’s “two portions,” not a ‘double yellow sprite’.      I like cereal the best when it go  crunchy-vroom-vroom !      Is it? I see it. I just haven’t heard it described like that before. Vroom-vroom toast, seriously.      We going to the   Neon Moon Festival   today?      That’s prononcence-ally very   fluffy  !      I think it’s “Neon Moon Event” again.      Neon Moon. I think we need to confirm the spelling again, but before that: are we leaving in ten minutes or not?      Yes, unless you want me to juggle your keys?      I once juggled Grandma’s knitting needles!   So fast  , she didn’t even see them go!      Well, don’t juggle anything with sharp edges.

Rather skip the new changes in the NHS funding regime, have they. I was just reading about it in  The Guardian  and it's all about cutting costs more than improving care. I've been where my brother was doing a full-time job and he couldn't wait as long for a hip operation as someone in Scotland apparently could.      Yeah,   it's true  . It’s not just a Welsh issue, though. I was at a seminar last week, and we had a delegate from Aberystwyth—his father-in-law has been waiting months for a scan, and the bloke’s grudgingly thankful because in Scotland they'd still be on a waiting list the length of the M4 for something like that.      Honestly though, I find this ridiculous. I’m from Wales as well, and I used to think our system was better—until I was at uni and saw how it doesn’t compare even to the north of England. I remember in my gap year, I volunteered in a health centre near Hay-on-Wye and saw the staff overworked and understaffed. They deserve better—personally, I’d vote for someone who puts healthcare first.      That’s the spirit, son. You always did have a good head on your shoulders. I remember when your nan had pneumonia, the chap in A&E barely had time to register her. I reckon she was waiting there longer than the whole journey from Swansea to Rhyl. Still, we’d better change lanes here—we’re near Bodmin and the road gets a bit snarly at this time.      I   agree  . It’s not just underfunding—it’s inefficient as well. Take my mum—she’s from a working-class background, right? Worked as a midwife in Birmingham for over thirty years. Every Sunday we’d have tea and she’d tell these amazing tales. My, the patients she’d seen! There was one lady who came in pregnant and turned out to be a farmer’s wife from the Borders.   She ended up helping her deliver the baby   in the shed because the ambulance got stuck in the snow!      Gracious, I’ve heard some wild ones in my day too, luv. My uncle—your granddad Walter go on about it for years—wanted to be a GP. Gave it up in the end, but I always remember the bloke who came in one day with a rabbit in his pocket.

Right, so today we're going to start working on your very own little story. We’ve read some Helen Moss, and I thought she’s great inspiration because her stories make you feel something, you know?      Do we get to have fairies?      Of course! Or if you’d rather have something different—dragons, knights, maybe even just animals in the forest? What would you like?      Can I have a robot?      Robot? That’s brilliant! So maybe the robot and the fairy are friends, or the robot has a problem it needs to solve. What does  your  robot do, then?      It goes into space and brings back sweets for aliens! The aliens like jelly and marshmallows, but the robot spills the sweets and the aliens get cross!      Oh, that’s a great start. So, the robot goes on a mission, has a funny mishap, and then maybe the aliens aren’t angry after all? Or maybe the robot has to find more sweets?      I want my character to be a little girl who talks to animals.      I love that! Tell me more. Why does she talk to animals?      Because they can’t talk to people, so she helps them. One day a squirrel asks her help to save the apple tree from the big tree-cutter machine.      Wow, that’s a big adventure. And what does your character do?      She goes to the city and tells the grown-ups to stop cutting the trees down and shows them how beautiful the forest is.      That’s amazing! She’s a real hero. And maybe the grown-ups listen to her and make a new park out of it? Something like the Linton Book Festival does, actually—brings people together for creative ideas!      Can my robot friend her?      Of course! What if the robot comes to Earth to find sweet resources and accidentally lands in the forest? Then he meets your squirrel-rescuing girl and helps her stop the machines by whizzing away the cutter with his laser?      He could sing the squirrels a lullaby on the way if he’s nice!      That would go down really well. And the aliens might even send her a thank-you note made of jelly.      And the robot could turn into a library?      Oh, yes! A robot library where animals can borrow books about how to make nests and how to grow flowers!      My animal friend could teach him how to read!

Okay, I just wanted to say, I think I'm going to try going fully vegetarian for a week. I got this idea from one of the lectures at uni about how much better it is for the environment and all that.      That's kind of you, Alice. But honestly, if it’s just a week, I don’t think you’ll notice a big difference. I’ve tried multiple times—it’s the cheese and stuff like that that mess me up. Still, easier said than done.      You can do it Alice. But what are you going to eat? I mean, meat’s like part of every meal, honestly—especially when you cook like us.      Well, that’s kind of why I’m asking. I thought maybe we could team up, the three of us, and plan some meals that don’t include meat. Or if we do, maybe try something like shmeat—synthetic meat? I remember reading a bit about it at work, you ever heard of that, Kenzie?      Oh yeah, I’ve seen some videos about it, and it is pretty interesting—lab-grown meat, right? It’s still early days though, and it’s way too expensive for us. I tried a meatless burger from the supermarket last week, and it’s alright, but I wouldn’t say it replaces the real thing.      Mate, you’re talking about trying to replace the real thing with a burger made from soy and pineapples. Spent my weekend bingeing an old  "Curb Your Enthusiasm"  episode—Larry’s all up in a farm and realises it’s a meat farm, but he’s too ignorant to know what about. I mean, he does everything wrong, right? But watching it made me think a lot more about where meat actually comes from.      Ugh, I still don’t get why anyone finds that funny. To each their own I guess. But speaking of where meat comes from—haven't you ever thought about how intense factory farming is?      I have, and it's honestly hard to look past. I've watched a couple of documentaries over the last month, and it’s just so upsetting. The idea of hunting or eating the animal is one thing, but the way it's done in abattoirs? It makes me sick. I’m trying to be more conscious, I guess.      Look, I get it. But to be fair, humans have been eating meat since the Stone Age.

Rather skip the new year’s dinner this year to be honest. I’m just knackered.      Never mind Anna, you’ll be fine. Just need something warm after. Beans on toast is always reliable.      Beans on toast wouldn’t beat a night in watching eeny weeny TV show and eating nachos with cheese dip if you ask me.      A lot of people would think that too, but honestly,.Grid? Out of all the programmes you could watch!      Oh come on it’s not  that  bad. I like the jokes, even if it’s a bit much with the drama.      Difficult one, but I’m with you Anna—it’s not a programme I can see myself watching for the third time, is it?      It is for about a million people! Why do we have to be the clever ones all the time?      Go on then, I’ll agree to spare the laptop and the cookies for once. It’s nearly over anyway, thank God.      I’m with you both. We can flick through the other programmes and still pretend we’re watching something.      Speak for yourself. I remember my nan used to say the same, and now it's  us  saying the same thing. It's gotten out of hand!      When did that happen? We all thought this was going to be fun and exciting when we got to a certain age.      Yeah, but now it's just real life being duller than the telly.      I mean, I know I don’t want to touch the washing machine this week. It’s doing some weird thumping again. Not like I can really handle it after a day in that hospital.      Same here. All that mucking about with patients at 6 a.m. and then coming home to trying to figure out why you’ve got half a sock in the machine. It’s unbelievable.      Do people not keep an eye on what they're doing anymore? My grandad used to say he'd throw stuff out the window if it go bad or smelly.
