I think he was just trying to get rid of clutter in the house, really.      Tom what your grandad was doing was just planning ahead for 30 years of his life.      It's a pity we don't have a bin this big. We’d just chuck half the house out every so often and be done with it.

Rather skip the salad fork and go straight for the main course one.      But Mum... What's the point of having a dining table set with  five  different forks?      Well, we do try to eat like continental Europeans on our special supper evenings. You know, all the butterfly forks and things.      Why are they called "butterfly forks," though? Do they have wings?      Haha, not quite. Look carefully. See how the tines are shaped like the wings of a butterfly? The serrated ones are usually for more delicate foods, like fish.      I still can't see the difference between the turkey fork and the dinner fork.      Probably because they look the same, but they're used for different courses. The turkey fork is slightly heavier, often with a taller back.      Shouldn't we have a course named after me, like "Harry’s Fork"?      Maybe. That would confuse everyone even more.      I still don’t see why we don’t just use the same one for everything. It’s all about ceremony, dear. And then of course, we have the knife and fork held with the same hand and none of this “left-handed nonsense” at the table.      You know what I hate more than the fancy forks, though? Our 2-minute silence song. It always plays at the wrong time.      What? We don’t have a 2-minute silence song.      Yeah, we do. It’s just that it plays during the "birthdays" part of the meal. Every year it’s the exact same shuffle of jazz and then suddenly the national anthem starts.      That’s for Remembrance Day, not your birthday. Although, if that’s your idea of a party, I suppose it works.      Not when I’m making a cake to sing "Happy Birthday" to. It’s always trying to play over the top of it!      Maybe you should get a Russian cake machine like Dad told us about. He said he saw one in Moscow that plays  Tchaikovsky  while the candles blow out.      Let’s stick to your normal birthdays, thank you. I’m still recovering from the Father’s Day violin recital last year.      That wasn’t a violin, that was a fiddle. There's a difference.      Are they even the same thing?      They are instruments, lads. Now, stop arguing and eat your vegetables before they go cold.      But what if I don’t like the butterfly ones?      What if I don’t like lectures about continental etiquette?

So did you two like the Adventure Island books I got for you last week? I remember reading them when I was little and I thought they might be nice for your Cornwalls holiday.      Yeah, they’re really good! I read one in bed yesterday. The one with the cave in it.      Me too! But I nearly got lost reading it all… finished most of it. A lot of people on the island!      Oh right, some of the characters do get a bit confusing at the start. Didn’t the boy get chased by a dog?      Yeah! And there was a hidden map and everything!      It was like a proper adventurer thing! So are we going on the Ten Tors Walk this time? Darcy, is it?      It is, yeah. But you better remember breakfast, no funny business with the banana bread again or I’m not giving you any.      But the banana bread was a mistake. I thought it was cereal!      Well it’s not. I put two slices out for both of you. And only one, since someone remembers having an allergic reaction last year.      That was my fault – I didn’t check the label, I swear it looked like regular bread.      You’re lucky you didn’t end up in A&E again!      I know. Let’s not test the system again. Now, have you thought about whether we should camp or just stay at a hotel in St Ives? The V&A has an exhibition about outsider art there, and I’d like to see it if the kids can manage without the tent this time.      Can’t we just do both? Camp one day, hotel the next? I quite fancy a ‘proper’ bed after the guesthouse last year.      Can we go to a surf shop as well? I saw someone with a cool little board there.      Only after we’ve seen the exhibition. And lunches sorted. No chips from the fish and chip shop every day like you did in Bournemouth.      That goody two-shoes! I wanted fish and chips!      Well sorry, but we need to box in the costs a bit due to exam marking. I have three big classes to finish and then one after that.      It’s your third summer of doing that, isn’t it?      It’s how my pay works, so I get a bit of holiday time off once all the marking’s done.

So did you actually hand in your English coursework yet or are you still pretending you’ll do it ‘later’?      Oh, I did it properly! Messed around a bit with the first draft, but my nan wouldn’t stop nagging me about it, so I finished it. Got a bit of help from my cousin Ruth with the structure. She’s doing A Levels in Lit and Stuff.      Fair enough. I’m waiting to send mine off. It was easier pulling teeth to do it than to write the whole thing. Didn’t even want to read the book properly. I just watched the film again and  pretended .      That’s how I managed like three assignments last year. Honestly, you get away with so much when you’re not the one who’s in on it.      Yeah, but I’m definitely not becoming one of those school prefects that actually care about the rules. You know the ones — the people who report  everything , even if it’s just a bit of chewing gum under someone’s chair.      Oh, I heard Ms. Farquhar from Year 9 is still trying to get people to wear the hideous grey hoodies. Doesn’t work, of course.      Mate, I got a sneaking suspicion that one of the prefects is the one who set up those camera things in the changing rooms. Like, who thinks that’s even a job they should be doing?      I reckon it was a teacher just playing it safe. Anyway, you biking to the party on Saturday? I might be, depends if I finish my bike chain.      Yeah, I’m all set. My mum still won’t let me out of the house without a failsafe snack. Bread with egg or something.      That’s rough. Mine made me take Nutella.      Oh, you’re a lucky one. My mate Tom can’t have it though — his sister’s got a nut allergy. She had a full-on reaction to  one flake  the other week. It was whack.      Still, I heard they’re showing like that new Marvel film at the cinema later on. If you wanted to go…      Nah, I’m not into superhero stuff. I’m more of a ‘YouTube and Fortnite’ kind of guy.      Fair enough. I just watched that new horror movie called  The Blinds  or something over the weekend. Cursed them glasses like 100 times over.      Oh right, the one where the girl sees ghosts only in the mirror?

Rather annoying driving up here isn't it?      Yeah, it’s mad busy. I got stuck behind some van on the A11 and I swear it stared like it’d never move.      No, I mean the roundabouts. They’re a nightmare in this part of the world, innit?      True. I’ve only been on a few trips up from Herts and I always end up relying on Waze like a right idiot.      Oh, I got lost once going to a football match and ended up in the middle of nowhere near a cattle field. Thought I was gonna get pecked by sheep.      You know, I’ve been thinking about picking up a bike. Maybe I could ditch the car for a bit and cut down on the traffic stress.      That’d be smart. I’ve been riding more this year. Less petrol for me, and more exercise. Only thing is, I’m not brilliant at changing gears—still end up huffing like I’ve been running the marathon.      I never thought about it as much. I play cricket for a local team, though. It’s not the same work rhythm as when I got into it at uni. Mate of mine got me back in and now it’s once a week. Keeps me out of trouble.      Oh, I went to a few matches last summer and tried to pretend someone at the bar noticed me. Just ended up alone with a half-finished pint.      Still, better than watching the telly all day like I do when it’s not raining. I did pick up a couple of mates who bikeride, though. Gotta be careful with what you say round them. One of them told me I looked like a student when I asked how he found a flat tire.      Tut, you were just worried he reckoned it was a woman’s flat tire.      You mad? No one would talk to me after that. They all just looked at me with that “oh right” face. Know what I mean?      Oh yeah, like you told the universe you go out of your way to be confused. If I go wrong, I just line it up and see what happens.      Anyway, if you ever fancy playing cricket, I’ll see if we’ve got a match where you can lend us someone to stand at the wicket and not fall over.

Okay, I’m starving, and I really want dumplings. But I’m just confused by the website—what’s the difference between soup dumplings and regular dumplings?      Soup dumplings are like… with a little bit of broth in them. They’re like jelly-like, and when you bite into them, the juices come out. It’s a bit of a mess actually.      Oh, but they’re so good though! The last time we ordered from   Golden Crisp  , the soup dumplings were amazing. But be warned, when you open the packet at home they can just gush everywhere.      Ugh, I had that once. I managed to get MySpace on my trousers and my best jeans got ruined. I haven’t spoken to the delivery guy in a month.      Dude, you can just hand him a hanky and say, “Here, mop this up. I’m holding you personally responsible for needing a dry cleaner again.”      Also, the Sweet and Sour Pork, like, is it any good? Last time I ordered it, I think there was more vinegar than pork. It was basically lemonade with meat in it.      Oh no, don’t get that. Go for the lemon chicken—it’s actually not bad, and they don’t throw vinegar at it quite as hard.      If we’re picking mains, I’m in for the chilli beef.      Just not the crispy ones. Those are oddly sour.      I second the chilli beef. Any veggie options? I don’t want to make it all about meat.      Oh right, you’re on your vibes. The broccoli with garlic sounds good. Don’t know why they put it on the menu, but it’s just standard broccoli with soy and garlic. Doesn’t hurt.      Let’s also order some fried rice just in case.      You mad? That’s the best part of the whole meal. Also, if you add the 'egg add on,' it’s like instant nostalgia from 2004.      Okay, so to go over everything: two chilli beefs, one lemon chicken, broccoli, fried rice, and six dumplings. Who lives nearest to the delivery area?      I can take it. I’ve got it out of hours so I’ll just leave it on the table.      Perfect. We can meet up in 40 minutes and all mourn over our fake meat while drinking instant noodles tea.      That’s the spirit. Oh, and if the dumplings run, I swear I will strangle the person who said ordering Chinese is a good idea.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You know what, I’ve been trying to get through to the university’s admin again about some funding for the poetry outreach programme and I’ve had their automated helpline on repeat since yesterday.      That sounds like what you get with the NHS these days too. I tried to sort out a referral last week for my son and he ended up on hold for over an hour with that awful robot voice. Honestly, you’d think they’d be easier to get into by now, given it’s one of the most overcrowded GPs in Liverpool.      You’re not wrong. I’ve even considered going to that new clinic over in the Isle of Man, heard it’s like a My turkey alternative. You fly over, get treated by a qualified healer in a barn, back home in time for the news.      Haha, now that’s an alternative! Wait, you said ‘qualified healer’—I’m a bit in two minds about that. Last year we had this new GP move in next door, and he claimed to treat everyone like family—though I don’t know what that means for the rest of us. Like a blood relative might, I dunno, get more time or something.      Oh right, like the way the Finns do healthcare—isn't it supposed to be way better than ours? I was there a couple of years back and they didn’t have long waits or all this back and forth with the paperwork. Just turn up, state your problem, and they seem to know what they’re doing.      Yeah, the Finns pride themselves on that. But their housing is a mess! We’ve got Prime Minister Johnson in about how we need to build more houses, but it still feels like we’re going backwards.      Definitely. I know my neighbour down the road—the one with the three dogs and a ‘ Burgundy Gazette’ garden guesthouse—just had to move his family into a caravan on the beach for three months while they sorted out his kitchen flat. Imagine waiting six months just to get a new kitchen.      That’s truly tragic. I keep meaning to ask him how he’s doing. My daughter keeps trying to play with his dogs, and the poor lad can go days without a hot meal if you ask me.      Yeah, I’m trying to teach her the ‘university’ approach to your living space—live with the chaos, it’ll all get sorted one day.

Rather skip the queue and take a shortcut through Upper Stanborough. Might save us an hour or two.      Shortcuts and poetry, more or less! Erm, I saw this long line of birds today, all sorts of pigeons and things, just marching like they were gonna fly off and start a new country.      I reckon it was crows actually. They tend to gather like that when they're sensing something's off. Trouble, you know.      Pigeons or crows, either way, they probably want a better education system than what we’ve got. My George couldn’t even fill out a form without the pen flying across the page.      I’m not surprised. I left mine in the back pocket, didn’t I? D’you know, I think he turned round and gave the form back to the nurse saying it hadn’t arrived yet.      Haha! And she was all, “Well, we can’t even give you the benefits if the form isn’t filled in.” He said, “I didn’t know it was a delivery I had to pick up.”      Typical George. Tell me there was something funny about the bus.      Oh, there was Mate. Bus got stuck trying to go round that big hill again. Whole queue of cars behind him waiting to turn like it was a bloody roundabout and the wheel came off.      And the driver said what?      He said, “Not today, guv,” and just drove off and left the bus stationary in the road like he hadn’t even seen it.      That’s gold.      It’s like a whole new level of welfare. Don’t you get a stipend if the bus leaves you?      Maybe George should start a union. “United Parents of the Lost Form.”      He’d be secretary-treasurer for sure. I reckon he’s the only one who can count beyond three.      D’you think the police do anything if the bus drivers start abandoning cars in the middle of roads like that?      I asked them about it once. They said, “If the line is busy, just leave a message.” That bloke on the phone said, “We’ll be in touch in 2024, after next year’s manifesto.”      Ha! Sounds like poetry to me—delayed buses and delayed benefits.      I like that. Maybe we could write a poem about it all. Start with something like, “They sent the form to the wind / But the wind just passed it to no one, left it behind….”

So did you lot see the article this weekend about how rural dialects are declining in the North? Honestly, it got me thinking—how long before we're all sounding like posh BBC clones?      Honestly? Not sure I mind that much. But it is a shame—Dee-dee eeny and "we’ve got a bad one 'ere" won’t die with me, that’s a promise. Aylesbury’s got its own quirks, but nothing quite like a Geordie’s "nowt" and "mardy". You lot never run out of words.      I totally agree with you, Ruth—those northern linguistic features are the real deal. Still, I have to admit the East Anglian "blether" and "sarnie" throw me off now and again, even after all these years in Cambridge. Sometimes I spend an hour just breaking down why someone said something "proper" when it’s just a regular "proper".      And I’m American, yet even I’m picked up the nuances. One time, I was recording a native setter near Hertford, and he used the phrase "good show" meaning "well done", and I thought he’d just been nice in general—it was hilarious.      That reminds me of when I was preparing a publication on regional curriculum adaptations, and I had to footnote “get us sommat to eat,” just in case the Pacific Northwest teachers weren’t sure what it meant. It’s all in the phrasing, isn’t it?      It really is. I do corpus work, so it boggles my mind how many unofficial synonyms pop up between towns just twenty miles apart. "Whippet” about means something different in Leeds than it does in Sunderland.      And "sparky,"! Going from an electrical plug to a really cute guy—unacceptable ambiguity if you ask me. But hey, it gives us color.      I think that’s the point—language is evolving all the time, and no amount of restricting regional slang will stop it. As long as people understand each other, what’s the issue with a bit of local flavor?      Absolutely. Even in ELT, we’ve found that exposing students to dialect variations go a long way in building confidence and comprehension. They stop thinking there's just one “right” way to say things.      And your accents alone could be a postgrad thesis! I’ve had students who think I'm American just because I drop the H's now and again—like, “ask” pronounces like “a’ask,” and they’re so confused.

Rather annoying isn't it? I mean I used to watch that programme ages ago.      What was it called? The one about Spain, wasn't it?      Yeah, Costa Divina or some name like that. It was on BBC Two.      I thought that was more about holidays than the country itself.      Oh aye but I used to think they got so much colour in it. You know, flamenco, tapas bars, and all that.      Mmm but the internet has changed everything hasn't it?      Oh absolutely, we used to plan our holidays based on bits like that.      So what made you want to start learning Spanish then?      Erm, I wanted to go to Costa Rica for my sabbatical.      Oh clever choice.      People usually go to Spain or Mexico, you know, but Costa Rica was refreshing.      I haven’t been there but I’d heard it's very environmentally conscious.      Oh absolutely, and the biodiversity is insane. I mean, you can have a beach then a rainforest in the next town.      Sounds way better than Texas and back.      Yeah, trying to survive the American educational system as an exchange teacher was an experience.      Let me guess, they tried to teach you how to do presentations with flannel graphs?      Exactly! I had to teach  Shakespeare  using a felt board about cosmic werewolves.      Oh man, I’m dying.      Don’t you remember the time we were teaching together in Brighton?      Oh yeah, that boy Eddie passed out after eating his lunch at 10 am.      We waited for an hour for the ambulance.      All that sprite and cheesy pasta... He probably went into orbit.      Some people. Anyway, you remember delivering the presentation with the dog on the leash?      The Cavalier King Charles?      Finally, someone asked if it could go further in the exam.      It was only fluency 3, though, we had to start with something simple.      I say, ‘fluency’ when I want them to talk 10 minutes without faltering.      That's an achievement in itself sometimes.      It’s not all flannel graphs and animated dogs, you know. Teaching in another culture is actually really satisfying. Reveals so much about ourselves.      So you think that’s why you learned Spanish?      Maybe. To understand a bit more of the people there. Languages really open you up.      Mmm. I’m rather jealous, actually.      How about you? Think about learning anything new?      I’ve actually been into German this year. Not for exams, just because it's part of my thesis.

Right then, John, take a seat love. That cup of tea looks like it's ready for you first.      Thanks, Grandma. I’ll help myself. I've been studying non-stop this morning—math revision can be a bit of a grind sometimes.      Aye, I know the feeling. I mark exams for a living and if I see one more "answer is a square" instead of "square number", I might just crawl out of my skin. It's basic stuff, for crikey's sake!      Oh, leave the kids well enough alone, Maureen. You had to make  us  study, didn't you? Still don’t know what Pythagoras did to you, bless him.      I reckon he ran off with the milkman in the '50s and left you with a dodgy division sum. Or maybe he was just cleverer than ye!      Yeah, Grandma, even Grandpa says he hated math once. So what was the big secret?      I don’t know what your Gran did to you, love, but it worked. He was failing every test—and then she gave him a right rollocking. After that, he passed every one!      That’s not true, John! I just told you to  try ! You know what it’s like when you don’t pay attention. And what about your music? What happened to that?      That’s another story. I’m still playing guitar a bit, just not as much as I’d like. I’ve been so busy with GCSE prep. I’m thinking about trying to make the school band again this year.      Good! Music is life, lad. I used to play a bit on the accordion. My sister had us in the chapel choir. Maureen here used to sing with them too, by the way—only she was too shy to ever sing a solo.      That’s not true, and I’ll have you know I once sang with the Town Band in Beverley! They asked me to join the choir for  The Mikado . Course, I told 'em no go—too many pond life scenes and no one to shout at.      You hate blokes in tights and strappy boots. It’s a big issue!      I think I’m starting to get the picture here. So where were you at when you were my age, Grandma? Were you busy marking math papers already?      Oh, no, I was in school too, you cheeky. I left at sixteen to work in the bakery, and before that, I counted eggs in the back room.

Rather skip the queue and just go through the side doors, do you think?      I got the free pass from Anna—she said to park on the visitor's lot and just walk through the back entrance. Not sure if they speak English in there, but well, you know how these old Chinese buildings are.      Yeah, I reckon it's best to stick with the plan. I don’t fancy standing in the queue this afternoon, not with the heat. It was sweltering today. We’ve been inside the house for what feels like forever, but the garden has been lovely.      It’s so bizarre, isn’t it? When we first got here and saw that the house still looked so much like an English country mansion, you know—from the outside anyway. And then walking into the interior: beams, chandeliers—everything in there is still very much British. I still can’t believe that this happened.      When’s the last time we walked without thinking about the property or the budget? Good to just enjoy walking around for a moment, you know? Speaking of, I really liked that room with the photos. Did you see them? All those old friends we’ve never met—Elizabeth, Geoffrey, Janice.      Oh yes, I saw them. I was actually scanning the room trying to see if I could pick out someone that looked like you at 22. There was a woman with the same nose. Our daughter could inherit either one of ours.      She’s already got your stature—look at the kid. Stretches up and towers over everyone at school. I don’t know how you do it, honestly. I walk into the same room the next week and feel like an undersized child.      Not you! I mean it. You’re not short—just... less ‘giants of the world’ than me. Although, personally, I’m not sure the world is a land of giants at the moment. With all the upheaval in the region, the crises we’re hearing about on the news—it’s always something with people on the move.      Yeah, it’s hard to believe these walls are still standing sometimes. I can go days walking through them and not see a soul. Just dust, sunlight, and the odd cat that’s taken up residence. I imagine someone from the house must still come in at some point, or perhaps conservationists manage it now.

So did you go out last night?      Aye, me and some mates went to that new club in Nottingham. You went to that one down Brickyard, right?      Yeah, I was there with Jo and Zara—  Lola   tried to make us go eeny meeny miny moe catch a nigger by his toe, but we were like, nope. A lot of people just roll their eyes and continue.        Lola   sounds like a nightmare. We had a laugh though. Me and Beth danced the whole night.      Oh yeah, Lola—she’s a bit much. I heard she got her GCSE results and MySpace still wouldn’t log her in though.      I’m not surprised. D’you know, I think she turned 18 and she was still using Myspace for breakfast, no Bucks Fizz this time. Honestly, I used to live on that site five years ago, now it’s just for dead folk and sad clowns.      She looked like a dead clown in a feather crop last I saw her. What did you wear to the club?      Boots and a mini skirt, extra sparkle in case of emergencies. You?      Just a dress, and way too much glitter. I swear the glitter didn’t come off for like three days. Me and Jo ended up doing a dance that made sense and then just kept someone at full song for ten mins.      That sounds oddly therapeutic. You ever think about doing dance class proper or just fake it being choreographed at parties?      Only if I get paid. I’m not charging you for the club liturgy, though. Honestly, I just need more failsafes for when   Lola   starts freestyling on my mobile. My sister texted me the other day and said my contacts are all called 'GROUP CHAT '.      I tried to change my theme songs a while ago. Me and Beth had that sprite of the month calendar, trying to find the right vibe each week—was like trying to play MySpace for real life.      I had a month go bad when my ringtone was 'Shape of You' and I made my line in the password that I genuinely could not remember, until Beth went to your house and you made her play it over and over.      Yeah, I panicked and had to send her to your IP address. Look, over this one’s food, I’m like 70% my mum and 30% MySpace ringtone.      You owe me for that.

So do you think you could bring gran up to Cumbria next weekend? I think it'd do her good to stretch her legs out of Dublin for a bit. I know she's been a bit down since she stopped teaching full-time.      Oh aye, I’d be more than happy to! I just need to check the bus times and see if we can book a taxi to the station. She’s never been too keen on the idea of trains, to be honest. The thought of it all just scares her stiff.      Funny you should mention it—I was talking to my sister earlier about arranging a visit from Mary too. We were hoping to plan something out of the house. It's like everyone’s shrivelling up living in-place!      I know what you mean, Frank. I think it's important for them to feel like they’ve still got a bit of purpose—like part of something.      Oh absolutely. I remember the day I walked into my first classroom—it was the most terrifying yet exciting thing I’d ever done. She just stood there for ten minutes, not saying a word, waiting for a student to solve an equation. Then, when someone did, she burst out laughing—and it was such a lovely sound.      Mate, you’re misty-eyed and I barely know you! But I imagine that sort of impact stays with you. You don't forget the looks on kids’ faces when they finally "get it"—it’s almost like a light bulbs switching on over their heads.      Exactly—yes. That is it. So, let’s be hopeful next weekend. I’m thinking we can take her to Appleby Castle. She does love the old stories, and the walk around the grounds is gentle enough for her and not too far.      That sounds brilliant! Maybe we can do something in the evening too—watch some football. Eddie will be playing in his club’s final on the Saturday. I assume he's still trying to relive his FIFA glory when he was younger?      Oh yeah, he’s still got that fire in his belly. At one point he asked if the simulation would accept a fake lawyer career path with virtual clients! I had to explain goaldust doesn’t work if you don’t get real stats in.      Oh, don’t go telling him that on Saturday.

Right, thanks a million for helping us out with the tea. I can’t believe how much stuff passed through that kitchen today.      Haha, it was chaos, but in a good way. I probably need to do a bit of a clear-out later—my laptop keeps bricking again and I might finally give up and take it to the shop.      You should. I’ve only had my laptop for ten years and I never had problems with it. It was a dump machine, mind—just nothing fancy, but it held up.      You’re a relic, Dad. These things are made to break every two years now. I’d rather use voice recognition software and MyPhone on my phone than try fixing my computer. It’s ridiculous.      Speaking of, how’s the new blackberry working for you, Tom?      Not bad—slower than I’d like, but I’ll live. I had to ring someone to help me set it up. I mean, why isn’t it obvious what you need to do to get it going?      Back in the day, you didn’t need ten apps to do one simple thing. You just grabbed a paper and a pen.      Mate, I don’t even know how to work the sat nav in my car. I nearly drove into the sea once when I stayed near Brighton.      Oh Brighton! Our walk around the pier was fun—did you see the man playing the didgeridoo on the seafront? That is either a red flag or the purest form of authenticity.      He looked about half-chip. I think he just wanted the chips first, then the vibes.      You young people shouldn’t be worrying about didgeridoo players—worry about where you put your glasses. I nearly lost mine in a tea mug. I told my wife it was a telephone call.      I know the feeling. My telly’s on as I fall asleep every night. I always promise myself I’ll switch it off, but the moment I grab the remote, I’m out. Then my head’s buzzing the next morning.      I do the same. But at least I don’t drink myself into that state. Although the other night I had a bit too much of that boxed wine. I made it to midnight and then decided it was my night off from being an adult.      Ah, boxed wine crime. We all do it.

I just checked my phone—did you see the results? No, not yet. Was it a big one? Yeah, Man Utd v Liverpool. It was a proper humdinger. Chants and the lot. Oh no, did they draw? I was  not  in the mood for that. Worse than that—it went to extra time, but United actually won this time.  What?!  That sounds like a dream to you, but for us northerners, it’s a nightmare. Honestly, I’m still trying to get used to the idea that United can do something right now and again. Feels like living in an alternative universe. I hear you. I miss the pick of the Premier League back home. Living in Poland, you’ve got to make do with streaming—half of which I can’t access anyway. And the time difference doesn’t help. You always have to choose between staying up too late or missing half the game. Oh, I’ve been thinking about going home for the weekend. I’ve started getting that homesick feeling properly… plus, the sun’s been out, and I swear it’s triggered my SAD. I know the feeling—it’s like the weather here is trying to test your emotional endurance. You know what I miss the most? A decent chicken tikka in a paper cone. Nothing like it. Oh yeah, I can’t buy what I want here either. Everything tastes like either sugar or salt. Speaking of which, your class about idioms last week—how are they doing? Honestly? I’ve been  obsessed  with that group. I feel like it’s up to me to do well, you know? They’re so hardworking, and I want them to pass their exams. That’s sweet—and very intense. I just keep thinking, “If  I  can get out of bed at 6 to teach and learn English, so can they.” That’s amazing. I remember you told me about one guy—Ignacy? The one who works on a farm. Oh yeah, Ignacy. He lives in the countryside and cycles an hour each way. I asked him why he botheres, and he said, “I want to teach people like me.” That’s beautiful. You must feel proud of yourself. I do, honestly. Only, sometimes I wonder if I’m pushing too hard. I don’t want to scare them off. It’s such a balance. You’re doing better than you think.

So did you lot see the meeting memo for next week? I’ve been trying to get my head around the guest speaker and the AV setup all day.      Erm, I dunno much about it. I don’t do events, I just turn up and do things when told, y’know? I sort out the builders and stuff for my mate’s firm.      Oh yeah, that sounds way less stressful. I had this project at work where we had to reorganize the entire production schedule and I nearly lost my mind. Paperwork chase from hell.      I like the events work even if it’s stressful. I get to meet people, plan stuff, make it look posh. Just wish I didn’t have to dress so prim and proper for it.      Speaking of which, what’s the deal with your suit last Thursday? Looked like it had a life of its own.      I only wore it once, thanks to Elaine! She told me to “dress the part” and I went full pyjamas of the boardroom, apparently. Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? Chuggers by the park gates again. Felt like I was being followed the whole way round Gordon Square this morning. Blimey, I've nearly got a heart attack spotting them sunbathing in those orange vests like mindless little vultures.      Aye, I understand the principle, but really? It's not like it’s a private garden anyway, the public doesn't chase through Hyde Park with a pound coin in hand like they're in some Disney film.      What I found fascinating was how some of my students at the university talked about parks in China though. The one in Chengdu, the one with the giant pandas, is very popular. A world away from here, of course.      I envy you that. I've been wanting to go for years ever since my old mate from uni took me on that trip to Hainan a decade ago. We camped by Lake Nansha, and had some of the best takes I've ever had.      I tell you, it's quite different in-country watching how people interact. I’m mentoring a PhD student who's interested in that very thing—mainly how language acquisition and exposure to English differ between rural and urban parts of China. One moment it's wildlife, the next it's overcrowded cities. I remember hearing that they've got a strict attitude towards drugs and the death penalty there—you hear about Tibet and the protests, but you don't get informed much about the everyday life.      I think it's more about balance. Just like in Devon, you can go from buzzing market towns to deserted moorland in minutes.

Right, so the client’s meeting’s tomorrow at 10. I was just double-checking the file you got from the design team. You sorted that yet?      Yeah, I uploaded it to the shared drive this afternoon. I’ve just got to make sure it all goes in clean. One wrong glyph and it throws everything out.      I remember that with the old system, even a misaligned comma would crash an entire batch. One tiny decimal point missed, and it looked like we’d made about five square meters of concrete fly off a bridge.      Honestly, I’ve seen some fails in the corpus data too. So did you go to the doctor yet, Tom? You’ve been off work for three days with that cough... sounds like a cold or maybe something worse.      Yeah, I went this morning. I had a chesty cough a few months back and it turned into pneumonia. Scary stuff.      Oh no! How long were you off for?      Like four weeks. It was a nightmare, honestly—Managed to get through work the whole time only because I was in an office job, but I felt like I was wasting away.      I’d rather be off work than feel crap every day. Oh come on, he’s not that bad. We’ve all seen you in the kitchen muttering at the kettle.      Okay, fair. But seriously—get better soon. We’ve got that friend’s wedding in a few weeks and I   really   need you being able to smile at photos  without  sneering because your throat about to close up.      She’s right. Both of you. Speaking of relationships, did I tell you about that guy I went out with last week?      No—you said "he took the M54 for fun," and I nearly spat out my tea. Don’t go there again.      Oh, no, he wasn’t that bad. We had a really good laugh, but… he kept trying to convert me to astrology.      Romans, crystals, stars—three truths never told in one go. Okay do you want some tea?      Yeah I'll take a green tea thank you.      You got that sorted. I can take something or      Yeah.      Be as long as you like. A few years ago a patient would make a pass at me during the sessions I was running. It was very uncomfortable. Right, so today we're going to talk about good and evil. But first, let’s start with a question: what do you think makes someone good or bad?      I think if you’re kind and help people, you’re good. But if you hurt them, you’re evil.      That’s a very wise answer, Evie. And what about you, Lucas? What do you think?      I think if someone steals or lies, they’re bad. But if you do nice things, like sharing and playing fair, you’re good.      Very good thinking, both of you. A lot of stories we read or watch are about people trying to do good things, even when it’s hard. Do you know the legend of King Arthur?      Is he the one in the castle? With the sword in the stone?      Yes, that’s the one! He was a king in a story long, long ago, and lots of people thought he was the best kind of king—a hero. He stood up for people, and he had a group of knights he trusted to do the right thing. They were called the Knights of the Round Table.      Like Superheroes?      Kind of! – but they were real people in the story, and they had to prove themselves brave and honest. It was their duty to do good for everyone.      Did he live in the old days?      Yes! That was in a time called the Middle Ages. That was hundreds and hundreds of years ago, and stories from that time are called legends. Some of them are made up, and others are based on real people but twisted a bit over the years.      Like witches and dragons?      Exactly! Some of the stories are about real things, like farmers and rulers, but they get mixed up with magic, giants, and dragons. One of the oldest folk tales was called  Tam Lin , where a girl had to rescue a prince who was trapped by a witch. Do you know what a faerie is?      Is that like fairies?      Close! Faeries or fairies are magical beings in stories from the UK and Ireland. Some are friendly, and some are very sneaky, making people do things. These stories often teach lessons—like always being honest, or never going with strangers.      Like the wolf that dressed up?      Oh, yes! That’s  Little Red Riding Hood . A very old story. The moral is to be careful, and also to listen to your parents.

Aye, gardening’s not a science—more like witchcraft. You can overwater and it’s gone, you don’t water enough and it’s also gone. It's like dating a plant.      Very deep. What go you think about that new 'streetwear meets tailoring' trend? I tried it, and I look like I tried to dress up but forgot what ‘match’ meant.      You and me both, mate. Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You think they'd do something about the internet in this house. We're barely getting a signal in the garden now.      Yeah, I mean I was trying to stream that new killer whale documentary I told you about —  Orca: The Killing Machine — and it kept buffering. It’s driving me   mad  .      I remember that one! I think I saw it when I was at uni. They used to show it during arts week. We had to write an essay on animal intelligence. Apparently, orcas can mimic human speech patterns. It's wild.      Honestly, the dumbest thing is people think blue Peter badges mean you're an adventurer or something. My niece’s school tried to do their own version for their D.T. projects and I think the head teacher called it an "explorer’s badge." Ridiculous, isn’t it?      Oh, don’t remind me. I remember we used to go to Blue Peter programmes in the summer. We built that crazy Water Feature with a jam jar and some tinfoil — I think it still sits in my mum’s shed like a relic from the Stone Age.      Haha, yeah. I mean it's amazing – that kind of stuff helped foster creativity in kids before they were glued to screens. Though honestly, don’t get me started on the amount of violence on kids’ TV these days. It’s out of control. The other week my nephew watched a cartoon where this kid gets chased by a literal robot dinosaur with lasers.      I know! Even in schools – I had a colleague last term who pulled me about how his four-year-old students kept mimicking scenes from  Peppa Pig  — only with softer actions, thank heavens. Still! I mean it is a  cartoon , but with all the squelching and roaring…      Speaking of shows, have you heard about this lecturer at my uni who used to teach media studies? She got suspended for posting about squatting as political art on her Twitter. Her students went  wild  over it.      Oh no, really? I did a module on participatory culture with an American guy who insisted on including Banksy and Banksy-like work. I thought I was in for it, but they just wanted more academic references than anything. Though to be fair, I have known plenty of artists who live off the grid now.      It's a contrast, isn’t it?

Rather skip the queue and just go through the side doors, do they?      Oh, I don’t know, Harold. I’m more than happy to wait my turn. It’s a little thing like that that makes things feel… fairer, you know?      I don’t mind, honestly. It’s an adventure. I reckon it builds character—standing in a queue with a coffee in your hand and the wind from the river tugging at your coat. It’s not like it’s raining again or anything.      It always bloody well is when you get like three months of summer!  Sigh.  I remember when the pubs had only two taps, and now you’ve got supermarkets selling craft beer with names longer than your arm. Ten pounds a pint and still called “craft” by these sad twats.      They’ve got to put something on the bottle, Harold. Otherwise, everyone would just be called “Brown Ale” or “Best Bitter.” They need puff for the price tag.      I worked with a lad—person, I mean—once, in a bar in Birmingham. He told me they only started calling it “craft” so they could charge extra. He said it was all just “style over substance.” Mate of mine bought a pint, and it barely tasted like beer. Like sweet cider crossed with apple juice and then someone threw in a lemon rind and called it a job.      Well, I for one still like a simple ale. Something that’s been around a while— oring’d out a while , as Harold might say—ya know?      That’s right, doll. I’m not about to waste the good money on something fizzy and full of what you might call “flavour enhancers.” I mean, if you wanted apples in your beer, go get a cider.      I did once. I bought a cider named something like “Bitter Bramble Bliss” or something daft like that. I told the shop assistant it was overpriced and weak. She looked at me like I was the one with the mismatched socks and a tinted glass reflection in the mirror.      That goon really doesn’t know if you’re joking or not these days, Mark.      And the worst thing is, when the proper pubs started going downhill, the only ones that were left had these blooming bar stewards with beards and belly rings who cost more than the establishment itself.      I remember one guy. He kept telling me I was paying for the  experience , not just the beer.

So did you used to work in recruitment full time before you moved into the academic space?      Yeah, I did—good luck guessing that from my accent! I worked for a few years in Sydney doing executive recruitment, mainly in the tech and finance sectors. It was wild—Deals were fast, high pressure, and I used to think I was good with time management until I stepped into academia!      I can only imagine! From my point of view, recruitment sounds like a whirlwind of emails and endless coffee meetings. So how did you transition into teaching, then? Was it a planned move?      Not entirely. I was tutoring privately at first, helping uni students with academic writing and assignments. Then one of my tutors who was heading up a course on academic literacy reached out and asked if I’d be interested in helping design the curriculum. Before I knew it, I was part of the teaching team—formal agreement, lectures, marks... the whole shebang!      That sounds like a pretty smooth transition—and a great use of your skills. I mean, communication, tailoring your message, listening—these are all parts of your old job that must carry over well into university teaching. Have you noticed that?      Oh, absolutely. You’re negotiating needs constantly—like with students who aren’t sure how to structure a paragraph, or clients who didn’t quite tell you what they needed at first. In the end, you’re both trying to get the best out someone else. That said, lecturing is way more fulfilling—at least for now.      That is such a fair point. It’s interesting how recruitment and university education both come down to coaxing people about how they present themselves. Speaking of which, I've been watching this academic literacy course a bit more closely. I know that one of the big topics is how unprepared many students are for tertiary level reading and writing. What are your thoughts?      I think it’s a huge issue—and something that's often underplayed. Many students come from very performance-driven secondary schools where writing good essays was about keywords and ticking boxes. Then you get to university and the demand is so different—critical thinking, source analysis, reflection, structure. You're expected to not just regurgitate, but map your own intellectual journey.      Exactly! And in the course design, we’ve tried to integrate that shift through what we call “guided autonomy.”

I’ll even endorse it on my LinkedIn as “empowering, witty, and genuinely relatable, if you spend most of your time waiting for Wi-Fi.”      You lot are mad. I’m just here doing a  ridiculously  overcomplicated metaphor assignment where I compare rain to my mother’s cooking. Searing my brain trying to make sense of it.      And you call me mad for wondering why people are stressed?

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You think they'd do something about the internet in this house by now... got me stuck rewriting this bloody email for the press conference I’m setting up next week. Thought it was perfect, until I found out he’d said something  racist  at a pub quiz.
